A subclass constructor that needs new attributes after <code>super().__init__</code> is blocked. Frozen dataclasses handle more mechanics but still provide shallow rather than transitive immutability.

### 9.16.11 Attribute delegation and descriptor binding

<code>getattr(target, name)</code> performs descriptor binding with <code>target</code> as the receiver. Returning that result from a proxy means a target method remains bound to the target, not the proxy. This is usually correct:

~~~python
class Target:
    def identity(self) -> object:
        return self


target = Target()
proxy = Proxy(target)
assert proxy.identity() is target
~~~

A framework that retrieves raw attributes from <code>type(target).__dict__</code> and invokes <code>__get__</code> manually can bind differently, but doing so changes semantics and must account for MRO and descriptor precedence. Ordinary delegation should prefer ordinary <code>getattr</code> unless intentional rebinding is part of the abstraction.

### 9.16.12 Compatibility aliases should be narrow and temporary

<code>__getattr__</code> can preserve a renamed attribute:

~~~python
import warnings


class Endpoint:
    def __init__(self, address: str) -> None:
        self.address = address

    def __getattr__(self, name: str):
        if name == "url":
            warnings.warn(
                "url is deprecated; use address",
                DeprecationWarning,
                stacklevel=2,
            )
            return self.address
        raise AttributeError(name)
~~~

The alias is explicit, warns at the caller’s location, and leaves unrelated spelling errors visible. An unrestricted mapping such as replacing all underscores with hyphens would create a difficult-to-enumerate API.

### 9.16.13 Auditing must avoid sensitive leakage and semantic change

A <code>__getattribute__</code> logger sees names for secrets, internal locks, authentication tokens, and diagnostic machinery. Logging values can disclose data; even logging names may reveal behaviour. The logger itself can recurse, acquire locks in an unsafe order, or change timing.

For high-assurance auditing, intercept at a narrower domain boundary and define event schemas, redaction, failure handling, and append guarantees. General attribute interception is a language mechanism, not automatically an audit trail.

### 9.16.14 Performance and optimisation

General interception adds work to every ordinary access and can inhibit interpreter optimisations. That cost may be irrelevant for a configuration proxy and material for millions of numerical records. Measure an application-representative workload before choosing interception for performance reasons. Descriptors attached only to relevant fields or explicit methods often localise both semantic and runtime cost.

### 9.16.15 Class access is governed one level higher

Defining <code>__getattr__</code> on an ordinary class governs missing attributes on its *instances*, not missing attributes on the class object itself. Since a class is an instance of its metaclass, class-level interception belongs to the metaclass.

~~~python
class Meta(type):
    def __getattr__(cls, name: str) -> str:
        if name == "generated_label":
            return cls.__name__.lower()
        raise AttributeError(name)


class Model(metaclass=Meta):
    pass


assert Model.generated_label == "model"
~~~

This is rarely needed. A class method or explicit registry usually communicates class-level computation more directly. The example reinforces the uniform model: behaviour of an object is defined by its type; the type of a class is its metaclass.

### 9.16.16 A safe selection hierarchy

Choose the narrowest mechanism that owns the requirement:

1. use an ordinary stored attribute for plain state;
2. use a property for one class-specific managed attribute;
3. use a descriptor for reusable per-attribute policy;
4. use <code>__getattr__</code> for a constrained missing-name space or compatibility fallback;
5. use <code>__getattribute__</code> only when virtually all retrieval must be mediated;
6. use a proxy with explicitly implemented protocols when object-level mediation is the real abstraction;
7. use a metaclass hook only when class objects themselves require interception.

This hierarchy is not a rule of prestige. Broader hooks increase the amount of ordinary language behaviour that must be reconstructed and tested.

> **Common misconception — “<code>__getattr__</code> sees every attribute read.”**  
> It is a missing-attribute fallback. <code>__getattribute__</code> sees every ordinary retrieval.

> **Common misconception — “A forwarding <code>__getattr__</code> makes a transparent proxy.”**  
> Many special operations bypass ordinary instance fallback and must be implemented on the proxy type. Identity, type checks, introspection, and lifecycle can remain observably different as well.

> **Common misconception — “<code>hasattr</code> only inspects metadata.”**  
> It performs retrieval and can run arbitrary descriptor and fallback code; <code>AttributeError</code> controls its result.

## 9.17 Slots and instance representation

Ordinary user-defined instances commonly own a dictionary mapping attribute names to values. This representation is flexible: a new name can be added at runtime, and different instances can have different sets of names. Its flexibility consumes memory and adds an indirection. A class declaration may instead use <code>__slots__</code> to request named storage positions represented by class-owned descriptors.

~~~python
class Point:
    __slots__ = ("x", "y")

    def __init__(self, x: float, y: float) -> None:
        self.x = x
        self.y = y
~~~

For this class, class construction creates a member descriptor for each declared name. An instance ordinarily stores references in fixed layout positions rather than in its own name-to-value dictionary.

### 9.17.1 Slots are descriptors, not declarations of static fields

Inspect the class namespace:

~~~python
point = Point(1.0, 2.0)

print(Point.__dict__["x"])
print(hasattr(point, "__dict__"))
~~~

<code>Point.__dict__["x"]</code> is a descriptor supplied by the runtime. Assignment to <code>point.x</code> invokes slot-setting behaviour; retrieval invokes slot-getting behaviour. Under the stated class, <code>point</code> ordinarily has no <code>__dict__</code>.

<code>__slots__</code> therefore participates in the same attribute model as §9.15. It is not a separate compile-time field system, and it does not make Python statically typed.

### 9.17.2 Undeclared names usually fail when no dictionary exists

~~~python
point = Point(1.0, 2.0)

try:
    point.z = 3.0
except AttributeError as error:
    print(error)
~~~

No slot named <code>z</code> and no instance dictionary can receive the assignment, so it fails. This catches some spelling mistakes and makes the intended per-instance namespace explicit.

It does not prove every assignment is meaningful. <code>point.x = "north"</code> succeeds unless another mechanism validates the value. Slots constrain attribute names and representation, not types or domain invariants.

### 9.17.3 Slot values need not exist yet

Declaring a slot creates capacity and access machinery, not an initial value.

~~~python
class Incomplete:
    __slots__ = ("value",)


item = Incomplete()

try:
    print(item.value)
except AttributeError:
    print("slot has not been assigned")
~~~

The descriptor reports absence until assignment. Constructors should establish every required slot before the object escapes. Optional state should be represented deliberately, perhaps with <code>None</code>, a sentinel, or a property that documents absence.

### 9.17.4 A subclass can restore a dictionary

If a subclass does not declare <code>__slots__</code>, it ordinarily gains an instance dictionary even when its base is slotted.

~~~python
class LabelledPoint(Point):
    def __init__(self, x: float, y: float, label: str) -> None:
        super().__init__(x, y)
        self.label = label


labelled = LabelledPoint(1.0, 2.0, "origin-ish")
assert labelled.__dict__ == {"label": "origin-ish"}
~~~

The inherited <code>x</code> and <code>y</code> remain in base slots; <code>label</code> lives in the subclass instance dictionary. Saying “the base has slots, so all descendants lack dictionaries” is false.

A subclass that wants only additional fixed positions declares its own slots:

~~~python
class FixedLabelledPoint(Point):
    __slots__ = ("label",)

    def __init__(self, x: float, y: float, label: str) -> None:
        super().__init__(x, y)
        self.label = label
~~~

The subclass lists only *new* slot names. Inherited slots remain available automatically.

### 9.17.5 An empty slot declaration preserves a base layout

A subclass that adds no instance state can declare an empty tuple:

~~~python
class Origin(Point):
    __slots__ = ()

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__(0.0, 0.0)
~~~

Without <code>__slots__ = ()</code>, the subclass would ordinarily acquire a dictionary. Empty slots are common in stateless mixins designed to coexist with a slotted hierarchy, although overall multiple-inheritance layout must still be valid.

### 9.17.6 Explicitly requesting <code>__dict__</code>

The special slot name <code>__dict__</code> requests dictionary support:

~~~python
class ExtensiblePoint:
    __slots__ = ("x", "y", "__dict__")

    def __init__(self, x: float, y: float) -> None:
        self.x = x
        self.y = y


point = ExtensiblePoint(1.0, 2.0)
point.label = "A"
assert point.__dict__ == {"label": "A"}
~~~

The named slots still exist, while arbitrary additional attributes use the dictionary. This hybrid can support frameworks that require <code>__dict__</code>, but it removes much of the fixed-namespace guarantee and some memory benefit.

### 9.17.7 Weak-reference support is separate

A weak reference observes an object without keeping it alive. Ordinary dictionary-based instances generally support weak references; a slotted class needs the special <code>__weakref__</code> slot unless support is inherited.

~~~python
from weakref import ref


class WeakPoint:
    __slots__ = ("x", "y", "__weakref__")

    def __init__(self, x: float, y: float) -> None:
        self.x = x
        self.y = y


point = WeakPoint(1.0, 2.0)
observer = ref(point)
assert observer() is point
~~~

Weak-reference capability affects caches, registries, descriptor external storage, and lifecycle observation. Omitting it can break collaborators even when ordinary attribute access works.

### 9.17.8 Slot names and name mangling

A slot name with two leading underscores and no trailing double underscore is name-mangled using the declaring class, just as corresponding source-level attribute references are.

~~~python
class SecretCoordinate:
    __slots__ = ("__x",)

    def __init__(self, x: float) -> None:
        self.__x = x
~~~

The generated slot is effectively associated with a mangled name such as <code>_SecretCoordinate__x</code>. This reduces accidental collision with a subclass’s own <code>__x</code>; it does not provide confidentiality or hostile-code protection.

### 9.17.9 Do not redeclare an inherited slot name

If a subclass declares a slot with the same name as one in a base, it can hide the base descriptor and make the original storage reachable only by directly invoking that base descriptor. Behaviour is obscure and not a stable design foundation. Treat inherited slot names as already owned and declare only genuinely new names.

Namespace collision is particularly damaging because overwriting the class’s slot descriptor can make stored values inaccessible through normal syntax:

~~~python
class OneSlot:
    __slots__ = ("value",)


# Assigning OneSlot.value = 10 here would replace the member descriptor.
~~~

A slot name cannot simultaneously use an ordinary class attribute as a default, because that class attribute would occupy the name needed by the descriptor. Establish defaults in <code>__init__</code>, <code>__new__</code>, or another constructor.

### 9.17.10 Multiple slotted bases can have incompatible layouts

Multiple inheritance among bases with non-empty instance layouts is restricted. A class definition may raise <code>TypeError</code> because no single instance layout can satisfy both. Empty-slot mixins often combine successfully because they contribute behaviour without another physical layout.

~~~python
class BehaviourMixin:
    __slots__ = ()

    def coordinates(self) -> tuple[float, float]:
        return (self.x, self.y)


class BehaviouralPoint(BehaviourMixin, Point):
    __slots__ = ()
~~~

The mixin assumes a host protocol containing <code>x</code> and <code>y</code> but adds no storage. This is a more compatible use than independently stateful bases that both demand layout ownership.

MRO consistency and memory-layout compatibility are separate checks. A graph can have a valid C3 order and still be impossible to represent as one object.

### 9.17.11 Memory savings require whole-object measurement

<code>sys.getsizeof(instance)</code> reports the shallow size of the instance object, not necessarily the separately allocated instance dictionary or referenced values. Comparing only two shallow numbers can therefore make an ordinary instance appear deceptively small.

### Worked example 9.5O — Measure representation cautiously

~~~python
import sys


class DictPoint:
    def __init__(self, x: float, y: float) -> None:
        self.x = x
        self.y = y


class SlotPoint:
    __slots__ = ("x", "y")

    def __init__(self, x: float, y: float) -> None:
        self.x = x
        self.y = y


ordinary = DictPoint(1.0, 2.0)
slotted = SlotPoint(1.0, 2.0)

ordinary_shallow = sys.getsizeof(ordinary)
ordinary_dictionary = sys.getsizeof(ordinary.__dict__)
slotted_shallow = sys.getsizeof(slotted)

print(ordinary_shallow, ordinary_dictionary, slotted_shallow)
~~~

Exact results depend on interpreter build, platform, allocator state, key-sharing optimisations, inheritance, and measurement method. Referenced floats are shared conceptually between both designs in this example and should not be double-counted differently. A serious comparison creates representative populations, uses a tool such as <code>tracemalloc</code>, includes peak allocations, and measures the workload on supported runtimes.

For ten objects, saved bytes may not justify reduced flexibility. For tens of millions of long-lived objects, representation can dominate memory. Scale converts a small per-instance difference into an architectural constraint.

### 9.17.12 Attribute speed is an empirical secondary effect

Slots can make some accesses faster by avoiding dictionary lookup, but interpreter specialisation and dictionary optimisations complicate blanket claims. Construction, mutation, garbage collection, cache locality, and surrounding work may dominate. “Use slots because attributes are faster” is not an adequate performance argument without a representative benchmark and memory profile.

### 9.17.13 Slots are shallow and mutable

Slots do not make an object immutable:

~~~python
point = Point(1.0, 2.0)
point.x = 9.0
~~~

Nor do they make referenced objects immutable:

~~~python
class Bucket:
    __slots__ = ("items",)

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.items: list[str] = []


bucket = Bucket()
bucket.items.append("changed")
~~~

Immutability requires a behavioural contract over all observable state transitions. A frozen, slotted dataclass can prevent ordinary field rebinding and reduce layout, yet referenced lists can still mutate.

### 9.17.14 Slots do not make attributes private

The slot descriptor lives on the class and is introspectable. Callers can read and assign public slots. Name-mangled slots remain reachable by determined code. Slots prevent unlisted ordinary storage; they do not enforce an authority boundary.

### 9.17.15 Copying and serialisation must know the representation

Code that serialises only <code>obj.__dict__</code> omits slotted state or fails because no dictionary exists. Robust generic machinery must inspect supported protocols rather than assume representation. Pickle often has support for ordinary slot state, but custom reduction methods, inheritance, external resources, and changed class versions still need explicit design.

~~~python
class Pair:
    __slots__ = ("left", "right")

    def __init__(self, left: object, right: object) -> None:
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

    def __getstate__(self) -> tuple[object, object]:
        return (self.left, self.right)

    def __setstate__(self, state: tuple[object, object]) -> None:
        self.left, self.right = state
~~~

These methods make one state representation explicit but do not make untrusted pickle data safe; unpickling remains code-execution-capable and is addressed in Chapter 11.

### 9.17.16 Dataclasses can generate slotted classes

Modern dataclasses support a slots option:

~~~python
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(slots=True, frozen=True)
class Coordinate:
    x: float
    y: float
~~~

The decorator creates or returns a class with generated slots and dataclass methods. Interactions with inheritance, <code>__init_subclass__</code>, weak-reference support, field defaults, and custom methods must follow the dataclass contract. Generated code reduces boilerplate; it does not remove representation decisions.

### 9.17.17 Slots affect subclass and framework extensibility

Libraries sometimes expect to attach instrumentation, cached values, ORM state, test doubles, or debugging metadata to instances. A class without a dictionary rejects such additions unless the framework has a slot-aware route. Publishing a slotted base therefore constrains downstream subclass and tooling behaviour.

That constraint may be desirable for a closed value type and harmful for an extension-oriented base class. Representation is part of extensibility even when the public documentation mentions only methods.

### 9.17.18 When slots are justified

Slots are well motivated when:

- measurement shows substantial aggregate memory benefit;
- a large homogeneous population has a stable fixed shape;
- prevention of accidental attribute creation is valuable;
- weak-reference, serialisation, subclassing, and tooling requirements are known;
- multiple-inheritance layout is controlled;
- the project accepts the representation as an API constraint.

They are poorly motivated as decoration intended to make a class look advanced. Begin with an ordinary class when flexibility is useful; adopt slots when the fixed-shape contract or measured resource saving outweighs compatibility cost.

> **Common misconception — “Slots are just a list of permitted attribute names.”**  
> They request a different instance representation implemented by descriptors, with inheritance, weak-reference, layout, and serialisation consequences.

> **Common misconception — “A slotted base means every subclass is slotted.”**  
> A subclass without its own slot declaration ordinarily receives an instance dictionary.

> **Common misconception — “<code>sys.getsizeof</code> proves the saving.”**  
> Shallow size can exclude a separate instance dictionary and all referenced objects. Measure representative populations and the complete allocation effect.

## 9.18 Metaclasses

Every class is an object and therefore has a type. A **metaclass** is the type of a class: an object whose instance-construction protocol constructs class objects. The ordinary metaclass is <code>type</code>.

~~~python
class Ordinary:
    pass


assert isinstance(Ordinary, type)
assert type(Ordinary) is type
assert isinstance(Ordinary(), Ordinary)
~~~

The two instance relations occur at adjacent levels. <code>Ordinary()</code> is an instance of <code>Ordinary</code>; <code>Ordinary</code> is an instance of <code>type</code>. Moreover, <code>type</code> is itself an instance of <code>type</code>. This self-description terminates the otherwise tempting infinite regress of “what is the class of the class of the class?”

Metaclasses exist because class creation sometimes needs programmable policy: collect field declarations, enforce class-level invariants, build registries, synthesise methods, customise instance checks, or integrate with a foreign runtime. They operate at a wide semantic boundary and can affect every subclass and instance, so they require proportionately strong justification.

### 9.18.1 A class statement executes

A class statement is not passive record syntax. Its body is executable Python run in a newly prepared namespace.

~~~python
events: list[str] = []


class Example:
    events.append("class body ran")
    scale = 2 + 3

    def apply(self, value: int) -> int:
        return value * self.scale


assert events == ["class body ran"]
assert Example.scale == 5
~~~

The body executes once when control reaches the statement. It binds <code>scale</code> and <code>apply</code> into the class namespace being assembled. Constructing each <code>Example</code> later does not rerun the class body.

Because bodies execute, class definitions can fail, perform I/O, register callbacks, or depend on ambient state. Production class bodies should ordinarily remain deterministic and lightweight; import-time class creation is part of module execution.

### 9.18.2 The conceptual creation pipeline

For a statement of the form:

~~~python
class Report(Base, metaclass=Meta, category="financial"):
    field = Descriptor()
~~~

the language performs a pipeline conceptually containing these stages:

1. evaluate the base expressions and explicit keyword arguments;
2. resolve non-type base entries that provide MRO-entry substitution;
3. determine a metaclass compatible with all bases and any explicit metaclass;
4. ask the metaclass to prepare a class namespace;
5. execute the class body in that namespace, adding compiler-supplied entries where required;
6. call the selected metaclass with class name, resolved bases, namespace, and class keywords;
7. within ordinary <code>type</code> construction, build the class, set metadata, establish the MRO, notify suitable attributes through <code>__set_name__</code>, and invoke the inherited subclass-initialisation hook;
8. apply class decorators from the innermost/bottom decorator upward;
9. bind the final returned object to the class statement’s name.

This ordering is a semantic guide. Custom metaclasses can alter parts of construction, and detailed implementation steps should not be inferred beyond the documented hooks. The decisive point is that the name <code>Report</code> is bound only after creation and decoration succeed.

### 9.18.3 Metaclass selection uses compatibility, not simple inheritance

If no explicit metaclass is supplied and there are no bases imposing another one, Python selects <code>type</code>. With bases, the selected metaclass must be a subclass of the metaclass of every base. Python chooses the most-derived compatible candidate among the explicit metaclass, if any, and the base metaclasses.

~~~python
class MetaA(type):
    pass


class MetaB(type):
    pass


class A(metaclass=MetaA):
    pass


class B(metaclass=MetaB):
    pass


# class Conflict(A, B):
#     pass
~~~

The commented definition raises a metaclass-conflict <code>TypeError</code>: neither <code>MetaA</code> nor <code>MetaB</code> is a subclass of the other, so neither can govern a class that must satisfy both base policies.

One mechanical repair is a combined metaclass:

~~~python
class CombinedMeta(MetaA, MetaB):
    pass


class Combined(A, B, metaclass=CombinedMeta):
    pass
~~~

This works only if the metaclasses themselves cooperate through compatible MRO, signatures, and invariants. Creating a combined metaclass to silence an error can unite contradictory policies. Composition or removal of one inheritance relation may be the semantic repair.

### 9.18.4 <code>type</code> can construct a class dynamically

The three-argument form of <code>type</code> demonstrates that a class object can be constructed from a name, bases, and namespace:

~~~python
def area(self) -> int:
    return self.width * self.height


Rectangle = type(
    "Rectangle",
    (object,),
    {
        "width": 3,
        "height": 4,
        "area": area,
        "__module__": __name__,
    },
)

assert Rectangle().area() == 12
~~~

This is broadly analogous to an ordinary class statement after its body has created a namespace, but a class statement additionally handles lexical context, <code>__class__</code> cells, decorators, source metadata, and other protocol details. Dynamic <code>type</code> construction is not a textual macro and should not be used merely to avoid writing clear class syntax.

### 9.18.5 Namespace preparation with <code>__prepare__</code>

Before executing a class body, Python calls the selected metaclass’s <code>__prepare__</code> if provided. It must return a mapping-like namespace into which body assignments are made.

~~~python
class RecordingNamespace(dict[str, object]):
    def __setitem__(self, key: str, value: object) -> None:
        print(f"binding {key}")
        super().__setitem__(key, value)


class RecordingMeta(type):
    @classmethod
    def __prepare__(
        mcls,
        name: str,
        bases: tuple[type, ...],
        **kwargs: object,
    ) -> RecordingNamespace:
        return RecordingNamespace()
~~~

Defining a class with <code>RecordingMeta</code> records assignments including compiler-provided names such as <code>__module__</code> and <code>__qualname__</code>. The prepared namespace can preserve metadata, reject duplicate declarations, or interpret field objects.

Ordinary dictionaries already preserve insertion order in modern Python, so order preservation alone no longer requires a custom mapping. A nonstandard namespace must support the operations the compiler and <code>type</code> expect; exotic semantics can break class creation and tooling.

### 9.18.6 Rejecting duplicate class-body bindings

Normal class bodies allow later assignment to replace an earlier one:

~~~python
class Replaced:
    value = 1
    value = 2
~~~

A specialised schema language may want duplicate fields to be an error. A prepared namespace can enforce this while permitting compiler-managed names carefully.

### Worked example 9.6 — A duplicate-aware declaration metaclass

~~~python
class UniqueNamespace(dict[str, object]):
    def __setitem__(self, key: str, value: object) -> None:
        if key in self and key not in {"__annotations__"}:
            raise TypeError(f"duplicate class binding: {key}")
        super().__setitem__(key, value)


class UniqueBindings(type):
    @classmethod
    def __prepare__(
        mcls,
        name: str,
        bases: tuple[type, ...],
        **kwargs: object,
    ) -> UniqueNamespace:
        return UniqueNamespace()


class Schema(metaclass=UniqueBindings):
    account_id = str
    balance = int
~~~

This policy is intentionally narrow and still simplified. Decorated methods can require deliberate rebinding patterns; augmented annotations mutate <code>__annotations__</code>; compiler or framework entries may need exceptions. A real declaration language specifies which duplicate forms are legal rather than rejecting blindly.

### 9.18.7 Class-body scope is not an enclosing function scope

Names assigned earlier in a class body can be used by later expressions in that body, but a method body does not normally close over arbitrary class-local names.

~~~python
class ScopeExample:
    factor = 3
    doubled = factor * 2

    def apply(self, value: int) -> int:
        return value * self.factor
~~~

The method uses <code>self.factor</code>. Writing <code>return value * factor</code> would seek a local or enclosing function/global/built-in name under LEGB, not automatically the class namespace. Class attribute lookup is explicit through an instance, class, or special <code>__class__</code> reference.

Methods using <code>super()</code> or <code>__class__</code> can cause the compiler to create a <code>__classcell__</code> entry. A metaclass that copies or transforms the namespace must pass that cell correctly to <code>type.__new__</code>; discarding it can cause a runtime error during class creation.

### 9.18.8 <code>__new__</code> creates the class object

A metaclass’s <code>__new__</code> receives the metaclass, proposed name, resolved bases, namespace, and applicable class keywords. It can validate or transform the namespace before delegating to <code>type.__new__</code>.

~~~python
class RequiresCategory(type):
    def __new__(
        mcls,
        name: str,
        bases: tuple[type, ...],
        namespace: dict[str, object],
        **kwargs: object,
    ):
        if name != "Categorised":
            category = namespace.get("category")
            if not isinstance(category, str) or not category:
                raise TypeError(f"{name} must define non-empty category")

        cls = super().__new__(mcls, name, bases, namespace, **kwargs)
        return cls


class Categorised(metaclass=RequiresCategory):
    pass


class Report(Categorised):
    category = "financial"
~~~

Validation before <code>super().__new__</code> sees the proposed namespace but not a completed class or its computed MRO. Validation after delegation can inspect inherited attributes and descriptors after ordinary class construction. The chosen timing should match the invariant.

The example deliberately requires the subclass body itself to define <code>category</code> by inspecting <code>namespace</code>. Using <code>getattr(cls, "category", None)</code> after creation would also accept an inherited category. Neither is universally correct; “must declare” and “must provide after inheritance” are different contracts.

### 9.18.9 <code>__init__</code> initialises the class object

After <code>__new__</code> returns a class object of the expected metaclass lineage, the metaclass initialiser can perform post-construction work.

~~~python
class CountedMeta(type):
    created: list[type] = []

    def __init__(cls, name, bases, namespace, **kwargs) -> None:
        super().__init__(name, bases, namespace, **kwargs)
        CountedMeta.created.append(cls)
~~~

As at the instance level, <code>__new__</code> creates and returns the object; <code>__init__</code> initialises it. Class registries created here hold strong references unless designed otherwise, execute during imports, and accumulate across tests or reloads. Their lifetime is part of the system architecture.

### 9.18.10 Descriptor notification and subclass initialisation

Ordinary <code>type.__new__</code> participates in two important hooks encountered elsewhere:

- it calls <code>__set_name__</code> on suitable objects in the new class namespace;
- after the class object exists, subclass-initialisation machinery calls the next <code>__init_subclass__</code> hook in the new class’s parent chain.

Consequently, a metaclass that fails to delegate through <code>type</code> correctly may prevent ordinary descriptor setup or subclass hooks. A class decorator runs later and attaching a descriptor there requires explicit <code>__set_name__</code> notification if the descriptor depends on it.

The exact relative ordering among custom metaclass code, descriptor notifications, and subclass hooks matters. Tests that record events can verify a framework’s intended lifecycle, but framework code should rely on documented hook guarantees rather than CPython-private implementation functions.

### 9.18.11 Metaclass <code>__call__</code> governs ordinary instance construction

Calling a class such as <code>Report()</code> actually invokes call behaviour supplied by its metaclass. <code>type.__call__</code> ordinarily coordinates the class’s <code>__new__</code> and <code>__init__</code>.

~~~python
class TracingMeta(type):
    def __call__(cls, *args: object, **kwargs: object):
        print(f"constructing {cls.__name__}")
        instance = super().__call__(*args, **kwargs)
        print(f"constructed {instance!r}")
        return instance


class Traced(metaclass=TracingMeta):
    def __init__(self, value: int) -> None:
        self.value = value


item = Traced(5)
~~~

The metaclass can cache, reject, wrap, or substitute constructed instances. Doing so changes identity, subclassing, exception, concurrency, and serialisation semantics globally for governed classes.

### 9.18.12 The singleton metaclass illustrates hidden complexity

A common demonstration caches one instance per class in metaclass <code>__call__</code>. It appears concise:

~~~python
class SingletonMeta(type):
    _instances: dict[type, object] = {}

    def __call__(cls, *args: object, **kwargs: object):
        if cls not in cls._instances:
            cls._instances[cls] = super().__call__(*args, **kwargs)
        return cls._instances[cls]
~~~

This code leaves unresolved:

- concurrent first construction;
- whether later arguments are ignored, rejected, or reinitialise state;
- subclass instance separation;
- garbage collection and test reset;
- process and interpreter boundaries;
- copying, pickling, and reconstruction;
- failure during partial construction;
- dependency injection and replacement.

An explicit module-owned instance or factory often makes lifetime and configuration clearer. The example is useful precisely because it shows how a few metaclass lines can imply a large contract.

### 9.18.13 Custom instance and subclass checks

A metaclass may define <code>__instancecheck__</code> and <code>__subclasscheck__</code>, influencing <code>isinstance</code> and <code>issubclass</code>. <code>abc.ABCMeta</code> uses related machinery for abstract base classes and virtual subclassing.

~~~python
class HasSerializeMeta(type):
    def __instancecheck__(cls, instance: object) -> bool:
        return callable(getattr(instance, "serialize", None))


class Serializable(metaclass=HasSerializeMeta):
    pass


class Message:
    def serialize(self) -> bytes:
        return b"message"


assert isinstance(Message(), Serializable)
~~~

This runtime check proves only that retrieval produced a callable at that moment. It does not verify the signature, return type, determinism, safety, or other behavioural laws. Structural <code>Protocol</code> annotations are generally clearer for static interface expression, while ordinary capability tests can suffice at runtime.

Custom instance checks should be fast, side-effect controlled, and recursion safe. Calling <code>getattr</code> can execute arbitrary dynamic access, as §9.16 showed.

### 9.18.14 Customising <code>mro</code> changes inherited meaning

A metaclass can override MRO computation. This changes which descriptors, methods, constructors, and cooperative hooks every instance sees. It can invalidate the assumptions of bases that were written for C3’s normal guarantees.

Such customisation belongs to specialised interoperability systems, not ordinary application architecture. If a design seems to require hand-authored lookup order, first make collaborators explicit through composition or refactor conflicting responsibilities.

### 9.18.15 Non-class bases and <code>__mro_entries__</code>

In a class statement, a base expression need not initially evaluate to a class. A non-type object may provide <code>__mro_entries__(bases)</code>, returning replacement classes used as actual bases. This mechanism supports generic-alias and class-adaptation facilities.

The original base expressions can be recovered through metadata such as <code>__orig_bases__</code> in applicable cases, while <code>__bases__</code> contains resolved class bases. The mechanism is advanced because visually written bases may differ from the final inheritance graph. Libraries using it must make introspection and error messages unusually clear.

### 9.18.16 Class subscription need not be metaclass subscription

An expression such as <code>Container[int]</code> may be handled by <code>Container.__class_getitem__</code>, commonly used to parameterise generic classes for annotations. A metaclass <code>__getitem__</code> can also govern subscription of its class objects and may take precedence under the language rules.

These operations create or return objects representing parameterisation; they do not necessarily construct new runtime subclasses, enforce element types on assignment, or change instance layout. Static generic meaning and runtime metaclass behaviour should not be conflated.

### 9.18.17 Metaclass state is shared at class scale

Attributes on a metaclass can be visible through governed class objects. Mutable metaclass state may be shared across many classes, modules, and tests. It needs ownership just like module globals or descriptor state.

~~~python
class RegistryMeta(type):
    registry: dict[str, type] = {}

    def __new__(mcls, name, bases, namespace, **kwargs):
        cls = super().__new__(mcls, name, bases, namespace, **kwargs)
        key = f"{cls.__module__}.{cls.__qualname__}"
        if key in mcls.registry:
            raise RuntimeError(f"duplicate class key: {key}")
        mcls.registry[key] = cls
        return cls
~~~

Even the qualified key is not universally stable: local classes include enclosing scopes, reload can create a new class object with the same key, and plugins may require unloading. A registry design must specify collision, replacement, discovery, and cleanup semantics.

### 9.18.18 Metaclass methods and class methods occupy different receivers

A method defined on a metaclass and accessed through a governed class binds that class as receiver. A class method defined in the class body also receives the governed class, but it participates in the class’s own inheritance namespace. Their placement conveys different ownership:

- a class method is behaviour of the domain class and is inherited by its subclasses;
- a metaclass method is behaviour governing class objects and may apply across unrelated classes sharing the metaclass.

Most domain factories belong as class methods. Metaclass methods suit operations over the class system itself, such as schema introspection across all governed classes.

### 9.18.19 Framework declaration versus ordinary object design

Metaclasses are common in frameworks because a class body can serve as a declarative language:

~~~python
class Customer(Table):
    identifier = Integer(primary_key=True)
    email = Text(unique=True)
~~~

Here field objects, descriptors, namespace order, inheritance, and class creation can be converted into a database schema. The metaclass is justified when the framework needs to transform an open-ended family of class declarations consistently.

In application code with three known variants, an explicit data structure may be clearer:

~~~python
customer_schema = TableSchema(
    name="customer",
    fields=(
        IntegerField("identifier", primary_key=True),
        TextField("email", unique=True),
    ),
)
~~~

The object form makes construction order, dependencies, and test isolation ordinary. Declarative class syntax is valuable when its ergonomic and integration benefits outweigh the hidden lifecycle.

### 9.18.20 Failure atomicity during class creation

If a metaclass registers a class and a later hook raises, external state may retain a class whose defining statement never bound successfully. Similar partial effects can occur when descriptors register themselves during <code>__set_name__</code> or subclass hooks mutate registries.

A robust framework validates before committing where possible. When commit must precede later work, it needs rollback. Import retry and module cleanup make this especially important because a failed import can leave external registries even if the partially initialised module is removed from ordinary import caching.

### Worked example 9.6A — Validate, build, then commit registration

~~~python
class CommandMeta(type):
    registry: dict[str, type] = {}

    def __new__(
        mcls,
        name: str,
        bases: tuple[type, ...],
        namespace: dict[str, object],
        *,
        command: str | None = None,
        **kwargs: object,
    ):
        if command is not None:
            if not command or any(char.isspace() for char in command):
                raise TypeError("command must be non-empty without whitespace")
            if command in mcls.registry:
                raise TypeError(f"duplicate command: {command}")

        cls = super().__new__(mcls, name, bases, namespace, **kwargs)

        if command is not None:
            mcls.registry[command] = cls
            cls.command_name = command
        return cls


class Command(metaclass=CommandMeta):
    pass


class ListCommand(Command, command="list"):
    pass
~~~

Validation precedes construction and registration follows successful ordinary class creation. Yet assignment of <code>cls.command_name</code> after registry insertion could itself fail under a more restrictive metaclass, leaving partial state. The most robust form completes all fallible class configuration before the single registry commit or removes the entry in an exception handler.

### 9.18.21 Interaction with class decorators

A class decorator receives the class object after metaclass construction and returns the object ultimately bound to the class statement name. It may return the same class, a modified class, a replacement class, or even a non-class object.

~~~python
def labelled(cls: type) -> type:
    cls.label = cls.__name__.lower()
    return cls


@labelled
class Event:
    pass
~~~

The metaclass has already selected and created <code>Event</code> before <code>labelled</code> runs. A decorator cannot retroactively change metaclass selection without returning a newly constructed replacement. Conversely, a metaclass does not automatically see transformations performed later by decorators.

With multiple decorators:

~~~python
@outer
@inner
class C:
    pass
~~~

creation is followed conceptually by <code>C = outer(inner(C))</code>. Decorator application order is bottom-up, just as for function decorators.

### 9.18.22 Choosing the least powerful class hook

Class-level customisation mechanisms differ in scope:

| Requirement | Usually smallest suitable mechanism |
|---|---|
| Transform one completed class explicitly | class decorator |
| Validate every subclass of one base | <code>__init_subclass__</code> |
| Reuse attribute-access policy | descriptor and <code>__set_name__</code> |
| Construct variants on request | factory function or class method |
| Inspect or alter the class namespace before creation | metaclass <code>__prepare__</code>/<code>__new__</code> |
| Control construction of instances across a class family | metaclass <code>__call__</code>, only if class-local factories cannot own it |
| Combine nominal abstract-class machinery | <code>ABCMeta</code> through <code>ABC</code> |

“Least powerful” means smallest affected semantic surface, not least sophisticated. A narrow mechanism is easier to compose because fewer unrelated behaviours pass through it.

### 9.18.23 Testing a metaclass as a lifecycle system

Tests should cover more than a valid class declaration:

1. invalid namespaces fail before external commit;
2. inherited versus directly declared values follow the stated rule;
3. descriptors receive correct names;
4. subclass hooks run once in cooperative order;
5. class keywords are consumed or forwarded correctly;
6. multiple bases either select a compatible metaclass or fail deliberately;
7. decorators observe the intended post-metaclass state;
8. repeated import, reload, and test isolation do not corrupt registries;
9. concurrent class creation, if supported, has defined synchronisation;
10. copying, pickling, and instance construction still satisfy their contracts;
11. error messages identify the source declaration, not only an internal hook;
12. static analysis and introspection can recover declared interfaces.

### 9.18.24 Metaclasses complete rather than violate the object model

Metaclasses can initially appear to be an exception to the simpler claim that classes create instances. They are instead a recursive application of it. Ordinary objects are created under class call semantics; class objects are created under metaclass call semantics. Descriptors govern attributes at either level. MRO governs lookup for classes and metaclasses. <code>__new__</code> and <code>__init__</code> retain their allocation/initialisation distinction.

This capstone revises no earlier rule. It exposes the level at which those same rules construct the objects that programmers normally treat as types.

> **Common misconception — “A metaclass is a class factory.”**  
> That phrase is directionally useful but incomplete. A metaclass is itself a class whose instances are classes; its protocols can govern namespace preparation, class construction, class behaviour, and instance construction.

> **Common misconception — “Metaclasses run when an instance is created.”**  
> Metaclass class-construction hooks run when the class is created. The metaclass’s <code>__call__</code> also participates later when that class is called to create an instance.

> **Common misconception — “A metaclass conflict is solved whenever a combined metaclass compiles.”**  
> A legal metaclass MRO proves structural compatibility only. The policies of the component metaclasses must also cooperate semantically.

## 9.19 `__init_subclass__` and class decorators

Metaclasses govern an entire class-creation regime, but many requirements are narrower. A base class may need to validate or register only its descendants; <code>__init_subclass__</code> supplies that hook. A particular class declaration may need explicit post-processing; a class decorator supplies that transformation. Both preserve ordinary metaclass selection unless their implementations deliberately construct replacements.

### 9.19.1 <code>__init_subclass__</code> observes new descendants

When a class is created as a subclass, Python calls an inherited <code>__init_subclass__</code> hook on the new class. The hook is implicitly a class method: <code>cls</code> is the newly created subclass, not the base on which the source definition appears.

~~~python
class ObservableBase:
    def __init_subclass__(cls, **kwargs: object) -> None:
        super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)
        print(f"created subclass {cls.__qualname__}")


class First(ObservableBase):
    pass


class Second(First):
    pass
~~~

The hook runs for both <code>First</code> and <code>Second</code>. It runs during their class creation, commonly while the defining module is being imported, not when their instances are constructed.

### 9.19.2 Class-header keywords form a configuration channel

Extra keywords in a class header can be consumed by subclass hooks:

~~~python
class Versioned:
    version: int

    def __init_subclass__(
        cls,
        *,
        version: int,
        **kwargs: object,
    ) -> None:
        super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)
        if version < 1:
            raise TypeError("version must be positive")
        cls.version = version


class CurrentFormat(Versioned, version=3):
    pass
~~~

The keyword is configuration for class creation; it is not an argument to <code>CurrentFormat.__init__</code>. A participating hook consumes keywords it owns and forwards the rest. Eventually <code>object.__init_subclass__</code> accepts no arbitrary class keywords, so an unconsumed keyword ordinarily exposes a <code>TypeError</code> rather than disappearing silently.

### 9.19.3 Cooperative hooks follow the MRO

Multiple bases can each own a class keyword if their hooks cooperate.

~~~python
class Versioned:
    def __init_subclass__(
        cls,
        *,
        version: int,
        **kwargs: object,
    ) -> None:
        cls.version = version
        super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)


class Labelled:
    def __init_subclass__(
        cls,
        *,
        label: str,
        **kwargs: object,
    ) -> None:
        cls.label = label
        super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)


class Message(Versioned, Labelled, version=2, label="event"):
    pass
~~~

The MRO determines the hook chain. Each method consumes one keyword and advances. As with cooperative initialisers, compatible signatures and exactly-once delegation are obligations. Calling <code>object.__init_subclass__</code> directly from <code>Versioned</code> would skip <code>Labelled</code>.

### 9.19.4 Validate inherited capability versus local declaration

After ordinary class creation, <code>cls</code> exposes inherited attributes. A hook using <code>hasattr(cls, "encode")</code> accepts an inherited implementation. Sometimes the requirement is instead that every subclass declare its own method. Then inspect <code>cls.__dict__</code>.

~~~python
class MustOverride:
    def process(self) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def __init_subclass__(cls, **kwargs: object) -> None:
        super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)
        if "process" not in cls.__dict__:
            raise TypeError(f"{cls.__name__} must declare process")
~~~

This exact policy can be too strict for intermediate abstract subclasses, generated methods, or deliberate inheritance. <code>abc.abstractmethod</code> ordinarily expresses abstract implementation requirements more accurately. The example illustrates the difference between namespace declaration and effective interface, not a recommended replacement for abstract base classes.

### 9.19.5 Registration is an import-time side effect

~~~python
class Plugin:
    registry: dict[str, type["Plugin"]] = {}

    def __init_subclass__(
        cls,
        *,
        plugin_name: str,
        **kwargs: object,
    ) -> None:
        super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)
        if not plugin_name:
            raise TypeError("plugin name cannot be empty")
        if plugin_name in Plugin.registry:
            raise ValueError(f"duplicate plugin name: {plugin_name}")
        Plugin.registry[plugin_name] = cls


class TextPlugin(Plugin, plugin_name="text"):
    pass
~~~

The registry becomes populated only if the module defining <code>TextPlugin</code> is imported. Discovery therefore depends on import topology. Retaining the class keeps its module objects and associated state reachable. Reloading can attempt to register a new class under the same name. Test suites that define temporary subclasses can pollute later tests.

A plugin architecture must specify:

- which modules are discovered and imported;
- whether names are global or namespaced;
- duplicate and version policy;
- whether replacement and unloading are supported;
- lifetime and weak/strong ownership;
- synchronisation during concurrent discovery;
- security, because importing a plugin executes code;
- how failures avoid partial registry state.

The hook makes registration concise; it does not answer those system questions.

### 9.19.6 Avoid accidentally sharing a registry across unrelated roots

Using <code>cls.registry</code> can allow a subclass to shadow the registry and split registration unexpectedly; always using <code>Plugin.registry</code> deliberately centralises it. Alternatively, each root may initialise its own registry when directly subclassed. The intended ownership must be explicit.

~~~python
class RegistryRoot:
    registry: dict[str, type] = {}

    def __init_subclass__(
        cls,
        *,
        abstract: bool = False,
        key: str | None = None,
        **kwargs: object,
    ) -> None:
        super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)
        if abstract:
            return
        if key is None:
            raise TypeError("concrete subclass requires key")
        if key in RegistryRoot.registry:
            raise TypeError(f"duplicate key: {key}")
        RegistryRoot.registry[key] = cls
~~~

An explicit <code>abstract</code> flag is one possible policy. Integration with <code>inspect.isabstract</code> and <code>ABC</code> may be preferable when abstractness already has formal meaning.

### 9.19.7 A class decorator is explicit at the declaration site

A **class decorator** is a callable applied to a completed class object. The syntax:

~~~python
@register
class JsonCodec:
    pass
~~~

is approximately equivalent, after class construction, to:

~~~python
class JsonCodec:
    pass


JsonCodec = register(JsonCodec)
~~~

The decorator’s visible presence is useful when only selected classes opt into behaviour. <code>__init_subclass__</code>, by contrast, applies implicitly to every descendant of a base.

### Worked example 9.6B — A parameterised class decorator

~~~python
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import TypeVar


C = TypeVar("C", bound=type)
codec_registry: dict[str, type] = {}


def codec(name: str) -> Callable[[C], C]:
    if not name or not name.isascii():
        raise ValueError("codec name must be non-empty ASCII")

    def decorate(cls: C) -> C:
        if name in codec_registry:
            raise ValueError(f"duplicate codec: {name}")
        cls.codec_name = name
        codec_registry[name] = cls
        return cls

    return decorate


@codec("json")
class JsonCodec:
    pass
~~~

Evaluation has two stages. <code>codec("json")</code> runs when Python evaluates the decorator expressions and returns <code>decorate</code>. After the class object is created, <code>decorate(JsonCodec)</code> runs and its return value is bound to <code>JsonCodec</code>.

The generic annotation expresses that this decorator returns the same class type it receives, although dynamically adding <code>codec_name</code> may not become visible to every static checker. A decorator that returns a different class or wrapper needs a different type contract.

### 9.19.8 Decorators can replace the class entirely

Python does not require a class decorator to return the original class:

~~~python
def replace_with_factory(cls: type):
    def make(*args: object, **kwargs: object):
        return cls(*args, **kwargs)
    return make
~~~

After decoration, the source-level class name would refer to a function. This can surprise <code>isinstance</code>, inheritance, introspection, pickling, documentation, and static analysis. Mutating and returning the original class is usually less disruptive when the abstraction remains a class. Replacement should be a conspicuous, documented semantic choice.

### 9.19.9 Attaching descriptors after creation requires notification

A decorator that adds a descriptor after <code>type.__new__</code> has completed does not receive automatic <code>__set_name__</code> handling:

~~~python
def add_identifier(cls: type) -> type:
    descriptor = Named()
    setattr(cls, "identifier", descriptor)
    descriptor.__set_name__(cls, "identifier")
    return cls
~~~

If the descriptor requires other class-creation integration, manual attachment may still be insufficient. A metaclass that places it in the namespace before delegating to <code>type.__new__</code>, or an explicit descriptor in the original class body, may be more correct.

### 9.19.10 Decorator stacking has directional effects

~~~python
@audit
@register
class Handler:
    pass
~~~

<code>register</code> receives the newly created class first. <code>audit</code> receives whatever <code>register</code> returned. If <code>register</code> stores its argument and <code>audit</code> later replaces it, the registry and public name refer to different objects. Decorators that register, wrap, or replace must document ordering requirements or be designed to commute.

### 9.19.11 Dataclass is a class transformation

<code>@dataclass</code> is a prominent class decorator. It inspects annotated fields and can add methods such as <code>__init__</code>, <code>__repr__</code>, and <code>__eq__</code>. Options such as slots can require returning a new class rather than merely mutating the old one. This explains why custom <code>__init_subclass__</code> hooks and decorator ordering can interact in non-obvious ways: subclass hooks occur during the original class construction, while decorators transform afterward.

Frameworks combining dataclasses, abstract bases, descriptors, and registration should test actual lifecycle order. Assumptions based only on surface decorator placement are insufficient.

### 9.19.12 Comparing the mechanisms

| Property | <code>__init_subclass__</code> | Class decorator | Metaclass |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opt-in form | inherit from a base | annotate a declaration | inherit governed base or specify metaclass |
| Scope | all descendants following hook chain | selected decorated class | all classes governed by metaclass |
| Runs relative to class creation | during ordinary subclass initialisation | after class object is created | controls class construction itself |
| Sees prepared namespace before class exists | no | no | yes |
| Can naturally affect metaclass selection | no | no | yes |
| Composition concern | cooperative MRO hooks | decorator ordering | metaclass compatibility and MRO |
| Typical use | descendant validation/registration | explicit transformation/registration | declaration frameworks and class-wide policy |

The table describes normal use, not absolute power. Any hook can call general Python code and construct replacements. Design should be based on the smallest truthful lifecycle, not on what is technically possible.

### 9.19.13 Error location and diagnostic quality

Class hooks run while a class statement is executing, often during import. Errors can therefore surface as import failures several frames removed from the declaration. A good error identifies:

- the class’s qualified name and module;
- the offending field, keyword, or method;
- the violated requirement;
- conflicting registered owner where applicable;
- corrective action without exposing secrets.

Raise <code>TypeError</code> for a malformed class interface or unsupported class-definition argument and <code>ValueError</code> for an unacceptable value of an otherwise accepted form, unless a framework documents a different exception taxonomy.

### 9.19.14 Test isolation and reversibility

Tests commonly create local subclasses. If creation mutates a permanent registry, garbage collection of the local name will not remove the registry entry. Options include:

- an explicit registry object injected into registration;
- a context manager that snapshots and restores registry state;
- weak-value storage when lifecycle semantics permit it;
- unique test namespaces;
- an explicit unregister operation with ownership checks;
- discovery that computes current plugins instead of mutating global state.

Do not solve contamination by clearing an unrelated global registry indiscriminately; another concurrent test or application component may own its contents.

### 9.19.15 Selection rules

Use <code>__init_subclass__</code> when inheriting from the base truthfully means accepting the policy for all descendants. Use a class decorator when transformation should be explicit on selected declarations. Use a descriptor when the policy belongs to individual attributes. Use a metaclass only when the namespace-before-class or class-of-classes level is essential. Use an ordinary function or data object when no class lifecycle is needed.

> **Common misconception — “<code>__init_subclass__</code> initialises instances of subclasses.”**  
> It runs when each subclass object is created. Instance initialisation remains the role of that class’s construction protocol.

> **Common misconception — “A class decorator always preserves a class.”**  
> The decorator’s return value replaces the name and can be any object. Replacement may disrupt type identity, inheritance, introspection, and serialisation.

> **Common misconception — “Registration means discovery is solved.”**  
> Registration occurs only for class definitions that execute. Module discovery, import authority, duplicate policy, failure recovery, and unloading remain system responsibilities.

## 9.20 Integrated object-model trace

The individual protocols become reliable only when their order is understood. This section follows one small class family from source execution to class objects, from class call to instance, and from attribute syntax to descriptor and method results. The event recorder is pedagogical instrumentation: it deliberately makes normally implicit protocol transitions visible.

### 9.20.1 Instrumented definitions

~~~python
from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any


events: list[str] = []


class TraceMeta(type):
    @classmethod
    def __prepare__(
        mcls,
        name: str,
        bases: tuple[type, ...],
        **kwargs: object,
    ) -> dict[str, object]:
        events.append(f"prepare:{name}")
        return super().__prepare__(name, bases, **kwargs)

    def __new__(
        mcls,
        name: str,
        bases: tuple[type, ...],
        namespace: dict[str, object],
        **kwargs: object,
    ) -> TraceMeta:
        events.append(f"meta-new-before:{name}")
        cls = super().__new__(mcls, name, bases, namespace, **kwargs)
        events.append(f"meta-new-after:{name}")
        return cls

    def __init__(
        cls,
        name: str,
        bases: tuple[type, ...],
        namespace: dict[str, object],
        **kwargs: object,
    ) -> None:
        events.append(f"meta-init:{name}")
        super().__init__(name, bases, namespace, **kwargs)

    def __call__(cls, *args: object, **kwargs: object):
        events.append(f"meta-call-before:{cls.__name__}")
        instance = super().__call__(*args, **kwargs)
        events.append(f"meta-call-after:{cls.__name__}")
        return instance


class Measured:
    def __set_name__(self, owner: type, name: str) -> None:
        self.public_name = name
        self.storage_name = f"_{name}"
        events.append(f"set-name:{owner.__name__}.{name}")

    def __get__(self, instance: object | None, owner: type | None = None):
        owner_name = owner.__name__ if owner is not None else "None"
        if instance is None:
            events.append(f"get-class:{owner_name}.{self.public_name}")
            return self
        events.append(f"get-instance:{type(instance).__name__}.{self.public_name}")
        raw = object.__getattribute__(instance, "__dict__")[self.storage_name]
        return raw * 2

    def __set__(self, instance: object, value: int) -> None:
        events.append(f"set-instance:{type(instance).__name__}.{self.public_name}")
        if value < 0:
            raise ValueError("measurement must be non-negative")
        object.__getattribute__(instance, "__dict__")[self.storage_name] = value


class HookRoot(metaclass=TraceMeta):
    def __init_subclass__(cls, **kwargs: object) -> None:
        events.append(f"init-subclass:{cls.__name__}")
        super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)


def mark(cls: type) -> type:
    events.append(f"decorate:{cls.__name__}")
    cls.marked = True
    return cls
~~~

Defining <code>TraceMeta</code> itself is governed by <code>type</code>, not by <code>TraceMeta</code>, so its own hooks do not log its definition. Defining <code>HookRoot</code> does produce events; clear them before isolating the next declaration:

~~~python
events.clear()


@mark
class Base(HookRoot):
    measured = Measured()

    def __new__(cls, value: int) -> Base:
        events.append(f"instance-new:{cls.__name__}")
        return super().__new__(cls)

    def __init__(self, value: int) -> None:
        events.append(f"instance-init:{type(self).__name__}")
        self.measured = value

    def report(self) -> int:
        events.append("report:Base")
        return self.measured
~~~

### 9.20.2 Class creation trace

After the <code>Base</code> statement completes, the relevant event order is:

~~~text
prepare:Base
meta-new-before:Base
set-name:Base.measured
init-subclass:Base
meta-new-after:Base
meta-init:Base
decorate:Base
~~~

The order can now be explained without invoking magic:

1. Python evaluates the decorator expression <code>mark</code> and base expression <code>HookRoot</code>.
2. <code>TraceMeta</code> is selected because it is the metaclass of <code>HookRoot</code>.
3. <code>TraceMeta.__prepare__</code> supplies the namespace.
4. The body executes, constructing one <code>Measured</code> object and several function objects, then binding them into that namespace.
5. Calling the metaclass enters <code>TraceMeta.__new__</code>.
6. Its delegation to <code>type.__new__</code> creates <code>Base</code>. During that ordinary construction, the descriptor receives <code>__set_name__</code>, then the inherited <code>HookRoot.__init_subclass__</code> runs with the new <code>Base</code> as <code>cls</code>.
7. Control returns to the remainder of metaclass <code>__new__</code>, then metaclass <code>__init__</code> initialises the new class object.
8. The decorator receives the completed class, adds <code>marked</code>, and returns it.
9. The module namespace is finally bound so <code>Base</code> refers to that returned class.

The event ordering also explains why <code>Base</code> cannot ordinarily refer to its eventual global name inside its own class body: that binding has not happened. Methods can use the compiler-supported <code>__class__</code> closure once invoked later.

### 9.20.3 Creating a subclass adds no descriptor copy

~~~python
events.clear()


class Child(Base):
    def report(self) -> int:
        events.append("report:Child")
        return super().report() + 1
~~~

The event order is:

~~~text
prepare:Child
meta-new-before:Child
init-subclass:Child
meta-new-after:Child
meta-init:Child
~~~

No <code>set-name:Child.measured</code> event occurs. <code>Child</code> inherits the descriptor object stored in <code>Base.__dict__</code>; the descriptor is not copied into the child namespace and is not automatically notified again. The dynamic <code>owner</code> argument supplied during later access can nevertheless be <code>Child</code>.

The decorator also does not recur: decorators apply to the particular class statement they annotate and are not inherited transformations. The attribute <code>marked</code>, however, is inherited through ordinary lookup.

### 9.20.4 Calling the class traverses the metaclass and class protocols

~~~python
events.clear()
item = Child(5)
~~~

The resulting events are:

~~~text
meta-call-before:Child
instance-new:Child
instance-init:Child
set-instance:Child.measured
meta-call-after:Child
~~~

Detailed derivation:

1. <code>Child(5)</code> is a call on a class object whose type is <code>TraceMeta</code>.
2. <code>TraceMeta.__call__</code> receives <code>Child</code> as <code>cls</code> and logs before delegation.
3. <code>type.__call__</code> locates inherited <code>Base.__new__</code> and calls it with dynamic class <code>Child</code> and argument <code>5</code>.
4. <code>Base.__new__</code> delegates allocation and returns a newly allocated <code>Child</code>.
5. Because the returned object is an instance of the class being constructed, ordinary construction locates inherited <code>Base.__init__</code> and calls it.
6. Assignment to <code>self.measured</code> finds a data descriptor in <code>Base</code> through <code>Child.__mro__</code> and invokes <code>Measured.__set__</code>.
7. The descriptor validates and stores <code>_measured: 5</code> in the instance dictionary.
8. Control returns through <code>type.__call__</code> and then <code>TraceMeta.__call__</code>, which logs completion and returns the instance.

The integer argument was passed to both <code>__new__</code> and <code>__init__</code> under ordinary construction. Neither the descriptor nor the metaclass invented the argument flow.

### 9.20.5 Stored representation differs from apparent attribute value

~~~python
assert item.__dict__ == {"_measured": 5}

events.clear()
answer = item.measured

assert answer == 10
assert events == ["get-instance:Child.measured"]
~~~

The public read does not return a stored <code>measured</code> entry. Lookup finds the data descriptor, which retrieves raw <code>_measured</code> and doubles it. Thus three distinct notions must not be conflated:

- **public attribute name:** <code>measured</code>;
- **physical storage key:** <code>_measured</code>;
- **retrieved semantic value:** <code>10</code> from stored raw value <code>5</code>.

Serialising the dictionary directly would expose the physical representation, not necessarily the public state contract.

### 9.20.6 Class access invokes the same descriptor differently

~~~python
events.clear()
descriptor = Child.measured

assert descriptor is Base.__dict__["measured"]
assert events == ["get-class:Child.measured"]
~~~

Lookup through <code>Child</code> finds the inherited descriptor and calls <code>__get__</code> with <code>instance=None</code> and dynamic owner <code>Child</code>. The descriptor returns itself. Directly indexing <code>Base.__dict__</code> retrieves the raw namespace entry without invoking its protocol.

### 9.20.7 Method binding precedes the call body

For <code>item.report()</code>, first evaluate <code>item.report</code>. Class lookup finds the function in <code>Child.__dict__</code>. The function is a non-data descriptor, so its <code>__get__</code> returns a bound method retaining <code>item</code>. Calling that bound method supplies <code>item</code> as <code>self</code>.

~~~python
bound = item.report
assert bound.__self__ is item
assert bound.__func__ is Child.__dict__["report"]
~~~

This binding stage is why the call syntax contains no explicit receiver argument even though the function definition names <code>self</code>.

### 9.20.8 <code>super</code> continues relative to the defining class

~~~python
events.clear()
result = item.report()

assert result == 11
assert events == [
    "report:Child",
    "report:Base",
    "get-instance:Child.measured",
]
~~~

The call chain is:

1. the bound <code>Child.report</code> logs its contribution;
2. zero-argument <code>super()</code> is parameterised by defining class <code>Child</code> and receiver <code>item</code>;
3. lookup after <code>Child</code> in <code>Child.__mro__</code> finds <code>Base.report</code> and binds it to the same <code>item</code>;
4. <code>Base.report</code> logs, then reads <code>self.measured</code>;
5. the descriptor sees an instance of <code>Child</code>, retrieves and doubles its stored value to <code>10</code>;
6. <code>Child.report</code> adds one and returns <code>11</code>.

The same receiver flows through both methods; <code>super</code> changes the lookup starting point, not the object.

### 9.20.9 Rejected descriptor assignment is commit-safe

~~~python
events.clear()

try:
    item.measured = -1
except ValueError:
    pass

assert item.__dict__ == {"_measured": 5}
assert item.measured == 10
~~~

<code>Measured.__set__</code> validates before updating the dictionary. The rejected value therefore leaves prior state intact. Had it written first and validated second, the raised exception would not automatically roll back mutation.

### 9.20.10 Shadowing cannot bypass this data descriptor

Even direct insertion of a same-named dictionary key does not change public retrieval:

~~~python
item.__dict__["measured"] = 999
assert item.measured == 10
~~~

Data-descriptor precedence selects <code>Measured.__get__</code> before the instance dictionary entry. The unused key still consumes memory and may confuse naive serializers. Encapsulation mechanisms should prevent or detect such representational debris where relevant.

### 9.20.11 Replacing the class attribute changes future lookup

If code performs <code>Base.measured = 100</code>, it replaces the descriptor in the class namespace. Existing raw <code>_measured</code> values remain in instances but ordinary <code>item.measured</code> now finds the ordinary class value unless a subclass overrides it. Class-level mutation can therefore change the semantics of all current instances without touching them.

This operation is omitted from the executable trace because destructive mutation would make later assertions dependent on repair. The principle is central: class namespaces are live shared objects, not immutable templates consumed at construction.

### 9.20.12 A compact lookup calculus

For an ordinary instance <code>x</code>, dynamic type <code>T</code>, and attribute name <code>n</code>, use the following decision sequence:

1. Does a custom <code>T.__getattribute__</code> intercept? If so, follow its semantics and delegation.
2. Under ordinary base semantics, find the first <code>n</code> in the MRO.
3. If that object is a data descriptor, invoke it.
4. Else, if <code>x.__dict__</code> contains <code>n</code>, return that entry.
5. Else, if the class result is a non-data descriptor, invoke it.
6. Else, if a class result exists, return it.
7. Else, invoke a suitable <code>__getattr__</code> fallback if defined.
8. Otherwise raise <code>AttributeError</code>.

For a class object <code>C</code>, repeat the object/type idea one level higher: <code>C</code> is an instance of metaclass <code>M</code>, and lookup can involve metaclass descriptors, the class MRO, and <code>M.__getattribute__</code>. Exact class lookup has additional precedence details, but no new ontological category is needed.

### 9.20.13 A compact construction calculus

For an ordinary call <code>C(args)</code> where <code>C</code> is a class:

1. dispatch callability through <code>type(C).__call__</code>;
2. under <code>type.__call__</code>, invoke <code>C.__new__(C, args)</code> through inherited lookup;
3. receive the created object <code>x</code>;
4. if <code>x</code> has the required instance relation, invoke the applicable <code>C.__init__(x, args)</code>;
5. ignore <code>__init__</code> as a value-producing operation—it must return <code>None</code>;
6. return <code>x</code> through the metaclass call chain.

Custom metaclass call behaviour and unusual <code>__new__</code> returns can change steps. Factories that are not classes simply follow their own call protocol.

### 9.20.14 A compact class-creation calculus

For <code>class C(Bases, keywords): body</code>:

1. evaluate header expressions;
2. resolve bases and select a compatible metaclass;
3. prepare namespace;
4. execute body into namespace;
5. ask metaclass to construct and initialise class object;
6. within ordinary type construction, compute MRO and integrate descriptors and subclass hooks;
7. apply decorators;
8. bind final object to <code>C</code>.

These three calculi—lookup, instance construction, and class construction—explain most “magic” attributed to Python OOP. The language supplies dispatch protocols; user code supplies policy.

### 9.20.15 Object orientation as coordinated namespaces and protocols

The full mental model can now replace the loose “blueprint” metaphor. A Python object-oriented program is a graph of objects. Some objects are classes; some classes are metaclasses. Namespaces bind names to objects. Attribute lookup walks instance storage, class MROs, and descriptor protocols under defined precedence. Function descriptors bind receivers. Class calling invokes construction protocols. <code>super</code> advances through an MRO. Special syntax invokes type-level protocols. Invariants and substitutability constrain which programmable behaviours remain coherent.

Nothing in that account requires mystical dispatch. The difficulty is real because several ordinary mechanisms compose, and each hook can run arbitrary code. Precision comes from identifying the receiver, its dynamic type, the definition site, the MRO, the descriptor category, the namespace containing each binding, and the exact protocol transition currently occurring.

## 9.21 Common misconceptions consolidated

The following false statements are plausible because each compresses several mechanisms into a familiar metaphor. The correction after each statement should be read as a compact diagnostic rule.

### 9.21.1 Classes, instances, identity, and construction

1. **“A class is a blueprint but not an object.”** A Python class is an object, ordinarily an instance of <code>type</code>, with identity, attributes, bases, an MRO, and callable construction behaviour.
2. **“Every object is an instance of <code>object</code> in exactly the same sense.”** Ordinary classes derive from <code>object</code>, while instance relationships can also be customised or virtual. Ask which runtime relation and protocol are relevant.
3. **“The class statement merely declares a shape.”** Its body executes immediately in a prepared namespace and can compute, fail, or cause effects.
4. **“Class body code runs for every instance.”** It runs during class creation; ordinary per-instance initialisation occurs through <code>__new__</code> and <code>__init__</code> when the class is called.
5. **“<code>__init__</code> creates the object.”** <code>__new__</code> produces it. <code>__init__</code> receives an already created instance and must return <code>None</code>.
6. **“Every call to a class yields a fresh instance of that class.”** A metaclass can customise calls, and <code>__new__</code> can return cached or different objects. Such behaviour requires an explicit identity contract.
7. **“If <code>__new__</code> succeeds, <code>__init__</code> always runs.”** An unusual return outside the required instance relation can skip the expected initialiser; an exception also terminates construction.
8. **“Constructor arguments belong only to <code>__init__</code>.”** Ordinary class calling can pass them through metaclass <code>__call__</code> to both <code>__new__</code> and <code>__init__</code>.
9. **“An object’s class is permanently described by the variable annotation holding it.”** An annotation informs tools; runtime dispatch follows the actual object and <code>type</code> relationships.
10. **“Equal objects are the same object.”** Equality is a programmable value relation; identity means one object and is tested with <code>is</code>.
11. **“A frozen object is deeply immutable.”** Preventing field rebinding does not freeze mutable objects reachable through its fields.
12. **“Private attributes are enforced by double underscores.”** Name mangling reduces accidental subclass collision; determined code can still reach the mangled binding.

### 9.21.2 Attributes, methods, and descriptors

13. **“Attributes reside inside an object as one flat table.”** Lookup can combine data descriptors, instance dictionaries, non-data descriptors, class namespaces, base-class MROs, and fallback hooks.
14. **“Class attributes are copied into each new instance.”** Instances normally find the shared class binding through lookup until an allowed instance binding shadows it.
15. **“Changing a mutable class attribute changes the class but not existing instances.”** Instances finding that same object observe its mutation unless they shadow the name or another protocol intervenes.
16. **“Assignment to <code>obj.name</code> always writes <code>obj.__dict__</code>.”** A data descriptor, slot, or custom <code>__setattr__</code> can mediate or reject assignment.
17. **“An entry in <code>obj.__dict__</code> always wins.”** A data descriptor with the same name has higher retrieval precedence.
18. **“A method is copied and given <code>self</code> when the instance is made.”** A class-owned function is a descriptor; access through an instance creates a bound-method object as needed.
19. **“<code>self</code> is a reserved word.”** It is a strong convention for the first instance-method parameter; binding depends on descriptors, not spelling.
20. **“A static method is faster because it is static.”** <code>staticmethod</code> changes binding semantics, not an optimisation guarantee.
