21. **“A class method is run only once per class.”** It is an ordinarily callable method whose first bound argument is the dynamic class.
22. **“A property is a method with omitted parentheses.”** It is a descriptor participating in attribute lookup. Attribute syntax should still have a defensible access-cost and side-effect contract.
23. **“A property without a setter is non-data.”** Property objects implement data-descriptor behaviour even when assignment is rejected, so an instance entry cannot ordinarily shadow retrieval.
24. **“A descriptor contains every instance’s value in its own simple field.”** The descriptor is shared; values may be stored in each instance, slots, weak mappings, external systems, or computed dynamically.
25. **“<code>__set_name__</code> runs whenever a descriptor is assigned to a class.”** Ordinary type construction invokes it for objects in the original class namespace. Later attachment needs explicit handling.
26. **“<code>__getattr__</code> intercepts all reads.”** It is a fallback for missing attributes; <code>__getattribute__</code> participates in all ordinary reads.
27. **“<code>hasattr</code> safely inspects without executing behaviour.”** It performs retrieval, can invoke arbitrary user code, and interprets <code>AttributeError</code> as absence.

### 9.21.3 Encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism

28. **“Encapsulation means no external code can mutate state.”** In Python it primarily assigns responsibility and exposes a controlled cooperative interface; it is not a hostile-code sandbox.
29. **“A leading underscore makes an attribute inaccessible.”** It communicates non-public API intent by convention.
30. **“Getters and setters automatically improve encapsulation.”** Accessors that merely mirror public storage add ceremony; a boundary is useful when it owns an invariant, abstraction, or change policy.
31. **“Inheritance is the normal mechanism for code reuse.”** Inheritance asserts a type/substitutability relation. Composition, delegation, or a function can reuse behaviour without that claim.
32. **“If <code>isinstance(child, Base)</code> is true, substitution is proven.”** The runtime nominal relation does not prove preservation of preconditions, postconditions, invariants, exceptions, or history constraints.
33. **“A subtype may reject more inputs because it is more specialised.”** Strengthening a base method’s preconditions breaks callers entitled to use the base contract.
34. **“A subtype may return less information if its implementation is simpler.”** Weakening promised postconditions breaks substitutability.
35. **“Overriding a method means copying and replacing it everywhere.”** The subclass binds another attribute; MRO lookup selects it for suitable receivers while the base implementation continues to exist.
36. **“Calling a base method directly and using <code>super</code> are equivalent.”** A named base freezes one route; <code>super</code> continues after a definition site in the receiver’s MRO.
37. **“<code>super()</code> calls the immediate parent.”** In a multiple-inheritance MRO it can call a sibling relative to the defining class.
38. **“Python searches one parent tree completely, then the next.”** C3 constructs one monotonic linearisation that keeps shared ancestors after their subclasses.
39. **“A legal MRO proves the bases work together.”** It proves consistent precedence only, not compatible signatures, state ownership, or behavioural laws.
40. **“One call to <code>super</code> guarantees every base runs.”** Every intervening implementation must continue the cooperative chain exactly as its contract requires.
41. **“A mixin is any small base class.”** A disciplined mixin contributes a narrow capability under explicit host and cooperation requirements; size alone is irrelevant.
42. **“Composition eliminates coupling.”** It makes collaborators and ownership explicit, but their interfaces and lifecycle still create intentional coupling.
43. **“Duck typing means there is no interface.”** Structural use still depends on operations and behavioural laws; only nominal declaration is unnecessary.

### 9.21.4 Special methods and operator protocols

44. **“Dunder methods are ordinary methods with funny names.”** They are ordinary attributes syntactically, but language syntax often looks them up specially on types and imposes result/fallback rules.
45. **“Calling <code>obj.__len__()</code> is always equivalent to <code>len(obj)</code>.”** The built-in owns special lookup, type checks, and error semantics; direct calling can observe different shadowing or invalid results.
46. **“Any integer from <code>__len__</code> is accepted.”** Length must satisfy the protocol’s non-negative integer and platform-size constraints.
47. **“Truth testing only calls <code>__bool__</code>.”** If absent, Python can use <code>__len__</code>; if both are absent, ordinary objects are truthy.
48. **“An iterable and iterator are synonyms.”** An iterable produces an iterator; an iterator is the stateful object whose <code>__next__</code> advances and exhausts.
49. **“Returning <code>NotImplemented</code> reports an unfinished method to the caller.”** It asks a cooperative operator protocol to try another route.
50. **“<code>NotImplementedError</code> and <code>NotImplemented</code> are interchangeable.”** One is an exception terminating the current call; the other is a sentinel value used by selected dispatch protocols.
51. **“The left operand always receives first operator dispatch.”** A strict right-hand subtype with a distinct reflected method can receive priority.
52. **“A reflected subtraction method computes receiver minus argument.”** It implements the original expression order: in <code>right.__rsub__(left)</code>, compute <code>left - right</code>.
53. **“<code>+=</code> necessarily mutates.”** It tries an in-place method and may otherwise compute an ordinary result and rebind the left target.
54. **“If augmented assignment raises, nothing changed.”** An inner mutable object can be changed before a later target rebinding fails; compound syntax is not transactional.
55. **“Implementing <code>__eq__</code> automatically gives a valid hash.”** Mutable or value-equal objects need an explicit hash policy; equal hashable objects must have equal hashes.
56. **“Operator syntax decides the mathematics.”** A type must choose meanings, coercions, closure, result types, and algebraic laws; syntax supplies dispatch only.
57. **“Returning a plausible result is enough.”** Special protocols include error, aliasing, resource, algebraic, and interoperability contracts as well as result shape.

### 9.21.5 Slots, metaclasses, and class lifecycle

58. **“Slots declare statically typed fields.”** They request named runtime storage descriptors; they do not constrain value types without additional policy.
59. **“Slots make instances immutable.”** Slot values can ordinarily be reassigned, and referenced objects can mutate.
60. **“Slots make attributes private.”** They constrain ordinary storage names, not access authority.
61. **“A slotted base forces all subclasses to have no dictionary.”** A subclass without its own slot declaration ordinarily gains a dictionary.
62. **“Slots always save a known number of bytes.”** Savings vary with interpreter, layout, key sharing, population, inheritance, and measurement boundary.
63. **“Shallow <code>getsizeof</code> compares complete object memory.”** Separately allocated dictionaries and referenced graphs may be excluded.
64. **“Every class has metaclass <code>type</code> exactly.”** Custom metaclasses are subclasses of <code>type</code>; <code>type(C)</code> may be such a subclass.
65. **“A metaclass is needed whenever classes are created dynamically.”** The three-argument <code>type</code>, factory functions, decorators, and ordinary closures cover many dynamic cases.
66. **“Metaclass <code>__new__</code> constructs ordinary instances.”** It constructs class objects; metaclass <code>__call__</code> later participates when those class objects construct instances.
67. **“<code>__prepare__</code> receives an already completed class.”** It supplies the namespace before the class body executes.
68. **“A metaclass conflict is only a syntax issue.”** It signals incompatible class-governance inheritance; a combined metaclass must reconcile policies, not merely types.
69. **“<code>__init_subclass__</code> runs on each instance.”** It runs on the newly created subclass during class creation.
70. **“A class decorator runs before the metaclass.”** It receives the object after metaclass construction and subclass hooks, then its return is bound.
71. **“Class decorators are inherited automatically.”** Their transformed attributes may be inherited, but the decorator call applies only to the annotated class statement.
72. **“Metaprogramming removes boilerplate for free.”** It moves work into implicit lifecycle machinery, increasing requirements for ordering, diagnostics, typing, introspection, failure recovery, and tests.

## 9.22 Exercises

The problems are cumulative. “Predict” means write the outcome and justify it from namespaces and protocols before executing code. “Prove” means state assumptions, derive the claim, and supply tests as evidence; a few passing examples alone are not a proof of all inputs.

### 9.22.1 Objects, classes, and namespaces

1. For the expressions <code>type(3)</code>, <code>type(int)</code>, <code>isinstance(3, int)</code>, <code>isinstance(int, type)</code>, and <code>issubclass(bool, int)</code>, predict each result and draw the two distinct instance/inheritance relations involved.
2. Define a class containing one integer class attribute. Create two instances, assign the same attribute name on one instance, and draw all three namespaces before and after assignment.
3. Delete the shadowing instance attribute from Exercise 2. Predict what retrieval yields and explain why deletion appears to “restore” a value without copying anything.
4. Bind the same mutable list as a class attribute and mutate it through one instance. Account for every reference and observation through the other instance.
5. Repair Exercise 4 by constructing per-instance lists. Then deliberately share one list between two instances through constructor arguments and explain why the repair cannot prevent explicit aliasing.
6. Write a function that receives an arbitrary object and reports its dynamic type, class MRO when applicable, instance dictionary when present, and raw class namespace entry for a requested name without triggering descriptor access. State every case it cannot safely or completely inspect.
7. Show that assigning a new class attribute after instances exist changes lookup on those instances. Add an instance shadow and determine which objects observe each later class rebinding.
8. Create a class body containing a loop that generates three class attributes. Explain when the loop runs, where its loop variable remains bound, and why instance construction does not repeat it.
9. Demonstrate that a method body does not automatically close over a class-local constant. Repair the method using instance/class attribute lookup and separately using a module constant; compare override behaviour.
10. Use <code>vars</code> on an instance, its class, and the metaclass. Classify returned mappings by ownership and mutability; do not mutate a mapping proxy.
11. Construct two distinct class objects with the same <code>__name__</code>. Prove that names do not establish type identity, and analyse the resulting representations.
12. Integration with Chapters 5 and 8: represent the object/class/metaclass relationships as a graph of nodes and typed edges using only dictionaries and tuples, then write pure query functions for “instances of” and “subclasses of.” Explain how this model differs from Python’s programmable runtime checks.

### 9.22.2 Methods, binding, and receiver semantics

13. Retrieve the same method through a class and an instance. Inspect <code>__func__</code> and <code>__self__</code> where available and reconstruct the bound call by calling the raw function explicitly.
14. Store a bound method in a variable, delete the original instance name, and show whether the instance remains reachable. Explain the lifetime edge.
15. Assign a plain function to one instance under an existing method name. Predict whether automatic receiver binding occurs and explain the non-data-descriptor precedence responsible.
16. Assign a function to a class after class creation and invoke it through an instance. Compare this with Exercise 15.
17. Implement the same operation as an instance method, class method, static method, and module function. For each, state the receiver or dependency it can access implicitly and select the truthful design.
18. Inherit a class method factory and call it through a subclass. Verify the dynamic class constructed. Then replace <code>cls(...)</code> with a named base call and identify the extensibility defect.
19. Create a static method that does not conceptually belong to the class. Move it to a module-level function and assess discoverability, coupling, and substitution; justify one location.
20. Shadow a non-data function descriptor on one instance, then make a data descriptor with the same retrieval behaviour. Demonstrate why the latter cannot be shadowed by ordinary assignment.
21. Pass an unbound class function as a callback. Specify the signature the callback consumer must use and compare it with passing a bound method.
22. Store bound methods from one thousand short-lived instances in a list. Explain and measure why the instances remain alive until the list is cleared.
23. Build a callback wrapper using <code>weakref.WeakMethod</code>. Define what should happen when the receiving instance has been collected.
24. Integration with Chapter 8: write a decorator that preserves metadata and works on an instance method. Trace decoration time, descriptor binding time, wrapper call time, and the identities of <code>self</code> and the original function.

### 9.22.3 Encapsulation, invariants, and record types

25. Define a bank-account invariant in pence using integers. Implement deposit and withdrawal so rejected operations leave state unchanged. Test zero, negative, boundary, and excessive values.

## 9.23 Cumulative glossary additions

- **Abstract base class (ABC):** nominal interface class that can mark required methods abstract and prevent ordinary instantiation until those requirements are resolved.
- **Adapter:** component translating one interface, representation, or exception vocabulary into another.
- **Ad hoc polymorphism:** selection of differing implementations for an operation according to involved types, as in overloaded operator dispatch.
- **Aggregate:** object or object cluster treated as one invariant and consistency boundary.
- **Aliasing contract:** specification of whether an operation preserves identity, mutates a shared object, or produces a separately owned value.
- **Attribute:** named value resolved through an object and its type’s access protocol rather than necessarily one direct storage entry.
- **Augmented assignment:** statement form such as <code>+=</code> that attempts an in-place protocol and can fall back to an ordinary operation plus rebinding.
- **Behavioural subtype:** type whose instances preserve every relevant observable contract of a supertype.
- **Bound method:** callable retaining a function and the instance or class supplied as its receiver.
- **C3 linearisation:** algorithm computing Python’s monotonic method resolution order while respecting local base order.
- **Capability:** reference or narrower interface conferring authority to perform a set of operations.
- **Class:** object used to construct instances and govern shared behaviour through attribute lookup and protocols.
- **Class attribute:** binding stored in a class namespace and potentially found by class or instance lookup.
- **Class decorator:** callable applied to a completed class object whose return becomes the class statement’s final binding.
- **Class method:** descriptor-wrapped function that binds the dynamic class as its first argument.
- **Class variable:** type-annotation category expressing state conceptually owned by the class rather than each instance.
- **Class-body namespace:** prepared mapping populated by execution of a class suite before construction of the class object.
- **Closed operation:** operation that maps operands from a set back into that set.
- **Coercion:** conversion of an operand into a representation accepted by an operation.
- **Composition:** construction of higher behaviour from explicit component objects rather than inherited implementation.
- **Composition root:** application location that creates concrete components and connects their dependencies.
- **Cooperative method:** method that contributes local behaviour and delegates continuation through <code>super</code> under a shared MRO contract.
- **Data descriptor:** descriptor whose type defines setting or deletion and which ordinarily precedes an instance dictionary entry during retrieval.
- **Dataclass:** class transformed to generate selected record-like methods from declared fields and configuration.
- **Delegation:** transfer of an operation from one object to a collaborating object.
- **Dependency injection:** supply of a collaborator from outside a component rather than hidden location or construction within it.
- **Descriptor:** class-owned object controlling attribute retrieval, assignment, or deletion through descriptor protocol methods.
- **Design-pattern Decorator:** wrapper object implementing a component interface while adding behaviour before or after delegation; distinct from <code>@</code> decorator syntax.
- **Double dispatch (limited operator form):** cooperation in which an operation may consult implementations associated with both operand types; Python binary operators provide a constrained form rather than a general multimethod system.
- **Duck typing:** structural use of an object according to behaviour it supports rather than a demanded nominal ancestry.
- **Dunder method:** informal name for a double-underscore special method participating in a Python protocol.
- **Encapsulation:** assignment of state and invariant ownership behind a controlled interface.
- **Entity:** domain object whose continuity and identity matter independently of equality of all present field values.
- **Equivalence relation:** relation that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive; the usual law expected of value equality.
- **Factory:** callable whose responsibility is constructing or selecting objects, possibly with validation, caching, or implementation choice.
- **Fluent interface:** interface whose operations return a suitable receiver-related value so calls can be chained.
- **Hash:** integer summary used with equality to select candidate locations in hash-based collections.
- **Hashable object:** object providing a stable hash during collection membership and equality coherent with equal objects’ hashes.
- **History constraint:** behavioural-subtyping requirement that a subtype not introduce state evolutions forbidden by the supertype abstraction.
- **Identity:** relation of being the very same object, tested with <code>is</code>.
- **Immutable value object:** value-semantic object whose observable equality-relevant state cannot change after construction.
- **In-place method:** special method such as <code>__iadd__</code> given first opportunity for augmented assignment; it may mutate or return a new object.
- **Inheritance:** derivation of a class from one or more bases, creating nominal type and MRO relationships and optionally reusing implementation.
- **Instance:** object related to a class through Python’s instance semantics and ordinarily governed by that class’s protocols.
- **Instance attribute:** per-instance attribute state, commonly but not necessarily stored in an instance dictionary.
- **Invariant:** condition that must hold at every publicly observable stable point in an object’s lifecycle.
- **Law of Demeter:** coupling heuristic that discourages reaching through long collaborator chains and favours asking the owner of a responsibility to act.
- **Liskov substitution principle:** requirement that subtype objects preserve the behavioural expectations available through their supertype interface.
- **Local precedence order:** requirement that direct bases retain their declared left-to-right precedence in an MRO.
- **Metaclass:** class whose instances are class objects and whose protocols can govern class creation and class behaviour.
- **Metaclass conflict:** absence of one selected metaclass that is a subclass of the metaclass of every proposed base and compatible explicit candidate.
- **Method resolution order (MRO):** linear class sequence used for inherited attribute search and cooperative <code>super</code> traversal.
- **Mixin:** narrowly purposed base class intended to contribute a capability within a compatible inheritance composition.
- **Monotonicity:** C3 property preventing a subclass from reversing precedence already established by a parent MRO.
- **Name mangling:** class-definition transformation of selected double-leading-underscore names intended to reduce accidental subclass collision.
- **Nominal subtype:** subtype relationship declared through class inheritance or another explicit nominal mechanism.
- **Non-data descriptor:** retrieval descriptor lacking descriptor-type setting/deletion methods and therefore ordinarily shadowable by an instance dictionary entry.
- **NotImplemented:** singleton result by which a selected binary/comparison method declines an operand combination and permits protocol fallback.
- **NotImplementedError:** exception indicating that invoked code deliberately lacks an implementation; not the operator-cooperation sentinel.
- **Null Object:** component implementing an interface with deliberately neutral behaviour to avoid repeated absence branching.
- **Object graph:** objects represented as nodes and references as directed edges, including sharing and cycles.
- **Observer-relative substitutability:** principle that compatibility is judged against behaviours visible to callers using the promised interface.
- **Partial order:** ordering relation that permits some pairs to be incomparable.
- **Polymorphism:** use of one operation or interface across values of differing types under a shared contract.
- **Postcondition:** property promised after an operation completes successfully, including result and permitted state changes.
- **Precondition:** condition a caller must satisfy before invoking an operation.
- **Property:** data descriptor exposing managed attribute syntax through getter, setter, or deleter functions.
- **Protocol:** behavioural interface defined by supported operations and their laws, whether expressed structurally, nominally, statically, or informally.
- **Proxy:** object mediating access to a target object while presenting some selected part of its interface.
- **Reflected operation:** right-operand special method that may implement the original ordered binary expression when selected by cooperative dispatch.
- **Representation exposure:** leakage of internal mutable or sensitive structure through a public return, iterator, representation, or alias.
- **Runtime-checkable protocol:** structural typing protocol opted into shallow <code>isinstance</code>/<code>issubclass</code>-style presence checks at runtime.
- **Slot:** named instance-storage position represented by a class-owned descriptor and requested through <code>__slots__</code>.
- **Static method:** descriptor wrapper suppressing automatic instance or class receiver binding for a class-namespaced function.
- **Strategy:** replaceable policy object or callable selected independently from the coordinator that uses it.
- **Structural subtype:** type accepted because it provides required interface structure rather than because it declares nominal ancestry.
- **Subclass hook:** <code>__init_subclass__</code> method invoked on a newly created subclass through its inherited cooperative hook chain.
- **Substitutability:** ability to use one object wherever an interface is promised without invalidating caller assumptions.
- **Total order:** ordering relation in which every relevant pair is comparable and ordering laws hold.
- **Type object:** class object used in runtime type relations and ordinarily callable to construct instances.
- **Value object:** domain object understood primarily by immutable or controlled value semantics rather than independent identity.
- **Variance:** rule governing how subtype relations between type arguments induce—or do not induce—relations between parameterised types.
- **Virtual subclass:** class recognised nominally by an abstract base mechanism without inheriting its implementation or entering its MRO.
- **Weak reference:** reference that observes an object without by itself keeping that object alive.
- **<code>__classcell__</code>:** compiler/metaclass handoff cell enabling methods that require a lexical <code>__class__</code> reference, including zero-argument <code>super</code>.
- **<code>__prepare__</code>:** metaclass hook returning the mapping used as a class body’s execution namespace.
- **<code>__set_name__</code>:** class-creation hook notifying a namespace value of the owner class and attribute name under which it was defined.

# Chapter 10 — Modules, Packages, Imports, and Distribution

## 10.1 Modularity is control over knowledge and change

A **module** is a Python object serving as a namespace for definitions loaded under the import system. A **package** is a module capable of containing submodules. Modularity solves more than file length: it assigns ownership, limits which facts one component must know, publishes stable interfaces, and controls the spread of change.

A module boundary is useful when it separates responsibilities with distinct invariants. Splitting every class into a file or collecting unrelated helpers in `utils.py` creates filenames without a coherent model. A module should answer a recognisable question and expose a deliberate public surface.

Example project:

```text
ledger/
    pyproject.toml
    README.md
    src/
        ledger/
            __init__.py
            __main__.py
            model.py
            parsing.py
            reporting.py
    tests/
        test_model.py
        test_parsing.py
```

The outer `ledger/` is the project root. `src/ledger/` is the import package. Reusing the name is conventional but the two roles differ. `pyproject.toml` describes a distribution project; `__init__.py` initialises an ordinary package; `model.py` and others define submodules.

### 10.1.1 Four boundaries that are often conflated

A Python project commonly contains at least four distinct organisational units:

1. a **source file**, which is a persistent filesystem artefact containing text;
2. a **module**, which is a runtime namespace object loaded under a name;
3. an **import package**, which is a module that can contain submodules;
4. a **distribution**, which is an installable versioned collection described by packaging metadata.

One source file can be executed under different module names and thereby produce distinct module objects. A module can be supplied by a built-in or custom loader without an ordinary source file. One distribution can install several top-level import packages, and several distributions can contribute portions of one namespace package. The repository name, distribution name, and import name are therefore mappings, not identities.

For the example, a repository and distribution might be named <code>careful-ledger</code> while callers write <code>import ledger</code>. Package installers reason primarily about the distribution name; the import machinery reasons primarily about <code>ledger</code> and its search path.

### 10.1.2 Cohesion determines what belongs together

**Cohesion** is the degree to which the responsibilities inside a component belong to one comprehensible purpose. A cohesive <code>parsing</code> module converts external representations into validated domain values. An incoherent <code>helpers</code> module may contain timestamp formatting, database retries, checksum calculation, and user authorisation merely because all four are “utilities.”

Cohesion is evaluated semantically, not by line count. A 1,500-line parser implementing one grammar may be more cohesive than a 70-line module containing seven unrelated conveniences. Size can signal a need to inspect responsibilities, but arbitrary size limits can fragment one abstraction into files whose changes must always travel together.

One practical test asks: can the module’s purpose be stated without “and” joining independent reasons to change? “Parses ledger transaction syntax” is cohesive. “Parses transactions and sends notification email” joins distinct boundary and policy concerns.

### 10.1.3 Coupling measures dependency knowledge

**Coupling** is the dependency between components: one component relies on another’s name, interface, data representation, timing, exceptions, side effects, or lifecycle. Coupling is not inherently bad. A program works because components deliberately depend on contracts. The design objective is to make essential coupling explicit and prevent dependence on accidental details.

~~~python
# reporting.py
from collections.abc import Iterable

from .model import Transaction


def total(transactions: Iterable[Transaction]) -> int:
    return sum(transaction.amount_pence for transaction in transactions)
~~~

This module intentionally knows the public <code>Transaction.amount_pence</code> interface. It need not know which file format produced transactions, which database stores them, or how the total is displayed. Those absences are reductions in coupling.

Coupling has several dimensions:

- **name coupling:** imported symbol and module paths;
- **representation coupling:** assumptions about private fields or concrete containers;
- **control coupling:** flags telling another component which internal branch to take;
- **temporal coupling:** operations required in a particular unstated order;
- **failure coupling:** dependence on exception types and partial effects;
- **deployment coupling:** components that must be released or configured together;
- **authority coupling:** access to resources or credentials broader than the task requires.

Counting imports detects only part of this structure.

### 10.1.4 Information hiding stabilises change

**Information hiding** means that a component publishes the smallest stable knowledge callers need while retaining freedom to change implementation decisions. A package can re-export <code>Transaction</code> from a public façade, allowing the source file that defines it to move without changing client imports.

Information hiding does not mean hiding all implementation source from inspection. Python code and objects are highly introspectable. It means declaring which facts are contractual and which are not supported dependencies. Leading underscores, documentation, re-export modules, protocols, and tests all communicate that boundary; none alone enforces it against determined access.

### 10.1.5 The dependency graph should reflect policy

Treat modules as nodes and imports as directed edges. If <code>reporting</code> imports <code>model</code>, draw <code>reporting → model</code>. A useful layered design directs volatile boundary concerns toward stable domain policy:

~~~text
command interface  ->  application coordination  ->  domain model
file adapter        ->  application coordination  ->  domain model
database adapter    ->  domain protocols
~~~

Arrows represent compile/load-time knowledge, not the direction data flows at runtime. A database adapter can send records “up” to an application while its source code depends “inward” on a domain-owned protocol.

A **dependency inversion** places an interface near the higher-level policy that needs it, then makes lower-level adapters implement that interface. Higher policy no longer imports one concrete database. This is the module-level form of dependency injection from Chapter 9.

### 10.1.6 Import graph and call graph differ

An **import graph** records which modules require names from which others during loading. A **call graph** records possible runtime calls among functions or methods. They need not point the same way.

~~~python
# policy.py
from typing import Protocol


class Writer(Protocol):
    def write(self, text: str) -> None: ...


def publish(writer: Writer, text: str) -> None:
    writer.write(text)
~~~

~~~python
# file_adapter.py
from .policy import Writer


class FileWriter:
    def write(self, text: str) -> None:
        # Filesystem boundary omitted here.
        pass
~~~

The adapter imports the policy protocol, so the import edge points from adapter to policy. At runtime, <code>policy.publish</code> calls a method on the injected adapter, so one call edge points from policy code to adapter behaviour. Dynamic dispatch inverts runtime control without reversing source dependency.

### 10.1.7 Stable and volatile modules

A stable module changes infrequently or has many dependants whose compatibility matters. A volatile module changes often because it represents user-interface decisions, vendor APIs, deployment configuration, or experimental policy. Directing many stable modules toward one volatile module amplifies change.

Stability is observed, not inferred from an attractive name such as <code>core</code>. Version history, ownership, interface breadth, and reasons for change provide evidence. A module with many incoming dependencies deserves a small, deliberate public surface and strong compatibility tests.

### 10.1.8 Granularity is an optimisation problem

Modules that are too large mix ownership and make independent testing or reuse difficult. Modules that are too small increase import edges, navigation cost, naming burden, and circular-dependency risk. Choose granularity so that:

- concepts that maintain one invariant remain near each other;
- code that changes together is usually reviewed together;
- public interfaces are smaller than implementation interiors;
- dependency direction remains legible;
- tests can exercise meaningful units without excessive mocking;
- names describe domain or architectural roles rather than accidental code shapes.

One-class-per-file is a convention from some ecosystems, not a Python design law. Related value classes and functions can form one cohesive module.

### 10.1.9 A public façade can decouple layout from API

Suppose version 1 defines <code>Transaction</code> in <code>ledger.model</code>. Callers that import its physical location are coupled to that layout. The package can instead publish:

~~~python
# ledger/__init__.py
from .model import Transaction

__all__ = ["Transaction"]
~~~

Clients use <code>from ledger import Transaction</code>. A later version can move implementation to <code>ledger.transactions</code> while preserving the façade import. The façade does not remove semantic compatibility obligations; it separates a public name from one internal file boundary.

Avoid re-exporting every internal name. A façade that mirrors the whole package exposes layout indirectly and creates import-time cycles or expense. Publish a curated interface.

### 10.1.10 The <code>src</code> layout tests installation assumptions

In a flat project layout, the repository root may contain the import package directly. Running tests from that root can import the working directory even if packaging configuration would omit files or use a different mapping. A <code>src</code> layout places import packages below a directory such as <code>src/</code>; normal development then uses an installation, commonly editable, to make them importable.

This layout helps reveal missing installation configuration. It does not itself prove the built wheel is correct and does not prevent tests from manipulating <code>sys.path</code>. Clean-wheel verification remains necessary.

### 10.1.11 Module state has process lifetime by default

Once imported ordinarily, a module object is retained in <code>sys.modules</code> and its namespace persists. Module-level caches, registries, locks, and clients thereby become shared process-lifetime state unless explicitly reset or replaced.

~~~python
# counters.py
count = 0


def next_count() -> int:
    global count
    count += 1
    return count
~~~

Every importer using the same cached <code>counters</code> module observes the same binding. That may be the intended owner of a monotonic process counter, but tests, subinterpreters, process forks, reload, and concurrency need defined semantics. A module is a convenient singleton-like namespace, not a magically safe state container.

### 10.1.12 Boundary review questions

For every proposed module or package, answer:

1. What invariant or responsibility does it own?
2. Which names and behaviours are public?
3. Which modules may depend on it, and why?
4. Which external effects occur on import versus explicit calls?
5. Which state persists in the module object?
6. What is the lifecycle and concurrency policy for that state?
7. Which exceptions cross the boundary?
8. Can implementation move without breaking callers?
9. How is the boundary tested as a unit and through integration?
10. Does its import direction create a cycle?
11. Which distribution installs it, and under which import name?
12. What authority is granted merely by importing it?

> **Common misconception — “Modularity means splitting code into more files.”**  
> Useful modularity assigns coherent responsibility and controls dependencies. More files can increase coupling and obscure invariants.

> **Common misconception — “If a name begins with an underscore, callers cannot depend on it.”**  
> The underscore communicates non-public status. Compatibility depends on social and tooling discipline, not access prevention.

## 10.2 Import is execution with caching

The statement

```python
import ledger.model
```

does not textually paste another file into the current one. The import system conceptually:

1. resolves the requested name through finders and the package context;
2. obtains a module specification describing how it can be loaded;
3. creates a module object when needed;
4. places it in `sys.modules` early enough to manage recursive imports;
5. executes its top-level code in its module namespace;
6. returns or binds the appropriate module object;
7. reuses the cached module on later ordinary imports in the same process.

`sys.modules` is a mapping from loaded module names to module objects. It is a runtime cache and registry, not a list of installed distributions. Removing or mutating entries is advanced and can create multiple module objects or inconsistent references.

### Worked example 10.1 — Top-level effects happen once per ordinary process import

`observed.py`:

```python
print("executing observed")
value = 42
```

`main.py`:

```python
import observed
import observed

print(observed.value)
```

A fresh ordinary run prints `executing observed` once and then 42. The second import finds the cached module. This is not a language promise that code can never be re-executed: explicit reload, separate module names, separate processes, test machinery, and custom import hooks can change circumstances. Top-level code should nevertheless be designed as import-time execution.

Import-time network calls, file mutation, expensive computation, or process startup create hidden effects for every importer. Prefer definitions and small deterministic registration; place application actions behind functions and entry points.

### 10.2.1 Import has a name, context, and search machinery

An import request is not merely a path lookup. It contains a module name, possibly a package context for resolving relative dots, and for submodules a parent package search path. The import machinery uses registered **finders** to obtain a **module specification** and a **loader** to create and execute the module when necessary.

The public <code>importlib</code> package exposes much of this machinery. Ordinary code should use <code>import</code> statements for statically known dependencies and <code>importlib.import_module</code> for deliberately dynamic names:

~~~python
from importlib import import_module


module = import_module("ledger.reporting")
report = module.build_report
~~~

Dynamic import is still code execution. If the string comes from untrusted input, an allowlist must decide which modules may execute; validating only that the text resembles a dotted name is not an authority policy.

### 10.2.2 <code>sys.modules</code> defines ordinary module identity

The cache maps fully qualified import names to module objects:

~~~python
import sys
import ledger.model


assert sys.modules["ledger.model"] is ledger.model
~~~

Ordinary repeated import under the same name reuses this object. Existing references do not consult the cache again on every attribute access. Replacing <code>sys.modules["ledger.model"]</code> later does not transform the module object already held by <code>ledger.model</code> or other variables.

The cache key matters. If the same source is made importable under two different names, it can execute twice and produce distinct class objects, registries, and exception types. Objects created from the two nominally identical class definitions may fail <code>isinstance</code> checks against one another.

### 10.2.3 Early cache insertion breaks recursive creation, not cycles of knowledge

Before a loader executes a new module’s body, import machinery normally places its module object in <code>sys.modules</code>. If execution recursively requests the same name, it can receive that in-progress object instead of allocating another indefinitely.

This solves recursion of module *creation*. It does not guarantee that requested attributes have already been assigned. A circular importer can observe the module after its first five statements but before its sixth. The resulting object is real and cached, yet **partially initialised**.

### 10.2.4 Failed imports do not imply global rollback

When execution of a newly loading module fails, import machinery ordinarily removes the failing module’s cache entry. Side effects already performed are not generally undone, and modules successfully imported as consequences can remain cached.

Suppose <code>plugin.py</code> registers a callback, imports <code>support</code>, then raises. A second import may execute <code>plugin.py</code> again and register a duplicate callback, while reusing the already loaded <code>support</code>. Import is not a transaction spanning the process.

Robust import-time registration should validate before commit, be idempotent under explicit repeated execution when feasible, or provide rollback around fallible later steps. The simplest policy is to defer mutable registration to an explicit application assembly phase.

### Worked example 10.1A — Observe retained side effects after failure

<code>registry.py</code>:

~~~python
entries: list[str] = []
~~~

<code>broken_plugin.py</code>:

~~~python
import registry

registry.entries.append("attempt")
raise RuntimeError("definition failed")
~~~

<code>probe.py</code>:

~~~python
import registry

for _ in range(2):
    try:
        import broken_plugin
    except RuntimeError:
        pass

print(registry.entries)
~~~

In an ordinary environment, each failed attempt can append, producing two entries. The failing module is retried because its incomplete cache entry was removed; <code>registry</code> remains successfully cached with mutated state.

### 10.2.5 A module specification describes loading

A module’s <code>__spec__</code> ordinarily refers to a <code>ModuleSpec</code> describing facts such as its name, loader, origin, parent package relationship, and submodule search locations where applicable.

~~~python
import importlib.util


spec = importlib.util.find_spec("ledger.model")
if spec is None:
    raise RuntimeError("ledger.model cannot be found")

print(spec.name)
print(spec.loader)
print(spec.origin)
~~~

Finding a specification can import the parent package for a submodule and can therefore cause effects. An origin may be <code>None</code> or a non-filesystem description for namespace, built-in, frozen, or custom-loaded modules. Do not assume every module has a meaningful <code>__file__</code>.

### 10.2.6 Meta-path finders and path-based discovery

Python consults finder objects in <code>sys.meta_path</code>. Built-in machinery can recognise built-in modules, frozen modules, and modules found through import paths. For path-based imports, path hooks and importer caches translate entries such as directories or archives into finders.

A finder answers “can I supply a specification for this fully qualified name in this context?” A loader answers “how is the module object created and executed?” Modern loader protocols commonly expose <code>create_module</code> and <code>exec_module</code>. The import system coordinates cache insertion and metadata.

Custom finders can load code from databases, encrypted stores, generated sources, or remote systems. Doing so broadens the trusted computing base and complicates debugging, caching, reproducibility, and audit. Most applications should not replace ordinary file/package loading.

### 10.2.7 <code>sys.path</code> is search configuration, not a dependency manifest

For top-level path-based imports, <code>sys.path</code> contains search entries assembled from launch context, interpreter installation, environment configuration, virtual environment, and site customisation. Exact entries depend on platform and invocation.

~~~python
import sys


for entry in sys.path:
    print(repr(entry))
~~~

The first matching candidate can determine what executes. This makes writable early entries security-sensitive and explains local shadowing. <code>sys.path</code> does not record which distribution declared a dependency, which version should be installed, or why an entry is trusted.

Editing it within library modules is usually an architectural defect. It makes import meaning depend on execution order and current filesystem layout. Configure installation, invocation, or a controlled application entry point instead.

### 10.2.8 Parent packages are loaded before submodules

Importing <code>ledger.model</code> requires a <code>ledger</code> package context. The parent package is imported first if necessary. Its <code>__init__.py</code>, for an ordinary package, therefore executes before the child module.

After the child loads, import machinery ordinarily binds it as an attribute of its parent package, so <code>ledger.model</code> refers to the submodule. Package <code>__init__.py</code> can also define or replace names, which makes overly elaborate initialisation a source of ambiguity and cycles.

### 10.2.9 Import locking coordinates concurrent attempts

Multiple threads can attempt imports concurrently. The import implementation coordinates module loading so one name is not ordinarily executed simultaneously as two independent initialisations in the same interpreter. This does not make arbitrary module body effects thread-safe, nor does it make imports across processes share state.

A module can release control, import other modules, start threads, or expose itself through external registries while only partly initialised. Do not use the existence of import locks as a substitute for lifecycle design.

### 10.2.10 Bytecode caches are an optimisation layer

For eligible source modules, Python may cache compiled bytecode in <code>__pycache__</code> files. A later process can avoid reparsing and recompiling unchanged source under applicable invalidation rules. The module body still executes to create runtime bindings.

Deleting bytecode caches should not change correct program semantics. A stale or unwritable cache can affect startup performance or diagnostics, but reinstalling dependencies because a module prints twice misunderstands the execution/cache distinction.

Bytecode is Python-version and implementation qualified, not a portable long-term source substitute. Chapter 15 examines bytecode itself.

### 10.2.11 Reload re-executes into an existing module context

<code>importlib.reload(module)</code> recompiles/re-executes a module using its specification while retaining the module object and generally its namespace dictionary. Names rebound by new code change; old names not overwritten may remain. External references bound earlier remain external references.

~~~python
from importlib import reload

import settings
from settings import Configuration


old_class = Configuration
reload(settings)
new_class = settings.Configuration

print(old_class is new_class)
~~~

If execution creates a new class, <code>old_class</code> and instances already made from it remain related to the old class object. Existing <code>from settings import Configuration</code> bindings are not automatically rebound. Registries may contain both generations; extension modules may not support meaningful repeated initialisation.

Reload is useful in controlled interactive development, not a general deployment update protocol. Application hot-reload needs explicit state migration and compatibility boundaries.

### 10.2.12 Import-time type-only dependencies

Annotations can create import cycles even when runtime computation does not need the imported class. Deferred annotations and <code>typing.TYPE_CHECKING</code> can separate static-only imports:

~~~python
from __future__ import annotations

from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from .model import Transaction


def describe(transaction: Transaction) -> str:
    return str(transaction)
~~~

Static checkers treat the guarded import as available; at runtime <code>TYPE_CHECKING</code> is false. This is appropriate only because the function body does not require the class object. Runtime introspection of annotations may need explicit resolution and imports, and hiding a genuine architectural cycle behind the guard is not a repair.

### 10.2.13 Import cost belongs to startup architecture

Every imported module consumes discovery, possible bytecode validation/compilation, body execution, and retained objects. A command that imports a large optional stack before parsing <code>--help</code> can have poor startup latency. Measure import profiles and move optional heavy dependencies behind the operation that needs them when doing so preserves clear failures and contracts.

Lazy import introduces its own complexity: failures occur later, first-use latency moves into an operation, thread races and partial setup need policy, and static tools see less direct dependency structure. Optimise measured startup paths rather than distributing imports unpredictably through function bodies.

### 10.2.14 Import invariants

A well-behaved library module should ordinarily satisfy:

- import either completes with a coherent public namespace or raises a meaningful exception;
- importing does not launch the application;
- import does not require unrelated network availability or mutable current-directory state;
- repeated ordinary import through the canonical name reuses compatible module state;
- public objects do not depend on a second alias import of the same source;
- optional dependencies fail at the capability boundary with actionable diagnostics;
- imports do not mutate unrelated global state without an explicit registry contract;
- import ordering among independent modules does not change semantics.

> **Common misconception — “Importing twice executes twice unless guarded.”**  
> The import cache normally prevents re-execution under the same canonical name within one interpreter. Guards inside a module do not create that cache behaviour.

> **Common misconception — “A failed import leaves no trace.”**  
> The failing cache entry is normally removed, but completed side effects and successfully imported dependencies can remain.

## 10.3 Import statement forms and bindings

```python
import ledger.model
```

binds name `ledger` in the importing namespace; `ledger.model` becomes accessible as an attribute after successful import.

```python
from ledger import model
```

binds local name `model` to the resolved object.

```python
from ledger.model import Transaction
```

binds local name `Transaction` to the object found under that attribute at import time. Later rebinding of `ledger.model.Transaction` does not automatically rebind the importing module’s local name.

Aliases change local spelling:

```python
import ledger.reporting as reporting
```

They do not rename the actual module in the import registry.

Wildcard import, `from module import *`, imports names selected by the module’s `__all__` or by fallback rules. It obscures name origin, can overwrite bindings, and makes static reasoning difficult. It is primarily suitable for carefully designed interactive or package-export contexts, not ordinary internal dependencies.

### Worked example 10.2 — Imported binding versus module lookup

`settings.py`:

```python
rate = 2
```

`consumer.py`:

```python
import settings
from settings import rate

settings.rate = 3
print(settings.rate)
print(rate)
```

Output is 3 then 2. The `from` import bound local `rate` to the earlier integer object. Assignment later changed the attribute binding in the module namespace; it did not reach into every importing namespace.

### 10.3.1 Import both loads and binds

An import statement has two distinguishable effects:

1. ensure the requested module objects are found and loaded under import-system rules;
2. bind one or more names in the namespace where the statement executes.

Caching concerns the first effect. Scope and alias syntax govern the second. Repeating an import inside a function can reuse the cached module while performing a local binding on every call.

~~~python
def calculate() -> float:
    import math
    return math.sqrt(81.0)
~~~

Here <code>math</code> is a local name because the import statement binds inside the function. The module is not re-executed on every call under normal caching, but the local binding operation still occurs.

### 10.3.2 Dotted import without alias binds the top-level name

After:

~~~python
import ledger.reporting
~~~

the local binding is ordinarily <code>ledger</code>, not <code>reporting</code>. Successful loading makes the child available through the package, so the caller writes <code>ledger.reporting</code>. By contrast:

~~~python
import ledger.reporting as reporting
~~~

binds local <code>reporting</code> directly to the submodule object. The alias changes only the importing namespace; <code>reporting.__name__</code> remains its canonical module name.

### 10.3.3 From-import binds a snapshot reference, not a live path

At import time:

~~~python
from settings import rate
~~~

Python obtains the object currently exposed as <code>settings.rate</code> and binds that object locally as <code>rate</code>. If the source module later rebinds its attribute, the two namespaces diverge. If the object itself is mutable and either side mutates it, both references can still observe the same object.

~~~python
# settings.py
options = ["safe"]
~~~

~~~python
import settings
from settings import options

options.append("verbose")
assert settings.options == ["safe", "verbose"]

settings.options = []
assert options == ["safe", "verbose"]
~~~

Mutation follows object identity; rebinding changes one namespace edge. Import introduces no special sharing model beyond the reference semantics of Chapter 5.

### 10.3.4 Import location determines monkeypatch location

Suppose <code>service.py</code> contains:

~~~python
from clock import now


def timestamp() -> float:
    return now()
~~~

Replacing <code>clock.now</code> after <code>service</code> imported it does not replace <code>service.now</code>. A test must patch the name looked up by the code under test: <code>service.now</code>. If <code>service</code> instead used <code>import clock</code> and called <code>clock.now()</code>, patching <code>clock.now</code> would affect that lookup.

This is not a testing-library peculiarity. It follows directly from which namespace contains the binding evaluated at call time. Dependency injection can avoid global patching and make the collaborator explicit.

### 10.3.5 Imports obey ordinary scope rules

An import at module top level creates a global binding in that module. An import inside a function creates a local binding unless declared otherwise. A conditional branch may leave the name unbound on paths where it did not execute.

~~~python
def formatter(use_json: bool):
    if use_json:
        import json
    return json.dumps({"ready": True})
~~~

Calling with false raises because local <code>json</code> was never bound. Static unconditional imports at module top usually make dependencies and failures clearest. Local or conditional imports are justified for optional capabilities, cycle management with explicit rationale, or measured startup cost—not as arbitrary style.

### 10.3.6 Catch optional-dependency failure narrowly

This broad pattern is defective:

~~~python
try:
    import optional_backend
except Exception:
    optional_backend = None
~~~

It treats syntax errors, runtime defects, transitive dependency failures, and even some interruption-like conditions as “not installed.” A narrower approach catches the import failure whose absence is actually optional and checks its identity where necessary:

~~~python
try:
    import optional_backend
except ModuleNotFoundError as error:
    if error.name != "optional_backend":
        raise
    optional_backend = None
~~~

If <code>optional_backend</code> exists but its body imports a missing <code>backend_dependency</code>, <code>error.name</code> differs and the real broken installation propagates. Even this logic should be placed near an explicit capability boundary with an actionable message.

### 10.3.7 <code>ImportError</code> and <code>ModuleNotFoundError</code>

<code>ModuleNotFoundError</code> is a subclass of <code>ImportError</code> used when a module cannot be found, including certain <code>None</code> cache cases. <code>ImportError</code> can also report failure to import a requested name from an existing module.

Do not assume every <code>ImportError</code> means “install a package.” Causes include a misspelled import name, incompatible version, circular initialisation, local shadowing, platform-specific extension load failure, or a source module explicitly raising the exception. Diagnose the resolved origin and traceback.

### 10.3.8 Aliases should reduce ambiguity without erasing provenance

Conventional aliases such as a well-known short library name can improve readability in domains where their meaning is established. An alias like <code>x</code> for an infrastructure module hides provenance. Renaming two different <code>config</code> modules as <code>application_config</code> and <code>database_config</code> can clarify ownership.

Avoid aliases that make a module look like a class or function, or that shadow built-ins and local domain names. Import readability is part of dependency documentation.

### 10.3.9 Importing a symbol couples to its defining interface

<code>from package import Name</code> may retrieve a re-export from the package façade, not necessarily a definition physically written in <code>package/__init__.py</code>. The supported import path is whichever path the package documents. Importing deeper internal paths because they reveal implementation can forfeit compatibility.

Conversely, a package’s convenient top-level API can import a large dependency graph. Internal performance-sensitive code may choose a documented submodule path when the project explicitly supports it. Publicness and cost are contractual facts, not deduced solely from path depth.

### 10.3.10 Wildcard import performs a runtime selection

For <code>from module import *</code>, the source module’s <code>__all__</code>, when present, supplies names to retrieve. Without it, fallback selection generally excludes names beginning with an underscore. The operation binds into the receiving namespace and can replace existing names.

~~~python
# palette.py
__all__ = ["RED", "BLUE"]

RED = "#ff0000"
BLUE = "#0000ff"
_CACHE = {}
~~~

<code>__all__</code> is a sequence of strings naming exports; it does not hold the exported objects themselves. Listing an absent name causes import failure when retrieval is attempted. It does not prevent explicit access to unlisted attributes.

Wildcard import is prohibited inside function scope by the language and is difficult for static readers because bindings depend on another module’s runtime state. A curated interactive namespace or package façade is its main defensible use.

### 10.3.11 Importing from a package can seek a submodule

In <code>from ledger import reporting</code>, import machinery can attempt to find the <code>ledger.reporting</code> submodule if the attribute is not already supplied in the expected way. This makes package imports more than a simple dictionary lookup. Package initialisation and submodule loading can interact, especially during cycles.

Do not rely on accidental prior imports to populate package attributes. Explicitly import and re-export supported submodules or symbols in the package API where that is the contract.

### 10.3.12 Dynamic names move errors from analysis to runtime

~~~python
from importlib import import_module


def load_codec(name: str):
    module = import_module(f"codecs_{name}")
    return module.Codec()
~~~

This design conceals the allowed set, dependencies, and required interface. A safer plugin loader maps validated identifiers to known entry points or obtains installed entry-point metadata, then validates the loaded object’s contract. Dynamic import should be an intentional extensibility boundary with error isolation and authority review.

### 10.3.13 Prefer module qualification when provenance matters

Compare:

~~~python
from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_EVEN
~~~

with:

~~~python
import decimal

amount = decimal.Decimal("1.25")
~~~

Direct symbol imports can be concise; qualified module access makes origin and patch location explicit. There is no universal rule. Frequently used domain types may deserve direct import, while operations with common names such as <code>open</code>, <code>parse</code>, or <code>load</code> often benefit from qualification.

> **Common misconception — “From-import copies a value.”**  
> It binds another reference to the current object. Later object mutation can be shared; later source-module rebinding is not propagated.

> **Common misconception — “An import inside a function reloads the module every call.”**  
> It normally reuses the cached module and creates a local binding. Deferred failure and hidden dependency remain design concerns.

## 10.4 Absolute and relative imports

An **absolute import** names a module from the import-system root:

```python
from ledger.model import Transaction
```

An **explicit relative import** uses leading dots from the current package:

```python
from .model import Transaction
from ..shared import Clock
```

One dot means the current package; additional dots move through parent packages under the import rules. Relative imports require a recognised package context. Running an internal module file directly can deprive it of that context, producing the familiar “attempted relative import with no known parent package” failure.

Launch package code through its package entry point:

```text
python -m ledger
```

rather than:

```text
python src/ledger/__main__.py
```

The `-m` route asks the import system to locate the module and establishes package metadata consistently.

Absolute imports make cross-package origin explicit. Relative imports can make internal refactoring and package cohesion clear. Choose a project policy and do not manipulate `sys.path` inside modules to conceal a broken installation or launch model.

### 10.4.1 “Absolute” is relative to configured import roots

An absolute name begins with a top-level module name rather than a filesystem root. <code>ledger.model</code> is resolved by import finders over configured locations, built-ins, archives, or custom sources. It does not necessarily mean <code>/ledger/model.py</code>, and a leading operating-system slash is not valid Python module syntax.

The same absolute name can resolve to different code in different virtual environments or launch configurations. Reproducibility therefore requires controlled distributions and search paths, not merely absolute import spelling.

### 10.4.2 Relative dots use package identity

Within <code>ledger.reporting.summary</code>:

- <code>from . import formatters</code> refers from current package <code>ledger.reporting</code>;
- <code>from .formatters import render</code> refers to a sibling submodule or exported attribute;
- <code>from ..model import Transaction</code> moves to parent package <code>ledger</code>;
- <code>from ...shared import Clock</code> attempts another parent level.

The first dot means “current package,” and each additional dot moves one level upward. A request beyond the top-level package fails. Relative syntax is supported in the <code>from</code> form; <code>import .model</code> is not the corresponding grammar.

### 10.4.3 <code>__package__</code> supplies relative context

Relative resolution uses package metadata, ordinarily based on <code>__package__</code> and the module specification. An imported module <code>ledger.reporting</code> has a recognised package parent. A source file launched directly as a bare script commonly has <code>__name__ == "__main__"</code> and no suitable package context, even if it physically resides inside a directory containing <code>__init__.py</code>.

Filesystem containment alone does not assign runtime package identity. The import system must load or execute the module under that identity.

### Worked example 10.2A — One file, two execution identities

Suppose <code>ledger/probe.py</code> contains:

~~~python
print(__name__)
print(__package__)
print(__spec__)
~~~

Direct invocation:

~~~text
python ledger/probe.py
~~~

typically executes it as top-level <code>__main__</code> with no package specification. Module invocation from the project’s configured import root:

~~~text
python -m ledger.probe
~~~

still uses <code>__name__ == "__main__"</code> for entry execution but supplies package/specification context identifying <code>ledger</code> as the parent. Exact displayed object representations vary, but the relative-import capability difference is contractual.

### 10.4.4 Entry execution can create a second module identity

Code run as <code>__main__</code> is stored under that name. If it or another module subsequently imports its canonical name, the same source may execute again as a distinct module object.

For example, directly executing a module that defines <code>class Token</code>, then importing that file canonically, can produce <code>__main__.Token</code> and <code>package.module.Token</code> as distinct classes. Instances fail identity-based nominal relationships across them.

Keep substantial definitions in canonically importable modules and make entry modules thin coordinators. Then <code>__main__</code> imports the canonical implementation rather than other modules importing definitions from <code>__main__</code>.

### 10.4.5 <code>-m</code> locates before executing

The <code>-m</code> command-line option asks Python to locate a module through the import system and execute its code as the top-level environment. For a package name, Python executes its <code>__main__</code> submodule. This preserves package context and tests that the module is discoverable through configured import roots.

It does not imply the distribution is installed globally; the current environment and search path still govern discovery. Nor does it make relative filesystem data paths safe. A module should use package-resource APIs for packaged data and explicit user paths for external data.

### 10.4.6 Absolute and relative imports encode different stability assumptions

An absolute internal import:

~~~python
from ledger.model import Transaction
~~~

asserts that the package’s top-level public identity is <code>ledger</code>. A relative import:

~~~python
from .model import Transaction
~~~

asserts a sibling relationship within the current package. If the whole package is vendored or renamed, relative internal edges may require fewer edits. If code moves to another subpackage level, dot depth changes.

For imports crossing architectural package boundaries, absolute names usually reveal provenance. For tightly cohesive internal siblings, explicit relative imports can make locality evident. Consistency matters because a mixture can make the same dependency appear to be two concepts.

### 10.4.7 Relative imports do not prevent cycles

Changing <code>from ledger import model</code> to <code>from . import model</code> changes resolution spelling, not dependency direction. If <code>model</code> imports the caller during top-level execution, the cycle remains. Resolve circular ownership structurally.

### 10.4.8 Running an internal file directly is not a package test

Developers sometimes insert the parent directory into <code>sys.path</code> so <code>python package/internal.py</code> works. This creates a launch mode different from installed use and can import sibling files as top-level modules under wrong names.

Use one of these patterns instead:

- execute a supported package or module entry with <code>python -m ...</code>;
- install the distribution into the active environment;
- expose a declared console-script entry point;
- keep standalone maintenance scripts outside the import package and make them import its public API.

### 10.4.9 Test runners can disguise package mistakes

A test runner may add the repository root to <code>sys.path</code>, import tests as packages, or use an editable installation. A test can pass while a built wheel omits the package or resolves different modules. Record <code>module.__file__</code> during diagnosis and run clean-wheel tests outside the repository.

Do not make tests rely on ambiguous relative imports between test files. Shared fixtures and helpers should have an explicit package/module structure or be provided through the testing framework’s supported discovery model.

### 10.4.10 Refactoring safely across package boundaries

When moving a public object:

1. choose and document the canonical public import path;
2. preserve a compatibility re-export at the old supported path for a deprecation window;
3. update internal imports toward the canonical path without creating a façade cycle;
4. test object identity across old and new imports;
5. ensure pickled or dynamically referenced qualified names have an evolution plan;
6. test type-checker stubs and documentation references;
7. remove the old path only under the versioning policy.

Simply copying the class definition to a new module creates two class identities. Re-export the same class object during migration.

### 10.4.11 Diagnosing a resolution surprise

Collect:

~~~python
import importlib.util
import sys


name = "ledger.model"
spec = importlib.util.find_spec(name)
print("spec:", spec)
print("cached:", sys.modules.get(name))

if name in sys.modules:
    module = sys.modules[name]
    print("file:", getattr(module, "__file__", None))
    print("package:", getattr(module, "__package__", None))
    print("loader:", getattr(module, "__loader__", None))
~~~

Perform this within the actual failing environment and invocation. A shell, notebook kernel, test worker, IDE, and deployed service may use different interpreters and search paths.

> **Common misconception — “A directory with <code>__init__.py</code> makes every direct file execution package-aware.”**  
> Package identity comes from how the import system loads or executes the module, not only its physical location.

> **Common misconception — “Absolute imports always select the project’s own package.”**  
> They select the first matching module under the active import machinery. Environment control and origin inspection establish which code was found.

## 10.5 `__name__` and entry execution

Every module has a `__name__` attribute. When imported normally, it contains the module’s import name. Code selected as the top-level entry environment receives `__name__ == "__main__"`.

```python
def main() -> int:
    print("application runs")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())
```

This guard distinguishes definition/import from application execution. Importing the module creates `main` but does not call it through the guarded path. Executing the file as the entry script calls `main` and turns its integer result into process status.

The idiom is not a security boundary and does not prevent all import effects. Every statement outside the guarded suite still executes on import. Nor does it make the module automatically distributable; packaging metadata and installation remain separate.

`__main__.py` gives a package or archive an executable module. `python -m ledger` locates and executes `ledger.__main__` as the entry module while the package remains importable.

### 10.5.1 <code>__main__</code> names the top-level execution environment

Python assigns <code>__name__ == "__main__"</code> to the top-level code environment, including code launched from a file, with <code>-m</code>, with <code>-c</code>, from standard input, or interactively. It does not mean that the file is literally named <code>__main__.py</code>.

The active top-level module is ordinarily available as <code>sys.modules["__main__"]</code>. Importing a module whose canonical name is <code>application.main</code> is a separate operation and normally sets that module’s <code>__name__</code> to <code>application.main</code>.

### 10.5.2 The guard tests execution role

~~~python
if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())
~~~

The condition asks whether this module currently occupies the top-level execution role. It does not ask whether the file was “opened by a user,” whether a function is called main, or whether the code is safe to execute.

Everything needed merely to define <code>main</code> remains outside the guard and runs on import. Keep that definition phase free of application-start effects.

### 10.5.3 Return values become process status through <code>SystemExit</code>

Operating systems expose a small integer-like **exit status** from a process. By convention, zero denotes success and nonzero denotes a class of failure. <code>raise SystemExit(status)</code> asks Python to terminate normally with the supplied status after ordinary cleanup paths.

~~~python
def main() -> int:
    try:
        run_application()
    except ConfigurationError as error:
        print(f"configuration error: {error}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    return 0
~~~

Passing a non-integer object such as a string to <code>SystemExit</code> can print it and produce a failure status under interpreter rules; returning explicit integers is clearer for command contracts. A Boolean is an integer subtype but obscures status meaning.

Do not call <code>sys.exit</code> deep inside reusable domain logic. It raises <code>SystemExit</code>, crossing normal application boundaries and making the code difficult to compose. Raise a domain exception or return a result; translate to status at the entry point.

### 10.5.4 Separate argument parsing, coordination, and computation

A testable command architecture has layers:

~~~python
from collections.abc import Sequence


def calculate_total(values: Sequence[int]) -> int:
    return sum(values)


def run(arguments: Sequence[str]) -> int:
    try:
        values = [int(argument) for argument in arguments]
    except ValueError as error:
        print(f"invalid integer: {error}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2

    print(calculate_total(values))
    return 0


def main() -> int:
    return run(sys.argv[1:])
~~~

<code>calculate_total</code> is pure. <code>run</code> accepts explicit arguments and owns textual boundary translation. <code>main</code> adapts process-global <code>sys.argv</code>. Tests can call <code>run(["2", "3"])</code> while capturing streams, or move streams into explicit parameters for still narrower effects.

### 10.5.5 Standard output and standard error have different contracts

Commands commonly write ordinary machine- or user-consumable results to standard output and diagnostics to standard error. This permits shell pipelines to consume valid output without mixing error text.

The distinction should be tested. A command returning status zero while printing a traceback to output violates likely automation expectations even if a human can read it. Command-line interface stability includes status codes, stream selection, encodings, line formats, and partial-output policy.

### 10.5.6 <code>__main__.py</code> is a package adapter

A thin package entry module can import canonical application code:

~~~python
# ledger/__main__.py
from .cli import main


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())
~~~

<code>python -m ledger</code> locates <code>ledger</code>, initialises the package, then executes this submodule as top-level code. Keeping implementation in <code>ledger.cli</code> avoids other modules importing definitions from <code>__main__</code> and acquiring a second execution identity.

### 10.5.7 Installed console scripts are metadata-driven adapters

A project can declare:

~~~toml
[project.scripts]
careful-ledger = "ledger.cli:main"
~~~

Installation tooling creates an environment-appropriate command wrapper. Invoking <code>careful-ledger</code> imports <code>ledger.cli</code>, retrieves <code>main</code>, calls it, and translates the result according to the generated entry-point convention.

The wrapper is generated at installation; merely adding metadata does not create a command in an environment until installed. Renaming or removing the target callable without rebuilding/reinstalling leaves a broken wrapper.

Console-script and <code>python -m ledger</code> entry paths should normally call the same implementation so they do not drift in status, arguments, or effects.

### 10.5.8 Import-safe does not mean side-effect-free

A module may legitimately create immutable constants, compile regular expressions, define classes, or register a small declared adapter during import. “Import-safe” means those effects satisfy an explicit, deterministic loading contract and do not unexpectedly launch work, prompt for input, alter user files, or require external service availability.

There is no absolute ban on computation. The relevant questions are cost, failure mode, authority, repeatability, and whether every importer consented to the effect.

### 10.5.9 The guard is required for some process-spawning patterns

Forward reference: Chapter 14 formally introduces multiprocessing, in which work runs in separate operating-system processes. Under start methods that import the entry module in a child process, unguarded top-level process creation can recursively create more processes. Placing application launch under the <code>__main__</code> guard prevents imported child setup from relaunching the parent entry path.

This does not mean every function needed by child processes belongs inside the guard. Importable worker functions should remain at module scope; only initiating calls belong behind the execution-role boundary.
