### 10.5.10 <code>runpy</code> executes modules under controlled naming

The standard <code>runpy</code> module underlies related execution use cases and can run a module or path while establishing a special globals dictionary. It is not an isolation mechanism: code executes in the current process and can mutate shared state. Thread-safety and alterations to <code>sys</code> state need attention under its documented options.

For ordinary applications, subprocess execution supplies a clearer process boundary. <code>runpy</code> is useful for tooling that intentionally reproduces Python’s script/module execution semantics.

### 10.5.11 Entry-point error policy

An entry point should classify failures:

- anticipated user/input errors: concise diagnostic and stable nonzero status;
- unavailable optional capability: actionable installation/configuration message;
- interrupted operation: cleanup and a status consistent with platform policy;
- internal defect: nonzero status and diagnostic evidence, possibly a traceback under debug configuration;
- partial external write: explicit warning and recovery instructions.

Do not catch <code>BaseException</code> and report success. <code>KeyboardInterrupt</code>, <code>SystemExit</code>, and process-control conditions have specialised meanings. Catch only failures the boundary can translate responsibly.

### 10.5.12 Entry-point tests

Test at three levels:

1. pure computation with ordinary unit tests;
2. coordinator function with explicit arguments and injected streams/dependencies;
3. installed command in a subprocess, asserting status, stdout, stderr, current-directory independence, and environment behaviour.

The subprocess test proves the generated wrapper or <code>-m</code> route, interpreter selection, import installation, and process-status integration. Directly calling <code>main()</code> cannot prove all of those.

> **Common misconception — “The name guard makes a file both library and application automatically.”**  
> It prevents one guarded launch path during import. Public API design, import-time effects, package context, and distribution entry points remain separate.

> **Common misconception — “Returning 1 from <code>main</code> exits with status 1.”**  
> A normal Python function return is just a value. The entry adapter must pass it to <code>SystemExit</code> or an equivalent wrapper.

## 10.6 Circular imports

A **circular import** occurs when modules depend on one another during import initialisation. Because a module is placed in `sys.modules` before its top-level execution completes, another module may observe it in a partially initialised state.

`a.py`:

```python
from b import value_b
value_a = "A"
```

`b.py`:

```python
from a import value_a
value_b = "B"
```

Importing `a` begins execution and immediately imports `b`. `b` imports `a`, but the cached `a` object has not yet executed `value_a = "A"`. Retrieval fails from the partially initialised module.

Moving imports inside functions can defer the cycle but may merely hide an architectural problem. Stronger repairs include:

- moving shared abstractions into a lower-level module;
- reversing a dependency through an injected interface;
- merging modules that are one responsibility;
- separating import-time registration from runtime collaboration;
- importing modules rather than early-bound attributes where appropriate.

A dependency graph should ordinarily be directed from higher policy towards lower stable mechanisms without cycles. Real plugin systems and mutual type references require deliberate patterns, but accidental circles indicate unclear ownership.

### 10.6.1 A cycle is both structural and temporal

In a directed import graph, a cycle exists when a path returns to its starting module. Graph theory calls a maximal mutually reachable group a **strongly connected component**. Every module in such a component depends, directly or indirectly, on every other for loading.

The runtime failure depends on timing. A cycle can appear to work if neither side retrieves a not-yet-bound name during initialisation, then fail after an innocent statement reorder. Structural cyclicity creates temporal coupling even when one current execution order succeeds.

### 10.6.2 From-import often demands the value too early

In the original <code>a.py</code>/<code>b.py</code> example, <code>from a import value_a</code> requires the attribute while <code>a</code> is incomplete. Replacing it with <code>import a</code> can defer attribute retrieval until a later function call:

~~~python
# b.py
import a


def describe() -> str:
    return a.value_a
~~~

If <code>describe</code> is not called until both imports complete, this variant may work. It has not removed the cycle; it has moved the temporal requirement. The graph remains harder to initialise, test, and refactor.

### 10.6.3 Error text identifies partial initialisation, not necessarily root ownership

Modern Python often reports that an attribute cannot be imported from a partially initialised module and suggests a circular import. The named line is where the temporal contradiction surfaced, not necessarily where architectural responsibility is misplaced.

Follow the full traceback and construct the import chain. Repeatedly moving the failing import downward can hide the symptom without clarifying which module should own the shared concept.

### 10.6.4 Package façades can create invisible cycles

Suppose <code>ledger/__init__.py</code> re-exports from <code>reporting</code>, while <code>reporting.py</code> writes <code>from ledger import Transaction</code>. Importing the package begins the façade, enters <code>reporting</code>, then asks the still-running façade for <code>Transaction</code>. A cycle exists even though no source line names <code>ledger.__init__</code> explicitly.

Internal modules should often import the lower-level defining module directly, while external callers use the public façade:

~~~python
# inside ledger/reporting.py
from .model import Transaction
~~~

This does not universally prohibit internal façade imports, but it prevents the root package initializer from becoming a hub through which every internal edge passes.

### 10.6.5 Extract a lower-level shared abstraction

Suppose <code>orders.py</code> imports <code>payments.py</code> to call a charger, while <code>payments.py</code> imports <code>Order</code> for type and state access. The responsibilities can be separated:

~~~text
orders.py   -> contracts.py
payments.py -> contracts.py
checkout.py -> orders.py
checkout.py -> payments.py
~~~

<code>contracts.py</code> can define value types and protocols needed by both. <code>checkout.py</code> coordinates an order and a payment adapter. The cycle becomes two inward edges plus one higher-level composition point.

Extraction is correct only if the new module is cohesive. A <code>common.py</code> dumping ground that every module imports creates a low-level dependency magnet and may eventually recreate cycles.

### Worked example 10.2B — Invert a concrete dependency

Defective <code>reporting.py</code>:

~~~python
from .database import Database


def build_report(database: Database) -> str:
    return str(database.load_rows())
~~~

If <code>database.py</code> imports report schemas from <code>reporting.py</code>, the modules cycle. Place the requirement with the policy:

~~~python
# reporting.py
from typing import Protocol


class RowSource(Protocol):
    def load_rows(self) -> list[tuple[str, int]]: ...


def build_report(source: RowSource) -> str:
    return "\n".join(f"{name}: {amount}" for name, amount in source.load_rows())
~~~

~~~python
# database.py
from .reporting import RowSource


class DatabaseRowSource:
    def load_rows(self) -> list[tuple[str, int]]:
        # Real database interaction omitted.
        return []
~~~

The adapter depends on the policy-owned protocol, while an application module imports both and injects the adapter. Runtime calls can flow from reporting to the adapter without reporting importing its concrete implementation.

### 10.6.6 Merge modules that are falsely separated

Sometimes a cycle indicates that two files are one abstraction. If nearly every change to <code>node.py</code> requires <code>edge.py</code>, both share private representation, and neither has independent clients, a single <code>graph.py</code> module may have higher cohesion and fewer false boundaries.

Splitting later remains possible when a genuine stable interface emerges. Maintaining two files solely to satisfy a small-file preference imposes dependency complexity without modular benefit.

### 10.6.7 Defer an import only when use is genuinely deferred

A local import can be correct for an optional backend or rarely invoked adapter:

~~~python
def export_pdf(report: Report) -> bytes:
    from .pdf_backend import render_pdf
    return render_pdf(report)
~~~

Now users who never request PDF need not load that backend. If this also avoids a cycle, document why the delayed dependency is semantically appropriate. If every call immediately needs both modules, local import is a tactical workaround that moves failure to runtime and should prompt architectural review.

### 10.6.8 Type annotations should not force a runtime cycle

Use deferred annotations and <code>TYPE_CHECKING</code> when only a static type relation crosses the edge, as §10.2.12 showed. Alternatively, define a protocol or shared value type in a lower module.

Do not quote annotations randomly without understanding runtime consumers. Frameworks may resolve annotations using module globals and need the referenced names importable when schemas are built. Test the actual reflection lifecycle.

### 10.6.9 Registration should not require mutual top-level imports

A plugin base importing every implementation while implementations import the base creates a classic cycle. Let an application discovery layer enumerate plugin modules or use distribution entry points. The base defines the contract without knowing implementations.

~~~text
plugin_contract.py <- plugin_text.py
plugin_contract.py <- plugin_json.py
application.py -> discovery metadata -> plugin modules
~~~

This also reverses authority: low-level contract code no longer decides which untrusted or optional plugin code to execute.

### 10.6.10 Diagnose with strongly connected components

For a large codebase:

1. extract module-level import edges with a static analysis tool;
2. distinguish runtime imports from type-check-only and platform-conditional edges;
3. compute strongly connected components;
4. inspect each component containing more than one node, or a self-loop;
5. classify shared abstraction, misplaced coordination, façade re-entry, registration, or genuine mutual recursion;
6. add architecture tests preventing forbidden layer edges from returning.

Static analysis can miss dynamic imports and over-report conditional ones. Runtime import traces show observed paths but miss unexecuted branches. Use both kinds of evidence.

### 10.6.11 Import order should not be a secret configuration

If <code>import a; import b</code> works while <code>import b; import a</code> fails, independent clients face a hidden ordering precondition. Tests should import public modules in fresh subprocesses and vary order. A package public surface should establish its own prerequisites or reject unsupported use clearly.

Notebook sessions can mask this defect because earlier cells have populated caches and globals. Reproduce in a fresh interpreter.

### 10.6.12 Cycles and module-level instances

Constructing service objects at module top level deepens cycles because construction may immediately request other module state. Move assembly to a composition root after all definitions are importable:

~~~python
def build_application() -> Application:
    repository = SqlRepository(...)
    reporter = Reporter(repository)
    return Application(reporter)
~~~

The function can still be called too early, but the lifecycle becomes explicit and test-controlled.

### 10.6.13 Deliberate mutual recursion belongs below the module boundary

Two algorithms can call one another recursively without residing in mutually importing modules. Place them in one cohesive module, pass callables explicitly, or extract a shared dispatcher. Runtime recursion is not a justification for load-time dependency recursion.

### 10.6.14 Cycle repair checklist

When a cycle appears, ask in order:

1. Is the edge only for an annotation? Remove its runtime requirement.
2. Is one import used only for a genuinely optional/late operation? Defer it at that boundary.
3. Do both modules depend on a smaller shared abstraction? Extract it downward.
4. Does higher-level coordination live in a lower module? Move it to an application layer.
5. Is a concrete dependency pointing from policy to infrastructure? Invert it through a policy-owned protocol.
6. Are two modules actually one cohesive responsibility? Merge them.
7. Is a package façade re-entering itself? Import internal defining modules directly.
8. Is automatic registration forcing discovery into the contract module? Externalise discovery.
9. If the cycle is intentional, what exact initialisation order and deferred lookup prove it safe under reload, tests, and concurrency?

> **Common misconception — “A cycle is repaired if moving one import inside a function stops the error.”**  
> The structural dependency remains. Deferral is correct only when the dependency’s semantic use is genuinely late or optional.

> **Common misconception — “Circular imports are forbidden by Python.”**  
> Python’s early module caching permits some cycles to complete. Their partial-initialisation and ordering contracts are fragile, so architecture should eliminate accidental ones.

## 10.7 Public APIs and `__all__`

A **public API** is the supported interface on which external callers may rely. In Python, names without a leading underscore are conventionally public unless documentation says otherwise; a leading underscore marks a non-public name by convention.

Package `__init__.py` can re-export a stable surface:

```python
from .model import Account, Transaction
from .parsing import parse_transaction

__all__ = ["Account", "Transaction", "parse_transaction"]
```

Callers can then use:

```python
from ledger import Account
```

instead of depending on internal file layout. The package may later move `Account` while preserving the re-export.

`__all__` controls wildcard export selection and documents intent for tools; it does not make other attributes inaccessible. API stability requires semantic compatibility: retaining a name while changing its exceptions, mutation, ordering, or timing can still break callers.

### Worked example 10.3 — Compatibility is behavioural

Version 1 contract:

```python
def lookup(identifier: str) -> Record | None:
    """Return a record, or None when absent."""
```

Version 2 retains the name but raises `KeyError` when absent. Source code still imports and calls, yet clients written to test `is None` now fail. The API break is semantic. Versioning must describe behaviour, not merely symbols.

### 10.7.1 Publicness is a support promise

A public API consists of names, call forms, types, behaviours, and evolution commitments that maintainers support for external callers. Accessibility is broader: Python callers can often reach underscore-prefixed names, module globals, implementation submodules, and class internals. Accessible does not mean stable.

The distinction allows implementation evolution. If every inspectable name were permanently public, refactoring would become impossible. Conversely, maintainers cannot erase a widely documented, deliberately exported function merely by later calling it internal.

### 10.7.2 API dimensions extend beyond signatures

For a public function, compatibility can include:

- import path and bound name;
- positional, keyword, variadic, and default argument acceptance;
- accepted value domain and coercions;
- return type, shape, identity, ownership, and mutability;
- exceptions and when they occur;
- external effects and their ordering;
- thread, process, and async safety;
- time and space complexity promises;
- determinism and ordering;
- resource lifetime;
- warning behaviour;
- subclass and override hooks;
- serialised or textual formats;
- security and authority assumptions.

Changing a return from list to generator may preserve iteration syntax while breaking repeatability, indexing, eager validation timing, resource closure, or truth testing. “The examples still run” is insufficient compatibility analysis.

### 10.7.3 Public façade versus implementation modules

A package façade can expose stable concepts while implementation remains distributed:

~~~python
# ledger/__init__.py
from ._model import Account as Account
from ._model import Transaction as Transaction
from ._parsing import parse_transaction as parse_transaction

__all__ = ["Account", "Transaction", "parse_transaction"]
~~~

The repeated <code>as</code> spelling can make an intentional re-export explicit to static tools. Underscore-prefixed implementation module names signal that callers should use the façade.

All internal modules importing through the façade can cause cycles. They should usually depend directly on lower internal definitions; external callers receive the façade. This creates asymmetric import policy by design.

### 10.7.4 <code>__all__</code> is export metadata with operational effects

When defined, <code>__all__</code> should contain strings naming attributes the module intends wildcard import to retrieve. Tools also read it as public-surface evidence.

~~~python
__all__ = [
    "Account",
    "Transaction",
    "parse_transaction",
]
~~~

It does not:

- prevent <code>from ledger import _internal</code>;
- remove other attributes from <code>dir</code> automatically;
- prove listed names satisfy documentation;
- recursively control submodule APIs;
- guarantee a name remains stable;
- hide imported implementation dependencies from memory.

Treat the list as one executable declaration backed by tests and documentation.

### 10.7.5 Re-export the same object during moves

Suppose <code>Record</code> moves from <code>ledger.model</code> to <code>ledger.records</code>. A compatibility module should import and bind the new class:

~~~python
# ledger/model.py during a compatibility period
from .records import Record as Record

__all__ = ["Record"]
~~~

Defining a subclass wrapper or copying source creates a different class identity, which can alter <code>isinstance</code>, equality policies, dataclass type checks, registries, pickling, and singledispatch registration. A re-export preserves identity:

~~~python
from ledger.model import Record as OldPathRecord
from ledger.records import Record as NewPathRecord

assert OldPathRecord is NewPathRecord
~~~

### 10.7.6 Signature compatibility is directional

Adding a new optional keyword-only parameter is often backward compatible for callers, while adding a required parameter is not. Renaming a parameter can break callers that used it by keyword even when positional calls still work. Making a formerly positional parameter keyword-only or the reverse changes accepted calls.

For methods designed to be overridden, compatibility is bidirectional across callers and subclasses. Adding a new argument that the base begins passing can break old overrides lacking it. Base-class evolution therefore requires an explicit extension protocol, not only caller-side signature review.

### 10.7.7 Broadening inputs can still break behaviour

Accepting more types appears monotonic, but it can alter overload selection, previously raised exceptions, ambiguity, and performance. If a function formerly rejected strings and a caller used <code>TypeError</code> to select another path, silently accepting strings changes control flow. Exception behaviour should not be used casually as feature detection, yet published behaviour can still have dependants.

Backward compatibility is an engineering judgement based on documented and reasonably relied-upon contracts, not a purely syntactic relation.

### 10.7.8 Deprecation is a staged protocol

A **deprecation** announces that a supported interface remains temporarily available but is scheduled for removal or change. A disciplined sequence is:

1. introduce the replacement and migration path;
2. document the old interface as deprecated with target policy/version where known;
3. emit an appropriate warning at the caller location;
4. retain compatibility for the stated interval;
5. test both old and new paths during that interval;
6. remove under a release boundary that permits the break;
7. document the removal and any automatic migration tooling.

Warnings must avoid secrets and excessive volume. The <code>stacklevel</code> should normally identify caller code rather than an internal compatibility wrapper.

### Worked example 10.3A — A module-level compatibility alias

Modern Python modules can define <code>__getattr__</code> for missing module attributes:

~~~python
# ledger/__init__.py
import warnings

from .records import Record

__all__ = ["Record"]


def __getattr__(name: str):
    if name == "Entry":
        warnings.warn(
            "ledger.Entry is deprecated; use ledger.Record",
            DeprecationWarning,
            stacklevel=2,
        )
        return Record
    raise AttributeError(name)
~~~

The fallback preserves an old attribute without listing it as a preferred wildcard export. Static type checkers may need a stub or explicit deprecated declaration to understand the alias. A direct top-level binding is simpler if warning-on-access is unnecessary.

### 10.7.9 Module <code>__dir__</code> can aid discovery

A module can define <code>__dir__</code> to customise names returned by <code>dir(module)</code>. This can advertise dynamic attributes, but it does not create them and does not establish public support by itself.

Dynamic module attributes complicate static analysis and documentation. Use them for narrow compatibility or lazy-loading boundaries with measured benefit, not to make an arbitrary dictionary look like a module API.

### 10.7.10 Lazy exports change failure timing

A package may defer importing an expensive optional submodule until a public attribute is requested through module <code>__getattr__</code>. This can reduce startup cost, but now:

- <code>import package</code> succeeds while <code>package.Feature</code> may fail later;
- first access bears latency and possible concurrency;
- type tools need separate declarations;
- <code>dir</code>, documentation, and pickling need coherent names;
- partial lazy-loading state needs rollback.

The optimisation should be backed by import-time measurements and tests across first use, failure, repeated use, and concurrent access.

### 10.7.11 Exceptions are public types

Callers catch exception classes by identity and hierarchy. Moving an exception while re-exporting the same class preserves catches; redefining a lookalike does not. Changing from <code>ValueError</code> to <code>KeyError</code>, wrapping without <code>raise ... from ...</code>, or expanding the set of routine failures can be an API change.

Publish a small exception hierarchy when callers need stable recovery categories. Do not expose every vendor exception from an implementation dependency unless binding callers to that vendor is intentional.

### 10.7.12 Mutability and ownership are API properties

If a function returns its internal list and version 2 returns a copy, callers that intentionally mutated shared state change behaviour. If version 1 returned a copy and version 2 returns the internal list, callers can now corrupt invariants. Both return annotations may remain <code>list[T]</code>.

Document whether results are borrowed live views, owned mutable values, immutable snapshots, iterators tied to resources, or cached shared objects.

### 10.7.13 Ordering can be contractual even without an annotation

A dictionary return type does not alone state iteration order semantics. If documentation promises insertion order, sorted order, or priority order, changing it can break deterministic output and caller selection. If order is explicitly unspecified, tests should avoid pinning one incidental implementation order.

### 10.7.14 Performance compatibility matters selectively

Changing a lookup from amortised constant time to linear time can break a caller processing millions of records even if values remain identical. Libraries need not promise exact timing, but may document complexity classes or suitable scale. Performance promises require representative benchmarks and account for worst-case/adversarial inputs where security matters.

### 10.7.15 Static typing surfaces and runtime surfaces can diverge

A package may ship <code>.pyi</code> stub files or a <code>py.typed</code> marker describing annotations. A symbol can exist at runtime but be absent from the supported typing surface, or vice versa because of a packaging defect. Test both runtime imports and static consumer examples.

Annotation changes can be breaking for statically checked clients even when runtime accepts the same calls. Overloads, generic variance, and protocol members form part of the type-level API.

### 10.7.16 Version discovery belongs to distribution metadata

A package may expose <code>__version__</code>, but the installed distribution’s authoritative version is recorded in metadata. <code>importlib.metadata.version("distribution-name")</code> queries that metadata when the mapping is known.

Hard-coding a second version string in source risks divergence. Build tools can derive both from one source or code can query metadata. Remember that distribution and import names may differ.

### 10.7.17 API contract tests

A public API test suite can assert:

- documented imports resolve to the intended identical objects;
- <code>__all__</code> names exist and match the support policy;
- signatures accept legacy call forms;
- return ownership, ordering, and repeatability remain stable;
- documented exception categories and causal chains hold;
- deprecations warn once or at the specified frequency and point to callers;
- pickled/serialised forms migrate or fail under an explicit policy;
- static consumer snippets type-check;
- clean installed artefacts expose the same API as source tests.

Snapshotting every <code>dir(package)</code> entry over-constrains implementation. Test the declared public surface and explicitly forbidden accidental exports.

### 10.7.18 API review table

For each proposed change, record:

| Dimension | Old contract | New contract | Existing caller effect | Migration |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| import path | | | | |
| accepted calls | | | | |
| value semantics | | | | |
| effects/lifetime | | | | |
| exceptions | | | | |
| typing | | | | |
| performance/order | | | | |
| security/authority | | | | |

An empty cell is a question, not evidence of no effect.

> **Common misconception — “Keeping the same function name preserves compatibility.”**  
> Call forms, values, effects, failures, ownership, ordering, typing, and complexity can break clients while the name remains.

> **Common misconception — “<code>__all__</code> makes unlisted names private.”**  
> It controls wildcard export selection and communicates intent. Explicit attribute access remains possible.

## 10.8 Module state and dependency injection

Module namespaces persist for the process lifetime under ordinary caching, which makes them convenient owners of immutable definitions and hazardous owners of mutable global state.

```python
cache: dict[str, object] = {}
```

This dictionary is shared by all importers of that module object. Tests can influence one another; concurrency requires coordination; state reset and memory growth require policy. If shared state is intentional, encapsulate it behind functions or an object and publish lifetime semantics.

**Dependency injection** supplies a collaborator from outside rather than having a component locate or construct it invisibly.

```python
from collections.abc import Callable


def generate_report(
    load: Callable[[], list[int]],
    write: Callable[[str], None],
) -> None:
    values = load()
    result = f"total={sum(values)}"
    write(result)
```

The function does not import a global database client or write a fixed path. Production and tests can supply different boundary implementations. Injection is not automatically superior for every constant or pure helper; it is valuable where variation, effects, or test control matter.

### 10.8.1 A module is one shared namespace per cached identity

Module globals are bindings in the module object’s dictionary. A function defined there resolves global names against that dictionary when called, subject to normal scope rules.

~~~python
# limits.py
threshold = 10


def accepts(value: int) -> bool:
    return value <= threshold
~~~

Rebinding <code>limits.threshold</code> changes what later <code>accepts</code> calls observe because the function performs a global lookup. A caller that used <code>from limits import threshold</code> holds a separate binding and does not control <code>accepts</code> by rebinding its local name.

### 10.8.2 <code>global</code> selects a namespace; it does not create process universality

Inside a function, <code>global name</code> means assignments target the defining module’s global namespace rather than a local. It does not mean one value shared across all modules, processes, interpreters, machines, or import aliases.

~~~python
count = 0


def increment() -> int:
    global count
    count += 1
    return count
~~~

Each process normally has its own memory and module cache. A second import identity can have another <code>count</code>. Threads share the module object but <code>count += 1</code> is not thereby a documented atomic transaction; Chapter 14 develops concurrency.

### 10.8.3 Constants are conventionally stable bindings

Uppercase spelling such as <code>SECONDS_PER_DAY = 86_400</code> communicates that callers should treat a binding as constant. Python does not generally enforce rebinding prohibition. Prefer immutable constant values and avoid deriving them from mutable environment state at unpredictable times.

A configuration value that changes between deployments is not necessarily a source constant. Parse it at an application boundary into a validated configuration object and inject that object.

### 10.8.4 Module-owned caches require a complete policy

~~~python
_cache: dict[str, bytes] = {}
~~~

Before adding this line, define:

- key and value semantics;
- maximum size and eviction;
- freshness and invalidation;
- negative-result caching;
- exception caching;
- thread/async/process coordination;
- memory ownership and weak references;
- reset for tests and configuration changes;
- observability and sensitive-data handling;
- behaviour across reload and fork.

An unbounded dictionary is a lifetime-long accumulation policy, even if the author did not intend one.

### 10.8.5 Import-time clients conflate loading with environment access

~~~python
# hazardous.py
client = DatabaseClient.from_environment()
~~~

Importing this module now reads environment configuration, may load credentials, and may establish resources before the caller selects an operation. Documentation tools, test collection, shell completion, and unrelated commands all inherit the requirement.

Prefer explicit assembly:

~~~python
def build_client(configuration: DatabaseConfiguration) -> DatabaseClient:
    return DatabaseClient(
        host=configuration.host,
        credentials=configuration.credentials,
    )
~~~

The composition root decides when to read configuration and how to close the client.

### 10.8.6 Parameter injection is the most local form

~~~python
from collections.abc import Callable
from datetime import datetime


def expired(
    deadline: datetime,
    *,
    now: Callable[[], datetime],
) -> bool:
    return now() >= deadline
~~~

The dependency is visible in the call signature and a test can supply a fixed clock. For a small number of collaborators, this is often clearer than building a class solely to store them.

Repeatedly threading many dependencies through many calls can signal that a cohesive service object or context value should own them. Do not hide them in globals merely to shorten signatures.

### 10.8.7 Constructor injection defines object capability

~~~python
from typing import Protocol


class TransactionSource(Protocol):
    def all(self) -> list[Transaction]: ...


class ReportService:
    def __init__(self, source: TransactionSource) -> None:
        self._source = source

    def total(self) -> int:
        return sum(item.amount_pence for item in self._source.all())
~~~

A <code>ReportService</code> can perform only operations exposed by its source reference and other reachable objects. Constructor injection makes the required capability part of valid construction. A setter-injected collaborator can leave the object temporarily unusable unless optionality or lifecycle is explicit.

### 10.8.8 Factory injection controls repeated construction

If each operation needs a fresh session, injecting one session object gives the wrong lifetime. Inject a factory or context-manager factory:

~~~python
from collections.abc import Callable
from contextlib import AbstractContextManager


SessionFactory = Callable[[], AbstractContextManager[Session]]


class ImportService:
    def __init__(self, sessions: SessionFactory) -> None:
        self._sessions = sessions

    def import_batch(self, batch: Batch) -> None:
        with self._sessions() as session:
            session.store(batch)
~~~

The factory dependency states that the service owns one scoped session per batch. Tests can supply a recording context manager and assert closure.

### 10.8.9 A service locator hides dependencies

A **service locator** is a registry from which code requests collaborators during execution:

~~~python
def generate() -> str:
    repository = services.resolve("repository")
    return repository.report()
~~~

The function signature does not reveal its requirement; missing configuration fails at runtime; any code with the locator may obtain broad capabilities. Dependency injection resolves collaborators at an outer assembly boundary and supplies only what a component needs.

A locator can be appropriate inside a plugin framework or application composition mechanism, but domain code should not use it as ambient global access.

### 10.8.10 Default arguments can freeze a dependency too early

~~~python
from clock import now


def stamp(value: str, clock=now) -> str:
    return f"{clock()}:{value}"
~~~

The default object is evaluated when the function is defined. Later patching <code>clock.now</code> does not change this default. Explicit required injection or a <code>None</code> sentinel resolved inside the function has different semantics.

Defaults are useful for stable pure policies, but hidden effectful collaborators create tests that patch the wrong namespace and applications that cannot reconfigure lifetime.

### 10.8.11 Configuration is data, not scattered global reads

Reading <code>os.environ</code> throughout modules creates implicit dependencies and inconsistent parse timing. Gather external strings at startup, parse and validate once, then pass an immutable configuration value:

~~~python
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Configuration:
    database_url: str
    timeout_seconds: float
    debug: bool
~~~

Secret-bearing fields need redacted representation or separate capability objects. Immutability means components share one configuration snapshot; dynamic reconfiguration requires an explicit versioned update protocol rather than silent environment rereads.

### 10.8.12 Pure core and effectful shell

A useful architecture concentrates deterministic transformation in a **functional core** and external effects in an **imperative shell**:

~~~python
def summarise(records: tuple[Record, ...]) -> Summary:
    # Pure domain transformation.
    ...


def run_import(source: Source, destination: Destination) -> None:
    records = tuple(source.read())
    summary = summarise(records)
    destination.write(summary)
~~~

The division improves testability and failure reasoning. It is not absolute: some domain rules concern time or transactions and need controlled effects. Injection turns those effects into explicit interfaces rather than pretending they are pure.

### 10.8.13 Module state and fork/spawn differ

Forward reference to Chapter 14: a new process may inherit a snapshot of memory under a fork-like mechanism or start a fresh interpreter that imports modules under a spawn-like mechanism. Neither produces a transparently shared mutable module dictionary. Updates require interprocess communication or shared external storage.

Code whose correctness depends on “the module singleton” should state whether uniqueness means per import name, interpreter, process, user, host, or distributed deployment. These scopes are not interchangeable.

### 10.8.14 Testing module state without global contamination

Prefer testing explicit owner objects. When module state is itself the contract:

1. expose narrow reset/close operations only if production lifecycle also needs them;
2. use test fixtures that restore exact prior state, even after failure;
3. avoid deleting unrelated cache entries;
4. isolate import-lifecycle tests in subprocesses;
5. test concurrent access if state is shared across threads;
6. avoid relying on test execution order;
7. assert that sensitive state is not leaked in representations.

Reload rarely provides a clean reset because external references and retained namespace entries can survive.

### Worked example 10.3B — Replace global patching with a composition root

Before:

~~~python
# service.py
from .database import global_database


def account_total(account_id: str) -> int:
    rows = global_database.query(account_id)
    return sum(row.amount for row in rows)
~~~

After:

~~~python
class AccountRows(Protocol):
    def query(self, account_id: str) -> list[Transaction]: ...


def account_total(source: AccountRows, account_id: str) -> int:
    rows = source.query(account_id)
    return sum(row.amount_pence for row in rows)


def build_application(configuration: Configuration) -> Application:
    database = Database(configuration.database_url)
    return Application(database=database)
~~~

The pure calculation still depends on transaction meaning but no longer on one module-owned connection. The application object or outer context owns database closure. A test supplies an in-memory source without patching import bindings.

> **Common misconception — “Module globals are bad by definition.”**  
> Immutable definitions and deliberately process-scoped state can have clear module ownership. Hidden mutable dependencies without lifecycle policy are the problem.

> **Common misconception — “Dependency injection means using a framework container.”**  
> Passing a value, protocol implementation, or factory as an argument is dependency injection. Containers are optional assembly machinery and can become service locators if used inside domain code.

## 10.9 Distribution projects and installed packages

A Python **distribution project** is a versioned unit that can be built and installed. It contains metadata and one or more import packages or modules. Distribution name, import name, and repository name need not match.

An installed distribution records metadata such as name, version, dependencies, files, and entry points. The import system ordinarily searches directories recorded in `sys.path`; it does not ask `pip` each time an import occurs. Installation arranges files and metadata so import finders can locate modules.

This distinction explains four separate questions:

1. Is a distribution installed in this environment?
2. Which version and metadata are installed?
3. Which import modules does it provide?
4. Which file and module object did this particular import resolve?

Use `python -m pip show distribution-name` for distribution metadata and inspect `module.__file__`, `module.__spec__`, and `importlib.metadata` under their contracts for runtime evidence. Do not infer one solely from the other’s spelling.

### 10.9.1 Project name and import name inhabit different registries

Distribution project names are compared under packaging normalisation rules; differences in case and runs of certain punctuation may normalise to one project key. Python import identifiers follow Python name syntax and are case-sensitive on the language level, even when filesystem behaviour adds platform complications.

A distribution named <code>careful-ledger</code> can provide import package <code>ledger</code>. The hyphen would not be an ordinary identifier in <code>import careful-ledger</code>. Never derive a pip command mechanically from an <code>ImportError</code> name without consulting project documentation or distribution metadata; attackers exploit plausible name confusion.

### 10.9.2 Installation places files and metadata into an environment

A standard wheel installation commonly places importable modules in an environment’s site-packages location and metadata in a <code>.dist-info</code> directory. Metadata can include project name, version, requirements, entry points, licences, and a record of installed files.

The exact paths depend on interpreter, environment, platform, and installation scheme. The import system sees search locations and loaders; <code>importlib.metadata</code> sees distribution metadata discoverable there. Neither requires that all files come from one installer or remain unmodified after installation.

### 10.9.3 Mapping packages back to distributions is many-to-many

The standard metadata API can offer a mapping from top-level import packages to distributions:

~~~python
from importlib.metadata import packages_distributions


providers = packages_distributions().get("ledger", [])
print(providers)
~~~

The result can be empty, one name, or several names. Editable source, modules without distribution metadata, namespace packages, and imperfect package declarations limit the inference. Use it as evidence, not an identity theorem.

### 10.9.4 Query an installed distribution explicitly

~~~python
from importlib.metadata import PackageNotFoundError, metadata, version


try:
    installed_version = version("careful-ledger")
    project_metadata = metadata("careful-ledger")
except PackageNotFoundError:
    print("distribution metadata not found")
~~~

Finding metadata does not prove a particular import resolves to its files when shadowing exists. Conversely, an import may succeed from the working tree without installed metadata. Diagnose both sides.

### 10.9.5 Editable installation changes the code-location contract

An **editable installation** makes a development source tree importable while recording project metadata in the environment, using a mechanism selected by the build backend/frontend. Edits can affect later imports without rebuilding a wheel.

Editable behaviour is intentionally development-oriented and can differ from a regular wheel in package discovery, generated files, extension builds, and resource inclusion. It is not the artefact shipped to users. Test both editable development and a clean regular installation.

Legacy descriptions that editable installation always creates one particular link file are too narrow; modern backend protocols can implement editability in different compliant ways.

### 10.9.6 Environment selection precedes package installation

The command <code>pip</code> found by a shell may belong to a different interpreter than <code>python</code>. Use:

~~~text
python -m pip install careful-ledger
~~~

to run pip as a module of the selected <code>python</code>. Then verify:

~~~python
import sys

print(sys.executable)
print(sys.prefix)
print(sys.base_prefix)
~~~

In a conventional virtual environment, <code>sys.prefix</code> identifies the environment while <code>sys.base_prefix</code> identifies the base interpreter. Environment managers may add further layers, so report the actual executable and paths during diagnosis.

### 10.9.7 Installation success and import success are distinct

A distribution can install successfully yet fail to import because:

- packaging omitted modules or native libraries;
- a runtime dependency was undeclared or incompatible;
- an import package has a different name;
- current-directory shadowing selects another file;
- platform dynamic linking fails;
- import-time configuration or code raises;
- the command and interpreter use different environments.

An import can succeed without an installation because the module is built in, on <code>PYTHONPATH</code>, in the current directory, injected by a notebook, or otherwise discoverable.

### 10.9.8 Multiple distributions can collide

Two distributions can install the same ordinary module path. The later file operation may overwrite another distribution’s file, or search-order paths may select one copy. Uninstalling one can remove files the other expected. Packaging metadata alone cannot make overlapping ownership safe.

Namespace packages intentionally permit different distributions to contribute distinct subpackages under one namespace. They must still avoid owning the same concrete module and coordinate naming and API policy.

### 10.9.9 Installation records support inspection, not perfect provenance

Wheel metadata records installed paths and hashes for many files. Administrators can compare records to detect modification. Some generated files and installer behaviours have special treatment, and privileged processes can alter both code and records.

For high-assurance supply chains, retain artefact hashes/signatures under organisational policy, use controlled indexes, build reproducibly where feasible, and deploy immutable environments. An installed directory is operational state, not by itself an authenticated source of truth.

### 10.9.10 Version is qualified by environment and artefact

“Version 2.1 is installed” is incomplete without the environment/interpreter and potentially build tag or direct-source revision. Local version identifiers, platform wheels, downstream rebuilds, and editable worktrees can contain different code under related version strings.

Record lock data, artefact hashes, Python version, platform, and deployment image identity when reproducibility matters. Do not mutate installed source files in place and continue relying on unchanged metadata.

### 10.9.11 Import names are not dependency declarations

Source code can import <code>yaml</code>, while project metadata must require the distribution that intentionally supplies it. Static import scanning cannot always infer dependencies because names differ, imports may be optional, and dynamic plugins may be discovered by metadata.

Declare direct runtime dependencies even if another direct dependency happens to install them transitively. Depending on an undeclared transitive package couples the project to another project’s internal requirement graph.

### 10.9.12 Diagnose environment identity end to end

For an unexpected version or module:

1. record <code>sys.executable</code> and interpreter version;
2. record virtual-environment prefixes;
3. inspect <code>sys.path</code> in the failing process;
4. inspect <code>module.__spec__</code> and <code>module.__file__</code> after import;
5. query the intended distribution metadata through the same interpreter;
6. map the top-level package to candidate distributions cautiously;
7. inspect installation files and hashes when necessary;
8. reproduce outside the repository to rule out shadowing;
9. compare the built artefact with source/editable state.

> **Common misconception — “The pip name and import name are the same with punctuation changed.”**  
> There is no universal one-to-one naming transformation. Consult authoritative project metadata.

> **Common misconception — “If distribution metadata reports a version, that exact code handled my import.”**  
> Search-path shadowing, editable sources, overlapping installations, or file modification can separate metadata from the resolved module. Inspect both.

## 10.10 `pyproject.toml`

`pyproject.toml` is the standard configuration file through which projects declare build-system requirements and project metadata. A fuller example:

```toml
[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling>=1.25"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[project]
name = "careful-ledger"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "A demonstrative transaction ledger"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
license = "MIT"
license-files = ["LICENSE*"]
authors = [
  { name = "Example Author" },
]
dependencies = []

[project.optional-dependencies]
test = [
  "pytest>=8,<9",
]

[project.scripts]
careful-ledger = "ledger.__main__:entry"

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]
```

The build-system table states which backend builds the project and which packages are required to run that backend in an isolated build context. The project table supplies core metadata. Optional dependencies group additional capabilities. A script entry point asks installation tooling to create a command that imports `ledger.__main__`, finds `entry`, and calls it under the entry-point contract.

The precise accepted fields and version syntax belong to packaging standards and selected tools. Tool-specific configuration lives under namespaced `[tool.NAME]` tables.

Do not execute `pyproject.toml` as Python; it is TOML data interpreted by build and development tools.

### 10.10.1 One file serves standard and tool-specific roles

<code>pyproject.toml</code> can contain:

- <code>[build-system]</code>, which tells a build frontend how to bootstrap the project’s build backend;
- <code>[project]</code>, which contains standard project metadata;
- standard companion tables such as entry-point and optional-dependency tables;
- namespaced <code>[tool.NAME]</code> tables interpreted only by the named tool.

The file is not one tool’s proprietary configuration. A formatter must ignore the build backend’s table; a backend must not reinterpret another tool’s namespace. Unknown standard fields and unknown tool tables follow their consumers’ respective validation rules.

### 10.10.2 TOML types are part of metadata correctness

TOML distinguishes strings, arrays, tables, integers, dates, and other values. These are not interchangeable textual spellings.

~~~toml
[project]
name = "careful-ledger"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
keywords = ["ledger", "accounting"]
~~~

<code>requires-python</code> is a string containing a version specifier; it is not a TOML number. <code>keywords</code> is an array of strings. Dotted table names and arrays of tables have structural meaning. Validate with build/metadata tools rather than assuming parse success means specification conformance.

### 10.10.3 Build frontend and backend are different roles

A **build frontend** is the user-facing tool requesting a standard build operation. A **build backend** is the project-selected implementation that knows how to turn this source tree into an sdist or wheel under defined hooks.

~~~toml
[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling>=1.25"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"
~~~

The frontend creates an isolated build environment when applicable, installs <code>requires</code> there, imports the backend object, and invokes standard hooks. The dependencies in <code>build-system.requires</code> are needed to run the build; they are not automatically runtime dependencies of the installed library.

The lower bound shown is illustrative, not a universal recommendation. A project should constrain build requirements to features it uses while avoiding unnecessary exclusion of compatible releases. Reproducible release pipelines additionally lock or retain the actual build environment outside the broad source metadata contract.

### 10.10.4 Build isolation prevents ambient accidental dependencies

Without isolation, a build might succeed only because the developer environment happens to contain an undeclared plugin or compiler helper. An isolated build asks whether declared build requirements suffice.

Isolation does not isolate from malicious build code: the backend and build requirements execute with process authority. It also does not supply operating-system compilers, headers, or libraries unless the broader environment provides them. Build reproducibility spans Python and non-Python inputs.

### 10.10.5 Static and dynamic metadata

Most <code>[project]</code> fields are written statically. A project can list selected fields in <code>dynamic</code> so its backend supplies them:

~~~toml
[project]
name = "careful-ledger"
dynamic = ["version"]
~~~

Backend-specific configuration then identifies the version source. A field cannot coherently be both statically specified and declared dynamic, and required metadata must ultimately be supplied.

Static metadata is easiest for generic tools to inspect without executing project code. Deriving a version by importing the package can create a build cycle when that package imports dependencies not yet installed. Prefer a backend-supported source that does not import the full runtime package.

### 10.10.6 Project name, version, and Python requirement

~~~toml
[project]
name = "careful-ledger"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
~~~

The name identifies the distribution under packaging normalisation. The version follows the packaging version scheme, which is richer than naive decimal comparison. <code>requires-python</code> filters interpreter compatibility during resolution; it does not itself prevent source from being run by an unsupported interpreter outside packaging tools.

Set the Python lower bound to the oldest version actually tested and supported. Raising it can exclude environments and is a compatibility change. A claim of <code>>=3.12</code> should be backed by continuous tests on supported versions and syntax/features consistent with that bound.

### 10.10.7 Readme and description metadata

~~~toml
[project]
description = "A transaction ledger with explicit integer-money semantics"
readme = "README.md"
~~~

The short description is plain project metadata. The readme path tells the backend to include/read long-description content with content type inferred or configured under specification rules. Links and rendered markup should be tested on the target index; repository-relative links may not resolve in an index page.

Packaging inclusion and documentation quality are distinct. A readme can be present in metadata yet omit API or migration contracts.

### 10.10.8 Licence expressions and files

Current packaging metadata supports an SPDX licence expression string and patterns for licence files:

~~~toml
[project]
license = "MIT"
license-files = ["LICENSE*"]
~~~

The expression identifies licensing under the packaging specification; it is not a substitute for including the actual licence notices required by the selected licence and dependencies. Compound expressions use SPDX operators under their grammar. A project-specific custom identifier follows the allowed <code>LicenseRef-...</code> form.

Older examples used a table such as <code>license = { text = "MIT" }</code>. That legacy table form has been superseded/deprecated by newer licence metadata. A long-lived reference should label it as compatibility history, not teach it as the preferred current form.

### 10.10.9 People and project URLs

~~~toml
[[project.authors]]
name = "Example Author"
email = "author@example.invalid"

[project.urls]
Documentation = "https://example.invalid/careful-ledger/docs"
Source = "https://example.invalid/careful-ledger/source"
Issues = "https://example.invalid/careful-ledger/issues"
~~~

Authors and maintainers are arrays of tables because there can be several people or organisations. Do not publish personal contact information without consent. URLs are labelled metadata for tools and indexes; labels are conventions rather than arbitrary code hooks.

### 10.10.10 Runtime dependencies use requirement strings

~~~toml
[project]
dependencies = [
  "platformdirs>=4,<5",
  "importlib-resources>=6; python_version < '3.12'",
]
~~~

Each string uses the dependency-specifier grammar and can include a project name, extras, version constraints, direct references under permitted policies, and an environment marker. The example’s backport marker is pedagogical; a project requiring Python 3.12 would not need that particular backport and should omit irrelevant dependencies.

Environment markers are evaluated for a target installation environment. They are not ordinary Python expressions and use defined marker variables/operators. Test resolution on every supported platform; a branch never exercised by the developer’s machine can remain broken.

### 10.10.11 Do not overconstrain library dependencies

A reusable library should state versions it is actually incompatible with, not freeze the entire environment to one lock set in its public metadata. Exact transitive pins from one development machine can make the library impossible to compose with others.

An application deployment needs a reproducible resolved environment and may maintain a lock file or constraints under its toolchain. Source metadata states compatibility intent; a lock records one selected solution. These are complementary artefacts.

Upper bounds should be evidence-based. Assuming every next major release is incompatible can be prudent for some dependencies and needlessly block security updates for others. Establish an update/testing policy.

### 10.10.12 Optional dependencies describe installable feature sets

~~~toml
[project.optional-dependencies]
postgres = ["psycopg[binary]>=3.2,<4"]
plot = ["matplotlib>=3.9"]
test = ["pytest>=8", "mypy>=1.11"]
~~~

Users can request a distribution extra through requirement syntax such as <code>careful-ledger[postgres]</code>. An extra groups additional distribution requirements; it does not automatically activate code at runtime. Application code still detects/configures the capability and reports absence meaningfully.

Using <code>test</code> as an extra is common but not the only development-dependency mechanism. Development tools may support dependency groups or lock configurations that need not become published extras. Choose deliberately which groups are part of public installation metadata.

### 10.10.13 Command entry points

~~~toml
[project.scripts]
careful-ledger = "ledger.cli:main"

[project.gui-scripts]
careful-ledger-gui = "ledger.gui:main"
~~~

The value names an import module and object reference consumed by installation tooling. It is not a shell command string and should not contain arbitrary command-line arguments. The object must be present in the installed artefact with all runtime dependencies declared.

GUI script behaviour differs by platform, particularly console/window handling. Test generated commands on target operating systems.

### 10.10.14 General entry-point groups

Frameworks can define named entry-point groups for plugin discovery:

~~~toml
[project.entry-points."careful_ledger.exporters"]
json = "ledger_json:JsonExporter"
csv = "ledger_csv:CsvExporter"
~~~

In a real ecosystem, plugin distributions ordinarily declare their own entries pointing to their implementations; the host queries installed metadata for the group. Loading an entry point imports code and requires interface validation and failure isolation. Group and entry names are public coordination namespaces and should be globally chosen with collision policy.

### 10.10.15 Classifiers and keywords are discovery metadata

Classifiers come from a controlled vocabulary used by package indexes. They can communicate supported Python versions, development status, audience, and topics. They do not override <code>requires-python</code>, licence expressions, or test evidence.

Do not list every conceivable platform as supported because pure Python source happens to parse there. Support includes dependencies, tests, documentation, and issue policy.

### 10.10.16 Backend-specific package discovery

The standard <code>[project]</code> table does not by itself tell every backend exactly which source packages and non-code files to include. Backend-specific tables may configure <code>src</code> layout, inclusion/exclusion, generated files, and extension builds.

Because this configuration is backend-specific, consult the selected backend’s primary documentation and pin required feature versions. Verify artefact contents rather than inferring them from a successful build.

### 10.10.17 Tool tables do not become runtime metadata automatically

~~~toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]

[tool.mypy]
python_version = "3.12"
strict = true
~~~

These tables configure named development tools. They are not automatically embedded as public distribution metadata, installed as dependencies, or enforced for downstream users. A misspelled tool table may be ignored unless the tool validates configuration strictly; CI should run configuration checks.

### 10.10.18 Environment-specific values do not belong in source metadata

Database passwords, deployment URLs, private tokens, and machine-specific absolute paths should not be committed to <code>pyproject.toml</code>. Build metadata is commonly published inside distributions and indexes. Keep secrets in an authorised deployment mechanism and feed them to runtime configuration without embedding them in built artefacts or logs.

### 10.10.19 Validate metadata at several stages

1. parse and validate <code>pyproject.toml</code> under the chosen backend/frontends;
2. build sdist and wheel in isolation;
3. inspect archive file lists and core metadata;
4. install the wheel into a clean environment;
5. query installed metadata with <code>importlib.metadata</code>;
6. run entry points and imports outside the repository;
7. resolve optional extras on supported targets;
8. render the long description as the target index will;
9. audit that secrets and unintended files are absent;
10. compare sdist-to-wheel rebuild behaviour.

### 10.10.20 A current minimal library skeleton

~~~toml
[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling>=1.25"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[project]
name = "careful-ledger"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Integer-valued transaction ledger"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
license = "MIT"
license-files = ["LICENSE*"]
authors = [
  { name = "Example Author" },
]
dependencies = []

[project.optional-dependencies]
test = [
  "pytest>=8",
]

[project.scripts]
careful-ledger = "ledger.cli:main"
~~~

This example is intentionally not universal. Backend choice, dependency ranges, licence, author, entry point, and Python support must match the actual project. Copying metadata without owning its claims produces a formally buildable but semantically false distribution.

> **Common misconception — “<code>pyproject.toml</code> installs dependencies when Python imports the package.”**  
> Installation/resolution tools consume metadata before runtime. The import system does not invoke them to repair missing dependencies.

> **Common misconception — “Build-system requirements are application dependencies.”**  
> They bootstrap the backend in the build environment. Runtime dependencies belong under <code>project.dependencies</code>.

## 10.11 Source distributions and wheels

A **source distribution**, commonly called an **sdist**, is an archive containing source and metadata sufficient for a compatible build frontend/backend to produce an installation artefact. A **wheel** is a built distribution format designed for installation without rerunning arbitrary project build steps in the target environment.

A **pure Python wheel** can be broadly platform-compatible when it contains no platform-specific compiled components. A wheel containing native extensions carries compatibility tags for Python/ABI/platform constraints. **ABI**, application binary interface, is the low-level calling, layout, and binary compatibility contract between compiled components.

Building and installing are distinct:

```text
python -m build
python -m pip install dist/careful_ledger-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
```

The `build` frontend is itself an external tool and must be present in the development environment. A build commonly produces both sdist and wheel under `dist/`. Installation should be tested in a clean environment; an editable working-tree install can conceal omitted files and undeclared dependencies.

### Worked example 10.4 — Clean-wheel verification

1. Create the project environment and run tests against source.
2. Build the wheel.
3. Create a new empty virtual environment.
4. Install only the wheel and its declared dependencies.
5. Change to a directory outside the repository.
6. Import the package, run its command entry point, and execute installed-distribution tests or smoke tests.

Leaving the repository prevents the current working tree from satisfying imports accidentally. This procedure tests the artefact users receive, not merely the source tree.

### 10.11.1 An sdist is a source release contract

A source distribution is not simply <code>git archive</code>. It has a standardised filename/container and project metadata, and should contain the source and configuration needed for a build frontend to ask the backend for a wheel on a compatible system.

An sdist may omit development-only files while requiring licence files, readme, build configuration, generated-source inputs, and package data. Whether generated C files or documentation sources belong depends on the project’s build contract. A user should not need the project’s unlisted version-control plugins merely to build.

### 10.11.2 A wheel is an installation-oriented archive

A wheel is a ZIP-based built distribution with a defined internal layout and metadata. It can contain pure Python modules, package data, scripts/entry metadata, and platform-specific compiled files. Installation mainly unpacks and arranges those contents under a scheme rather than running the project’s arbitrary source build process.

Wheel installation can still execute installer/tooling code and later imports execute package code. “Built” reduces target-side build work; it does not make the artefact inert or trusted.

### 10.11.3 Wheel filename tags express compatibility

A wheel filename includes distribution/version components and a triple of Python, ABI, and platform tags. The familiar suffix:

~~~text
py3-none-any.whl
~~~

means a broadly Python-3-compatible wheel with no specific compiled ABI and no platform-specific tag. A native extension wheel might use tags identifying a CPython version/ABI and an operating-system/architecture family.

Installers compare wheel tags with tags supported by the target interpreter. A matching tag means claimed binary compatibility, not proof that every external shared library or CPU feature is available. Projects must build and test appropriate artefacts for supported targets.

### 10.11.4 ABI compatibility is below Python source compatibility

Pure Python code depends on language and library interfaces. A compiled extension additionally depends on an application binary interface: calling conventions, symbol availability, object layouts, and binary formats. An extension built for one CPython ABI may not load in another even if source syntax is identical.

Some extensions target a limited stable ABI to cover several CPython versions; others use version-specific internal APIs for features or performance. The choice affects wheel tags, test matrix, and release burden.

### 10.11.5 Build wheels from a release source boundary

A disciplined release can:

1. create an sdist from the version-controlled release state;
2. inspect and verify the sdist;
3. build a wheel from that sdist in an isolated environment;
4. compare expected metadata and run tests on the installed wheel;
5. build platform wheels in controlled target builders where needed;
6. publish exactly the verified artefacts and hashes.

Building the wheel from the sdist tests that the source archive is sufficient. Building only from a rich checkout can hide omitted generated inputs or accidental dependence on untracked files.

### 10.11.6 Artefact contents are the truth delivered

List both archives:

~~~text
python -m build
python -m zipfile --list dist/careful_ledger-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
python -m tarfile --list dist/careful_ledger-0.1.0.tar.gz
~~~

Exact commands depend on filenames and available tools. Inspect for:

- every intended import module;
- type stubs or <code>py.typed</code> marker;
- licence and notice files;
- package resources;
- core metadata and entry points;
- absence of tests, secrets, local databases, credentials, and enormous unintended artefacts according to project policy.

A successful upload does not validate application completeness.

### 10.11.7 Package data versus user data

Read-only templates, schemas, and small reference datasets required by the package can be **package resources**. Runtime configuration, caches, mutable databases, and user documents do not belong inside the installed package directory.

Installed package locations may be read-only, replaced during upgrades, shared by users, or loaded from non-directory sources. Use platform-appropriate configuration/cache/data directories and explicit user paths for mutable data.

### 10.11.8 Reproducible builds require deterministic inputs

Two builds from logically identical source can differ because of archive timestamps, file ordering, generated identifiers, compiler versions, locale, paths, dependency versions, or nondeterministic code generation. A **reproducible build** is one whose defined inputs produce bit-for-bit identical outputs under the project’s reproduction specification.

Techniques include fixed source-date metadata, deterministic archive ordering, pinned/retained build tools, path normalisation, stable code generation, and controlled compiler flags. Reproducibility does not prove source safety; it lets independent builders compare that an artefact corresponds to declared inputs.

### 10.11.9 Installation integrity and <code>RECORD</code>

Wheel metadata includes a record of installed files and hashes/sizes under specification rules. This supports uninstall and integrity inspection. Some generated entries have special treatment, and an attacker able to modify the environment may modify records too.

Operational deployments can verify environments against immutable images or retained artefact hashes. A mutable developer environment is convenient but weak provenance evidence.

### 10.11.10 Native builds expand the toolchain

A package with C, C++, Rust, Fortran, or other native components may require compilers, headers, linkers, platform SDKs, and external libraries when no compatible wheel is available. Source installation can therefore fail even though a pure Python dependency resolver found compatible versions.

Error logs distinguishing “no compatible wheel was available” from “native build failed” guide remediation. Installing random compiler packages is not appropriate on a production host when policy requires prebuilt reviewed wheels.

### 10.11.11 Cross-compilation and target testing

Building on one platform for another requires a target toolchain and correct compatibility tags. A successful link does not prove runtime behaviour on the target. Execute tests in actual or faithfully emulated target environments, including architecture, operating-system baseline, and external library versions.

### 10.11.12 Wheel caching can conceal build defects

Installers often cache downloaded or locally built wheels. A second installation command may reuse a cached success instead of rebuilding changed source. During diagnosis, inspect logs, cache keys, resolved artefact hashes, and whether the command built or reused.

Do not disable caches permanently as a substitute for versioning artefacts correctly. Caches improve performance when their identity inputs are sound.

### 10.11.13 Test the installed interface outside source

A clean verification script might run:

~~~python
from importlib.metadata import version

import ledger


assert version("careful-ledger") == "0.1.0"
assert ledger.__file__ is not None
assert ledger.Transaction is not None
~~~

It should execute from a temporary directory that does not contain the checkout, run the installed command, load every required package resource, and perhaps type-check a consumer fixture. A full test suite may be omitted from the wheel, so retain external integration tests in the release pipeline.

### 10.11.14 Build and installation are security boundaries

Build backends and requirements execute code. Source distributions can cause target-side builds. Wheels contain code that executes when imported and can install entry-point wrappers. Security policy should control indexes, hashes, allowed build systems, network access during builds, and secrets available to builders.

A sandboxed builder with no publishing credential should create artefacts; a separate controlled step can verify and publish them. This limits what compromised build code can steal or release.

### 10.11.15 Artefact version must match code semantics

Every published artefact for one distribution version should represent one coherent release contract. Re-uploading different bytes under the same filename/version, where repositories permit any analogous mutation, destroys cache and provenance assumptions. Increment version for changed release content under repository policy.

### 10.11.16 Release verification matrix

For each artefact, record:

| Concern | Sdist | Pure wheel | Native wheel |
|---|---|---|---|
| archive format/name | verify | verify | verify |
| metadata/version | verify | verify | verify |
| source sufficiency | build wheel | not applicable | not applicable |
| import package files | source inputs | installed files | installed files |
| resources/licences | verify | verify | verify |
| target compatibility | build environments | supported Python range | Python/ABI/platform matrix |
| clean installation | build then install | install | install on target |
| command entry points | after installation | test | test |
| reproducible hash | compare under policy | compare | compare per toolchain |

> **Common misconception — “An sdist is for developers and a wheel is the source with a new extension.”**  
> They are distinct standard distribution formats: one supplies a source-build boundary; the other supplies an installation-oriented built layout.

> **Common misconception — “A wheel never runs code.”**  
> It avoids project source build steps during ordinary installation, but installers still operate, generated commands execute later, and importing installed modules runs code.

## 10.12 Dependency specifications and resolution

A dependency requirement combines a distribution name with optional version constraints, environment markers, and extras. A **resolver** selects a mutually compatible set of distribution versions from available candidates.

Broad requirements support libraries that should interoperate with many environments. Applications often need a locked, reviewed environment for deployment. Exact pins alone do not guarantee reproducibility if artefacts disappear, platform markers vary, or build inputs remain uncontrolled. Hash checking, retained indexes or artefacts, interpreter constraints, and operating-system dependencies can matter.

**Semantic Versioning** is one project policy using major, minor, and patch numbers to communicate compatibility intent. Python packaging does not force every project to follow SemVer, and dependency solvers cannot infer behavioural compatibility beyond declared metadata. Read each project’s actual version policy.

Transitive dependencies are code brought into the environment without direct source imports in the application. They remain part of the attack surface and compatibility graph. Review and update policy must cover the solved graph, not only top-level declarations.

### 10.12.1 Anatomy of a requirement

An illustrative requirement is:

~~~text
http-client[http2]>=4.2,<5; python_version >= "3.12"
~~~

Its components are:

- distribution project name <code>http-client</code>;
- requested extra <code>http2</code>;
- version specifier set <code>>=4.2,<5</code>;
- environment marker restricting when the requirement applies.

This string does not name an import package, guarantee that version 4.9 is compatible, or select one artefact by itself. It defines constraints consumed by a resolver for a target environment.

### 10.12.2 Version ordering is specified, not lexical

Packaging versions have parsed components covering epochs, release segments, pre-releases, post-releases, development releases, and local versions under defined rules. Lexical string sorting gives wrong results for values such as <code>1.10</code> and <code>1.9</code>.

Use packaging-aware tools and classes when interpreting versions. Do not convert versions to floats: <code>1.10</code> as a decimal-like float becomes indistinguishable from <code>1.1</code>, and pre-release labels cannot be represented.

### 10.12.3 Specifier operators communicate sets

Common forms include:

- <code>>=2</code>: releases at or above a lower bound;
- <code><3</code>: releases below an upper bound;
- <code>!=2.4.1</code>: exclusion of a known bad release;
- <code>==2.4.*</code>: prefix matching under version-specifier rules;
- <code>~=2.4</code>: compatible-release constraint with a defined lower bound and compatible prefix.

Do not translate <code>~=</code> into an informal “approximately” without deriving its exact release-clause boundary. Test the set with a packaging version/specifier implementation.

Exact <code>==2.4.1</code> in published library metadata sharply restricts composition. Exact selections are usually recorded in application locks or constraints when reproducibility requires them.

### 10.12.4 A resolver solves a graph of constraints

Suppose application <code>A</code> requires <code>B>=2</code> and <code>C>=4</code>. Candidate <code>B 2.5</code> requires <code>D<3</code>; candidate <code>C 4.1</code> requires <code>D>=3</code>. No single <code>D</code> satisfies both, so that candidate combination is unsatisfiable.

A modern resolver may backtrack to other versions of <code>B</code> or <code>C</code>. Failure does not mean either top-level requirement is invalid alone; it means the combined graph has no found solution under indexes, markers, Python version, platform, pre-release policy, and other constraints.

### 10.12.5 Resolution may have many valid answers

If requirements allow ten versions of each of several packages, many graphs may satisfy them. Resolver strategy, index state, release time, and preferences determine one selection. Re-running broad resolution months later can legitimately choose newer versions without source metadata changing.

A lock captures one selection and, ideally, artefact identities for intended target environments. It converts repeated solving into verification of a recorded solution, subject to the lock format and installer.

### 10.12.6 Constraints differ from requirements

A requirement causes a project to be part of the desired environment and constrains it. A constraints file or analogous mechanism limits versions of projects that are otherwise required; it does not necessarily request their installation independently.
