The term **content-addressed** means an identifier is derived from object content under Git’s object format. Altering any hashed part yields a different identifier with overwhelming probability. This detects accidental or malicious alteration relative to a trusted identifier, but the hash alone does not establish who authored content, whether it is safe, or whether the repository’s reference was itself substituted.

Git historically uses SHA-1 object identifiers and supports a SHA-256 repository format in relevant versions. Algorithm and interoperability details are implementation/version facts; never infer identifier length from examples when writing long-lived tooling.

> **Common misconception 12.46 — “A commit hash proves who wrote the commit.”**  
> It identifies hashed content. Authorship fields are data inside that content and can be chosen freely. Authenticity requires a trusted distribution channel or a verified cryptographic signature under an identity policy.

### 12.13.2 A commit is a snapshot with ancestry

Git presents diffs because humans review change, but a commit names a complete project tree. Unchanged subtrees and blobs are shared, so snapshots need not duplicate all bytes. A diff is computed by comparing two trees, often with rename similarity heuristics.

This distinction matters:

- a file rename is not necessarily stored as an explicit rename event;
- the same commit can be compared with different parents or working states;
- merge commits have more than one parent and therefore more than one parent-relative diff;
- path history is derived and can become ambiguous through copies and rewrites.

Commit identity includes the root tree, parents, author, committer, message, and relevant timestamps/headers. Amending a message therefore produces a new commit even if every file is unchanged.

### Worked example 12.5A — Inspect objects without changing history

In a disposable repository:

~~~text
git rev-parse HEAD
git cat-file -t HEAD
git cat-file -p HEAD
git ls-tree HEAD
git show --stat --oneline HEAD
git diff HEAD^ HEAD
~~~

<code>rev-parse</code> resolves a revision expression; <code>cat-file -t</code> reports object type; <code>cat-file -p</code> prints an object in an appropriate representation; <code>ls-tree</code> lists a tree; <code>show</code> presents commit and derived change; <code>diff</code> compares the first parent with the commit. Commands and revision syntax are Git interfaces and should be checked against the installed manual.

If the commit is the repository’s first, <code>HEAD^</code> has no parent and the final command fails. This is a boundary case in history structure, not file content.

### 12.13.3 The working tree and index are independent states

For an ordinary tracked path, there can be three relevant versions:

1. the version in <code>HEAD</code>;
2. the version in the index;
3. the version in the working tree.

Consequently:

| Command | Principal comparison |
|:---|:---|
| <code>git diff</code> | working tree versus index |
| <code>git diff --cached</code> | index versus <code>HEAD</code> |
| <code>git diff HEAD</code> | working tree versus <code>HEAD</code> |

The index is not merely a list of filenames. It records path, mode, object identifier, and conflict stages. <code>git add</code> copies selected working content into the index; later working edits do not alter the staged blob until another add.

Interactive staging can select hunks, but a hunk is a textual partition generated by diff heuristics. If two conceptual changes occupy the same line, edit deliberately or sequence commits in a temporary working state. Never leave the working file broken merely to manufacture tiny commits without verifying each snapshot.

> **Common misconception 12.47 — “Staging saves my work.”**  
> It prepares content for the next commit and stores associated objects, but it is not a durable substitute for a named commit and remote backup. Later index operations can replace it.

### 12.13.4 References, HEAD, and detached state

A local branch name is usually a reference under <code>refs/heads/</code>. A remote-tracking reference, such as <code>refs/remotes/origin/main</code>, records the last locally fetched state of a remote reference; it does not update continuously. A tag normally resides under <code>refs/tags/</code>.

<code>HEAD</code> is usually a symbolic reference to the current branch. In a **detached HEAD** state it identifies a commit directly. New commits are valid objects but no branch name advances to retain them. Before switching away, create a branch or tag if the work should remain conveniently reachable.

A **revision expression** such as <code>main~3</code> or <code>release^2</code> resolves relative to graph ancestry. The tilde follows first parents repeatedly; a numbered caret selects a particular parent. Merge topology makes this different from “three chronological commits ago”.

### 12.13.5 Remotes, fetch, pull, and push

A **remote** is a named set of repository locations and refspec configuration. It is not inherently central; Git remains distributed. Common operations:

- <code>fetch</code> obtains objects and updates configured remote-tracking references;
- <code>merge</code> integrates another history into the current branch;
- <code>rebase</code> copies selected commits onto another base;
- <code>pull</code> normally performs fetch followed by a configured integration strategy;
- <code>push</code> asks a remote to update references after transferring needed objects.

Because <code>pull</code> combines two conceptual operations, explicit <code>fetch</code> followed by inspection and chosen integration can be clearer. A push can be rejected if the remote reference would cease to contain its current tip under a fast-forward policy.

Authentication proves control of credentials to a transport endpoint. It does not make fetched code trustworthy. Review repository identity, protected reference policy, signatures where used, and dependency changes.

> **Common misconception 12.48 — “origin is the authoritative repository.”**  
> <code>origin</code> is a conventional remote name created by many clone workflows. Authority comes from project governance and verified location, not from the spelling of a local configuration entry.

## 12.14 Branching, merging, and conflicts

A branch permits a line of commits to advance independently. Merging relates histories and combines tree changes. A **merge conflict** means Git cannot safely choose one combined content automatically; it does not mean the developers are personally in conflict or that one side is correct.

Conflict resolution requires understanding the intended post-merge program, not merely deleting marker lines. After editing resolved content:

1. inspect every conflict region and adjacent invariant;
2. run focused and integration tests;
3. stage the resolved files;
4. inspect the resulting diff;
5. complete the merge commit under the repository workflow.

Rebasing copies a sequence of changes onto a new base by creating new commit objects. It rewrites commit identities. Do not rebase shared published history without a team policy because collaborators’ references still point to the original commits.

`git revert` creates a new commit applying the inverse of an earlier change under current context. It preserves public history and is distinct from resetting references or discarding working files.

### 12.14.1 Fast-forward and true merges

Suppose branch <code>feature</code> descends directly from <code>main</code> and <code>main</code> has not advanced. Moving <code>main</code> to the feature tip is a **fast-forward**: no new merge commit is required because the feature tip already contains the previous main tip as an ancestor.

If both branches have new commits, a three-way merge uses:

1. the merge base, representing shared ancestry;
2. one branch tip;
3. the other branch tip.

Changes from base to each side are combined. A clean textual merge is not necessarily a correct semantic merge. One branch may rename a configuration value while the other adds a new use of the old name on different lines; no markers appear, yet the combined program is wrong.

### Worked example 12.5B — A semantic conflict without markers

Base:

~~~python
TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 5


def fetch(client: Client) -> Response:
    return client.get(timeout=TIMEOUT_SECONDS)
~~~

Branch A changes units:

~~~python
TIMEOUT_MILLISECONDS = 5_000


def fetch(client: Client) -> Response:
    return client.get(timeout=TIMEOUT_MILLISECONDS / 1_000)
~~~

Branch B adds:

~~~python
def refresh(client: Client) -> Response:
    return client.get(timeout=TIMEOUT_SECONDS * 2)
~~~

A textual merge can retain Branch A’s renamed constant and Branch B’s new function referring to the removed name. Tests and static analysis detect what the merge algorithm cannot infer. Integration review must reason about the combined tree.

> **Common misconception 12.49 — “No conflict markers means the merge succeeded.”**  
> It means Git produced a textual tree automatically. Semantic compatibility remains an engineering claim requiring build, analysis, and tests.

### 12.14.2 Conflict stages and resolution

During an unresolved merge, the index can hold up to three staged entries for a conflicted path: merge base, “ours”, and “theirs”. These labels are contextual and can be surprising during rebase, where the checked-out side and replayed commit have roles different from a simple branch merge.

Conflict markers in a working file delimit candidate regions:

~~~text
<<<<<<< current-side
selected content
=======
other-side content
>>>>>>> other-side
~~~

Resolution is not “choose ours”, “choose theirs”, or concatenate both by default. Reconstruct the intended post-integration requirement, inspect surrounding changes and history, edit a coherent result, stage it, and test. Generated files should normally be regenerated from resolved sources rather than hand-merged.

Binary files require domain-specific merge tools or selection because line merging has no meaningful general rule. Database migrations, lock files, and generated schemas may be textual yet still require specialised semantic resolution.

### 12.14.3 Rebase as change replay

If commits <code>F1</code> and <code>F2</code> descend from base <code>B</code>, rebasing onto <code>M</code> computes their changes and applies equivalents, producing new commits <code>F1'</code> and <code>F2'</code>. Content can match while identifiers differ because parents and metadata differ.

Interactive rebase can reorder, combine, edit, or omit commits. It is useful for preparing an intelligible unpublished change series. It can also destroy review context if used to conceal the actual evolution of a risky change. Project policy should distinguish cleanup from falsification.

After rebase, test the resulting series. Resolving the same conceptual conflict at several replayed commits may produce intermediate states that do not build. Whether every intermediate commit must pass depends on the project’s history policy, but bisectability and review improve when it does.

Force-updating a remote reference can discard another contributor’s new tip. A lease-protected force operation checks the expected remote state and is safer than unconditional force, but it still rewrites history and requires authorisation and coordination.

> **Common misconception 12.50 — “Rebase moves existing commits.”**  
> It normally creates new commits representing replayed changes on a new parent chain. Names are then updated to reach the new objects.

### 12.14.4 Merge, rebase, squash, and cherry-pick

These operations answer different history questions:

| Operation | Result |
|:---|:---|
| merge | combines ancestries, possibly with a multi-parent commit |
| rebase | replays changes as new commits on another base |
| squash merge | integrates the net change as one new commit without feature ancestry in the main line |
| cherry-pick | applies the change introduced by selected commit(s) as new commit(s) elsewhere |
| revert | applies an inverse change as new history |

Cherry-picking duplicates a change but not its ancestry relation. Later merging branches containing both original and cherry-picked changes can require careful reasoning. Record the source commit in the message when policy supports traceability.

No strategy is universally cleanest. Merge commits preserve topology; a linear rebased history can simplify first-parent reading; squashing hides internal steps; cherry-picking is useful for targeted backports. Choose based on collaboration, audit, release, and recovery needs.

### 12.14.5 Reset, restore, and revert

These commands are often confused:

- <code>git revert</code> creates a new commit that attempts to reverse an earlier commit’s change;
- <code>git reset</code> moves the current branch reference and, depending on mode, may also change index and working tree;
- <code>git restore</code> replaces selected working-tree or index content from another source;
- <code>git checkout</code> historically combines branch switching and path restoration, which newer commands separate.

Reset and restore can discard uncommitted work. Before any destructive mode, inspect status and diffs, identify the exact path/reference, and create a recoverable commit or stash when appropriate. This book shows concepts, not an invitation to run destructive commands in a valuable working tree.

Reverting a merge requires choosing a mainline parent: the inverse depends on which parent represents the line being retained. Later attempts to merge the same topic can be surprising because ancestry records that it was already merged. Consult the official manual and rehearse in a disposable clone.

> **Common misconception 12.51 — “Revert returns the repository to exactly an old state.”**  
> It applies an inverse patch in current context. Intervening changes remain, conflicts can occur, and external effects—deployments, messages, migrations—are not undone by source history.

### 12.14.6 Stashes and worktrees

A **stash** records selected working/index states in commit-like objects and restores a cleaner working tree. It is useful for brief context switches, not a substitute for named, reviewed history. Stash application can conflict after the base changes; include untracked content only deliberately.

A Git **worktree** permits multiple working trees associated with one repository, often with different branches checked out. Worktrees reduce the need to stash when switching between a release repair and ongoing work. They share object storage and some repository administration; deleting directories manually can leave administrative records requiring repair.

Both mechanisms manage local workflow. Neither communicates intent to collaborators until commits and references are exchanged.

### 12.14.7 Reflogs and recovery

A **reflog** records local updates to a reference or to <code>HEAD</code>, including previous object identifiers. If a branch is reset or deleted, a recent commit may be recoverable while its object and reflog entry remain.

~~~text
git reflog
git show <candidate-object-id>
git branch recovered-work <candidate-object-id>
~~~

The safe conceptual sequence is inspect, verify, then create a new retaining reference. Reflogs are normally local, expire under configuration, and may not exist for every reference or server. Do not promise recovery based on them; commit coherent work and push authorised references.

> **Common misconception 12.52 — “Git can always recover anything.”**  
> Recovery depends on whether content was stored as an object and remains reachable through a reference, reflog, or retention window. Never-added working bytes may never have entered Git.

### 12.14.8 Automated bisection and testable history

The debugging section introduced <code>git bisect</code>. Its effectiveness depends on a history whose intermediate commits can build and on a predicate that classifies them. A **bisectable history** makes each commit coherent enough that regression tests have meaning.

If a schema change and application change must deploy together, an intermediate commit containing only half may be untestable. The solution is not arbitrary splitting; use backward-compatible steps:

1. add schema capable of serving old and new code;
2. deploy code that writes/reads compatible forms;
3. migrate existing data with verification;
4. stop using old form;
5. remove old schema after compatibility window.

Each step has a rollback and mixed-version story. This history is both deployable and diagnosable.

### 12.14.9 Tags, releases, and signatures

A lightweight tag is a reference directly to an object. An **annotated tag** normally points to a tag object containing a name, tagger, message, and target, and can carry a cryptographic signature. Release policy should specify which form is authoritative.

A signature establishes that a holder of a private key signed specified bytes. Trust additionally requires validating key ownership, key status, algorithm policy, and the relationship between signed commit/tag and built artefact. A signed tag does not prove that an uploaded wheel was built from it unless the build and provenance chain connects them.

Release names should be immutable. Moving a published version tag makes caches and users disagree about what the version means. Correct an erroneous release with a new version and explicit advisory under ordinary package practice.

### 12.14.10 Collaborative integration policy

A maintainable collaboration policy answers:

- which branches or references are protected;
- which checks and approvals are required;
- whether review authors may approve their own changes;
- whether force updates are permitted;
- merge strategy and commit-message requirements;
- how emergency changes are authorised and reviewed afterwards;
- how release tags and artefacts are produced;
- retention and audit requirements.

Automation enforces only encoded policy. An administrator bypass may be necessary during an incident, but it should be visible, narrowly authorised, and followed by retrospective verification.

> **Common misconception 12.53 — “A protected branch guarantees good code.”**  
> Protection can require checks and approvals. It cannot make weak tests discriminating, reviewers knowledgeable, credentials uncompromised, or requirements correct.

## 12.15 `.gitignore` and secret history

`.gitignore` prevents untracked matching paths from being considered by ordinary add operations. It does not remove files already tracked and does not erase secrets from prior commits.

Typical Python exclusions include environment directories, bytecode caches, build outputs, coverage data, tool caches, and local secret/configuration files. The exact file should follow project tools and deployment model rather than copy every global template entry.

If a secret enters Git history, deleting the current file is insufficient. Treat the secret as compromised: revoke or rotate it, then follow repository policy for history rewriting where necessary. Rewriting does not retract clones, caches, logs, or already used credentials.

### 12.15.1 Ignore rules are path-selection rules

An ignore pattern affects untracked paths considered by commands such as status and add. Rules can come from repository files, per-repository exclusions, and user-level configuration. Negation can re-include a path only under the documented traversal constraints; pattern order and directory matching matter.

Use:

~~~text
git check-ignore -v path/to/file
~~~

to inspect which rule applies to an ignored path. This is more reliable than guessing from a large template.

Repository <code>.gitignore</code> should contain project-wide generated or local-only paths. A developer’s editor backups can live in a global excludes file. Files required for a reproducible build must not be ignored merely because they are generated locally; either version their source and reproduce them or version the artefact under explicit policy.

> **Common misconception 12.54 — “Ignoring a directory makes its contents private.”**  
> Ignore rules are client-side convenience. Any process can read the local files, and explicit force-add can store them. Confidentiality requires access controls and secret-management practice.

### 12.15.2 Secret prevention and response

Secrets include passwords, private keys, bearer tokens, signing material, and connection strings containing credentials. Keep them out of source through:

- environment or secret-manager injection at runtime;
- committed example configuration containing no real secret;
- least-privilege, short-lived credentials;
- pre-commit and server-side secret scanning;
- review of generated artefacts and logs;
- separate authorised storage for development secrets.

Scanning is probabilistic. High-entropy detectors miss structured low-entropy secrets and can flag harmless test values. A test credential must be visibly non-production and unusable outside its isolated service.

If a secret is committed:

1. contain risk and rotate or revoke first;
2. determine scope, privileges, access logs, and exposure;
3. remove it from current source;
4. decide whether history rewriting is necessary;
5. coordinate rewritten references and cached copies;
6. invalidate derived credentials or sessions;
7. record the incident without reproducing the secret;
8. add preventive controls.

History rewriting changes commit identities for every descendant. Collaborators must replace or carefully rebase old clones so the secret is not reintroduced. Hosted pull requests, CI logs, package artefacts, and forks may retain copies beyond repository history.

### 12.15.3 Large and generated files

Git stores content versions efficiently when they share compressible structure, but repeated large binary artefacts can make clone and maintenance expensive. Systems such as Git LFS replace selected working paths with small pointer files while storing payloads separately. This introduces a second storage, authentication, retention, and availability dependency.

Do not commit virtual environments, caches, ordinary build directories, database dumps, or credentials. Whether to commit generated source, lock files, migrations, or documentation output is project-specific:

- commit when consumers cannot reliably regenerate it or review needs the exact form;
- omit when deterministic generation from versioned sources is established;
- never hand-edit a generated file without changing its source;
- verify generated output is current in CI.

### 12.15.4 Hooks and trust

Git hooks are programs invoked at selected client or server operations. Client hooks can format, scan, or validate before commit; server controls can enforce policy independent of a contributor’s local configuration.

Local hooks are not a security boundary because users can bypass or lack them. A repository does not ordinarily activate cloned hook scripts automatically, which avoids executing untrusted code merely by cloning. Hook-distribution tools themselves become dependencies to review.

Build scripts, test plugins, package configuration, and hooks from an untrusted repository can execute code. Inspect before running, use least-privileged environments, and do not expose unrelated credentials to arbitrary builds.

> **Common misconception 12.55 — “Pre-commit hooks enforce repository policy.”**  
> They provide fast local feedback. Authoritative enforcement belongs on controlled integration infrastructure, because local execution is voluntary and environment-dependent.

## 12.16 Code style and PEP 8

**PEP 8** is the principal style guide for Python code. Style supports consistent reading, diff quality, and tool cooperation. It does not define language semantics and is not an argument against domain-appropriate exceptions.

Important principles include:

- four spaces per indentation level;
- meaningful naming conventions;
- readable line structure;
- separation of top-level definitions;
- imports organised and normally placed near the top;
- whitespace that exposes grouping;
- comparisons to `None` with `is`/`is not`;
- truth testing rather than unnecessary equality to `True`;
- consistency with the surrounding maintained project.

Automated formatters can settle presentation mechanically. Linters detect selected defects and policy violations. A formatter does not improve names, contracts, decomposition, or algorithm choice. A linter warning should be understood before suppression; a suppression should be narrow and justified.

### Worked example 12.6 — Style reveals semantics

Obscure:

```python
def f(x=[]):
    if x==None:return []
    else:x.append(1);return x
```

Formatted source remains semantically defective because the mutable default persists and `x == None` permits equality dispatch. A meaningful repair is:

```python
def append_marker(values: list[int] | None = None) -> list[int]:
    if values is None:
        values = []
    values.append(1)
    return values
```

Style made the flow inspectable, but the repair required object and identity reasoning.

### 12.16.1 Readability is an engineering property

Source code is read to predict behaviour, review change, diagnose failure, and construct new behaviour. **Readability** is the degree to which an intended reader can form an accurate mental model with bounded effort. It is not identical to visual beauty or brevity.

Readable code makes important distinctions visible:

- domain concepts have stable names;
- units and representations are explicit;
- state mutation and external effects are localised;
- ordinary and exceptional paths can be followed;
- control nesting is bounded;
- invariants are expressed near the operations that depend on them;
- interfaces expose required variation without incidental mechanism;
- similar structures mean similar things.

Empirical measurement of readability is difficult and context-dependent. Style rules serve as standardised defaults that reduce unproductive variation. They are strongest where consistency assists scanning and weakest when applied as substitutes for semantic judgement.

### 12.16.2 Naming as model construction

A name asserts a category. <code>elapsed_seconds</code> asserts duration and unit; <code>deadline</code> asserts a point against a clock; <code>user</code> may ambiguously denote an authenticated principal, database row, customer, or display profile.

Good names distinguish:

- identifier from the identified object;
- raw input from parsed value;
- current state from requested transition;
- collection from one element;
- predicate from command;
- unit and coordinate system;
- trusted from untrusted representation.

~~~python
def schedule_retry(
    request_id: str,
    attempt_count: int,
    delay_seconds: float,
) -> ScheduledRetry:
    ...
~~~

This signature is more informative than <code>retry(id, n, timeout)</code>, but it still needs contracts: whether attempt count includes the first try, which clock schedules delay, permissible range, and idempotency.

Avoid encoding mutable type information in names such as <code>customer_dict</code> when the conceptual object is a customer. Conversely, representation distinctions such as <code>payload_bytes</code> and <code>payload_text</code> can prevent encoding errors.

> **Common misconception 12.56 — “Long names are self-documenting.”**  
> Length can carry distinctions, but a long name can still assert the wrong model or repeat obvious context. Documentation includes contracts, structure, examples, and rationale—not identifier length alone.

### 12.16.3 Formatting and line structure

PEP 8 recommends a consistent indentation and layout vocabulary. Modern projects often delegate many choices to an opinionated formatter. A formatter:

- parses source;
- emits a canonical or narrowly variable layout;
- reduces review noise;
- makes formatting reproducible across editors and CI.

It does not preserve every hand-aligned visual table, and that loss is often intentional: manual alignment creates large diffs when one name grows. Formatting should be applied as a separate mechanical change when introducing it to an established repository, so semantic review is not buried.

Line length is a readability and tooling constraint, not a Python parser limit. Long URLs, generated code, string literals, tables, and mathematical expressions can justify exceptions. Configure one policy and let tools agree.

Parentheses are preferable to a backslash for most explicit line continuation because comments and editing are safer:

~~~python
accepted = (
    request.authenticated
    and request.account_id in permitted_accounts
    and not request.expired
)
~~~

The layout reveals three conditions. Whether the policy is correct still requires a decision table.

### 12.16.4 Linters and rule provenance

A **linter** performs static checks for selected suspicious or non-conforming patterns. Rules may concern:

- definite errors, such as an undefined name;
- probable errors, such as a mutable default;
- maintainability, such as excessive complexity;
- style, such as import ordering;
- security patterns, such as unsafe temporary-file use;
- project architecture, such as forbidden dependencies.

Not every diagnostic has the same epistemic status. An undefined name is usually a specification-level source error. A “too many arguments” threshold is a maintainability heuristic. A security pattern can be a real vulnerability only under particular input trust. Configure severity accordingly.

A suppression is an assertion that the rule is inapplicable at one site. Make it narrow, include the rule identifier, and explain non-obvious reasoning:

~~~python
payload = pickle.loads(trusted_fixture_bytes)  # noqa: S301
~~~

Even this comment is insufficient unless “trusted fixture” provenance is genuinely controlled. Prefer formats that do not require a hazardous primitive. Periodically review suppressions because surrounding assumptions change.

> **Common misconception 12.57 — “A clean linter run means the code follows best practice.”**  
> It means enabled rules found no reportable pattern. Disabled rules, dynamic behaviour, architecture, domain contracts, and runtime evidence lie outside that conclusion.

### 12.16.5 Complexity measures and decomposition

**Cyclomatic complexity** is a control-flow measure related to the number of linearly independent paths through a graph. Tools approximate it from source constructs. A high value suggests many decisions to understand and test, but a low value does not guarantee simplicity: a one-line regular expression or call into a complex framework can be cognitively difficult.

**Cognitive complexity** and similar measures attempt to model human comprehension by weighting nesting and flow disruption. They are heuristic and tool-specific. Use thresholds to identify review candidates, not to force mechanical extraction.

Extracting every condition into a tiny function can scatter one policy across files. Good decomposition groups a coherent rule behind a name and reduces the amount of state considered at once.

### Worked example 12.6A — Refactor a decision, preserving its table

Before:

~~~python
def can_refund(order: Order, actor: Actor, now: datetime) -> bool:
    return (
        actor.is_staff
        or (
            actor.customer_id == order.customer_id
            and order.status == Status.PAID
            and now <= order.paid_at + timedelta(days=30)
            and not order.has_chargeback
        )
    )
~~~

After:

~~~python
def is_customer_refund_window_open(
    order: Order,
    *,
    customer_id: str,
    now: datetime,
) -> bool:
    return (
        customer_id == order.customer_id
        and order.status is Status.PAID
        and now <= order.paid_at + timedelta(days=30)
        and not order.has_chargeback
    )


def can_refund(order: Order, actor: Actor, now: datetime) -> bool:
    if actor.is_staff:
        return True
    return is_customer_refund_window_open(
        order,
        customer_id=actor.customer_id,
        now=now,
    )
~~~

The helper names one policy and the outer function reveals the staff override. The refactor could accidentally change equality semantics by using <code>is</code> for an enum; that is correct only because <code>Status</code> members are singleton enum objects. Regression tests derived from the original decision table must run before and after.

### 12.16.6 Refactoring and semantic preservation

**Refactoring** is a change to internal structure intended to preserve externally observable behaviour. The boundary of “observable” must be stated. Improving query count changes performance; renaming a public symbol changes API; changing exception text may affect callers; changing object identity can affect code even if equality remains.

A safe refactoring workflow:

1. identify the behaviour boundary to preserve;
2. strengthen characterisation tests where specification is incomplete;
3. make one structural transformation;
4. run focused static and dynamic checks;
5. inspect the diff for unintended semantic changes;
6. measure relevant performance if structure affects cost.

A refactoring can expose a latent defect without creating it. Treat the observation causally: compare traces and invariants rather than reverting reflexively.

> **Common misconception 12.58 — “Refactoring means cleaning code without changing features.”**  
> The intent is behavioural preservation under a declared observation boundary. Without evidence, a large cleanup can be a high-risk semantic change wearing a reassuring label.

## 12.17 Documentation

Documentation serves distinct audiences and timescales:

- **reference** precisely records an interface;
- **explanation** develops a mental model and reasons about design;
- **tutorial** guides a learner through a controlled first result;
- **how-to** gives steps for a specific task under stated conditions;
- architecture records explain boundaries and decisions;
- comments explain constraints, non-obvious reasons, and invariants near code.

A **docstring** is a string literal in the designated first statement position of a module, class, function, or method, available through `__doc__` and documentation tools.

```python
def withdraw(amount_pence: int) -> None:
    """Withdraw a positive amount.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the amount is not positive or exceeds the balance.
    """
```

Docstrings should state semantic facts not already obvious from the signature: units, mutation, failure, ordering, ownership, and constraints. Comments that restate syntax become stale:

```python
count += 1  # Increment count by one.
```

A valuable comment explains *why* the update occurs or which invariant it maintains.

Examples in documentation should be tested when practical. Untested examples become plausible-looking obsolete programs.

### 12.17.1 Documentation genres answer different questions

Combining every genre into one page serves none well. Four useful categories are:

| Genre | Reader’s question | Typical structure |
|:---|:---|:---|
| tutorial | How do I learn this through a guided first experience? | controlled sequence with explanation |
| how-to guide | How do I accomplish this specific task? | goal-directed steps and conditions |
| reference | What exactly does this interface mean? | systematic, complete, precise entries |
| explanation | Why is the system designed or behaving this way? | concepts, alternatives, reasoning |

This classification is a documentation design model, not a law. A page can link genres and small projects may combine them, but the author should know which reader problem each passage addresses.

Operational runbooks are another genre: executable procedures for diagnosis, containment, recovery, and verification. A runbook must state prerequisites, authority, irreversible steps, expected output, abort conditions, and escalation. A command list without interpretation is dangerous during an incident.

### 12.17.2 API reference as a contract

For each public function, class, command, or endpoint, reference documentation should state as applicable:

- purpose and stability;
- parameters, types, units, ranges, and defaults;
- return value and ownership;
- mutation and external effects;
- exceptions or failure results;
- ordering and concurrency;
- complexity or resource bounds when contractual;
- security and confidentiality constraints;
- version introduced, deprecated, or changed;
- examples of ordinary and boundary use.

Type hints remove some repetition but not semantics. <code>timeout: float</code> does not say seconds, whether zero disables or immediately expires, whether it covers connection and response together, or which exception signals expiry.

### Worked example 12.6B — A contract-bearing docstring

~~~python
def read_prefix(
    path: Path,
    limit_bytes: int,
) -> bytes:
    """Read at most limit_bytes bytes from the start of path.

    Args:
        path: Regular file to open for binary reading. Symbolic-link handling
            follows the host platform and is not restricted by this function.
        limit_bytes: Maximum byte count. Must be non-negative.

    Returns:
        Between zero and limit_bytes bytes. An empty file returns an empty
        byte string.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If limit_bytes is negative.
        OSError: If the path cannot be opened or read.

    The function does not promise that the file remains unchanged while it is
    read. Callers requiring a stable snapshot must provide that synchronisation.
    """
    if limit_bytes < 0:
        raise ValueError("limit_bytes must be non-negative")
    with path.open("rb") as stream:
        return stream.read(limit_bytes)
~~~

The docstring identifies a security-relevant omission—symbolic-link restriction—rather than implying safety. It distinguishes byte count from character count and states concurrent mutation semantics. A project’s chosen docstring convention may format sections differently; semantic completeness matters more than one syntax.

> **Common misconception 12.59 — “Type annotations make parameter documentation redundant.”**  
> Annotations classify values and relationships. They rarely encode units, side effects, authority, ordering, error policy, or operational limitations.

### 12.17.3 Comments explain constraints and reasons

A comment should reduce the gap between code and the reasoning needed to maintain it. Valuable comments include:

- a non-obvious invariant;
- a compatibility constraint and removal condition;
- why an apparently simpler algorithm is invalid;
- provenance for a protocol constant;
- security assumptions;
- relationship to a standard or issue;
- deliberate complexity or performance trade-off.

Example:

~~~python
# The provider can commit a charge before this request times out. Reuse the
# persisted key on every retry; generating a new key can duplicate the charge.
result = gateway.charge(
    amount_pence=amount_pence,
    idempotency_key=operation.provider_key,
)
~~~

The comment explains a distributed failure mode. A comment such as “call gateway” would restate syntax.

Outdated comments are defects because readers may trust them over code. Review comment validity during changes and attach external references that are expected to remain stable.

### 12.17.4 Doctest and executable examples

Python’s <code>doctest</code> module can discover interactive-looking examples in docstrings and compare output. It is effective for small deterministic expressions:

~~~python
def slugify_words(words: list[str]) -> str:
    """Join lowercase words with hyphens.

    >>> slugify_words(["Ada", "LOVELACE"])
    'ada-lovelace'
    >>> slugify_words([])
    ''
    """
    return "-".join(word.lower() for word in words)
~~~

Exact output comparison becomes brittle for unordered representations, paths, tracebacks, floating values, timestamps, and version-specific <code>repr</code>. Doctest examples can prioritise readable narrative and delegate thorough testing to ordinary tests. If examples are copied into separate tests, establish a process that prevents divergence.

Examples must not contain real credentials or destructive commands. Use reserved domains such as <code>example.test</code> and visibly fictional values.

### 12.17.5 Architecture and decision documentation

Architecture documentation should offer several **views**, each selected for a concern:

- context: system and external actors/systems;
- container or deployment: independently running/storage units;
- component: internal responsibility boundaries;
- data: schemas, ownership, flow, retention;
- runtime: important interactions and failure paths;
- security: trust boundaries, assets, threats, controls;
- decision history: ADRs and supersession.

One giant diagram becomes stale because it cannot serve every question. Generate mechanical API/schema facts from source where possible and write human reasoning around them.

Diagrams need legends, version/context, direction, and omitted-detail statements. A box labelled “service” says little without responsibility and boundary semantics.

### 12.17.6 Documentation build and verification

Treat documentation as source:

- version it with related code where appropriate;
- review it;
- check links and code snippets;
- build it in CI;
- publish the version matching a release;
- retain old-version reference when users still operate old releases.

An example that imports the working tree while documenting the last release can silently use future behaviour. Documentation tooling should install or select the intended artefact.

Accessibility applies: meaningful headings, alternative text for informative images, sufficient contrast, keyboard navigation in generated sites, and explanations that do not depend on colour alone.

> **Common misconception 12.60 — “Documentation can be generated from source.”**  
> Tools can extract signatures, docstrings, schemas, and cross-references. They cannot infer stakeholder intent, rationale, operational procedure, examples, or which caveats readers need.

## 12.18 Type hints

A **type hint** is metadata expressing intended relationships among values. Python’s runtime generally preserves annotations without automatically enforcing them. A **static type checker** analyses source without executing every path, approximating which values can flow where.

```python
from collections.abc import Iterable


def mean(values: Iterable[float]) -> float:
    collected = list(values)
    if not collected:
        raise ValueError("mean requires at least one value")
    return sum(collected) / len(collected)
```

The annotation admits any iterable of values compatible with float use. The implementation materialises because it needs length and repeated aggregate access. A more memory-efficient one-pass implementation could accept `Iterable[float]` without storage.

**Nominal typing** relates types through declarations and inheritance. **Structural typing** relates them through supported operations. `Protocol` expresses static structural interfaces.

Use unions for alternatives:

```python
def find(identifier: str) -> Account | None:
    ...
```

Callers must narrow the possibility before using account-only operations. `None` is not automatically ignored.

Generics preserve relationships:

```python
from collections.abc import Iterable
from typing import TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")


def first(values: Iterable[T]) -> T:
    iterator = iter(values)
    try:
        return next(iterator)
    except StopIteration as error:
        raise ValueError("values must be non-empty") from error
```

The same type variable states that the result type is the produced element type, rather than losing it to `object`.


### 12.18.1 Three different meanings of type

The word **type** can refer to related but distinct things:

1. a runtime class or type object used by Python’s execution semantics;
2. a static type expression interpreted by a checker;
3. a domain category, such as AccountIdentifier, that may share a runtime representation with other categories.

For example, <code>list[int]</code> is a runtime generic-alias object when evaluated in modern Python and a static expression denoting lists whose elements are integers. CPython does not inspect every append to enforce that expression. A static checker analyses source and reports incompatible operations before execution, subject to its model.

Annotations reside in <code>__annotations__</code> under version-dependent evaluation rules. Tools may inspect them at runtime, but library code should use documented facilities such as <code>typing.get_type_hints</code> rather than assuming every annotation is already an object. Forward references, deferred evaluation policy, imports, and Python version affect runtime introspection. Static meaning is governed by the typing specification and checker behaviour, not solely by the runtime dictionary.

> **Common misconception 12.61 — “Python becomes statically typed when annotations are added.”**  
> Python’s runtime semantics remain dynamic unless explicit runtime validation is introduced. An external checker supplies a separate analysis whose guarantees depend on coverage, configuration, and soundness limits.

### 12.18.2 Gradual typing and the boundary of precision

Python uses **gradual typing**: annotated and unannotated code can coexist, and precision can be introduced incrementally. This supports adoption but creates boundaries at which information may be lost.

The special static type <code>Any</code> is dynamically permissive. Operations on an <code>Any</code> value are largely accepted, and results often remain <code>Any</code>. It therefore acts as both top and bottom in many compatibility rules, allowing values to flow through checks unsafely.

<code>object</code> is different. Every ordinary Python value is compatible with <code>object</code>, but a value known only as <code>object</code> supports only operations guaranteed by that type until narrowed:

~~~python
def length_if_text(value: object) -> int | None:
    if isinstance(value, str):
        return len(value)
    return None
~~~

The <code>isinstance</code> branch narrows <code>value</code> to <code>str</code>. Had the parameter been <code>Any</code>, the checker would permit <code>len(value)</code> even without proof. Use <code>object</code> to represent an unknown value that must be validated; use <code>Any</code> only when deliberately crossing a dynamic boundary.

At the opposite extreme, <code>Never</code> denotes no possible values in the static model. It can describe functions that do not return normally or prove exhaustiveness. Checker support and import location are version-dependent.

### Worked example 12.6C — Validate dynamic JSON into a precise model

~~~python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ImportRequest:
    account_id: str
    amounts_pence: tuple[int, ...]


class SchemaError(ValueError):
    pass


def parse_import_request(value: Any) -> ImportRequest:
    if not isinstance(value, dict):
        raise SchemaError("request must be an object")

    account_id = value.get("account_id")
    amounts = value.get("amounts_pence")

    if not isinstance(account_id, str) or not account_id:
        raise SchemaError("account_id must be non-empty text")
    if not isinstance(amounts, list):
        raise SchemaError("amounts_pence must be an array")
    if not all(
        isinstance(amount, int) and not isinstance(amount, bool)
        for amount in amounts
    ):
        raise SchemaError("every amount must be an integer")

    return ImportRequest(account_id, tuple(amounts))
~~~

The dynamic value is confined to the boundary. After validation, internal code receives a frozen record with a precise tuple. The checker cannot prove that arbitrary JSON conforms; runtime validation and static analysis cooperate.

For very large arrays, <code>all</code> followed by tuple construction traverses twice. A one-pass parser can validate while appending to a local list, then freeze it. That is a performance refinement whose correctness needs separate tests.

> **Common misconception 12.62 — “Replacing Any with object fixes the type problem.”**  
> It makes unsafe operations visible to the checker. The programmer must still narrow or parse the value according to a real runtime contract.

### 12.18.3 Union types and narrowing

A union <code>A | B</code> denotes a value compatible with either alternative. Narrowing uses control-flow evidence:

~~~python
def display_name(account: Account | None) -> str:
    if account is None:
        return "anonymous"
    return account.display_name
~~~

The checker understands that after the guard, <code>account</code> cannot be <code>None</code>. Narrowing mechanisms include identity checks, <code>isinstance</code>, discriminant literals, pattern matching, and checker-specific inference.

A **discriminated union** gives each variant a literal tag:

~~~python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Accepted:
    kind: Literal["accepted"]
    identifier: str


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Rejected:
    kind: Literal["rejected"]
    reason: str


type SubmissionResult = Accepted | Rejected


def describe(result: SubmissionResult) -> str:
    match result:
        case Accepted(identifier=identifier):
            return f"accepted as {identifier}"
        case Rejected(reason=reason):
            return f"rejected: {reason}"
~~~

The <code>type</code> statement and generic syntax introduced in Python 3.12 create a type alias; they do not create a runtime subclass enforcing values. Checkers differ in exhaustiveness diagnostics. A final assertion helper accepting <code>Never</code> can make an omitted variant reportable, but runtime defence may still be required at untrusted boundaries.

<code>Literal["accepted"]</code> expresses one exact static value. It does not cause an ordinary string read from JSON to acquire that type without validation or inference.

### 12.18.4 Type aliases, NewType, and domain distinction

A **type alias** gives another name to a type expression:

~~~python
type AccountId = str
type BalanceTable = dict[AccountId, int]
~~~

<code>AccountId</code> and <code>str</code> remain statically interchangeable because the alias is transparent. When two concepts share a representation but must not mix, <code>NewType</code> creates a distinct static type with an identity-like runtime constructor:

~~~python
from typing import NewType


AccountId = NewType("AccountId", str)
RequestId = NewType("RequestId", str)


def load_account(identifier: AccountId) -> Account:
    ...


account_id = AccountId("A-7")
request_id = RequestId("R-4")
~~~

A checker rejects passing <code>request_id</code> to <code>load_account</code>. At runtime these values are still strings and <code>isinstance(value, AccountId)</code> is not a valid nominal check. If runtime methods, validation, or invariant-bearing construction are needed, define a class or frozen dataclass.

### 12.18.5 Typed mappings and structural records

<code>TypedDict</code> describes dictionary-shaped records for static checking, including required and optional keys:

~~~python
from typing import NotRequired, TypedDict


class AccountPayload(TypedDict):
    identifier: str
    balance_pence: int
    note: NotRequired[str]
~~~

At runtime an <code>AccountPayload</code> value is an ordinary dictionary. Construction does not validate external JSON. Typed dictionaries are useful at serialisation and interoperability boundaries where mapping shape is intrinsic. For rich behaviour and invariants, a class or dataclass is often clearer.

Width and mutability make compatibility subtle. A mapping with extra fields can sometimes be used where fewer fields are read, but writable fields and deletion permissions constrain substitutability. Follow the typing specification rather than assuming structural records behave like immutable mathematical records.

> **Common misconception 12.63 — “TypedDict creates a typed dictionary class.”**  
> It supplies a static structural description. Runtime values are dictionaries unless another validation system is deliberately used.

### 12.18.6 Generic functions and classes

A **generic** definition expresses relationships while abstracting over one or more types. Python 3.12’s parameter syntax makes the variable local to the definition:

~~~python
from collections.abc import Sequence


def first_or[T](values: Sequence[T], default: T) -> T:
    if values:
        return values[0]
    return default
~~~

The repeated <code>T</code> relates sequence elements, default, and result. Replacing it with <code>object</code> would lose that relation:

~~~python
result = first_or(["a", "b"], "none")  # Inferred as str.
~~~

A generic class:

~~~python
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Cell[T]:
    value: T

    def replace(self, value: T) -> None:
        self.value = value
~~~

<code>Cell[int]</code> and <code>Cell[str]</code> share one runtime class in ordinary implementation terms but receive different static specialisations. Generic parameters can have bounds or constraints when operations require more than arbitrary <code>object</code>.

The older <code>TypeVar</code> syntax remains important for supported Python versions before 3.12 and for tools not yet implementing every new form. A project should declare its minimum Python and checker versions.

### 12.18.7 Bounds, constraints, and overloads

A bounded type variable permits any subtype of a bound and preserves the specific input type. A constrained variable selects among enumerated alternatives. The distinction affects inference.

An **overload** describes multiple call signatures for one runtime implementation:

~~~python
from typing import Literal, overload


@overload
def decode(data: bytes, *, as_text: Literal[False] = False) -> bytes: ...


@overload
def decode(data: bytes, *, as_text: Literal[True]) -> str: ...


def decode(data: bytes, *, as_text: bool = False) -> bytes | str:
    plain = decompress(data)
    if as_text:
        return plain.decode("utf-8")
    return plain
~~~

The overloads relate a literal argument to result type. They have no independent runtime implementation; the final function executes. The implementation must accept every overload and return accordingly. Tests must still establish decompression and decoding behaviour.

Too many overloads can signal an interface whose behaviour depends on hidden combinations. Separate methods or a generic protocol may be clearer.

### 12.18.8 Callable types, ParamSpec, and decorators

<code>Callable[[A, B], R]</code> describes positional parameter types and a result but cannot express every keyword, overload, or parameter-kind relation. A callback <code>Protocol</code> can name a precise <code>__call__</code> signature.

Decorators often preserve an arbitrary callable’s parameters. <code>ParamSpec</code> captures a parameter specification and a result type variable captures its return:

~~~python
from collections.abc import Callable
from functools import wraps
from typing import ParamSpec, TypeVar


P = ParamSpec("P")
R = TypeVar("R")


def traced(function: Callable[P, R]) -> Callable[P, R]:
    @wraps(function)
    def wrapper(*args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> R:
        logger.debug(
            "call_started",
            extra={"function": function.__qualname__},
        )
        return function(*args, **kwargs)

    return wrapper
~~~

Static preservation does not make the decorator semantically transparent. It adds logging, cost, and possible confidentiality exposure. <code>wraps</code> copies selected metadata and establishes <code>__wrapped__</code>; it does not make object identity equal.

### 12.18.9 Protocols and structural subtyping

A <code>Protocol</code> defines required operations for static structural compatibility. Implementing classes need not inherit from it:

~~~python
from typing import Protocol


class ByteReader(Protocol):
    def read(self, size: int = -1) -> bytes: ...


def read_header(stream: ByteReader) -> bytes:
    header = stream.read(8)
    if len(header) != 8:
        raise EOFError("incomplete header")
    return header
~~~

Any statically compatible class can be supplied. The protocol should be as small as the client’s need, avoiding coupling to a concrete file class.

Protocols can contain writable attributes, properties, methods, and generic parameters. Mutation affects variance and safety. <code>@runtime_checkable</code> permits limited <code>isinstance</code> checks against member presence, but runtime checks do not validate full signatures or type annotations. Do not mistake them for schema validation.

> **Common misconception 12.64 — “Protocols formalise duck typing at runtime.”**  
> Their principal role is static structural checking. Optional runtime checks are shallow and obey separate documented rules.

### 12.18.10 Self types and fluent interfaces

The special type <code>Self</code> expresses that a result has the same most-specific class as the receiver:

~~~python
from typing import Self


class Query:
    def limit(self, count: int) -> Self:
        if count < 0:
            raise ValueError("limit cannot be negative")
        self._limit = count
        return self
~~~

A subclass call can remain typed as the subclass. <code>Self</code> is appropriate only when implementations return a compatible instance of their actual class. A factory that always returns the base class should annotate that base class instead.

Fluent mutation remains mutation. Returning <code>self</code> can make aliasing and partial configuration less visible; an immutable builder returning new values may offer clearer semantics.

### 12.18.11 Recursive and recursive-looking types

Data structures can refer to themselves:

~~~python
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Directory:
    name: str
    children: tuple["Directory", ...] = ()
~~~

The quoted reference is a forward reference under relevant runtime evaluation behaviour. Static checkers resolve it from scope. Recursive aliases can describe JSON-like structures, but unrestricted recursion can make error messages and narrowing difficult.

A common alias:

~~~python
type JsonValue = (
    None
    | bool
    | int
    | float
    | str
    | list["JsonValue"]
    | dict[str, "JsonValue"]
)
~~~

This models parsed JSON-like Python values but is not identical to the JSON standard: non-finite floats and arbitrary-size integer interoperability need runtime policy. Types are approximations of permitted structure, not the entire serialisation contract.

### 12.18.12 Types and exceptions

Annotations describe normal returns but Python’s ordinary function type does not enumerate checked exceptions. A callable annotated <code>-> Account</code> can still raise <code>OSError</code>, <code>ValueError</code>, or terminate. Document public failure policy and test it.

Some designs represent expected domain alternatives as a union, reserving exceptions for unexpected or boundary failures:

~~~python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Found:
    account: Account


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Missing:
    identifier: AccountId


type LookupResult = Found | Missing
~~~

This makes callers handle absence through narrowing, but it can create verbose wrappers. <code>Account | None</code> may be sufficient when one absence category exists. Type design should expose distinctions consumers must act upon.

> **Common misconception 12.65 — “If the type checker accepts a function, every return path has the declared runtime type.”**  
> The conclusion is bounded by the checker’s soundness, typed dependencies, suppressions, dynamic operations, and configuration. Exceptions and non-termination are also possible.


## 12.19 Static analysis with `mypy`

`mypy` is a static type checker for Python. Under configured strictness it can detect missing annotations, incompatible assignments, impossible member access, unchecked `None`, inconsistent overrides, and other flow errors.

Example defect:

```python
def label(account: Account | None) -> str:
    return account.name
```

A checker reports that `None` has no `name`. Repair by handling the state:

```python
def label(account: Account | None) -> str:
    if account is None:
        return "unknown"
    return account.name
```

The branch narrows the type and, more importantly, forces a domain policy for absence.

Run through the selected environment:

```text
python -m mypy src tests
```

Static typing is deliberately unsound in some practical respects and interacts with untyped code, `Any`, dynamic imports, decorators, mutation, variance, and reflection. A clean report is evidence under the checker version and configuration, not a proof of runtime correctness.

`Any` is an escape from type checking that propagates permissiveness. Use it at truly dynamic boundaries, validate, and convert into precise internal types. Do not use `Any` merely to silence a misunderstanding.

### 12.19.1 Static analysis is an abstract execution

A static analyser computes an approximation of possible program behaviours without running every concrete input. It represents sets of values and control states abstractly, propagates them through source, and emits a diagnostic when an operation is inconsistent with the model.

Exact prediction of arbitrary program behaviour is impossible in general. Useful analysers therefore trade:

- **soundness**: whether all behaviours of interest are conservatively included;
- **completeness**: whether every reported issue corresponds to a real defect;
- precision;
- termination;
- performance;
- compatibility with dynamic idioms.

Mypy is intentionally practical rather than a proof system for all Python execution. Untyped functions, <code>Any</code>, unchecked external data, reflection, native extensions, monkeypatching, and unsound library stubs create escape routes. The relevant goal is to reduce defect classes and make interfaces explicit, while retaining runtime tests and validation.

### 12.19.2 Configuration defines the claim

A statement such as “mypy passes” is incomplete without:

- mypy version;
- Python language target;
- modules/files included and excluded;
- import-following policy;
- enabled strictness and optional error codes;
- per-module overrides;
- plugin set;
- stub/package versions;
- cache assumptions if relevant.

Illustrative project configuration:

~~~toml
[tool.mypy]
python_version = "3.12"
files = ["src", "tests"]
strict = true
warn_unreachable = true
show_error_codes = true
pretty = true

[[tool.mypy.overrides]]
module = ["untyped_legacy.*"]
disallow_untyped_defs = false
~~~

The override acknowledges a migration boundary. It should be narrowed by module and tracked; a global relaxation lets new untyped code spread. Exact option names and their membership in <code>strict</code> are tool-version facts, so the checked-in configuration and official manual take precedence over this illustration.

Run analysis from the same declared environment as dependencies. A globally installed checker may see different stubs and Python target:

~~~text
python -m mypy
~~~

> **Common misconception 12.66 — “Strict mode is one timeless guarantee.”**  
> It is a versioned bundle of checker options plus project-specific scope. Record the effective configuration; new releases can add diagnostics or change inference.

### 12.19.3 Revealed types, casts, and assertions

Mypy’s <code>reveal_type</code> is a diagnostic form recognised during checking:

~~~python
def process(value: str | bytes) -> int:
    if isinstance(value, str):
        reveal_type(value)  # Revealed as str by the checker.
        return len(value.encode("utf-8"))
    reveal_type(value)  # Revealed as bytes.
    return len(value)
~~~

Depending on Python/runtime context, leaving diagnostic forms in executable code can have runtime consequences; use them temporarily or through documented typing facilities.

<code>cast(Target, value)</code> tells the checker to treat a value as <code>Target</code>. It returns the value unchanged at runtime and performs no validation:

~~~python
from typing import cast


account = cast(Account, cache.get(key))
~~~

This can silence a genuine <code>None</code> defect. Prefer a runtime check or redesign the cache API. A cast is justified when the programmer possesses evidence the checker cannot express; document that evidence near the cast.

An exhaustiveness helper:

~~~python
from typing import Never, assert_never


def outcome_code(result: SubmissionResult) -> int:
    match result:
        case Accepted():
            return 0
        case Rejected():
            return 1
        case unreachable:
            assert_never(unreachable)
~~~

If a new statically known variant is added, a capable checker reports that the final value is not <code>Never</code>. At runtime <code>assert_never</code> also raises if reached under the standard library’s implementation contract.

### 12.19.4 Error suppression is local unsoundness

A line-specific ignore typically has the form:

~~~python
legacy_value = plugin.load()  # type: ignore[no-untyped-call]
~~~

The error code documents which diagnostic is suppressed. The suppression should answer:

- why the analyser cannot prove safety;
- what runtime validation or test supplies evidence;
- who owns removal;
- what version or upstream fix changes the condition.

Warnings for unused ignores prevent obsolete suppressions from masking future errors. Never use a file-wide ignore to make an unfamiliar error disappear without studying the resulting unchecked surface.

Generated code may require configured exclusions or generated stubs, but its boundary still needs runtime and integration evidence.

### 12.19.5 Stubs and typed distributions

A **stub file**, with suffix <code>.pyi</code>, declares static interfaces without ordinary runtime implementations. Stub bodies commonly use ellipses. A stub can accompany a library, reside in a separate stub distribution, or be supplied by the checker ecosystem.

~~~python
class Client:
    def __init__(self, endpoint: str, *, timeout: float = ...) -> None: ...
    def fetch(self, identifier: str) -> bytes: ...
~~~

If the implementation accepts <code>timeout=None</code> but the stub does not, correctly working caller code can be rejected. If the stub claims <code>fetch</code> always returns bytes while runtime can return <code>None</code>, checked code can still fail. Stub accuracy is a maintained compatibility obligation.

PEP 561 defines mechanisms by which distributions advertise inline typing information, including a <code>py.typed</code> marker, and how type checkers resolve stub packages. Shipping annotations in source is not enough if consumers’ tools cannot discover the intended typed package under the relevant rules.

Test public stubs against runtime signatures with specialised tools where appropriate, and include representative downstream type-check cases.

### 12.19.6 Incremental adoption

For an untyped codebase, adding <code>Any</code> everywhere satisfies annotation-count metrics while providing little protection. Adopt types along dependency and trust boundaries:

1. configure a reproducible checker baseline;
2. type a coherent leaf module or domain model;
3. replace dynamic input with parsing at its boundary;
4. expose precise public interfaces;
5. prevent new untyped definitions in migrated modules;
6. ratchet diagnostics rather than accepting a permanent broad ignore list;
7. measure <code>Any</code> ingress and propagation.

A **type-coverage** percentage needs interpretation. Annotated declarations can still contain <code>Any</code>, wrong stubs, or unsound casts. Use it to monitor migration, not to claim correctness.

### 12.19.7 Checker disagreement and specification

Different checkers can infer differently while conforming to much of the shared typing specification. Some behaviour is intentionally checker-specific or evolving. A library intended for broad typed use should test against chosen supported checkers or state one normative target.

When a checker rejects code:

1. determine whether the runtime behaviour is valid;
2. determine whether the annotation expresses the intended contract;
3. consult the typing specification and tool documentation;
4. minimise a suspected checker defect;
5. redesign a needlessly dynamic interface where that improves the program;
6. otherwise use the narrowest justified suppression.

Do not distort a clear runtime design solely to satisfy an analyser’s incidental limitation; equally, do not dismiss a diagnostic merely because Python executes the happy case.

> **Common misconception 12.67 — “A type error is either definitely a runtime bug or merely tool noise.”**  
> It can reveal a real path, a contract mismatch, an imprecise stub, unsupported dynamic design, or analyser limitation. Classification requires reasoning and evidence.

## 12.20 Variance and mutable containers

Suppose `Cat` is a subtype of `Animal`. It might seem that `list[Cat]` should be usable as `list[Animal]`. That would be unsafe:

```python
def add_animal(animals: list[Animal]) -> None:
    animals.append(Dog())
```

If a `list[Cat]` were admitted, the function would insert a `Dog`, violating the original list’s element invariant. Mutable lists are therefore invariant in their type parameter under ordinary static typing.

Read-only producer interfaces can be covariant because callers cannot insert a broader value. `Sequence[Cat]` can often be used where `Sequence[Animal]` is required under the type system’s declared variance. **Variance** describes how a generic type’s subtype relationship follows or reverses its parameter subtype relation.

This is not abstract bureaucracy; it is mutation and substitutability expressed statically.

### 12.20.1 Covariance, contravariance, and invariance

Let <code>Cat</code> be a subtype of <code>Animal</code>. For a generic constructor <code>G</code>:

- **covariance** means <code>G[Cat]</code> is a subtype of <code>G[Animal]</code>;
- **contravariance** means <code>G[Animal]</code> is a subtype of <code>G[Cat]</code>;
- **invariance** means neither relationship follows merely from the parameter relation.

Producers tend towards covariance: a source of Cats can serve a consumer needing Animals. Consumers tend towards contravariance: a handler capable of every Animal can handle a Cat. Mutable structures both produce and consume values and are commonly invariant.

### Worked example 12.6D — Why callback parameters reverse

~~~python
from collections.abc import Callable


class Animal:
    pass


class Cat(Animal):
    pass


def describe_animal(animal: Animal) -> str:
    return animal.__class__.__name__


def render_cats(
    cats: list[Cat],
    describe: Callable[[Cat], str],
) -> list[str]:
    return [describe(cat) for cat in cats]


names = render_cats([Cat()], describe_animal)
~~~

<code>describe_animal</code> accepts any Animal, so it certainly accepts every Cat supplied by <code>render_cats</code>. A function accepting only a particular Cat subtype would not be safe where arbitrary Cats can arrive. Callable parameter types therefore vary contravariantly in the static model, while return types vary covariantly.

### 12.20.2 Read-only views and aliasing

Annotating a parameter as <code>Sequence[Animal]</code> prevents that function from calling list mutation methods through the parameter. It does not make the underlying object immutable. Another alias can mutate a list during or after the call.

If a stable snapshot is required, copy to an immutable representation:

~~~python
def snapshot_names(animals: Sequence[Animal]) -> tuple[str, ...]:
    snapshot = tuple(animals)
    return tuple(animal.name for animal in snapshot)
~~~

Even the tuple only freezes references; mutable Animal objects can change internally. “Read-only interface”, “shallow immutable container”, and “deep immutable value” are different contracts.

### 12.20.3 Variance declarations and inferred variance

Traditional <code>TypeVar</code> declarations can explicitly mark covariance or contravariance for user-defined generics. Newer generic syntax can permit checker inference under specified rules. The correct declaration follows how the parameter appears in public operations, not the author’s preferred assignability.

A supposedly covariant box with a setter is unsafe: after viewing <code>Box[Cat]</code> as <code>Box[Animal]</code>, a caller could insert a Dog. Hide mutation or remain invariant.

Private attributes, properties, and checker conventions can influence inferred variance. Treat unexpected inference as a reason to inspect interface semantics, not merely to force a flag.

> **Common misconception 12.68 — “Immutable syntax makes a generic covariant.”**  
> Variance follows substitutability of the exposed interface. Runtime immutability, static read-only access, and absence of writable aliases are related but distinct facts.

## 12.21 Continuous integration

**Continuous integration** (**CI**) is the practice and automation of frequently combining changes and running repeatable verification. A CI pipeline commonly performs:

1. clean checkout;
2. declared interpreter/tool setup;
3. dependency installation from controlled inputs;
4. formatting or format check;
5. lint and static analysis;
6. unit and integration tests;
7. build of distributable artefacts;
8. clean-artefact smoke tests;
9. security or licence checks under policy;
10. publication only from authorised reviewed state.

CI does not make tests more true. It removes dependence on one developer’s hidden environment and makes the evidence repeatable for every change.

A failing CI job should preserve logs, versions, and artefacts needed to reproduce the failure. Automatically rerunning until green can conceal nondeterminism; a flaky test is an uncontrolled experiment and requires diagnosis.

### 12.21.1 A pipeline is a dependency graph

A CI pipeline is better modelled as a directed acyclic graph of jobs than as one long script. A node consumes declared inputs, executes in an environment, and produces status and artefacts. An edge states that a downstream job requires an upstream result.

For example:

~~~text
source checkout
    -> source-format check
    -> lint
    -> static types
    -> unit tests
    -> integration tests
    -> build sdist and wheel
    -> install-wheel smoke test
    -> provenance and publication
~~~

Independent jobs can run concurrently, while publication depends on every required gate. The apparent sequence is not itself evidence: each node must fail on tool failure, retain meaningful output, and use exactly the source revision claimed.

A command hidden behind <code>|| true</code>, a shell pipeline that returns only the final command’s status, or a test runner configured to accept zero tests can produce false green. CI code deserves the same review as production code because it defines the evidence and release authority.

### 12.21.2 Clean construction and environmental parity

A fresh runner detects undeclared dependencies that a long-lived developer machine supplies accidentally: an environment variable, global package, cached generated file, local database schema, or earlier build output.

“Works in CI” still does not guarantee production parity. Compare:

- operating system and CPU architecture;
- Python implementation and patch version;
- dependency resolution;
- native libraries;
- locale, timezone, and filesystem;
- permission model;
- network topology and proxies;
- service versions and schemas;
- resource limits;
- secrets and identity.

Exact identity is rarely attainable or desirable; tests need controlled fidelity for the relevant claim. A Linux CI runner cannot establish Windows path behaviour. A matrix can test declared supported platforms and Python versions, with expensive cases scheduled under risk policy.

### 12.21.3 Matrices, fail-fast, and evidence preservation

A **test matrix** evaluates combinations such as Python 3.12/3.13, Linux/Windows/macOS, and minimum/latest dependencies. The Cartesian product can become expensive. Select combinations deliberately:

- every supported Python version on a primary platform;
- every supported platform on a primary Python version;
- minimum dependency versions where compatibility is promised;
- latest compatible dependencies to detect upcoming conflict;
- special native or optional features in targeted jobs.

This “covering” matrix omits some interactions. Add a full matrix periodically or when a risk suggests one.

Fail-fast saves resources after one failure but can discard independent diagnostic evidence. For a small matrix, allowing remaining jobs to finish can show whether failure is platform-specific. For an expensive deployment stage, stopping immediately is safer. Choose by cost and information value.

### Worked example 12.6E — Distinguish source tests from artefact tests

An illustrative local sequence:

~~~text
python -m pytest
python -m mypy
python -m build
python -m venv .wheel-test
.wheel-test/bin/python -m pip install --no-deps dist/example_pkg-1.4.0-py3-none-any.whl
.wheel-test/bin/python -c "import example_pkg; print(example_pkg.__version__)"
~~~

Platform-specific activation paths differ, and a real pipeline should create its environment in disposable workspace rather than a retained project path. The conceptual distinction is critical:

- tests against the checkout establish source-tree behaviour;
- installation of the built wheel establishes that packaging included the necessary modules, metadata, data files, and entry points;
- an import/smoke test in a directory outside the repository avoids accidental imports from the working tree.

A package can pass every source test and produce a broken wheel. Build artefacts are subjects of verification, not by-products assumed correct.

> **Common misconception 12.69 — “CI reproduces the developer’s commands on a server.”**  
> A sound pipeline reconstructs declared state, evaluates policy, preserves evidence, and authorises later actions. Its identity, permissions, artefacts, and failure semantics are part of the engineered system.

### 12.21.4 Caches and reproducibility

CI caches trade isolation for speed. A cache key should incorporate every input affecting cached output: operating system, architecture, Python ABI, dependency declaration or lock hash, tool version, and relevant build options. An overly broad key can reuse incompatible artefacts; an overly narrow key wastes storage.

Treat caches as untrusted accelerators. A clean build without cache should succeed, and cache corruption should cause a miss or rebuild rather than silently alter a release. Do not cache secrets. Control who can populate caches used by privileged release jobs, because cache poisoning can cross trust boundaries.

A **reproducible build** yields bit-for-bit identical output from the same declared source and build inputs under the specified process. Deterministic timestamps, file order, paths, locale, compression, and dependency tooling all matter. Reproducibility allows independent parties to compare artefacts, but identical malicious builds remain malicious; source and build-environment trust still matter.

### 12.21.5 Pipeline identity and least privilege

CI executes repository-controlled code, often automatically on contributions. Grant untrusted change jobs the least privilege:

- read-only source access;
- no production credentials;
- no release-signing key;
- no ability to alter protected policy;
- bounded network and compute where feasible;
- isolated caches from privileged branches.
