| (Theta(2^n)) | enumerate every subset |
| (Theta(n!)) | enumerate every permutation |

Logarithm base differs only by a constant factor for asymptotic classification. Binary search naturally uses base two because each comparison halves the remaining interval.

Polynomial growth can still be impractical; exponential algorithms can be appropriate for small fixed (n), pruned search, or unavoidable exact problems. Complexity informs design but does not decide requirements.

### 13.3.1 A hierarchy, not a stopwatch

For sufficiently large \(n\), the familiar hierarchy is

\[
1
\prec \log n
\prec n^\alpha
\prec n
\prec n\log n
\prec n^2
\prec n^3
\prec c^n
\prec n!
\prec n^n,
\]

where \(0<\alpha<1\), \(c>1\), and \(f\prec g\) here means \(f\in o(g)\). The ordering is asymptotic. It makes no assertion about the crossing point: a cubic algorithm with small constants may outperform a linear one with costly remote I/O for all deployed sizes.

A thought experiment nevertheless reveals scale. If an abstract machine performs \(10^8\) charged operations per second, an \(n^2\) procedure at \(n=10^6\) requires \(10^{12}\) operations, or approximately \(10^4\) seconds under the deliberately unrealistic assumption of uniform operations. A \(2^n\) procedure crosses \(10^{12}\) operations near \(n=40\). The arithmetic is not a benchmark; it exposes why growth rate constrains feasible input size.

The most relevant size is the largest admitted by the service contract, not the size used in a demonstration. If a batch currently contains 200 items but an unbounded API accepts 200,000, a quadratic duplicate check carries operational risk even if today’s timing appears negligible.

> **Common misconception 13.13 — “A better asymptotic class is always faster.”**  
> Growth classes compare eventual scaling under a model. Constants, locality, vectorised native work, allocation, input distribution, and maximum deployed size decide measured performance within the relevant range.

### 13.3.2 Output-sensitive and parameterised bounds

An **output-sensitive algorithm** expresses its cost partly in terms of output size. Reporting every match between two collections may inherently require \(\Omega(z)\) time merely to emit \(z\) matches. A bound such as \(O((n+m)\log n+z)\) distinguishes search overhead from production of results.

A **parameterised analysis** isolates a structural parameter \(k\) in addition to total input size \(n\). A procedure with cost

\[
O(2^k n^3)
\]

is exponential in \(k\) but polynomial in \(n\). It may be practical when \(k\) is guaranteed small. A problem is **fixed-parameter tractable** with respect to \(k\) if it admits a bound \(f(k)n^{O(1)}\) for some computable function \(f\). This vocabulary will be used only as a classification in this chapter; parameterised-complexity theory is substantially deeper.

Input-sensitive bounds can also use disorder measures. Insertion sort takes \(\Theta(n+I)\) movements and comparisons under suitable counting, where \(I\) is the number of **inversions**—pairs out of desired order. This explains its adaptiveness more precisely than giving only quadratic worst-case cost.

> **Common misconception 13.14 — “Exponential dependence makes an algorithm categorically useless.”**  
> Dependence on a small parameter, aggressive pruning, approximation, or tiny bounded instances can make exponential worst-case methods appropriate. The bound must identify which quantity is in the exponent.

### 13.3.3 Polynomial does not mean practical

An algorithm is commonly called **polynomial-time** when its worst-case cost is bounded by \(O(n^k)\) for some fixed \(k\), under a conventional machine and encoded input length. This boundary is theoretically significant because polynomial algorithms compose and are comparatively robust under reasonable machine simulations. It is not a synonym for feasible.

\(n^{100}\) is polynomial and almost never usable for non-trivial \(n\). An \(O(n^3)\) dense matrix algorithm may be entirely appropriate for \(n=200\) and prohibitive for \(n=10^6\). A pseudo-polynomial \(O(nT)\) dynamic program may be excellent when numeric target \(T\) is below ten thousand despite not being polynomial in \(\log T\).

Likewise, worst-case exponential algorithms can solve large structured instances while failing on much smaller adversarial ones. **Combinatorial explosion** refers to a search space whose number of candidates grows exponentially or faster; it identifies a scaling mechanism, not an observed duration.

> **Common misconception 13.15 — “Polynomial-time means efficient in practice.”**  
> Polynomial-time is a coarse theoretical tractability category. Exponent, constants, representation, memory traffic, input structure, and operational limits remain decisive.

## 13.4 Amortised analysis

Amortised analysis bounds the total cost across a sequence without assuming random inputs. A dynamic array append may cost 1 when capacity remains and proportional to current length when resizing. If capacity grows geometrically, each existing reference participates in only a bounded number of copies relative to later appends.

For capacities 1, 2, 4, 8, ..., reaching (n) elements copies fewer than

\[
1+2+4+\cdots+\frac{n}{2}<n
\]

existing elements across resizes, plus (n) ordinary writes. Total work is (O(n)), so average charge across (n) appends is amortised (O(1)).

Amortised is not probabilistic and does not promise each operation is cheap. Real-time systems may reject an occasional (O(n)) pause even when throughput is excellent.

### 13.4.1 Aggregate analysis

The **aggregate method** bounds the total cost \(T(n)\) of a sequence of \(n\) operations and divides by \(n\). Consider a stack supporting <code>push</code>, <code>pop</code>, and <code>clear</code>, where <code>clear</code> pops every current item:

~~~python
class ClearingStack:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._items: list[int] = []

    def push(self, item: int) -> None:
        self._items.append(item)

    def pop(self) -> int:
        return self._items.pop()

    def clear(self) -> None:
        while self._items:
            self._items.pop()
~~~

One <code>clear</code> may cost \(\Theta(n)\), but across any sequence beginning empty, an item can be popped only after it was pushed and at most once before being pushed again. There are at most \(n\) pushes and at most \(n\) removals among \(n\) public operations. Ignoring dynamic-array resizing already analysed separately, total abstract stack work is \(O(n)\), hence \(O(1)\) amortised per operation.

This conclusion applies to the entire operation set and the stated initial condition. Starting with \(m\) pre-existing elements gives \(O(n+m)\) total removal work. Amortised claims must identify the sequences over which cost is spread.

### 13.4.2 The accounting method

The **accounting method** assigns an artificial **amortised charge** to each operation. Cheap operations may be overcharged; the surplus is stored as conceptual credit that pays for later expensive operations. Credits must never become negative if the proof is to establish an upper bound.

For the clearing stack, charge 2 units to <code>push</code>: one pays for insertion and one is stored on the pushed item. Charge 0 or 1 to removal depending on the primitive convention; the stored credit pays for the item’s eventual pop. Because every removable item carries its credit, a mass clear is prepaid.

For a table that doubles when full, a constant charge on each insertion can pay for its own write and reserve credits for future reference copies. Exact credit placement depends on the growth rule. The accounting currency is not real time or memory; it is a proof device whose total dominates actual charged work.

> **Common misconception 13.16 — “Amortised cost is average cost over random inputs.”**  
> Amortised analysis places a deterministic bound on every admitted operation sequence as a whole. It requires no probability distribution.

### 13.4.3 The potential method

The **potential method** summarises stored credit with a non-negative function \(\Phi(D)\) of data-structure state \(D\). If operation \(i\) changes state \(D_{i-1}\) to \(D_i\) with actual cost \(c_i\), define amortised cost

\[
\widehat c_i
=c_i+\Phi(D_i)-\Phi(D_{i-1}).
\]

Summing telescopes:

\[
\sum_{i=1}^n\widehat c_i
=
\sum_{i=1}^n c_i+\Phi(D_n)-\Phi(D_0).
\]

If \(\Phi(D_0)=0\) and \(\Phi(D_n)\ge0\), then total actual cost does not exceed total amortised cost.

For a binary counter, represent a non-negative integer as bits. Increment flips trailing ones to zero and the following zero to one. Let actual cost be the number of flipped bits and potential be the number of one bits. If an increment encounters \(t\) trailing ones, actual cost is \(t+1\); potential changes by \(1-t\). Therefore

\[
\widehat c=(t+1)+(1-t)=2.
\]

Every increment has amortised cost at most 2 although incrementing \(0111\ldots1\) flips many bits.

~~~python
def increment_little_endian(bits: list[int]) -> None:
    index = 0
    while index < len(bits) and bits[index] == 1:
        bits[index] = 0
        index += 1
    if index == len(bits):
        bits.append(1)
    else:
        bits[index] = 1
~~~

The list stores the least significant bit first. Its representation invariant requires every entry to be 0 or 1 and, if canonical representation is required, the final bit of a non-empty list to be 1. The amortised proof concerns bit flips; list resizing contributes its own amortised cost.

> **Common misconception 13.17 — “An amortised \(O(1)\) operation never pauses for linear work.”**  
> Individual operations may remain expensive. Amortised bounds control total cost across a sequence, not per-operation latency.

### 13.4.4 Resizing in both directions

A dynamic table that grows at load 1 and shrinks immediately whenever one element is removed can **thrash**: alternating insert and delete around the boundary repeatedly copies the table. A design uses hysteresis—different thresholds for growth and shrinkage. For example, double when full but halve only when occupancy falls below one quarter. The unused interval absorbs oscillation.

A suitable potential rises as the table approaches either resize threshold and falls when a resize restores slack. This establishes constant amortised update cost while keeping capacity within a constant factor of logical size. It also illustrates a general principle: an amortised guarantee depends on policy, not merely on the data structure’s name.

CPython’s list growth and shrinkage policies are implementation details rather than Python language guarantees. Their exact constants can change across releases. The portable semantic fact is that a list is a mutable sequence; complexity statements about its current implementation should be labelled and verified against the relevant implementation.

> **Common misconception 13.18 — “Amortised analysis hides an assumption about favourable input order.”**  
> A valid amortised proof covers every sequence satisfying its preconditions. A policy vulnerable to an adversarial oscillation has not earned the claimed bound.

## 13.5 Correctness through invariants and induction

Mathematical **induction** proves a claim for non-negative integers by establishing a base case and showing that truth for an arbitrary (k) implies truth for (k+1). A loop-invariant proof has the same structure across iterations: initialisation, maintenance, and termination.

For recursive algorithms, **structural induction** follows the constructors of the input structure. To prove a property for a binary tree, establish it for the empty tree and show that if it holds for left and right subtrees, it holds for a node combining them.

Correctness proof stages:

1. state precondition and postcondition;
2. choose an invariant strong enough to imply the postcondition;
3. prove it before the first iteration;
4. prove every body path preserves it;
5. prove termination separately;
6. combine exit condition and invariant.

An invariant can be true but useless. “The processed count is non-negative” is preserved by a maximum scan but does not imply the returned value is maximal.

### 13.5.1 Partial and total correctness

A program is **partially correct** with respect to precondition \(P\) and postcondition \(Q\) when: if execution begins in a state satisfying \(P\) and terminates, the final state satisfies \(Q\). **Total correctness** adds termination for every state satisfying \(P\).

This distinction prevents a non-terminating program from being called correct merely because it never returns a wrong answer. A proof of total correctness commonly contains:

1. a safety argument: an invariant and exit condition establish \(Q\);
2. a progress argument: a **variant** or **ranking function** takes values in a well-founded set and strictly decreases.

A relation is **well-founded** when it admits no infinite descending chain. Non-negative integers under \(>\) are the usual choice. Saying only that a numeric variant decreases is insufficient if it can descend without bound through negative integers or real values.

> **Common misconception 13.19 — “A loop invariant proves termination.”**  
> An invariant constrains reachable states. Termination requires a separate progress argument, usually a well-founded decreasing variant.

### Worked example 13.5A — Prove a maximum scan

~~~python
from collections.abc import Sequence
from typing import TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")


def maximum(values: Sequence[T]) -> T:
    if not values:
        raise ValueError("maximum requires a non-empty sequence")

    best = values[0]
    index = 1
    while index < len(values):
        if values[index] > best:
            best = values[index]
        index += 1
    return best
~~~

The annotation does not statically express orderability; the semantic precondition is that comparisons used by the function form a suitable total preorder and do not fail. Let \(n=\lvert values\rvert\).

The loop invariant is:

\[
1\le index\le n
\quad\text{and}\quad
best\text{ is a maximum of }values[0:index].
\]

**Initialisation.** Before the loop, \(index=1\), and <code>best</code> is the sole element of the one-element prefix.

**Maintenance.** Assume the invariant at loop entry. Comparing \(values[index]\) with <code>best</code> and retaining the larger produces a maximum of the prefix ending at that position. Incrementing <code>index</code> makes that prefix precisely <code>values[0:index]</code> for the next entry.

**Termination.** The variant \(n-index\) is a non-negative integer at each loop entry and decreases by one. At exit \(index=n\). Combining this with the invariant proves that <code>best</code> is a maximum of the entire sequence.

The function performs exactly \(n-1\) greater-than comparisons for \(n>0\), regardless of value order. Its comparison complexity is therefore \(\Theta(n)\), and an adversary argument shows this is optimal in the comparison model for finding a maximum: every non-maximum candidate must lose at least one comparison.

### 13.5.2 Preconditions are part of the theorem

A proof does not establish correctness beyond its hypotheses. Binary search’s theorem requires sorted input; Dijkstra’s theorem requires non-negative edge weights; a hash table requires stable hashes while keys are stored. Code may enforce a precondition, document it, or rely on a type or constructor that makes violations unrepresentable.

A **postcondition** describes the result and relevant state after successful completion. For an in-place sort it must cover both order and preservation:

\[
\forall i<j:\ key(a_i)\le key(a_j)
\]

and the output must be a permutation of the input. Proving only order would permit replacing the entire list with repeated copies of its minimum.

A **frame condition** states what is not modified. If a procedure promises to rearrange one list without mutating its elements or external collections, that non-interference belongs to the specification.

Exceptions also require specification. “Returns the maximum” leaves undefined what happens on an empty input or failed comparison. The implementation above explicitly raises <code>ValueError</code> for emptiness but can propagate arbitrary comparison exceptions. Stronger contracts would need to specify mutation state on failure.

> **Common misconception 13.20 — “If tests pass, the algorithm is proven correct.”**  
> Tests establish observations for selected executions. A proof covers every instance satisfying stated preconditions, subject to the validity of its model and premises. Tests remain essential for implementation errors and premise violations.

### 13.5.3 Weakening, strengthening, and proof usefulness

A predicate \(A\) is **stronger** than \(B\) when \(A\Rightarrow B\). Strengthening an invariant makes more claims and may allow the postcondition to follow, but makes initialisation and preservation harder to prove. Weakening does the reverse.

For insertion sort, “the prefix is sorted” is not by itself sufficient to prove permutation preservation. A useful invariant states both:

1. the processed prefix is sorted;
2. it contains exactly the multiset of elements originally in that prefix.

The word **multiset** denotes a collection retaining multiplicity without order. Ordinary set equality would lose duplicates and could not establish that two equal-valued input records remain represented twice.

Proof discovery often proceeds backwards from the postcondition. Ask what must be true at loop exit, replace the final bound with the current loop index, and add the facts needed to preserve that statement. This is a design technique, not an automatic recipe.

> **Common misconception 13.21 — “The strongest possible invariant is always best.”**  
> An unnecessarily strong claim can be false or needlessly difficult. The goal is an inductive assertion strong enough, together with exit conditions, to imply the required postcondition.

### 13.5.4 Ordinary, strong, and structural induction

**Ordinary induction** assumes \(P(k)\) to prove \(P(k+1)\). **Strong induction** assumes every earlier case \(P(0),\ldots,P(k)\) to prove \(P(k+1)\). The two principles have equal logical power over natural numbers, but strong induction often matches algorithms with several possible subproblem sizes.

To prove merge sort correct for every list length \(n\), use strong induction:

- base: lengths 0 and 1 are already sorted;
- hypothesis: recursive calls correctly sort every list shorter than \(n\);
- step: both halves are shorter than \(n\), so each recursive result is sorted and a permutation of its half; the verified merge operation produces a sorted permutation of their concatenation.

Structural induction follows data constructors rather than a numeric counter. For the binary-tree definition “empty, or a node with two binary trees”, prove the empty case and then prove the node case assuming the claim for both children. This form aligns with recursive traversals.

A recursive implementation additionally needs a termination argument. Every recursive call must move to a smaller value under a well-founded measure. “Calls itself on something that looks simpler” is insufficient, especially when aliasing or cyclic structures are possible.

> **Common misconception 13.22 — “Recursion is correct because it eventually reaches the base case.”**  
> One must prove that every admitted call moves toward a base case and that combining correct subresults establishes the current result.

### 13.5.5 Counterexamples and minimal falsification

A universal algorithmic claim is disproved by one admitted counterexample. Constructing a **minimal counterexample**—one smallest under a chosen size measure—often reveals the broken invariant.

Suppose an attempted binary search updates <code>high = middle - 1</code> while maintaining a half-open interval <code>[low, high)</code>. A target at position <code>middle - 1</code> can be discarded because <code>high</code> itself is already excluded. Very small arrays expose the disagreement among interval convention, update, and exit condition.

Property-based testing operationalises counterexample search by generating many inputs and shrinking failures. It does not turn finite execution into a mathematical proof, but it complements proof: the proof identifies intended invariants; generated tests challenge the implementation and assumptions.

For optimisation algorithms, a counterexample must distinguish feasibility from optimality. A greedy schedule can produce a valid schedule yet select fewer intervals than possible. Showing only that its output violates no constraints does not test the optimality theorem.

> **Common misconception 13.23 — “A plausible explanation of the main idea is a correctness proof.”**  
> A proof must cover initial conditions, every transition, termination, preservation of required data, and all admitted boundary cases. An unexamined phrase such as “clearly optimal” often hides the disputed step.

## 13.6 Linear search

Linear search applies to an arbitrary iterable and makes no sortedness assumption.

```python
from collections.abc import Iterable
from typing import TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")


def find_index(values: Iterable[T], target: T) -> int | None:
    for index, value in enumerate(values):
        if value == target:
            return index
    return None
```

Invariant: before each comparison at index (i), none of the prior produced values at indices (0\ldots i-1) equals target. If a match is returned, it is the first index. On finite exhaustion, no item equals target.

Time is (O(n)) equality operations in the worst case. The function supports one-pass iterables and does not retain them. A set or dictionary can make repeated membership queries expected (O(1)) after (O(n)) preprocessing and memory, but building one for a single query may add cost and discard order/duplicate information.

### 13.6.1 The search contract determines the answer

“Find \(x\)” can denote several problems:

- decide whether any equal value exists;
- return the first position in encounter order;
- return every matching position;
- return one matching object;
- count matches;
- find a value satisfying a predicate rather than equality;
- find the minimum-cost or nearest match.

These specifications have different outputs and sometimes different lower bounds. A Boolean membership test may terminate at the first match. Enumerating every match has an \(\Omega(z)\) output cost for \(z\) results. Returning the first position presupposes a defined encounter order; a mathematical set has none, although a concrete Python set produces some iteration sequence that is not a portable ordering contract.

For a general iterable, <code>find_index</code> consumes values. If the iterable is an iterator, a failed search exhausts it and a successful search leaves it positioned after the match:

~~~python
stream = iter([10, 20, 30, 40])
assert find_index(stream, 30) == 2
assert list(stream) == [40]
~~~

Consumption is an observable effect and belongs in the function’s contract. A sequence can be revisited; an iterator represents evolving traversal state.

Equality also has cost and semantics. Searching a list of length-\(m\) strings can require \(O(nm)\) character work in a worst-case model, even though it performs \(n\) equality operations. User-defined equality can raise an exception or mutate state. The algorithmic comparison count remains useful, but it is not a complete wall-clock model.

> **Common misconception 13.24 — “Linear search has no preconditions.”**  
> It avoids sortedness, but still depends on finite traversal when a no-match result is expected, meaningful equality or predicate behaviour, and an understood consumption policy.

### 13.6.2 Predicate search and retained witnesses

A **witness** is an object demonstrating that a condition holds. Returning a witness often carries more information than returning <code>True</code>:

~~~python
from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable
from typing import TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")


def first_where(
    values: Iterable[T],
    predicate: Callable[[T], bool],
) -> T | None:
    for value in values:
        if predicate(value):
            return value
    return None
~~~

This interface is ambiguous when <code>None</code> can itself be an element satisfying the predicate. One remedy is to raise on absence; another returns an explicit tagged result. A sentinel object can distinguish the cases internally:

~~~python
_MISSING = object()


def first_where_or(
    values: Iterable[T],
    predicate: Callable[[T], bool],
    default: object = _MISSING,
) -> T | object:
    for value in values:
        if predicate(value):
            return value
    if default is _MISSING:
        raise LookupError("no matching value")
    return default
~~~

The sentinel is tested by identity because its purpose is to be one unique object, not a value equal to some input. This revisits Chapter 5’s distinction between identity and equality.

The invariant is: before each iteration, no previously encountered value satisfies <code>predicate</code>. If the call returns a value, that value satisfies the predicate and is the earliest such witness. If finite iteration ends, the invariant covers every element and justifies absence.

### 13.6.3 Sentinels as an algorithmic transformation

In low-level presentations, **sentinel linear search** temporarily places the target at the final position so that the loop needs no bounds check at each step. After finding a match, it determines whether the match was original or the sentinel. This can reduce a constant factor in a machine model, but it mutates storage and demands restoration even if comparison fails.

In ordinary Python, the transformation is rarely justified: interpreter dispatch and equality dominate the saved branch, mutation may violate caller expectations, and a one-pass iterable has no writable last cell. The example remains conceptually useful because it shows that algorithms trade preconditions and mutation for operation count.

~~~python
def sentinel_find(values: list[int], target: int) -> int | None:
    if not values:
        return None

    final = values[-1]
    values[-1] = target
    index = 0
    try:
        while values[index] != target:
            index += 1
    finally:
        values[-1] = final

    if index < len(values) - 1 or final == target:
        return index
    return None
~~~

The <code>finally</code> suite restores the final reference if equality raises. This supplies only a basic exception-safety guarantee: arbitrary equality code could mutate the list in other ways. The function is pedagogical, not a recommendation over a straightforward <code>for</code> loop.

> **Common misconception 13.25 — “Fewer source-level tests necessarily means faster Python.”**  
> An abstract operation saving must survive interpreter, method-dispatch, allocation, cache, and mutation costs. Measure a semantically equivalent implementation on representative workloads.

### 13.6.4 Preprocess when questions repeat

For one membership query over \(n\) unsorted values, a scan uses \(O(n)\) time and \(O(1)\) auxiliary storage. For \(q\) queries it uses \(O(qn)\) worst-case comparisons. Preprocessing changes the trade:

| Representation | Build | One query | Extra storage | Preserves multiplicity/order? |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| original sequence | none | \(O(n)\) | \(O(1)\) | yes |
| sorted copy + binary search | \(O(n\log n)\) | \(O(\log n)\) | \(O(n)\) | yes, in sorted rather than original order |
| hash set | expected \(O(n)\) | expected \(O(1)\) | \(O(n)\) | no |
| key-to-indices dictionary | expected \(O(n)\) | expected \(O(1+z)\) | \(O(n)\) | yes, if indices are stored |

The break-even point depends on constants, key costs, mutation frequency, and required outputs. If the source changes, an index must be updated or rebuilt; stale derived data is a correctness fault, not merely a performance issue.

A maintained summary can answer specialised searches. Keeping a minimum makes minimum retrieval \(O(1)\), but updating after arbitrary deletion may require a heap, balanced tree, counts map, or full rescan. No representation accelerates every operation simultaneously.

> **Common misconception 13.26 — “A hash set makes searching \(O(1)\), so conversion is always an improvement.”**  
> It adds construction and memory, offers expected rather than unconditional constant lookup, requires hashable stable keys, and discards information unless that information is stored separately.

## 13.7 Binary search

Binary search requires a sorted random-access sequence under a coherent ordering. Maintain a half-open candidate interval `[low, high)`.

```python
from collections.abc import Sequence


def binary_search(values: Sequence[int], target: int) -> int | None:
    low = 0
    high = len(values)

    while low < high:
        middle = low + (high - low) // 2
        candidate = values[middle]

        if candidate < target:
            low = middle + 1
        elif candidate > target:
            high = middle
        else:
            return middle

    return None
```

Invariant:

- (0\leq low\leq high\leq n);
- if target occurs in the sequence, at least one occurrence remains in `[low, high)`.

When `candidate < target`, sortedness proves positions through `middle` cannot contain target, so `low = middle + 1` preserves the candidate claim. When greater, positions from `middle` onward cannot be target, so `high = middle` preserves it. Equality returns a valid occurrence.

Variant is interval length `high - low`. Every non-returning iteration strictly reduces it. On exit it is zero; by the invariant no occurrence exists.

Each iteration approximately halves the interval, yielding (Theta(\log n)) comparisons. Indexing must be sufficiently direct; binary search over a linked list does not gain the same time bound because finding the middle costs linear traversal.

### Bound variants

Finding the first insertion position uses a related invariant:

```python
def lower_bound(values: Sequence[int], target: int) -> int:
    low = 0
    high = len(values)
    while low < high:
        middle = low + (high - low) // 2
        if values[middle] < target:
            low = middle + 1
        else:
            high = middle
    return low
```

At exit, all positions before `low` contain values less than target; all at or after contain values at least target. This returns the first equal occurrence when present and insertion point otherwise.

Off-by-one errors arise when interval convention, midpoint, update, and exit condition do not agree. Copying individual lines between closed and half-open variants breaks the proof.

### 13.7.1 Partition points unify the variants

Binary search is more general than equality lookup. Let a finite random-access domain be divided by a monotone Boolean predicate:

\[
\underbrace{False,\ldots,False}_{\text{possibly empty}},
\underbrace{True,\ldots,True}_{\text{possibly empty}}.
\]

The **partition point** is the first position where the predicate is true, or \(n\) if it is never true. Maintain

- every index below <code>low</code> is known false;
- every index at or above <code>high</code> is known true;
- the unknown interval is <code>[low, high)</code>.

At initialisation the known regions are empty, so the invariant holds without inspecting an element.

~~~python
from collections.abc import Callable


def first_true(length: int, predicate: Callable[[int], bool]) -> int:
    low = 0
    high = length

    while low < high:
        middle = low + (high - low) // 2
        if predicate(middle):
            high = middle
        else:
            low = middle + 1

    return low
~~~

If the predicate is not monotone, the invariant’s inference is invalid: observing true at <code>middle</code> would not prove all later positions true. The function cannot detect arbitrary violations without sacrificing the logarithmic advantage by checking the domain.

Lower bound uses <code>predicate(i) = values[i] &gt;= target</code>. Upper bound—the first index strictly greater than target—uses <code>values[i] &gt; target</code>. Equal values then occupy the half-open interval <code>[lower_bound, upper_bound)</code>.

~~~python
from collections.abc import Sequence


def upper_bound(values: Sequence[int], target: int) -> int:
    return first_true(
        len(values),
        lambda index: values[index] > target,
    )


def equal_range(values: Sequence[int], target: int) -> range:
    left = first_true(
        len(values),
        lambda index: values[index] >= target,
    )
    right = first_true(
        len(values),
        lambda index: values[index] > target,
    )
    return range(left, right)
~~~

The two searches use at most \(O(\log n)\) key comparisons and return all matching positions symbolically as a range. Materialising the matching elements additionally costs \(\Theta(z)\) for \(z\) matches.

> **Common misconception 13.27 — “Binary search is fundamentally a search for equality.”**  
> Its core operation locates a boundary in a monotone partition. Equality lookup is derived by choosing an ordering predicate and interpreting the boundary.

### 13.7.2 Exact comparison count and information

Each unsuccessful iteration reduces unknown interval length \(s>0\) to at most \(\lfloor s/2\rfloor\). After \(k\) iterations its length is at most \(\lfloor n/2^k\rfloor\). It reaches zero once \(2^k>n\), giving at most \(\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1\) predicate evaluations for \(n>0\).

There is a matching comparison lower bound for locating one among \(n+1\) insertion gaps with binary yes/no outcomes. A decision tree of height \(h\) distinguishes at most \(2^h\) outcomes, so \(2^h\ge n+1\) and

\[
h\ge\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil.
\]

Binary search is therefore asymptotically optimal for this task in the binary-comparison, random-access model. The qualification matters: interpolation search can exploit numeric distribution assumptions, and a maintained direct-address table can answer different key domains by indexing.

The familiar midpoint formula <code>(low + high) // 2</code> is safe for Python integers because they do not overflow at a fixed word boundary. The alternative <code>low + (high - low) // 2</code> remains valuable because it generalises to fixed-width languages and makes interval dependence explicit.

> **Common misconception 13.28 — “Python’s arbitrary-size integers remove binary-search boundary errors.”**  
> They remove one overflow hazard. Inconsistent interval conventions, non-shrinking updates, invalid sortedness, and incoherent comparisons remain.

### 13.7.3 The standard <code>bisect</code> operations

The standard-library <code>bisect</code> module supplies partition-point operations over sorted sequences:

~~~python
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right, insort_left

scores = [10, 20, 20, 20, 40]

first = bisect_left(scores, 20)
after = bisect_right(scores, 20)
assert (first, after) == (1, 4)
assert scores[first:after] == [20, 20, 20]

insort_left(scores, 30)
assert scores == [10, 20, 20, 20, 30, 40]
~~~

The search is \(O(\log n)\), but insertion into a Python list remains \(O(n)\) because later references must move. The module documentation explicitly notes that the linear insertion step dominates. A logarithmic insertion-point search does not turn a dynamic array into a logarithmic-update ordered structure.

Python 3.10 and later accept a <code>key</code> parameter for relevant bisect functions. The key is applied to sequence elements during search; for insertion functions it is also used to search for the new value but not to transform the value stored. Repeated calls may recompute keys. If key extraction is expensive, maintain a parallel key list or cache results, while preserving synchronisation with the records.

The module’s functions use less-than ordering rather than calling equality to find a value. This permits insertion boundaries even for types whose ordering notion is more useful than equality, but it still requires the sequence to be sorted consistently with the same key and ordering.

The official documentation also warns that the functions are not thread-safe for concurrent operations on the same sequence. Synchronisation and mutation discipline remain the caller’s responsibility.

> **Common misconception 13.29 — “Using <code>bisect.insort</code> gives \(O(\log n)\) insertion into a list.”**  
> Locating the position is logarithmic; shifting the list suffix is linear. The complete insertion is \(O(n)\).

### Worked example 13.7A — Search an implicit answer space

Suppose a production line can make a known number of units per hour for each machine. Find the minimum integer hours needed to make at least a target number of units. The answer predicate “capacity by \(h\) hours is at least target” is monotone.

~~~python
def minimum_hours(rates: list[int], target: int) -> int:
    if target < 0:
        raise ValueError("target must be non-negative")
    if target == 0:
        return 0
    if not rates or any(rate <= 0 for rate in rates):
        raise ValueError("rates must be positive")

    def sufficient(hours: int) -> bool:
        return sum(rate * hours for rate in rates) >= target

    low = 0
    high = 1
    while not sufficient(high):
        high *= 2

    while low < high:
        middle = low + (high - low) // 2
        if sufficient(middle):
            high = middle
        else:
            low = middle + 1
    return low
~~~

The first loop performs **exponential search** for an upper bound: doubling reaches an answer \(H\) after \(O(\log H)\) predicate calls. The second locates the first sufficient integer in \(O(\log H)\) calls. If summing over \(m\) rates costs \(\Theta(m)\), total time is \(O(m\log H)\).

This method searches a numeric answer domain without materialising a sorted array. Its correctness depends entirely on predicate monotonicity and on existence of a finite sufficient bound.

### 13.7.4 Discrete search and numerical bisection

Numerical **bisection** locates a root of a continuous real-valued function by maintaining endpoints with opposite signs and repeatedly halving an interval. It resembles binary search but has different foundations: continuity via the intermediate value theorem rather than discrete sorted order.

Floating-point bisection needs an accuracy or iteration stopping rule. Exact equality with zero may never occur, and <code>(low + high) / 2</code> can round to an endpoint when the interval is extremely narrow. A robust specification states whether error is bounded in the input coordinate, function value, or number of representable values.

~~~python
from collections.abc import Callable


def bisect_root(
    function: Callable[[float], float],
    low: float,
    high: float,
    *,
    iterations: int = 80,
) -> float:
    low_value = function(low)
    high_value = function(high)
    if low_value == 0.0:
        return low
    if high_value == 0.0:
        return high
    if (low_value < 0.0) == (high_value < 0.0):
        raise ValueError("endpoints must bracket a sign change")

    for _ in range(iterations):
        middle = low + (high - low) / 2.0
        middle_value = function(middle)
        if middle_value == 0.0:
            return middle
        if (middle_value < 0.0) == (low_value < 0.0):
            low = middle
            low_value = middle_value
        else:
            high = middle

    return low + (high - low) / 2.0
~~~

The code assumes finite meaningful function values; NaN breaks sign reasoning. Eighty iterations is a modelling choice, not a universally correct tolerance. Numerical analysis must account for representation and conditioning, subjects developed in the numerical-computing branch.

> **Common misconception 13.30 — “Binary search and floating-point bisection have the same correctness proof.”**  
> They share interval halving. Discrete binary search relies on a monotone partition; root bisection relies on analytic and floating-point assumptions that must be stated separately.

### 13.7.5 Subsequence and substring search

Binary search exploits order across candidate positions. Substring search instead exploits overlap among comparisons. Given a text \(T\) of length \(n\) and pattern \(P\) of length \(m\), the exact substring-search problem asks for an index \(s\) such that

\[
T[s:s+m]=P,
\]

or an absence result. A specification must say whether it returns the first match, every match, or overlapping matches, and what an empty pattern means.

A direct algorithm tests every feasible alignment:

~~~python
from collections.abc import Sequence
from typing import TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")


def naive_find(
    text: Sequence[T],
    pattern: Sequence[T],
) -> int | None:
    if len(pattern) == 0:
        return 0

    final_start = len(text) - len(pattern)
    for start in range(final_start + 1):
        for offset, expected in enumerate(pattern):
            if text[start + offset] != expected:
                break
        else:
            return start
    return None
~~~

The <code>else</code> belongs to the inner <code>for</code> and runs only when that loop is not terminated by <code>break</code>. The algorithm performs at most

\[
(n-m+1)m
\]

equality comparisons when \(0<m\le n\), hence \(O(nm)\). On ordinary mismatching text it often rejects an alignment quickly, but an input such as many repeated <code>a</code> elements followed by a differing final pattern element approaches the worst case.

The code compares indexed elements rather than slices. Forming and comparing <code>text[start:start+m]</code> can allocate or copy a subsequence for types such as lists and strings, adding representation-level cost.

#### Prefix information in Knuth–Morris–Pratt search

Suppose a mismatch occurs after several pattern elements have already matched. Those matched elements may contain a suffix that is also a pattern prefix. Reusing that fact avoids moving the text position backwards.

For each pattern prefix ending at index \(i\), define \(prefix[i]\) as the length of its longest proper prefix that is also a suffix. A **proper prefix** is shorter than the entire sequence.

~~~python
def prefix_lengths(pattern: Sequence[T]) -> list[int]:
    prefix = [0] * len(pattern)
    border = 0

    for index in range(1, len(pattern)):
        while border > 0 and pattern[index] != pattern[border]:
            border = prefix[border - 1]
        if pattern[index] == pattern[border]:
            border += 1
        prefix[index] = border

    return prefix
~~~

For <code>pattern = "ababaca"</code>, the table is \([0,0,1,2,3,0,1]\). At the prefix <code>ababa</code>, length 3 records that <code>aba</code> is both prefix and suffix. At the following <code>c</code>, border candidates fall from length 3 to the longest border of that border, then to zero.

The nested loop remains linear. Every successful outer progression can increase <code>border</code> by at most one; each failure fallback strictly decreases it. Across the whole construction, total decreases cannot exceed prior increases plus the initial value. Thus at most \(O(m)\) equality tests and table transitions occur.

The search maintains the number <code>matched</code> of pattern elements matching a suffix of the text processed so far:

~~~python
def kmp_find(
    text: Sequence[T],
    pattern: Sequence[T],
) -> int | None:
    if len(pattern) == 0:
        return 0

    prefix = prefix_lengths(pattern)
    matched = 0

    for text_index, value in enumerate(text):
        while matched > 0 and value != pattern[matched]:
            matched = prefix[matched - 1]
        if value == pattern[matched]:
            matched += 1
        if matched == len(pattern):
            return text_index - len(pattern) + 1

    return None
~~~

At the end of each processed text position, <code>matched</code> is the length of the longest pattern prefix equal to a suffix ending there. A mismatch discards only border lengths proven impossible and never re-examines a text element at an earlier index. As in table construction, increases and decreases of <code>matched</code> give \(O(n)\) search transitions after \(O(m)\) preprocessing. Auxiliary storage is \(O(m)\).

If every match is required, after emitting a match reset <code>matched = prefix[matched - 1]</code> and continue; this preserves overlapping occurrences. The additional output cost is \(\Omega(z)\) for \(z\) match indices.

Knuth–Morris–Pratt’s theoretical benefit is worst-case \(O(n+m)\) equality work. It is not necessarily the fastest implementation for every concrete string. Python’s built-in <code>str.find</code> and membership operations may use highly optimised implementation-specific algorithms, native loops, specialised character widths, and platform-aware routines. Portable code should rely on their documented result semantics rather than asserting a particular internal search family.

#### Rolling hashes

Rabin–Karp search compares a numeric fingerprint for each length-\(m\) window with the pattern fingerprint. A **rolling hash** updates the next window from the previous one in constant modular-arithmetic steps rather than rehashing every element.

~~~python
def rabin_karp_find(text: bytes, pattern: bytes) -> int | None:
    if not pattern:
        return 0
    if len(pattern) > len(text):
        return None

    base = 257
    modulus = 1_000_000_007
    high_place = pow(base, len(pattern) - 1, modulus)

    pattern_hash = 0
    window_hash = 0
    for pattern_byte, text_byte in zip(
        pattern,
        text[: len(pattern)],
    ):
        pattern_hash = (
            pattern_hash * base + pattern_byte
        ) % modulus
        window_hash = (
            window_hash * base + text_byte
        ) % modulus

    for start in range(len(text) - len(pattern) + 1):
        if (
            window_hash == pattern_hash
            and text[start : start + len(pattern)] == pattern
        ):
            return start

        if start + len(pattern) < len(text):
            outgoing = text[start]
            incoming = text[start + len(pattern)]
            window_hash = (
                (window_hash - outgoing * high_place) * base
                + incoming
            ) % modulus

    return None
~~~

Equal substrings produce equal fingerprints, but distinct substrings may collide. The explicit byte comparison after a hash match preserves correctness. Under a suitable collision model, expected work is \(O(n+m)\) plus match verification; adversarial or unlucky collisions can cause \(O(nm)\) verification. The modulus and base here are pedagogical and are not a cryptographic authentication mechanism.

Rolling hashes are particularly useful when searching several patterns of one length or comparing many windows. KMP uses deterministic prefix structure for one pattern; Rabin–Karp uses fingerprints and accepts collision verification. Aho–Corasick extends trie structure with failure links to search many patterns in one text. These are distinct answers to distinct workload structures.

#### Text is not always a sequence of user-perceived characters

Python strings are sequences of Unicode code points at the language level. A user-perceived grapheme can contain several code points, and canonically equivalent text can have different code-point sequences. Exact substring algorithms operate on the representation supplied. Searching human text may first require a documented Unicode normalisation and case policy; security-sensitive identifiers may deliberately forbid such equivalence.

**Audit caution — “substring” is not self-defining.** Byte substring, code-point substring, normalised linguistic match, locale-aware case-insensitive match, token sequence, and regular-expression match are different problems. Algorithmic correctness begins only after choosing one.

## 13.8 Comparison sorting

A **sorting algorithm** rearranges elements into non-decreasing order under a comparator or key. Additional properties include:

- **stability:** equal keys preserve relative input order;
- **in-place:** uses bounded or sublinear additional element storage under a defined model;
- **adaptive:** exploits existing order;
- worst-, average-, and best-case time;
- comparison and movement costs.

### Insertion sort

```python
def insertion_sort(values: list[int]) -> None:
    for index in range(1, len(values)):
        item = values[index]
        position = index

        while position > 0 and values[position - 1] > item:
            values[position] = values[position - 1]
            position -= 1

        values[position] = item
```

Outer invariant: before iteration at `index`, prefix `values[:index]` is sorted and contains exactly the original prefix elements. The inner loop shifts larger prefix elements right until `item` belongs at `position`. It is stable because equal elements are not shifted past one another under strict `>`.

Worst-case reversed input causes approximately (n(n-1)/2) comparisons and shifts, (Theta(n^2)). Already sorted input makes one comparison per outer iteration, (Theta(n)), showing adaptivity. Insertion sort is effective for small arrays and nearly sorted runs and appears as a component in hybrid algorithms.

### Merge sort

Merge sort divides the sequence, recursively sorts halves, and merges two sorted sequences.

```python
def merge_sort(values: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    if len(values) < 2:
        return values.copy()

    middle = len(values) // 2
    left = merge_sort(values[:middle])
    right = merge_sort(values[middle:])
    return merge(left, right)


def merge(left: list[int], right: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    result: list[int] = []
    i = 0
    j = 0

    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            result.append(left[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            result.append(right[j])
            j += 1

    result.extend(left[i:])
    result.extend(right[j:])
    return result
```

Merge invariant: `result` is sorted and contains exactly the consumed prefixes; every unconsumed item is no smaller than the final result item. Selecting the smaller front preserves it. `<=` selects from the left on equality, preserving stability.

The recursion has (log n) levels and performs (Theta(n)) merge work per level, giving (Theta(n\log n)) time. This implementation allocates slices and result lists, using (Theta(n)) peak auxiliary element-reference space plus recursion overhead under a careful accounting.

### Lower bound

Any deterministic comparison sort distinguishing arbitrary orders needs (Omega(n\log n)) comparisons in the worst case. A decision-tree argument has at least (n!) leaves, one per permutation, and a binary comparison tree of height (h) has at most (2^h) leaves. Thus (2^h\geq n!), so (h\geq\log_2(n!)=\Omega(n\log n)).

Non-comparison algorithms such as counting sort can beat this bound by exploiting key structure and range; they do not contradict it because their operations reveal more than pairwise relative order.

### 13.8.1 Selection sort separates selection from placement

**Selection sort** repeatedly finds the minimum of the unsorted suffix and exchanges it with the suffix’s first position.

~~~python
def selection_sort(values: list[int]) -> None:
    for boundary in range(len(values) - 1):
        minimum = boundary
        for index in range(boundary + 1, len(values)):
            if values[index] < values[minimum]:
                minimum = index
        values[boundary], values[minimum] = (
            values[minimum],
            values[boundary],
        )
~~~

At the start of iteration <code>boundary</code>:

1. the prefix before <code>boundary</code> contains the globally smallest elements in sorted order;
2. the suffix contains exactly the remaining elements.

The inner invariant says <code>minimum</code> indexes a minimum of the suffix portion inspected so far. After the scan, swapping places a suffix minimum at the boundary and preserves the outer invariant.

For every input order, the number of less-than comparisons is

\[
(n-1)+(n-2)+\cdots+1=\frac{n(n-1)}2.
\]

At most \(n-1\) swaps occur. Selection sort can therefore be useful in an abstract setting where comparisons are cheap but writes are unusually expensive. The implementation is not stable: swapping a later minimum forward can move one equal-key record behind another. Stability can be engineered by shifting rather than swapping, but then movement cost rises.

Selection sort and insertion sort share \(\Theta(n^2)\) worst-case time yet behave differently. Insertion sort is adaptive and stable as written; selection sort performs its full comparison count regardless of presortedness. Complexity class alone does not describe an algorithm.

> **Common misconception 13.31 — “Algorithms in the same \(\Theta\) class are interchangeable.”**  
> Stability, adaptiveness, writes, auxiliary storage, comparison cost, locality, and failure behaviour can differ substantially within one asymptotic class.

### 13.8.2 Bubble sort and the value of a weak algorithm

Bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps inverted pairs. A pass moves at least one maximal remaining element to its final suffix position.

~~~python
def bubble_sort(values: list[int]) -> None:
    unsorted_end = len(values)
    while unsorted_end > 1:
        last_swap = 0
        for index in range(1, unsorted_end):
            if values[index] < values[index - 1]:
                values[index - 1], values[index] = (
                    values[index],
                    values[index - 1],
                )
                last_swap = index
        unsorted_end = last_swap
~~~

If no swap occurs, <code>last_swap</code> remains zero and the algorithm terminates. More precisely, after a pass, every position from <code>last_swap</code> onward is already in final sorted relation to what follows, so the next pass can stop there.

Adjacent swaps under strict less-than preserve stability. The algorithm is \(\Theta(n)\) on sorted input with this early-exit rule and \(\Theta(n^2)\) in the worst case. It usually performs more movements than insertion sort and has no advantage over Python’s production sort. Its pedagogical value lies in inversion reasoning: each adjacent swap removes exactly one inversion, so any adjacent-swap-only sorting algorithm requires at least \(I\) swaps for an input with \(I\) inversions.

> **Common misconception 13.32 — “Bubble sort is a reasonable default because it is simple.”**  
> Simplicity is one engineering criterion, but Python already supplies a stable, extensively tested, adaptive \(O(n\log n)\)-worst-case sort. Bubble sort is primarily an object of analysis and specialised adjacent-exchange constraints.

### 13.8.3 Merging without recursive slices

The earlier merge-sort implementation is clear but allocates list slices at every recursive division. A bottom-up implementation alternates source and destination arrays and makes allocation explicit:

~~~python
from typing import TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")


def bottom_up_merge_sort(values: list[T]) -> list[T]:
    source = values.copy()
    destination = source.copy()
    width = 1

    while width < len(source):
        for start in range(0, len(source), 2 * width):
            middle = min(start + width, len(source))
            end = min(start + 2 * width, len(source))
            merge_into(source, destination, start, middle, end)
        source, destination = destination, source
        width *= 2

    return source


def merge_into(
    source: list[T],
    destination: list[T],
    start: int,
    middle: int,
    end: int,
) -> None:
    left = start
    right = middle

    for output in range(start, end):
        if right >= end or (
            left < middle and not source[right] < source[left]
        ):
            destination[output] = source[left]
            left += 1
        else:
            destination[output] = source[right]
            right += 1
~~~

The two input runs <code>[start, middle)</code> and <code>[middle, end)</code> are sorted. The merge condition chooses the left item unless the right item is strictly smaller. Avoiding <code>&lt;=</code> means the generic type needs only less-than, matching Python sorting’s preference for that relation; choosing left on equivalence preserves stability.

After passes of widths \(1,2,4,\ldots\), all runs of the resulting doubled width are sorted. There are \(\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\) passes, each reading and writing \(\Theta(n)\) references, so time is \(\Theta(n\log n)\). Two full lists exist during the operation; auxiliary reference storage is \(\Theta(n)\). The implementation returns a new list and does not mutate the caller’s list, although references to mutable elements are shared.

External merge sort extends the same invariant to storage too large for memory. It creates sorted runs that fit in memory, writes them, and performs a multiway merge with buffered I/O. Its chief cost model counts block transfers and seeks rather than only comparisons. An algorithm’s decomposition can survive while its relevant resources change.

> **Common misconception 13.33 — “Merge sort necessarily copies each element object.”**  
> A Python list implementation normally copies or moves references. Element objects remain shared unless the algorithm explicitly clones them.

### 13.8.4 Quicksort and partition invariants

Quicksort selects a **pivot**, partitions elements around it, and recursively sorts the partitions. Its attraction is good locality and small auxiliary arrays in common in-place implementations. Its hazard is unbalanced partitioning.

A three-way functional version makes duplicate handling clear:

~~~python
from typing import TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")


def quicksort(values: list[T]) -> list[T]:
    if len(values) < 2:
        return values.copy()

    pivot = values[len(values) // 2]
    lower: list[T] = []
    equal: list[T] = []
    upper: list[T] = []

    for value in values:
        if value < pivot:
            lower.append(value)
        elif pivot < value:
            upper.append(value)
        else:
            equal.append(value)

    return quicksort(lower) + equal + quicksort(upper)
~~~

This treats values as equivalent when neither is less than the other. It allocates partitions and is stable only under assumptions about equivalence and recursive concatenation; it is not the traditional in-place quicksort.

If partition sizes are \(k\) and \(n-k-1\), the recurrence is

\[
T(n)=T(k)+T(n-k-1)+\Theta(n).
\]

Balanced partitions yield \(\Theta(n\log n)\). Repeated \(0\) and \(n-1\) partitions yield

\[
T(n)=T(n-1)+\Theta(n)=\Theta(n^2)
\]

and \(\Theta(n)\) recursion depth. Selecting the first element as pivot makes already sorted input adversarial for a common two-way formulation.

A uniformly random pivot gives expected \(\Theta(n\log n)\) comparisons for every fixed input arrangement, assuming randomness independent of the input. Randomisation does not remove the quadratic worst case; it makes consistently bad partition sequences unlikely under the model. Median-of-three and introspective fallback policies offer different engineering protections.

**Introsort** begins with quicksort-like partitioning, switches to heapsort if recursion depth indicates persistent imbalance, and often uses insertion sort for small partitions. It demonstrates hybrid design: retain common-case locality while imposing an \(O(n\log n)\) worst-case bound.

> **Common misconception 13.34 — “Randomised quicksort is worst-case \(O(n\log n)\).”**  
> Its expected cost can be \(\Theta(n\log n)\) for each fixed input, while some random pivot sequences still produce \(\Theta(n^2)\) work.

### 13.8.5 Heap sort

A max-heap places a maximum at its root. Heap sort builds a max-heap, swaps the root with the final unsorted element, reduces the heap boundary, and restores the heap.

~~~python
def heap_sort(values: list[int]) -> None:
    length = len(values)

    for root in range(length // 2 - 1, -1, -1):
        sift_down(values, root, length)

    for end in range(length - 1, 0, -1):
        values[0], values[end] = values[end], values[0]
        sift_down(values, 0, end)


def sift_down(values: list[int], root: int, end: int) -> None:
    while True:
        left = 2 * root + 1
        if left >= end:
            return

        larger = left
        right = left + 1
        if right < end and values[larger] < values[right]:
            larger = right

        if not values[root] < values[larger]:
            return

        values[root], values[larger] = values[larger], values[root]
        root = larger
~~~

During extraction:

- <code>values[:end]</code> is a max-heap;
- <code>values[end:]</code> is sorted and contains the largest values;
- every heap value is no greater than every suffix value.

The swap places the heap maximum immediately before the sorted suffix. Sifting restores the heap over the reduced prefix.

One sift costs \(O(\log n)\). Repeating it \(n-1\) times costs \(O(n\log n)\). Bottom-up heap construction is \(O(n)\), not \(O(n\log n)\): most nodes lie near the leaves and travel only a few levels. If a node of height \(h\) costs \(O(h)\), summing heights over a complete binary tree is linear:

\[
\sum_{h\ge0} O\left(\frac{n}{2^{h+1}}h\right)=O(n).
\]

Heap sort is in-place under an \(O(1)\)-word auxiliary convention and has \(O(n\log n)\) worst-case time. It is not stable in this form and often has poorer locality than highly engineered alternatives.

> **Common misconception 13.35 — “Building a heap by repeated insertion and bottom-up heapify have the same cost.”**  
> Repeated insertion is \(O(n\log n)\) in the worst case. Bottom-up heapify is \(O(n)\) because few nodes can move far.

### 13.8.6 Sorting beyond the comparison model

If keys have exploitable structure, sorting need not learn order solely through comparisons. **Counting sort** handles integer keys in a bounded range:

~~~python
from collections.abc import Callable, Sequence
from typing import TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")


def counting_sort(
    values: Sequence[T],
    *,
    key: Callable[[T], int],
) -> list[T]:
    if not values:
        return []

    keys = [key(value) for value in values]
    minimum = min(keys)
    maximum = max(keys)
    counts = [0] * (maximum - minimum + 1)

    for item_key in keys:
        counts[item_key - minimum] += 1

    for index in range(1, len(counts)):
        counts[index] += counts[index - 1]

    result = [values[0]] * len(values)
    for value, item_key in zip(reversed(values), reversed(keys)):
        bucket = item_key - minimum
        counts[bucket] -= 1
        result[counts[bucket]] = value

    return result
~~~

Let \(n\) be item count and \(k=maximum-minimum+1\) the key range. Time and auxiliary storage are \(\Theta(n+k)\), excluding key-function cost beyond one call per item. Reverse traversal during placement preserves stability: later equal-key items claim later positions.

When \(k\gg n\), the counts array can be prohibitive. A dictionary of counts reduces storage for sparse keys but recovering sorted key order then costs at least sorting distinct keys or using another ordered structure.

**Radix sort** processes key digits using a stable sub-sort. Least-significant-digit radix sorting \(d\) digits in radix \(b\) costs \(O(d(n+b))\) under a fixed digit-extraction model. It is linear in \(n\) only when \(d\) and \(b\) are treated as suitably bounded. For arbitrary-size integers, \(d\) grows with bit length.

**Bucket sort** distributes values among ranges and sorts within buckets. Its expected linear claims require distribution assumptions; an adversarial concentration in one bucket can recover the inner sort’s worst case.

These algorithms do not violate the comparison lower bound. Array indexing by an integer digit reveals information unavailable to a pure comparison decision tree and may allocate storage proportional to the key universe.

> **Common misconception 13.36 — “Counting or radix sort proves the \(\Omega(n\log n)\) sorting lower bound false.”**  
> The lower bound is for arbitrary keys in the comparison model. Structured-key algorithms use stronger operations and carry range, digit, or distribution costs.

### 13.8.7 Sorting properties and selection

The principal algorithms can be compared only after fixing implementations:

| Algorithm | Best time | Worst time | Typical auxiliary element storage | Stable as presented | Adaptive |
|---|---:|---:|---:|:---:|:---:|
| insertion | \(\Theta(n)\) | \(\Theta(n^2)\) | \(\Theta(1)\) | yes | yes |
| selection | \(\Theta(n^2)\) | \(\Theta(n^2)\) | \(\Theta(1)\) | no | no |
| bubble with boundary | \(\Theta(n)\) | \(\Theta(n^2)\) | \(\Theta(1)\) | yes | yes |
| merge, array-backed | \(\Theta(n\log n)\) | \(\Theta(n\log n)\) | \(\Theta(n)\) | yes | weakly without run detection |
| randomised quicksort | expected \(\Theta(n\log n)\) | \(\Theta(n^2)\) | recursion/partitions vary | varies | no |
| heap sort | \(\Theta(n\log n)\) | \(\Theta(n\log n)\) | \(\Theta(1)\) | no | no |
| counting | \(\Theta(n+k)\) | \(\Theta(n+k)\) | \(\Theta(n+k)\) | yes as presented | no |

Sorting is unnecessary when the problem asks only for the \(k\)-th order statistic. **Quickselect** partitions as quicksort does but recurses into only the partition containing the requested rank. It has expected linear time with suitable randomisation and quadratic worst case. Deterministic median-of-medians pivot selection guarantees linear worst-case time, with larger constants and a more involved proof.

For a tiny number \(k\) of extreme items, a heap can produce top-\(k\) results in \(O(n\log k)\) time and \(O(k)\) storage. If fully sorted output is required, an \(\Omega(n\log n)\) comparison cost returns. Solve the requested output problem rather than sorting by habit.

> **Common misconception 13.37 — “To find the minimum, median, or top ten, first sort everything.”**  
> Full sorting computes more order information than selection may require. A scan finds an extremum in \(\Theta(n)\); selection and bounded heaps offer other task-specific bounds.

## 13.9 Python sorting and Timsort

Python’s `list.sort` and `sorted` are stable and use Timsort, an adaptive hybrid algorithm exploiting existing ordered runs and merging under carefully engineered invariants. Worst-case comparison growth is (O(n\log n)), while ordered structure can reduce work substantially.

Use key functions rather than comparators when possible:

```python
ordered = sorted(records, key=lambda record: (record.surname.casefold(), record.identifier))
```

The key is computed once per element under the sorting contract, then cached for comparisons. A comparator adapter can be built with `functools.cmp_to_key` for legacy interfaces, but a comparator must define a coherent ordering and can run many times.

Sorting a list containing incomparable keys raises `TypeError`; partial mutation can occur before a `list.sort` failure under documented cautions. Validate and derive keys before mutating critical original order where failure atomicity matters.

### 13.9.1 Language guarantees and implementation facts

The Python language/library contract guarantees that <code>list.sort()</code> modifies a list in place and returns <code>None</code>, while <code>sorted()</code> consumes an iterable and returns a new list. Both accept keyword-only <code>key</code> and <code>reverse</code> arguments and guarantee stability.

The fact that CPython 3.12 implements these operations with Timsort is an implementation fact documented in the sorting HOWTO and CPython source material; alternative conforming Python implementations may use another algorithm while preserving specified behaviour. Even within CPython, tuning constants and merge policies are not stable application interfaces.

Timsort identifies naturally ascending or descending **runs**, extends short runs using insertion-like techniques, and merges runs while maintaining size invariants. Existing order can therefore reduce comparisons. Its “galloping” mode accelerates certain merges when consecutive selections repeatedly come from one run. A complete proof and engineering account resides in implementation literature; applications should depend on stability and ordering results, not internal run-stack thresholds.

The key function is evaluated once for each input element during a successful ordinary sort invocation. Key caching converts repeated potentially expensive derivation into one derivation plus comparisons of cached keys. It does not imply that the key is pure: calls can have side effects or fail, which makes such a key hard to reason about.

> **Common misconception 13.38 — “Python guarantees Timsort forever.”**  
> Python guarantees documented sorting semantics, including stability. Timsort is the current CPython implementation strategy, not a necessary part of every conforming implementation’s contract.

### 13.9.2 Stability as a composition tool

Stability means that if two elements have equal keys, their relative input order is retained. It enables multi-pass sorting from least significant criterion to most significant criterion:

~~~python
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Student:
    name: str
    cohort: int
    mark: int


students = [
    Student("Ada", 2, 78),
    Student("Grace", 1, 91),
    Student("Edsger", 2, 91),
]

by_mark_then_cohort = sorted(students, key=lambda item: item.mark)
by_mark_then_cohort.sort(key=lambda item: item.cohort)
~~~

The second stable pass makes cohort primary while preserving mark order within each cohort. A tuple key expresses the same policy more directly:

~~~python
equivalent = sorted(
    students,
    key=lambda item: (item.cohort, item.mark),
)
assert equivalent == by_mark_then_cohort
~~~

Descending one field but ascending another requires care. Negating a numeric key works for ordinary finite numbers but not all types and interacts with NaN. A stable multi-pass approach can apply different <code>reverse</code> settings from the least significant field upward.

The historical **decorate–sort–undecorate** pattern constructs tuples containing derived keys, possibly an original index, and the value; sorts them; then removes decoration. Python’s built-in key support internalises the common key-caching need, but explicit decoration remains useful for mixed direction, audited key validation, or deterministic tie policies.

~~~python
decorated = [
    (student.cohort, -student.mark, index, student)
    for index, student in enumerate(students)
]
decorated.sort()
ordered_students = [entry[-1] for entry in decorated]
~~~

The index prevents Python from needing to compare <code>Student</code> objects when the preceding keys tie and makes original-order tie breaking explicit.

> **Common misconception 13.39 — “A stable sort leaves equal-valued objects at their original indices.”**  
> It preserves their relative order with respect to one another. Other elements can move around them, so absolute indices generally change.

### 13.9.3 Ordering must be coherent

Sorting algorithms assume a comparison relation with enough order structure. A **strict weak ordering**, the common algorithmic requirement, is irreflexive and transitive and induces transitive equivalence among values incomparable in either direction. Python does not dynamically prove these laws. A user-defined <code>__lt__</code> that changes over time or creates cycles can yield meaningless order.

Floating-point NaN is a prominent boundary: comparisons such as \(x&lt;\mathrm{NaN}\), \(\mathrm{NaN}&lt;x\), and \(\mathrm{NaN}==\mathrm{NaN}\) are false. A robust application defines a total placement policy:

~~~python
from math import isnan


def numeric_sort_key(value: float) -> tuple[bool, float]:
    if isnan(value):
        return (True, 0.0)
    return (False, value)


readings = [3.0, float("nan"), -1.0, 2.0]
ordered = sorted(readings, key=numeric_sort_key)
assert ordered[:3] == [-1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
assert isnan(ordered[-1])
~~~

Heterogeneous values such as integers and strings have no default cross-type numerical/text order in modern Python. Derive a tagged key only if the domain has a defensible policy:

~~~python
def mixed_key(value: int | str) -> tuple[int, int | str]:
    if isinstance(value, int):
        return (0, value)
    return (1, value.casefold())
~~~

Case folding can make distinct strings share a primary key; stability or an explicit secondary original string determines ties. Locale-aware collation is a separate policy and may require specialised facilities.

Mutation during <code>list.sort</code>, inconsistent comparisons, and exceptions from keys or comparison methods can expose partially transformed state or specified implementation restrictions. If preserving the original is essential, sort a copy or compute and validate decorations before committing:

~~~python
def safely_sorted_numbers(raw: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    decorated: list[tuple[int, int, str]] = []
    for index, text in enumerate(raw):
        parsed = int(text)
        decorated.append((parsed, index, text))
    decorated.sort()
    return [text for _, _, text in decorated]
~~~

All integer conversions finish before sorting begins. If conversion fails, <code>raw</code> remains unchanged. This is a transaction-like design choice, not a special guarantee supplied by sorting.

> **Common misconception 13.40 — “If <code>__lt__</code> returns a Boolean, the object is sortable correctly.”**  
> A comparator must obey order laws consistently over the operation. Returning Boolean values is syntactically sufficient but not semantically sufficient.

## 13.10 Linked lists built from scratch

A **linked list** stores each element in a node containing a value and a reference to another node. It avoids a contiguous reference array but introduces per-node allocation and pointer traversal.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Generic, Iterator, TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")


@dataclass(slots=True)
class Node(Generic[T]):
    value: T
    next: "Node[T] | None" = None


class SinglyLinkedList(Generic[T]):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._head: Node[T] | None = None
        self._tail: Node[T] | None = None
        self._length = 0

    def append(self, value: T) -> None:
        node = Node(value)
        if self._tail is None:
            self._head = node
        else:
            self._tail.next = node
        self._tail = node
        self._length += 1

    def prepend(self, value: T) -> None:
        node = Node(value, self._head)
        self._head = node
        if self._tail is None:
            self._tail = node
        self._length += 1

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        return self._length

    def __iter__(self) -> Iterator[T]:
        current = self._head
        while current is not None:
            yield current.value
            current = current.next
```

Invariants:

- length zero iff head and tail are both `None`;
- non-empty tail’s `next` is `None`;
- following `next` from head visits exactly `_length` nodes and ends at tail;
- no cycle exists.

Prepend and append are (O(1)) with retained tail. Index lookup is (O(n)) because nodes must be followed. Removing after a known node is (O(1)), but finding that node may be (O(n)). Compared with CPython list, linked nodes have poor spatial locality and substantial object overhead. The structure is not automatically more efficient because insertion notation looks direct.

### Cycle detection

Floyd’s tortoise-and-hare algorithm advances one reference by one edge and another by two. If a finite linked structure has a cycle reachable from head, they eventually meet; if the fast pointer reaches `None`, no cycle exists.

```python
def has_cycle(head: Node[object] | None) -> bool:
    slow = head
    fast = head
    while fast is not None and fast.next is not None:
        slow = slow.next if slow is not None else None
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:
            return True
    return False
```

Time is (O(n)); additional space is (O(1)). Identity comparison is required because the question is whether pointers reach the same node, not whether node values compare equal.

### 13.10.1 Abstract data type and representation

An **abstract data type** (**ADT**) specifies values and operations independently of a concrete storage arrangement. A sequence ADT might promise length, iteration, insertion, and deletion. A dynamic array and linked list are representations that realise some version of that interface with different costs.

The abstraction boundary matters because “linked list” is often used for both an interface and a node representation. A caller should not receive internal node references unless those references are deliberately part of the API. Exposing them permits external rewiring that can invalidate length, tail, and acyclicity.

The teaching class above owns its nodes but not the values referenced from them. Appending a mutable object stores a reference; later mutation through another alias is visible during iteration. This follows Python’s reference semantics and is not specific to linked lists.

Memory differs from the sketch of boxes and arrows. Each Python node is an object with runtime metadata and two references; allocation may scatter nodes. A CPython list stores references in a contiguous internal array, enabling compact iteration and efficient indexed access. The linked list saves suffix shifts for an insertion after a known node but often costs more memory per element and more cache misses.

> **Common misconception 13.41 — “A linked list is an abstract sequence, while a list is a physical array.”**  
> Both names can be used ambiguously. Separate the ADT contract from the representation that implements it before comparing costs.

### 13.10.2 Complete singly linked operations

Removing the first equal value illustrates predecessor tracking and boundary repair:

~~~python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Generic, Iterator, TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")


@dataclass(slots=True)
class Link(Generic[T]):
    value: T
    next: "Link[T] | None" = None


class LinkedSequence(Generic[T]):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._head: Link[T] | None = None
        self._tail: Link[T] | None = None
        self._length = 0

    def append(self, value: T) -> None:
        node = Link(value)
        if self._tail is None:
            self._head = node
        else:
            self._tail.next = node
        self._tail = node
        self._length += 1

    def remove_first(self, value: T) -> None:
        previous: Link[T] | None = None
        current = self._head

        while current is not None and current.value != value:
            previous = current
            current = current.next

        if current is None:
            raise ValueError("value is absent")

        if previous is None:
            self._head = current.next
        else:
            previous.next = current.next

        if current is self._tail:
            self._tail = previous

        self._length -= 1
        current.next = None

    def __iter__(self) -> Iterator[T]:
        current = self._head
        while current is not None:
            yield current.value
            current = current.next

    def assert_invariants(self) -> None:
        count = 0
        current = self._head
        final: Link[T] | None = None
        seen: set[int] = set()

        while current is not None:
            identity = id(current)
            if identity in seen:
                raise AssertionError("cycle in linked sequence")
            seen.add(identity)
            count += 1
            final = current
            current = current.next
~~~
