    PyObject *pair = PyTuple_New(2);
    if (pair == NULL) {
        return NULL;
    }

    /* Valid only because pair is fresh and both indices are in range. */
    PyTuple_SET_ITEM(pair, 0, Py_NewRef(first));
    PyTuple_SET_ITEM(pair, 1, Py_NewRef(second));

    return pair;
}
~~~

Each <code>Py_NewRef</code> creates a strong ownership claim and <code>PyTuple_SET_ITEM</code> steals it. The unchecked macro is valid only because <code>pair</code> is newly allocated with exactly two empty positions and the indices are proved. It would leak a prior item if used as a general replacement operation and can corrupt memory when its preconditions fail. In real extension code, prefer <code>PyTuple_Pack</code> for this task:

~~~c
static PyObject *
make_pair_safely(PyObject *first, PyObject *second)
{
    return PyTuple_Pack(2, first, second);
}
~~~

The higher-level constructor owns the balancing logic and returns a new reference or <code>NULL</code>. The design principle is general: choose an API whose ownership contract matches the operation rather than assembling a fragile sequence of low-level transfers.

Where several owned temporaries are necessary, a single cleanup label can make balance auditable:

~~~c
static PyObject *
normalised_mapping(PyObject *input)
{
    PyObject *result = NULL;
    PyObject *items = PyMapping_Items(input);
    if (items == NULL) {
        goto done;
    }

    PyObject *sorted = PySequence_List(items);
    if (sorted == NULL) {
        goto done;
    }

    if (PyList_Sort(sorted) < 0) {
        Py_DECREF(sorted);
        goto done;
    }

    result = sorted;

done:
    Py_XDECREF(items);
    return result;
}
~~~

<code>Py_XDECREF</code> tolerates <code>NULL</code>; <code>Py_DECREF</code> requires a valid non-null reference. The result variable receives ownership only on success. This example is illustrative rather than a complete semantic “normalisation”: sorting arbitrary mapping items can invoke user comparison and can fail.

The safest modern style often uses helper APIs and ownership conventions available in the minimum supported CPython version, keeps owned lifetimes short, and tests forced allocation and protocol failures. C++ wrappers can encode RAII—resource acquisition is initialisation—but must interoperate correctly with Python exceptions and interpreter attachment.

> **Common misconception 15.44 — “Reference leaks matter only on the successful return path.”**  
> Any allocation, conversion, callback, comparison, or container operation can fail. Each early return must preserve the exception and release exactly those references still owned on that path.

### 15.11.3 Borrowed references require a stability argument

A borrowed reference is safe only while its owner remains alive and no permitted action invalidates the borrowed access. The dangerous interval is often hidden in a call that can execute arbitrary Python:

~~~c
/* Conceptual hazard: do not copy as production code. */
PyObject *item = PyList_GetItem(list, 0);  /* borrowed */
if (item == NULL) {
    return NULL;
}

if (PyObject_CallNoArgs(callback) == NULL) {
    return NULL;
}

/* callback may have mutated list and released its former item */
return PyObject_Repr(item);
~~~

Even in a conventional GIL build, the callback can mutate <code>list</code>, delete the element, and cause the object’s last strong reference to disappear. The GIL prevents simultaneous execution during portions of the C call; it does not preserve a container element across re-entrant Python code.

Acquire an owned reference before the re-entrancy boundary. On CPython versions offering APIs that return strong references directly, prefer them; otherwise increment while validity is established under the required synchronisation:

~~~c
PyObject *item = PyList_GetItem(list, 0);  /* borrowed */
if (item == NULL) {
    return NULL;
}
Py_INCREF(item);                          /* retain across callback */

PyObject *ignored = PyObject_CallNoArgs(callback);
if (ignored == NULL) {
    Py_DECREF(item);
    return NULL;
}
Py_DECREF(ignored);

PyObject *representation = PyObject_Repr(item);
Py_DECREF(item);
return representation;
~~~

Free-threaded builds strengthen the need for fetch-style APIs and explicit container locking where documented. A separate thread can mutate a shared container after a borrowed pointer is obtained. An increment performed after removal may already be too late. APIs introduced for strong-reference retrieval close this race within their contract.

> **Common misconception 15.45 — “A borrowed reference is safe as long as the GIL was held when it was obtained.”**  
> Re-entrant callbacks can invalidate it in a GIL build, and concurrent mutation can invalidate assumptions in a free-threaded build. Safety requires owner lifetime and stability across the entire use interval.

### 15.11.4 Stealing references moves rather than duplicates an obligation

When an API steals a reference, the caller must treat the reference as transferred according to the exact success/failure rule. It must not decrement the transferred ownership again, yet it may retain a separate owned reference if it incremented beforehand.

This is analogous to moving a resource in a language with explicit ownership, but C provides no automatic invalidation. A useful local convention sets a pointer to <code>NULL</code> immediately after an unconditional transfer, making accidental cleanup less likely:

~~~c
PyObject *value = PyLong_FromLong(42);
if (value == NULL) {
    return NULL;
}

/* Suppose documented_api_steals(value) always steals on this path. */
if (documented_api_steals(value) < 0) {
    value = NULL;
    return NULL;
}
value = NULL;
~~~

This pseudo-call intentionally has no real declaration: the reader must consult a real function’s documentation rather than assume a universal steal-on-failure pattern. Setting the local to <code>NULL</code> is a review convention, not reference-count machinery.

The C API provides helpers such as <code>Py_NewRef</code> and <code>Py_XNewRef</code> in supported versions to express “return this object while acquiring a new strong reference”. These improve expression clarity and reduce the split between increment and return:

~~~c
static PyObject *
return_selected(PyObject *selected)
{
    return Py_NewRef(selected);
}
~~~

For replacement of an owned field, APIs/macros such as <code>Py_SETREF</code> and <code>Py_XSETREF</code> can encode “replace then release the old object” with important null preconditions. Under free-threading or shared published state, atomicity and locks remain separate concerns; ownership helpers do not by themselves make a compound state transition thread-safe.

> **Common misconception 15.46 — “If an API steals a reference, it creates another owned reference internally while the caller keeps its own.”**  
> Stealing transfers an existing ownership obligation. Continued caller ownership requires a distinct strong reference acquired before the transfer.

Reference-ownership rules explain local correctness at the native boundary. The next mechanism explains how conventional CPython turns those acquire/release operations into object lifetime—and why the simple integer-counter picture now needs qualification.

## 15.12 Reference counting

In conventional CPython, each object participates in reference counting. When a strong reference is acquired, a count-like ownership state increases; when released, it decreases. Reaching zero ordinarily triggers immediate deallocation under that implementation context, recursively releasing contained references.

Advantages:

- many unreachable acyclic objects are reclaimed promptly;
- resource wrappers may appear to finalise promptly in CPython;
- lifetime follows explicit ownership operations in the C API.

Costs and complications:

- every reference transfer requires bookkeeping;
- deallocation pauses can occur where the final reference is released;
- long recursive container destruction can cascade;
- cycles do not reach zero through reference counting alone;
- free-threaded operation requires different synchronisation and biased/deferred strategies internally.

Python code should use `with` for deterministic external-resource release rather than relying on reference count timing. Other implementations can use tracing garbage collection and delay finalisation.

`sys.getrefcount(obj)` in CPython reports a value affected by the temporary reference supplied to the call and by interpreter/compiler details. It is a diagnostic observation, not a stable ownership API.

### 15.12.1 Counts approximate strong ownership, not all machine pointers

The conventional model associates each object with the number of strong references recognised by CPython ownership rules. A local binding, container element, function default, closure cell, module global, and temporary evaluation-stack entry can each contribute. A raw C pointer that has not acquired ownership contributes nothing. Conversely, an internal owner can contribute without an obvious Python-level name.

Reference counting maintains an invariant, not a census of every address-sized bit pattern. Increment when acquiring an independent strong ownership claim; decrement when releasing it. If the last claim is released, deallocation begins. Missing an increment can leave a dangling pointer; missing a decrement leaves an unreachable object artificially alive; an extra decrement can destroy a live object.

At Python level, rebinding demonstrates transfers:

~~~python
class Payload:
    pass


first = Payload()
second = first
container = [first]

del first
assert second is container[0]

container.clear()
# The object remains alive through second.
assert isinstance(second, Payload)
~~~

Deleting <code>first</code> removes one binding. Clearing the list releases its element reference. Neither operation “deletes the object” because <code>second</code> remains an owner. The language account is reachability and binding; the CPython mechanism includes corresponding reference transfers.

Not every runtime reference is strong. Weak references do not retain the referent. Borrowed C pointers rely on someone else’s strong ownership. Some internal temporary references can be protected by precise invariants. Immortal objects no longer behave like ordinary decrement-to-zero counts. The model remains useful when stated as ownership, not when reduced to one publicly meaningful integer.

> **Common misconception 15.47 — “The reference count equals the number of Python variable names pointing at an object.”**  
> Strong owners also include containers, frames, cells, defaults, interpreter structures, and native code; names can be absent or multiple, and weak/borrowed pointers do not count as independent owners.

### 15.12.2 The zero transition invokes type-specific destruction

When ordinary reference state reaches zero in conventional CPython, the object’s type-specific deallocator runs. It must place the object into a consistent state, release owned child references, clear weak references and finalisation state under applicable rules, and return memory through the matching allocator. Releasing children can make their counts reach zero, causing a cascade.

For a container chain, destruction depth and timing can be non-trivial:

~~~python
class Marker:
    def __init__(self, label: str, log: list[str]) -> None:
        self.label = label
        self.log = log

    def __del__(self) -> None:
        self.log.append(self.label)


events: list[str] = []
values = [Marker("first", events), Marker("second", events)]
values.clear()
print(events)
~~~

The observed order and promptness should not become application semantics. List clearing must release element ownership, but external aliases, cycles, interpreter implementation, and finaliser behaviour can change when hooks run. A <code>__del__</code> method can execute arbitrary code and even mutate structures involved in destruction.

This produces a central implementation rule: decrement operations can be re-entrant. Consider a native setter replacing an owned field. If it decrements the old value before publishing the new consistent state, the old value’s finaliser can inspect a half-updated owner. Safer patterns first retain the new value if needed, update the field, and then release the old value, using documented replacement helpers where suitable.

Errors during finalisation cannot propagate to the vanished caller. Python reports unraisable exceptions through <code>sys.unraisablehook</code>. Libraries can customise that hook for observation, but must not let the hook itself become a source of recursive failure or retained exception graphs.

### Worked example 15.14 — Observe an unraisable finaliser error safely

~~~python
import gc
import sys


records: list[tuple[type[BaseException], str]] = []


def capture_unraisable(event) -> None:
    records.append((type(event.exc_value), str(event.exc_value)))


class FaultyFinaliser:
    def __del__(self) -> None:
        raise RuntimeError("cleanup failed")


previous = sys.unraisablehook
sys.unraisablehook = capture_unraisable
try:
    value = FaultyFinaliser()
    del value
    gc.collect()
finally:
    sys.unraisablehook = previous

assert records and records[0][0] is RuntimeError
~~~

The explicit collection makes the example more tolerant of implementation timing but does not make finalisers a sound cleanup primitive. Modifying a process-wide hook requires isolation in concurrent programs.

> **Common misconception 15.48 — “Py_DECREF is always a tiny non-observable arithmetic operation.”**  
> It can trigger type deallocation, recursive child release, weak callbacks, finalisers, arbitrary Python execution, and memory return. Native code must establish consistent state before a potentially final decrement.

### 15.12.3 getrefcount is a perturbed observation

<code>sys.getrefcount</code> is a CPython diagnostic returning a reference-count value as observed while its argument is being passed. The call itself creates at least one temporary reference, and compiler/interpreter temporaries can add more. Immortal objects can report very large implementation values unrelated to an actionable owner count.

### Worked example 15.15 — Compare deltas, not mythical absolute counts

~~~python
import sys


class Sample:
    pass


value = Sample()
before = sys.getrefcount(value)
aliases = [value, value, value]
during = sys.getrefcount(value)
aliases.clear()
after = sys.getrefcount(value)

assert during >= before + 3
assert after == before
~~~

Even this controlled delta is CPython-specific. The <code>>=</code> acknowledges possible temporaries, while equality after clearing is expected for this simple compiled context but should not be used as a production invariant. A tracing tool, debugger, notebook display, or alternate compiler optimisation can retain another reference.

Reference counts cannot prove that an object is “unused”. A reachable cache entry can have one owner and still be a leak relative to the application’s intended lifetime. A borrowed pointer can be semantically in use while adding no count. Diagnose ownership paths and application roots instead.

The <code>gc.get_referrers</code> function can expose selected tracked containers referring to an object, but it omits untracked and non-GC references, can return partially constructed objects, and creates new references during inspection. It is a debugging aid, not a complete inverse pointer map.

> **Common misconception 15.49 — “sys.getrefcount reveals the exact stable number of program references.”**  
> Calling it perturbs the count; temporaries, tooling, immortality, and implementation strategies affect the value. At most it supports carefully controlled, version-scoped experiments.

### 15.12.4 Immortality removes hot shared objects from ordinary zero-count lifetime

PEP 683 introduced **immortal objects** as a CPython mechanism: selected objects are marked so their reference state never reaches ordinary deallocation during runtime. Common singletons and statically allocated objects are natural candidates. This reduces reference-count write traffic and supports later free-threading mechanisms.

Immortality is not a new Python semantic category. <code>None</code> is still a singleton because the language specifies its role; its internal immortal state is a CPython implementation technique. User code must not infer immortality from a large value returned by <code>getrefcount</code>, retain raw pointers without ownership discipline, or assume every interned object is immortal.

At the C API level, increment/decrement operations on an immortal object become harmless with respect to its lifetime under the documented implementation, but extensions should still perform them according to contract. Omitting correct ownership merely because a test object happened to be immortal makes the code fail when another object arrives.

### 15.12.5 Free-threaded reference counting is distributed and deferred

Removing one global lock makes a single shared counter a highly contended cache line and exposes races in ordinary increments. The free-threaded design accepted through PEP 703 combines mechanisms including biased reference counting, deferred reference counting for selected references, immortalisation, and stop-the-world coordination for cyclic collection. Exact fields and state transitions are implementation details of each supporting version.

**Biased reference counting** gives an object an owning-thread bias so that common local increments/decrements can avoid an atomic operation, while references from other threads update shared state. Ownership transfer or merging reconciles state. **Deferred reference counting** omits immediate updates for selected interpreter-stack references and later accounts for them during coordinated scanning. These meanings differ from “reference counting was removed”.

The observable consequences are important:

- a raw numeric reference count is even less suitable as a truth oracle;
- deallocation timing can differ from conventional builds;
- borrowed-reference patterns that depended on global exclusion need strong-reference fetch APIs or locks;
- container integrity locks do not make multi-step application operations atomic;
- extension modules must use public ownership and thread-state APIs rather than direct field arithmetic.

### Worked example 15.16 — State a lifetime contract without relying on prompt destruction

~~~python
from contextlib import contextmanager
from io import StringIO
from collections.abc import Iterator


@contextmanager
def output_buffer() -> Iterator[StringIO]:
    stream = StringIO()
    try:
        yield stream
    finally:
        stream.close()


with output_buffer() as output:
    output.write("complete")
    assert output.getvalue() == "complete"

assert output.closed
~~~

The context manager gives deterministic lexical release independent of whether a reference count falls immediately. It remains correct on a tracing collector, conventional CPython, or a free-threaded configuration. Prompt reclamation is an optimisation of object memory lifetime; external resource correctness belongs to explicit protocols.

> **Common misconception 15.50 — “Free-threaded CPython simply makes every reference increment atomic and otherwise preserves the old model exactly.”**  
> Its design combines biased, deferred, immortal, atomic, and coordinated mechanisms to control contention and lifetime. Extensions must follow the supported API rather than assume one counter field.

Reference counting efficiently handles acyclic ownership. It cannot by itself distinguish an isolated cycle from a still-useful strongly connected structure, because every member of either structure can have a positive count.

## 15.13 Cyclic garbage collection

Reference counting cannot reclaim a cycle whose objects refer to each other after all external references disappear:

```python
left: list[object] = []
right: list[object] = [left]
left.append(right)

del left
del right
```

The two lists retain each other even though program roots no longer reach them. CPython’s cyclic garbage collector tracks selected container objects and periodically analyses groups to identify unreachable cycles.

The collector is **generational** in the broad sense that it uses generations or age-based policies whose exact count and scheduling have changed across versions. The empirical observation underlying generational collection is that many objects die young, so scanning younger candidates more often can reduce work. Consult the documentation for the target CPython version; do not hard-code historical generation counts.

The collector’s analysis conceptually distinguishes references internal to a candidate group from references arriving from outside. If subtracting internal support leaves no external reachability, the group is unreachable and can be cleared/finalised under applicable rules.

### Finalisation and resurrection

`__del__` is a finaliser hook, not a dependable resource manager. It can run at difficult times, during interpreter shutdown, on an arbitrary thread context under implementation rules, or not before abrupt termination. A finaliser can **resurrect** an object by creating a new reachable reference. Exceptions in `__del__` cannot propagate normally to a caller and are reported specially.

Use context managers for resources, `weakref.finalize` for selected fallback cleanup without embedding the same cycle hazards, and finalisers only with a complete lifecycle analysis.

### 15.13.1 The collector augments rather than replaces reference counting

The cyclic collector considers objects capable of participating in reference cycles, principally containers and user instances whose types support traversal. Such an object is **tracked** when registered with the collector’s tracking structures. Many atomic immutable objects need not be tracked because they cannot point into a cycle. CPython can also untrack containers such as selected dictionaries or tuples when their contents make cycle participation impossible, and later track them if contents change.

~~~python
import gc


observations = {
    "integer": gc.is_tracked(42),
    "list": gc.is_tracked([]),
    "atomic tuple": gc.is_tracked((1, 2, 3)),
    "nested tuple": gc.is_tracked(([],)),
    "dictionary": gc.is_tracked({"key": 1}),
}

for label, tracked in observations.items():
    print(label, tracked)
~~~

Only broad expectations should be asserted: a list capable of holding itself is normally tracked, while an integer is not a cycle-forming container. Tuple and dictionary tracking can change after a collection or mutation as an optimisation. “Untracked” does not mean unmanaged, immortal, outside reference counting, or invisible to all diagnostic tools. It means the cyclic collector need not include that object in the relevant traversal population at that moment.

The collector is not a moving/compacting collector in conventional CPython. It ordinarily leaves live object addresses stable and reclaims detected unreachable groups by clearing and reference-count consequences. That fact supports parts of the existing C API but also contributes to fragmentation; it is an implementation property, not a Python language guarantee.

> **Common misconception 15.51 — “Every CPython object is periodically traced by the cyclic garbage collector.”**  
> Reference counting manages all ordinary strong ownership, while cyclic collection tracks selected cycle-capable objects. Atomic and optimisably acyclic objects may be untracked.

### 15.13.2 Trial deletion identifies external support

Reference counts cannot distinguish a reachable cycle from an unreachable one using each count alone. The collector therefore performs a graph analysis over a candidate set. A useful conceptual account, sometimes called **trial deletion**, is:

1. copy each candidate’s reference-count support into temporary GC state;
2. traverse candidate-to-candidate strong references and subtract them from the target’s temporary support;
3. candidates with positive remaining support have references from outside the candidate graph or from roots represented outside the subtraction;
4. propagate reachability from those externally supported candidates through their outgoing edges;
5. the remaining candidates are unreachable cyclic trash, subject to finalisation and clearing rules.

This is conceptual, not a line-for-line specification of current internal functions or bit encodings. The key proof idea is that internal edges cancel. If a pair refers only to each other, both ordinary counts may be one; subtracting their mutual edges leaves zero. If a module global also points to one member, positive external support remains and reachability propagates to the other.

### Worked example 15.17 — Distinguish an unreachable cycle from a live cycle

~~~python
import gc
import weakref


class Node:
    def __init__(self, label: str) -> None:
        self.label = label
        self.next: Node | None = None


left = Node("left")
right = Node("right")
left.next = right
right.next = left

left_reference = weakref.ref(left)
right_reference = weakref.ref(right)

root = left
del left, right
gc.collect()
assert left_reference() is root
assert right_reference() is root.next

del root
gc.collect()
assert left_reference() is None
assert right_reference() is None
~~~

The local <code>root</code> is an external path during the first collection. After it is removed, only the internal cycle remains. Explicit <code>gc.collect</code> makes the observation deterministic enough for CPython tests but should not be inserted into normal hot paths as a substitute for lifecycle design.

An object graph can be unreachable from the program’s intended data model yet still reachable from the runtime—for example through a forgotten global cache, a trace function, a task registry, or a traceback. The collector correctly preserves it. Such a **logical leak** requires finding and removing the unwanted root, not changing cycle thresholds.

> **Common misconception 15.52 — “The collector frees every object the application no longer wants.”**  
> It can reclaim only objects unreachable under runtime roots and supported traversal. A stale cache or retained traceback is still reachable even if its lifetime violates the application design.

### 15.13.3 Generations trade collection frequency against survivor scanning

CPython 3.12 exposes three generations numbered 0, 1, and 2. Newly tracked objects enter the youngest generation. Survivors are promoted; younger generations are collected more often. Allocation-minus-deallocation counters and thresholds influence automatic collection. This exact three-generation policy must not be projected onto later releases: free-threaded and newer collector designs have revised generation counts and scheduling.

The public interface exposes configuration and statistics:

~~~python
import gc


print("thresholds", gc.get_threshold())
print("current counts", gc.get_count())

for generation, statistics in enumerate(gc.get_stats()):
    print(generation, statistics)
~~~

<code>get_count</code> values are scheduling counters, not numbers of live objects in each generation. <code>get_stats</code> reports cumulative collections, collected objects, and uncollectable objects for each exposed generation under the running interpreter. Allocation patterns in extensions or untracked types can escape a simplistic inference.

Calling <code>gc.collect(generation)</code> requests collection through a specified generation under that version’s semantics and returns the documented number of unreachable objects found. A full collection can clear certain built-in free lists as a side effect, changing subsequent memory and performance observations. Collection during another collection is undefined; callbacks must not recursively force it.

Applications sometimes disable automatic collection during a verified short phase that creates no cycles and then restore it. This is an advanced latency optimisation requiring measurement and exception-safe restoration:

~~~python
import gc


was_enabled = gc.isenabled()
if was_enabled:
    gc.disable()
try:
    records = [{"index": index} for index in range(10_000)]
finally:
    if was_enabled:
        gc.enable()

assert records[-1]["index"] == 9_999
~~~

The code does not prove no cycles were formed by surrounding hooks, subclasses, trace functions, or later mutations. Disabling automatic collection never disables reference counting. A server that forgets to re-enable it can accumulate cycles indefinitely.

> **Common misconception 15.53 — “Generation numbers and thresholds have one timeless meaning across CPython versions.”**  
> CPython 3.12’s three-generation policy is version-specific. Later collector and free-threaded designs alter generations, triggers, and scanning fractions; tools must interrogate and document their target runtime.

### 15.13.4 Extension containers must describe their outgoing graph

A native extension type that can participate in cycles must opt into GC support and implement traversal correctly. Its <code>tp_traverse</code> slot visits every owned Python reference that can lead to a cycle. Its <code>tp_clear</code> slot breaks such references safely. Allocation/initialisation tracks the object only after its traversable fields are in a state the collector can inspect, and deallocation untracks before invalidating them.

A conceptual skeleton is:

~~~c
typedef struct {
    PyObject_HEAD
    PyObject *peer;
} LinkObject;

static int
Link_traverse(LinkObject *self, visitproc visit, void *argument)
{
    Py_VISIT(self->peer);
    return 0;
}

static int
Link_clear(LinkObject *self)
{
    Py_CLEAR(self->peer);
    return 0;
}

static void
Link_dealloc(LinkObject *self)
{
    PyObject_GC_UnTrack(self);
    Link_clear(self);
    Py_TYPE(self)->tp_free((PyObject *)self);
}
~~~

The type definition must also set the documented GC flag and use a GC-compatible allocation/free path. <code>Py_VISIT</code> applies the visitor to a non-null child and propagates non-zero results. <code>Py_CLEAR</code> clears the field before decrementing the former value, helping make re-entrant finalisation observe a consistent owner.

Omitting an edge from <code>tp_traverse</code> can hide a cycle forever. Visiting a pointer that is not an owned Python reference can corrupt analysis. Clearing a mandatory invariant without making remaining methods tolerate the cleared state can cause use-after-clear errors during finalisation. GC support is therefore part of the type’s formal ownership design.

Inheritance adds requirements: a subtype’s traversal and clear logic may need to call the base implementation. The exact allocation helpers differ for fixed/variable-sized and limited-API use. Follow the C API documentation and model tests on each supported release.

> **Common misconception 15.54 — “The cyclic collector can discover native extension pointers by scanning raw memory.”**  
> CPython depends on each GC-aware type’s traversal contract. Hidden owned edges are invisible to graph analysis and can make cycles leak.

### 15.13.5 Finalisation, clearing, resurrection, and uncollectable state

PEP 442 established safe finalisation of cyclic isolates containing Python-level finalisers. Broadly, weak references are handled, finalisers are called under controlled ordering, the isolate is checked for resurrection, and cyclic links are cleared if it remains isolated. The exact implementation steps and distinctions among legacy C finalisers, modern finaliser slots, and weak callbacks require the target-version documentation.

**Resurrection** occurs when finalisation creates an externally reachable path to an object that was otherwise unreachable. A finaliser is normally called at most once under the modern protocol even if the resurrected object later becomes unreachable again.

### Worked example 15.18 — Demonstrate one-shot resurrection

~~~python
import gc
import weakref


resurrected: list[object] = []
events: list[str] = []


class Phoenix:
    def __del__(self) -> None:
        events.append("finalise")
        resurrected.append(self)


value = Phoenix()
reference = weakref.ref(value)
del value
gc.collect()

assert events == ["finalise"]
assert resurrected and reference() is resurrected[0]

resurrected.clear()
gc.collect()
assert events == ["finalise"]
~~~

Weak-reference timing around resurrection is subtle and version-specific; this example targets ordinary CPython behaviour and deliberately checks only after explicit collection. Resurrection makes reasoning difficult: state may have been partially torn down, external invariants may no longer hold, and ownership becomes global. It should almost never be an application technique.

<code>gc.garbage</code> stores objects the collector found uncollectable under the active policy, and <code>DEBUG_SAVEALL</code> deliberately appends all unreachable objects rather than freeing them. Turning on that flag creates retention by design:

~~~python
import gc


previous_flags = gc.get_debug()
try:
    gc.set_debug(previous_flags | gc.DEBUG_SAVEALL)
    cycle: list[object] = []
    cycle.append(cycle)
    del cycle
    gc.collect()
    saved = len(gc.garbage)
    gc.garbage.clear()
finally:
    gc.set_debug(previous_flags)

gc.collect()
assert saved >= 1
~~~

Global GC flags and <code>gc.garbage</code> affect the process. Diagnostic code must restore flags and clear intentionally saved state. The example should run in an isolated test process when other threads or tests may allocate cycles concurrently.

### 15.13.6 Collection callbacks enable measurement but can perturb it

<code>gc.callbacks</code> receives phase information at collection start and stop. A callback can measure duration and counts, but must remain fast, avoid retaining object graphs, and avoid causing nested collection.

~~~python
import gc
import time


starts: dict[int, int] = {}
durations: list[tuple[int, int]] = []


def observe_gc(phase: str, info: dict[str, int]) -> None:
    generation = info["generation"]
    if phase == "start":
        starts[generation] = time.perf_counter_ns()
    elif phase == "stop" and generation in starts:
        durations.append(
            (generation, time.perf_counter_ns() - starts.pop(generation))
        )


gc.callbacks.append(observe_gc)
try:
    gc.collect()
finally:
    gc.callbacks.remove(observe_gc)

assert durations
~~~

The measured interval includes callback overhead and whatever system scheduling occurs. It does not by itself identify pause attribution in a concurrent/free-threaded collector. Pair GC statistics with allocation traces, latency distributions, application phase, and runtime metadata.

> **Common misconception 15.55 — “Calling gc.collect is a general cure for high memory use.”**  
> It addresses eligible unreachable cycles. Reachable caches, native allocations, allocator retention, fragmentation, memory maps, and large still-live objects require different diagnoses; forced collection can only add cost when no cyclic trash exists.

Cyclic collection answers whether selected strongly connected objects remain externally reachable. Weak references answer a different design need: observing or indexing an object without becoming an external owner.

## 15.14 Weak references

A **weak reference** designates an object without keeping it alive. It permits caches, registries, and observer structures that should not own object lifetime.

```python
import weakref


class Record:
    pass


record = Record()
reference = weakref.ref(record)
print(reference() is record)

del record
print(reference())
```

In ordinary CPython execution, the final result becomes `None` after the object is collected. The timing is implementation-sensitive; the interface requires callers to handle the object disappearing between operations.

Not every type supports weak references. Slotted classes require a weak-reference slot. Weak mappings use identity/lifetime-aware weak references and have concurrency/liveness subtleties.

### 15.14.1 Dereference and test must be one operation

Calling a weak reference returns the referent if it is still alive or <code>None</code> after death. The race-safe idiom obtains one strong local result and tests it:

~~~python
from weakref import ReferenceType


def use_if_alive(reference: ReferenceType[object]) -> str | None:
    value = reference()
    if value is None:
        return None
    return type(value).__name__
~~~

Do not first call <code>reference()</code> to test and call it again to use. The last external strong reference can disappear between the two calls—through another thread in a free-threaded build, a callback, or other permitted execution. Assigning the result to <code>value</code> creates a strong local reference for the rest of the function’s use interval.

The referent itself can legitimately be <code>None</code> only if the weak-referenceable type permits an object identical to <code>None</code>; the built-in singleton is not weak-referenceable, so <code>None</code> serves unambiguously as a dead-result sentinel for <code>weakref.ref</code>.

A weak-reference callback is invoked when the referent is about to be finalised under applicable implementation rules. The callback receives the weak-reference object, not a live strong reference to the dying referent. Capturing the referent strongly in the callback would prevent the callback condition from arising:

~~~python
import gc
import weakref


events: list[str] = []


class Document:
    pass


document = Document()
reference = weakref.ref(
    document,
    lambda ref: events.append("document released"),
)

del document
gc.collect()

assert reference() is None
assert events == ["document released"]
~~~

The variable <code>reference</code> keeps the weak-reference object alive so its callback remains registered. Exceptions raised by weak callbacks are treated as unraisable and reported similarly to finaliser exceptions. Callback order among several weak references is implementation/documentation-sensitive and should not coordinate correctness.

> **Common misconception 15.56 — “Checking weak() is not None and then calling weak() again safely retrieves the same object.”**  
> The referent can die between calls. Call once, bind the result strongly, test that local, and use it only while the local remains in scope.

### 15.14.2 Weak containers encode non-ownership policies

<code>WeakValueDictionary</code> holds values weakly and removes entries when those values die. <code>WeakKeyDictionary</code> holds keys weakly and removes entries when keys die. <code>WeakSet</code> holds its members weakly. These structures are appropriate only when some independent owner controls lifetime.

### Worked example 15.19 — An interning cache that does not own results

~~~python
import gc
import weakref


class Symbol:
    def __init__(self, spelling: str) -> None:
        self.spelling = spelling


symbols: weakref.WeakValueDictionary[str, Symbol] = (
    weakref.WeakValueDictionary()
)


def symbol(spelling: str) -> Symbol:
    existing = symbols.get(spelling)
    if existing is not None:
        return existing
    created = Symbol(spelling)
    symbols[spelling] = created
    return created


first = symbol("alpha")
second = symbol("alpha")
assert first is second

del first, second
gc.collect()
assert "alpha" not in symbols
~~~

In concurrent use the get/create/store sequence requires a lock if identity uniqueness is an invariant. The container’s own memory integrity does not make the compound interning operation atomic.

Weak-key mappings have an equality/identity subtlety. Inserting a distinct but equal key can update the value associated with the original stored weak key; when that original object dies, the entry can disappear even if the equal object remains. Identity-keyed semantics should use an explicit identity wrapper or a registry designed and tested for that requirement.

Classes using <code>__slots__</code> do not automatically support weak references. Include <code>__weakref__</code> unless a base class already supplies support:

~~~python
import weakref


class SlottedRecord:
    __slots__ = ("name", "__weakref__")

    def __init__(self, name: str) -> None:
        self.name = name


record = SlottedRecord("entry")
assert weakref.ref(record)() is record
~~~

<code>weakref.finalize</code> registers a callback to run at most once when an object dies, or optionally at interpreter exit. It keeps itself alive, but its callback arguments must not own the monitored object, directly or through a bound method:

### Worked example 15.20 — A finaliser whose callback does not capture its owner

~~~python
import gc
import weakref


released: list[int] = []


class NativeHandle:
    def __init__(self, identifier: int) -> None:
        self.identifier = identifier
        self._finalizer = weakref.finalize(
            self,
            released.append,
            identifier,
        )

    def close(self) -> None:
        self._finalizer()


handle = NativeHandle(17)
handle.close()
assert released == [17]

del handle
gc.collect()
assert released == [17]
~~~

Explicit <code>close</code> gives deterministic cleanup and invoking the finaliser makes it inactive, so later collection does not duplicate the release. For a real handle, the callback must be idempotent or guarded and must tolerate shutdown conditions. A context manager should expose the primary ownership protocol; finalisation is a fallback.

> **Common misconception 15.57 — “weakref.finalize guarantees prompt and unconditional external-resource cleanup.”**  
> Process termination, retained referents, shutdown ordering, and callback failure can prevent or delay it. Use explicit close/context management for correctness and finalization only as a fallback.

Weak references help diagnose reachability without adding ownership. They do not explain why deallocated objects may leave process memory high; that question belongs to allocator layers and operating-system accounting.

## 15.15 Memory allocators

CPython layers memory management. Object-specific free lists, small-object allocation, arenas/pools, and platform allocators may retain freed memory for reuse rather than returning it immediately to the operating system. Therefore:

- object deallocation does not imply resident process memory immediately falls;
- `sys.getsizeof` does not include allocator fragmentation or all referents;
- a stable high-water resident set is not alone proof of a live-object leak;
- native extensions can allocate outside Python-traced domains.

Diagnose in layers: count live objects or allocation traces, inspect reachability, compare resident memory, and include native profilers where relevant. Choose the measure corresponding to the claim.

### 15.15.1 Allocator domains encode distinct contracts

The CPython memory C API separates three allocator domains:

| Domain | Representative family | Intended use |
|:---|:---|:---|
| raw | <code>PyMem_RawMalloc</code>, <code>PyMem_RawRealloc</code>, <code>PyMem_RawFree</code> | general memory, callable without an attached Python thread state under documented rules |
| memory | <code>PyMem_Malloc</code>, <code>PyMem_Realloc</code>, <code>PyMem_Free</code> | buffers associated with interpreter-managed memory and requiring an attached thread state |
| object | <code>PyObject_Malloc</code>, <code>PyObject_Realloc</code>, <code>PyObject_Free</code> | Python-object storage and related private allocations under object-domain rules |

The three families can route to different allocator implementations or hooks. Memory obtained from a family must be resized and freed with its matching family. Mixing <code>malloc</code> with <code>PyMem_Free</code>, or <code>PyObject_Malloc</code> with <code>free</code>, is undefined and can corrupt heaps even if it appears to work in one release build.

~~~c
static int
copy_bytes(const char *source, Py_ssize_t length, char **output)
{
    if (length < 0) {
        PyErr_SetString(PyExc_ValueError, "negative length");
        return -1;
    }

    char *buffer = PyMem_Malloc((size_t)length + 1);
    if (buffer == NULL) {
        PyErr_NoMemory();
        return -1;
    }

    memcpy(buffer, source, (size_t)length);
    buffer[length] = '\0';
    *output = buffer;
    return 0;
}

/* The eventual owner must call PyMem_Free(*output). */
~~~

The calculation casts a non-negative <code>Py_ssize_t</code> before adding one; on supported models its maximum plus one is representable by <code>size_t</code>. More general element-count times element-size calculations still require explicit overflow checks or checked-size helpers. Allocator ownership and size arithmetic form one proof, not separate afterthoughts.

Since Python 3.12, custom allocators installed for all domains must be thread-safe under the documented requirement. After full runtime initialisation, replacement allocators generally need to wrap the existing allocator rather than substitute arbitrary nonconforming state. Debug hooks may need reinstalling. Embedder code must follow the preinitialisation/initialisation phase restrictions for that version.

> **Common misconception 15.58 — “All CPython allocation functions are interchangeable wrappers around C malloc.”**  
> Raw, memory, and object domains have distinct attachment and instrumentation contracts. Allocation, reallocation, and free must remain within the same documented family.

### 15.15.2 pymalloc organises small blocks into pools and arenas

In the default conventional build, the specialised allocator commonly called **pymalloc** serves object-domain requests up to 512 bytes. It groups equal-size blocks into pools and obtains pools from larger arenas. In CPython 3.12, an arena is 1 MiB on 64-bit platforms and 256 KiB on 32-bit platforms; pool and size-class details are version/build mechanisms. Larger requests go to underlying platform allocation paths.

This hierarchy reduces the cost of repeated small allocations and internal fragmentation between unlike sizes. A pool dedicated to one size class can recycle a freed block immediately. An arena can return to the platform only when all its pools are sufficiently free under allocator policy. One long-lived object can therefore pin a pool or arena containing mostly free capacity.

The following Python experiment observes shallow allocation patterns, not internal pools directly:

### Worked example 15.21 — Separate live size from resident high-water behaviour

~~~python
import gc
import os
import tracemalloc


tracemalloc.start()
before = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()

objects = [bytearray(400) for _ in range(50_000)]
during = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
del objects
gc.collect()
after = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()

during_growth = sum(
    statistic.size_diff
    for statistic in during.compare_to(before, "lineno")
)
remaining_growth = sum(
    statistic.size_diff
    for statistic in after.compare_to(before, "lineno")
)

print(os.getpid(), during_growth, remaining_growth)
tracemalloc.stop()
~~~

The trace should show substantial allocation growth and later reduction, but exact numbers are deliberately not asserted. The process’s resident set may remain high because pools, arenas, the platform allocator, or operating-system page policy retain address space for reuse. <code>bytearray</code> can include a separately allocated buffer whose path is not reducible to the object header’s shallow size.

Three quantities answer different questions:

- **live traced allocation** estimates blocks currently attributed to traced Python allocator domains;
- **allocator reserved memory** includes free blocks kept in pools/arenas or platform heaps;
- **resident set size** counts pages currently resident according to operating-system accounting and can include code, shared libraries, mappings, native buffers, and allocator metadata.

A decline in the first need not immediately produce a decline in the third. Conversely, a native extension leak may grow resident memory without appearing in ordinary tracemalloc domains unless it integrates tracing.

> **Common misconception 15.59 — “If an object is deallocated, its bytes must immediately be returned to the operating system.”**  
> CPython and platform allocators commonly retain freed blocks, pools, or arenas for reuse. Object death, allocator availability, address-space release, and resident-page reduction are separate events.

### 15.15.3 Debug hooks expose family and boundary errors

CPython’s memory debug hooks can surround allocated blocks with forbidden-byte regions, fill newly allocated and freed memory with recognisable patterns, record requested size and API family, and use tracemalloc information to report allocation origin. A debug build enables substantial checks by default; the <code>PYTHONMALLOC=debug</code> environment setting can enable debug hooks in other supported builds.

These hooks help detect:

- writes before or after an allocated block;
- use of an inappropriate allocator family to free a block;
- selected calls without required thread-state attachment;
- use-after-free patterns when overwritten bytes retain debug markers.

They do not prove absence of all memory errors. An out-of-bounds write can corrupt unrelated data before a guard is checked; data races can evade deterministic detection; a pointer can target a still-allocated but semantically wrong object. AddressSanitizer, UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, Valgrind-like tools, debug builds, and stress tests provide complementary evidence.

Allocator selection can be reported rather than guessed:

~~~python
import os
import sys


print("implementation", sys.implementation.name)
print("malloc setting", os.environ.get("PYTHONMALLOC", "<default>"))
print("tracemalloc setting", os.environ.get("PYTHONTRACEMALLOC", "<default>"))
~~~

Changing <code>PYTHONMALLOC</code> requires starting a new process; setting it after initialisation does not retroactively rebuild allocator state. Comparing default, system-malloc, and debug configurations can isolate allocator-retention effects, but each configuration changes overhead and timing.

> **Common misconception 15.60 — “A release build that passes tests proves a C extension has correct allocation boundaries.”**  
> Heap corruption can remain latent. Debug hooks and native memory sanitizers deliberately change layout and timing to expose family mismatches, overruns, use-after-free, and races.

### 15.15.4 tracemalloc attributes selected allocations to Python stacks

<code>tracemalloc</code> records traceback metadata for traced allocation blocks. It can compare snapshots by source line, filename, or traceback, filter domains/locations, and report current and peak traced size. Starting it early captures more of program startup; deeper traceback limits improve attribution at additional memory/time cost.

### Worked example 15.22 — Compare a bounded allocation phase

~~~python
import tracemalloc


def build_index(size: int) -> dict[int, str]:
    return {number: str(number) for number in range(size)}


tracemalloc.start(10)
baseline = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()

index = build_index(20_000)
populated = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()

statistics = populated.compare_to(baseline, "traceback")
for statistic in statistics[:3]:
    print(statistic)

del index
tracemalloc.stop()
~~~

Snapshot comparison is differential: unrelated concurrent activity appears too. Run controlled workloads repeatedly, use filters, and preserve the allocation stack rather than blaming whichever line happens to retain the final container. A positive difference can represent intended cache growth; a leak is growth that violates the required lifetime and remains unbounded under a representative workload.

Native extensions can register allocations in non-zero tracemalloc domains through the C API, enabling separation from default Python allocations. Tracking metadata itself consumes memory. The module does not trace arbitrary <code>malloc</code> calls without cooperation.

### 15.15.5 Free lists and caches complicate before-and-after tests

Object implementations can retain recently freed structures in type-specific free lists or caches. Integer/string interning, tuple/frame-related caches in selected versions, import caches, regular-expression caches, and application-level pools all change allocation reuse. A full generation-2 collection clears some built-in free lists, but not necessarily every retained block.

<code>sys.getallocatedblocks</code>, where available, reports the number of memory blocks allocated by the interpreter and can return zero or an approximate value when tracking is unavailable. It is not a byte count and includes activity caused by the measurement environment:

### Worked example 15.23 — Treat allocated-block counts statistically

~~~python
import gc
import statistics
import sys


def allocated_blocks() -> int | None:
    getter = getattr(sys, "getallocatedblocks", None)
    return None if getter is None else getter()


measurements: list[int] = []
for _ in range(7):
    gc.collect()
    value = allocated_blocks()
    if value is not None:
        measurements.append(value)

if measurements:
    print(statistics.median(measurements), min(measurements), max(measurements))
~~~

Variation is expected. The act of building the list creates blocks. A valid leak test repeats a representative create/use/release cycle, discards warm-up, checks the slope or plateau across many rounds, and corroborates with object/reachability evidence.

> **Common misconception 15.61 — “One memory metric can distinguish every leak, cache, fragmentation, and allocator effect.”**  
> Live object graphs, traced blocks, native allocations, reserved arenas, virtual memory, and resident pages are different quantities. Diagnosis requires several aligned measurements and a lifetime hypothesis.

Allocator and reference-count designs were historically protected by a process-wide execution lock. Free-threaded builds must preserve memory safety and ownership without making that lock the universal exclusion mechanism.

## 15.16 The GIL and free-threaded internals

In conventional builds, the GIL permits CPython object and interpreter internals to rely on broad mutual exclusion for many operations, though extensions release it around blocking work or independent native computation. Thread switching can occur between bytecodes and within operations that release the lock or invoke arbitrary code.

Free-threaded CPython builds remove that global exclusion and use finer-grained, deferred, atomic, biased, or immortal-object techniques as the version implements them. Built-in containers employ internal synchronisation sufficient to protect their own memory integrity under documented conditions, but application-level sequences remain non-atomic unless explicitly synchronised.

Extension modules must advertise and implement compatible thread behaviour. Importing an extension not marked safe can alter runtime mode under version-specific policy. Performance can improve for parallel Python work and regress for single-thread or contention-heavy work; measurement is required.

The language-level conclusion is stable: never use the GIL as the specification of a program invariant.

### 15.16.1 The conventional GIL serialises attached bytecode execution, not all process activity

In a conventional CPython build, a thread must hold the **global interpreter lock** while operating on most Python objects and executing Python bytecode. Broad mutual exclusion makes ordinary reference-count updates and many object invariants cheaper than if every field required separate synchronisation. The lock is associated with an interpreter/runtime arrangement, not with a source line, and its policy has evolved.

Only one thread holding that GIL executes Python interpreter work at an instant, but other activity can proceed:

- a thread can release the lock while blocking in operating-system I/O;
- extension code can release it around native computation that does not touch Python objects;
- subprocesses execute in distinct processes with distinct interpreters;
- devices, kernels, databases, and network peers continue independently;
- some extension libraries manage their own worker threads and release the GIL.

This explains why threading can improve throughput for I/O-bound workloads even though CPU-bound pure Python bytecode remains serialised in one conventional interpreter. It does not guarantee improvement: lock hand-offs, scheduling, cache pressure, oversubscription, and task granularity add overhead.

The GIL is not held forever by one thread. The evaluator responds to switching requests and blocking operations. A configurable switch interval influences how often the interpreter asks long-running Python execution to yield, but it is not a strict maximum latency, instruction count, or real-time scheduling guarantee.

~~~python
import sys


original = sys.getswitchinterval()
try:
    sys.setswitchinterval(0.01)
    assert sys.getswitchinterval() > 0
finally:
    sys.setswitchinterval(original)
~~~

Changing a process-wide scheduling hint to “fix” a race is invalid. A correct algorithm uses locks, queues, conditions, futures, immutable messages, or transactional storage. The interval can be varied in stress tests to expose accidental scheduling assumptions.

> **Common misconception 15.62 — “The GIL means a multithreaded CPython program has no concurrency.”**  
> It serialises much Python-object/bytecode execution in a conventional interpreter. Threads can overlap blocking I/O and GIL-releasing native work, while external systems and processes execute concurrently.

### 15.16.2 Detaching thread state permits blocking or independent native work

Native extension code commonly brackets a region that neither accesses Python objects nor calls most Python C APIs. The <code>Py_BEGIN_ALLOW_THREADS</code> and <code>Py_END_ALLOW_THREADS</code> macros save/detach the current thread state and later restore/attach it; in a GIL build this releases and reacquires the lock.

~~~c
static PyObject *
wait_for_device(PyObject *self, PyObject *arguments)
{
    int descriptor;
    if (!PyArg_ParseTuple(arguments, "i", &descriptor)) {
        return NULL;
    }

    int status;
    Py_BEGIN_ALLOW_THREADS
    status = blocking_device_wait(descriptor);
    Py_END_ALLOW_THREADS

    if (status < 0) {
        return PyErr_SetFromErrno(PyExc_OSError);
    }
    Py_RETURN_NONE;
}
~~~

The native function names the intended shape; a real implementation must handle EINTR, platform handles, cancellation, descriptor lifetime, and whether its external API is thread-safe. Inside the detached region, it must not manipulate Python objects, adjust ordinary Python ownership through non-permitted APIs, or raise a Python exception. It records native status and constructs the Python result after reattachment.

In free-threaded builds these macros still detach/attach thread state even though they do not release a global lock in the same sense. The thread-state invariant remains. A callback from a foreign native thread must use documented attachment APIs and target the intended interpreter; convenience APIs historically assume the main interpreter and can be unsuitable for subinterpreters.

Long C loops that retain the GIL can starve other Python threads and delay signal handling. Releasing it is safe only when all accessed data has a non-Python lifetime and appropriate native synchronisation. Holding a raw pointer into a mutable Python buffer across detachment requires a specific export/pinning contract; “I do not call the API” alone is insufficient.

> **Common misconception 15.63 — “Between ALLOW_THREADS macros, C code may keep using Python object fields as long as it does not create objects.”**  
> Detachment permits other execution or free-threaded mutation. The region must avoid Python C API/object access unless an explicit API guarantees safety and lifetime independently.

### 15.16.3 Per-interpreter GILs partition exclusion, not arbitrary objects

PEP 684 moved the GIL into interpreter state and enabled subinterpreters configured with their own GIL in supporting CPython versions. Two such interpreters can execute Python code in parallel while retaining a GIL within each interpreter. This requires isolation of runtime state that was historically process-global.

A subinterpreter is not a lightweight thread sharing one arbitrary Python heap. Module dictionaries, built-ins, imported module instances, and many stateful resources are interpreter-specific. Cross-interpreter communication must use objects/data supported by explicit channels, copying, serialisation, or carefully designed shareable representations. Passing a normal <code>PyObject *</code> from one interpreter to another violates ownership and allocator assumptions.

Extension modules are a central constraint. A traditional single-phase extension with mutable static globals can accidentally share state across interpreters, retain objects from the wrong interpreter, or assume one finalisation event. Multi-phase initialisation and per-module state let each module instance own its state and support traversal, clearing, and freeing under the correct interpreter.

Conceptually:

~~~c
typedef struct {
    PyObject *cache;
} module_state;

static module_state *
get_state(PyObject *module)
{
    return (module_state *)PyModule_GetState(module);
}
~~~

The complete module definition must specify state size and lifecycle slots, traverse/clear owned objects, and declare multi-interpreter/GIL support through APIs appropriate to the target version. A pointer returned from module state remains governed by the module instance’s lifetime.

Per-interpreter isolation also affects process facilities that cannot be duplicated cleanly: environment variables, file descriptors, locale, signal disposition, C library globals, and third-party library singletons remain process-wide unless mediated. “Separate interpreter” is a carefully bounded isolation unit, not an operating-system security sandbox.

> **Common misconception 15.64 — “A per-interpreter GIL makes every extension and global resource safely independent.”**  
> Parallel interpreters require per-interpreter module state and explicit treatment of process-global native resources. Ordinary Python objects cannot be shared across interpreter heaps by raw pointer.

### 15.16.4 Free-threaded CPython replaces broad exclusion with several mechanisms

PEP 703 specifies an optional build mode in which Python threads can execute bytecode in parallel without one process/interpreter-wide GIL. In the 3.13 experimental era and subsequent development, the implementation combines techniques rather than applying one lock to every object:

- biased and deferred reference counting reduce atomic update traffic;
- selected objects are immortalised;
- built-in containers use fine-grained internal locks for memory integrity;
- optimistic dictionary/list access paths attempt common reads with validation;
- stop-the-world phases coordinate selected garbage-collection work;
- allocator changes and page reuse constraints support safe lock-free/optimistic reads;
- critical-section APIs let extension operations follow container locking policy;
- borrowed-reference APIs gain strong-reference alternatives for concurrent safety.

Each item is implementation- and version-scoped. The stable application consequence is that two threads may truly execute Python operations simultaneously. Data races that the conventional GIL happened to mask can become visible. The language still does not promise that compound read-modify-write sequences are atomic.

### Worked example 15.24 — Protect a semantic invariant, not a container method

~~~python
from threading import Lock, Thread


class Account:
    def __init__(self, balance: int) -> None:
        self._balance = balance
        self._lock = Lock()

    def withdraw(self, amount: int) -> bool:
        if amount < 0:
            raise ValueError("amount must be non-negative")
        with self._lock:
            if amount > self._balance:
                return False
            self._balance -= amount
            return True

    @property
    def balance(self) -> int:
        with self._lock:
            return self._balance


account = Account(100)
threads = [
    Thread(target=account.withdraw, args=(60,))
    for _ in range(2)
]
for thread in threads:
    thread.start()
for thread in threads:
    thread.join()

assert account.balance == 40
~~~

An internal lock on the integer object or instance dictionary would not make “check then subtract” one transaction. The account lock covers the invariant. The example is correct under both conventional and free-threaded builds and under scheduling changes.

Built-in list/dictionary locks preserve internal memory safety and give operations behaviour consistent with their documented critical regions. They do not supply a durable transaction across two calls, prevent logical lost updates, or replace ordering between application objects. Iteration while another thread mutates still requires an application protocol.

### 15.16.5 Extension compatibility is an explicit declaration and audit

A binary extension targeting a free-threaded build must be compiled for the appropriate ABI/configuration and declare support through the version’s module initialisation mechanism. The declaration is a claim backed by an audit:

- all process-global and module state has defined locking/ownership;
- borrowed references cannot outlive stable protected sources;
- direct reference-count and object-layout access is replaced by supported APIs;
- container mutations follow critical-section rules;
- callbacks and thread-state attachment target the right interpreter;
- released-GIL/detached regions have independent memory lifetimes;
- third-party native libraries are themselves safe under parallel calls.

In early free-threaded releases, importing an extension that does not declare support can cause the runtime to enable the GIL under documented policy and emit a warning. Exact behaviour and command-line/environment controls vary; test the actual deployment executable.

### Worked example 15.25 — Record the execution configuration in a benchmark

~~~python
import json
import sys
import sysconfig


def concurrency_configuration() -> dict[str, object]:
    gil_enabled = getattr(sys, "_is_gil_enabled", None)
    return {
        "version": sys.version,
        "gil_disabled_build": bool(
            sysconfig.get_config_var("Py_GIL_DISABLED")
        ),
        "gil_currently_enabled": (
            gil_enabled() if gil_enabled is not None else None
        ),
    }


print(json.dumps(concurrency_configuration(), indent=2))
~~~

The runtime query is only available in versions that expose it; <code>None</code> means “not observable through this interface”, not “the GIL is disabled”. A benchmark record should also list imported native extensions because one can affect runtime mode or parallel scalability.

> **Common misconception 15.65 — “No-GIL mode makes every threaded workload faster.”**  
> Parallelism introduces synchronisation, atomic operations, cache coherence, allocation, scheduling, and contention costs. Speedup depends on workload, thread count, extensions, memory bandwidth, and single-thread overhead, and must be measured against a stated baseline.

Function-call overhead is one frequently executed part of this picture. Vectorcall reduces argument-container construction while preserving the language’s call and binding semantics.

## 15.17 Native calls and vectorcall

Function calls are frequent, so modern CPython uses calling conventions such as **vectorcall** to reduce temporary tuple/dictionary construction when passing positional and keyword arguments internally. Exact structures and flags are C API details.

At Python level, call semantics remain:

- evaluate callable;
- evaluate arguments in order;
- perform signature binding or callable-specific processing;
- execute and return or raise.

An implementation optimisation may avoid allocating an argument tuple while preserving the observable call. Benchmarking a call must therefore target a CPython version and callable kind; built-ins, Python functions, bound methods, and extension callables have different fast paths.

### 15.17.1 Call semantics and call representation are separate contracts

Python call syntax first evaluates the primary expression naming the callable, then argument expressions in specified order, expands starred positional and double-starred keyword inputs under defined rules, rejects duplicate keywords, and invokes the object’s call protocol. A Python function then binds supplied arguments to positional-only, positional-or-keyword, variadic positional, keyword-only, and variadic keyword parameters, applying retained defaults where permitted.

Vectorcall changes how an already evaluated call is carried across an internal/API boundary. Instead of necessarily constructing a tuple of positional arguments and a dictionary of keywords, the caller supplies a contiguous vector of object pointers plus compact metadata. The callee consumes that representation directly when it supports the protocol.

The following language-level experiment proves evaluation order, not vectorcall internals:

~~~python
events: list[str] = []


def argument(label: str, value: int) -> int:
    events.append(label)
    return value


def combine(left: int, right: int, *, scale: int) -> int:
    events.append("body")
    return (left + right) * scale


result = combine(
    argument("left", 2),
    argument("right", 3),
    scale=argument("scale", 4),
)

assert result == 20
assert events == ["left", "right", "scale", "body"]
~~~

An optimised calling convention cannot reorder these visible effects. It begins after or participates consistently in evaluation while retaining the specified sequence. Nor may it omit duplicate-key detection, positional-only restrictions, or descriptor binding.

> **Common misconception 15.66 — “Vectorcall is a different kind of Python function with different argument rules.”**  
> It is a CPython calling representation and protocol. Python-level evaluation, expansion, binding, defaults, and error semantics remain the governing contract.

### 15.17.2 nargsf and kwnames describe a packed argument vector

At the C API level, a vectorcall function receives a callable, an array of <code>PyObject *</code> arguments, a <code>size_t nargsf</code>, and a keyword-name tuple. Masking <code>nargsf</code> with the documented operation obtains the positional count; a flag can indicate that a writable scratch slot exists immediately before the argument vector. The keyword tuple contains names only, while corresponding values follow the positional values in the same vector.

Conceptually, a call such as <code>function(10, 20, scale=3, mode="fast")</code> is represented as:

| Vector index | Object role |
|:---:|:---|
| 0 | positional value 10 |
| 1 | positional value 20 |
| 2 | value 3 for keyword <code>scale</code> |
| 3 | value <code>fast</code> for keyword <code>mode</code> |

and <code>kwnames</code> is a tuple equivalent to <code>("scale", "mode")</code>. It is not a dictionary and need not allocate one unless callee semantics require a <code>**kwargs</code> object. Keywords in <code>kwnames</code> must satisfy the protocol’s string/name requirements; callers must not mutate argument arrays in violation of flags.

A simplified custom type slot has this form:

~~~c
static PyObject *
Example_vectorcall(PyObject *callable,
                   PyObject *const *arguments,
                   size_t nargsf,
                   PyObject *keyword_names)
{
    Py_ssize_t positional = PyVectorcall_NARGS(nargsf);
    /* Parse without retaining borrowed array entries across callbacks. */
    return parse_and_execute(
        callable,
        arguments,
        positional,
        keyword_names
    );
}
~~~

The placeholder helper would need a complete parsing, ownership, error, recursion, and thread-safety implementation. C extensions should normally use maintained parsing helpers or generated Argument Clinic code instead of hand-parsing every vector. Vector entries are not automatically new owned references.

The <code>PY_VECTORCALL_ARGUMENTS_OFFSET</code> flag permits selected callers to let a callee temporarily use <code>arguments[-1]</code>, enabling efficient insertion of a bound receiver. It does not authorise arbitrary out-of-bounds access. The callee must restore any temporarily changed value before return.

> **Common misconception 15.67 — “kwnames contains the keyword values or is an ordinary keyword dictionary.”**  
> It contains keyword-name objects. Their values occupy the argument vector after positional values, allowing a call to avoid constructing a dictionary when the callee does not need one.

### 15.17.3 Descriptors and method calls motivate allocation avoidance

Ordinary attribute access to a function stored on a class produces a bound method object whose receiver is recorded as <code>__self__</code>. If code immediately calls that method, allocating a transient bound-method object is often avoidable. CPython’s method-load/call paths can carry callable and receiver separately into vectorcall.

### Worked example 15.26 — Bound-method semantics survive an optimised call

~~~python
class Counter:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.value = 0

    def add(self, amount: int) -> int:
        self.value += amount
        return self.value


counter = Counter()

bound = counter.add
assert bound.__self__ is counter
assert bound.__func__ is Counter.add
assert counter.add(3) == 3
assert bound(4) == 7
~~~

The explicit <code>bound</code> access materialises a method object observable through identity and attributes. The immediate <code>counter.add(3)</code> expression can use an optimised path while producing the same receiver binding. A custom descriptor may implement arbitrary <code>__get__</code>, so the optimiser must preserve descriptor semantics and guard fast paths.

Callable categories differ. A Python function parses against its code/signature metadata. A built-in C function can implement method flags or vectorcall directly. A class call passes through metaclass/type construction machinery. A callable instance uses the type’s call slot. <code>functools.partial</code> and bound methods prepend stored arguments. Benchmarking “the cost of a Python call” without identifying the category conflates distinct paths.

### Worked example 15.27 — inspect semantic signatures rather than native flags

~~~python
import inspect
from functools import partial


def affine(value: float, scale: float, offset: float) -> float:
    return value * scale + offset


shifted = partial(affine, scale=2.0, offset=1.0)

signature = inspect.signature(affine)
assert tuple(signature.parameters) == ("value", "scale", "offset")
print(inspect.signature(shifted))
assert shifted(3.0) == 7.0
~~~

The structural assertion avoids coupling the test to whether annotations are stored as objects or postponed strings and to formatted spelling. The point is that <code>inspect.signature</code> provides callable binding semantics while vectorcall flags describe a native transport.

Argument Clinic is a CPython source-generation system that turns declarative signatures into C parsing wrappers, documentation signatures, and method definitions. It reduces repetitive error-prone conversion code and lets maintainers evolve calling conventions centrally. It is a CPython development mechanism, not a Python packaging dependency every extension must use.

> **Common misconception 15.68 — “Avoiding a temporary tuple means a call performs no allocations or argument processing.”**  
> The callee may create locals, <code>*args</code>, <code>**kwargs</code>, defaults, conversion results, a frame, or returned objects. Vectorcall removes selected transport overhead, not the semantic work of calling.

Calls cross module boundaries through name and attribute resolution. Import creates those module objects through a protocol whose early caching and failure behaviour are essential to circular-import reasoning.

## 15.18 Import internals and module objects

Import uses `sys.meta_path` finders to produce module specifications, loaders to create/execute modules, and `sys.modules` to cache them. Import locks coordinate concurrent loading. Package path entries and hooks permit filesystem, archive, frozen, and custom sources.

During import, the module is inserted in `sys.modules` before execution completes to manage recursion. If execution fails, cleanup rules remove or retain related entries according to the import path, and already imported side-effect modules can remain. Import is not a transaction rolling back every effect.

Instrumenting import time can expose expensive top-level code:

```text
python -X importtime -c "import ledger"
```

`-X` options are implementation-specific. The output describes one environment and cache state.

### 15.18.1 Import is a protocol with an early cache entry

An import first checks <code>sys.modules</code> for the fully qualified name. If no usable entry exists, finders on <code>sys.meta_path</code> are asked for a <code>ModuleSpec</code>. The chosen loader can create a module or allow default creation; import-related attributes are initialised; the module is placed in <code>sys.modules</code>; and the loader executes its code. The early insertion is what lets a recursive import encounter the same partially initialised module instead of creating an infinite series of copies.

The protocol separates discovery, module creation, and execution. A spec records name, loader, origin, package/submodule information, and optional loader state. It is not necessarily a filesystem record: built-in, frozen, namespace-package, zip, database, remote, or application-defined finders can participate.

### Worked example 15.28 — Observe a module specification without re-executing it

~~~python
import importlib.util
import json


for name in ("json", "sys"):
    specification = importlib.util.find_spec(name)
    if specification is None:
        raise RuntimeError(f"no specification for {name}")
    print(
        name,
        type(specification.loader).__name__,
        specification.origin,
        specification.submodule_search_locations,
    )

assert json.__spec__ is not None
assert json.__spec__.name == "json"
~~~

<code>find_spec</code> can import a parent package while locating a submodule, so it is not universally side-effect-free. Printing a custom loader can execute its representation. Inspection tools should work within a controlled finder environment.

During a circular import, a module can be present but incomplete. Suppose <code>alpha</code> imports <code>beta</code> before binding <code>alpha.ready</code>, while <code>beta</code> immediately reads that attribute. The cache correctly returns <code>alpha</code>; the attribute is absent because execution has not reached its assignment. Reordering imports sometimes hides the cycle but does not improve architecture. Extract shared declarations into a lower-level module, import modules rather than eager attributes where suitable, or delay a dependency explicitly.

If execution of a newly loaded module fails, import removes the failing module’s cache entry under the standard protocol, while modules successfully loaded as side effects can remain cached. Mutations, files written, network requests, thread creation, and registrations performed before failure are not rolled back. Retrying the import can repeat them.
