Signatures and digests must specify whether they cover encoded transfer bytes or decoded representation bytes.

Language, profile, and API-version information can be represented through media-type parameters, fields, or resource identifiers. Each approach affects caches, links, deprecation, and client implementation. “Versionless” APIs still evolve; compatibility rules simply move elsewhere.

> **Common misconception 18.22 — “<code>Content-Type</code> tells the server what response the client wants.”**  
> It describes enclosed request or response content. <code>Accept</code> and related negotiation fields describe acceptable response representations.

### 18.10.2 Negotiation and the <code>Vary</code> contract

An <code>Accept</code> value can list media ranges with quality weights. The server combines client preferences, representation availability, and policy. A missing <code>Accept</code> commonly means broad acceptance, not specifically JSON. A 406 can report that no acceptable representation exists, though APIs often define one fixed representation instead.

If response selection depends on <code>Accept-Encoding</code>, <code>Accept-Language</code>, or another request field, a shared cache needs that field in <code>Vary</code>. Otherwise it can reuse a compressed, language-specific, or otherwise incompatible representation for another request. Excessive <code>Vary</code> dimensions fragment cache effectiveness.

~~~python
from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Representation:
    media_type: str
    body: bytes


def choose_representation(accept: str | None) -> Representation:
    html = Representation(
        "text/html; charset=utf-8",
        b"<p>device A17</p>",
    )
    json = Representation(
        "application/json",
        b'{"device_id":"A17"}',
    )
    if accept is None or "*/*" in accept:
        return json
    if "application/json" in accept:
        return json
    if "text/html" in accept:
        return html
    raise LookupError("no acceptable representation")


assert choose_representation("application/json").media_type == (
    "application/json"
)
~~~

This deliberately incomplete parser cannot implement quality weights, specificity, parameters, or quoted syntax. It exposes why applications should use maintained negotiation utilities or define a narrow documented contract.

Streaming JSON as one giant array delays valid closure and complicates recovery. Newline-delimited JSON, server-sent events, or format-specific streaming can define incremental records, but each needs framing, per-record limits, cancellation, and partial-delivery semantics.

> **Common misconception 18.23 — “Content negotiation is just checking whether a header contains the word JSON.”**  
> It is selection under typed syntax, weights, specificity, availability, and cache variation. Substring tests misparse valid fields.

### 18.10.3 HTML is a semantic document language

HTML represents a document tree with elements whose names carry structure and behaviour. A browser parses bytes under the response encoding and HTML parsing algorithm, repairs some malformed structures, constructs a Document Object Model (DOM), loads referenced resources, and exposes interactive semantics.

Elements are not chosen only for appearance. A heading establishes document hierarchy; a button is keyboard-focusable and activates under platform input conventions; a label associates text with a form control; navigation and main landmarks support assistive technology. Replacing them with generic <code>div</code> elements plus click handlers discards behaviour that then has to be reconstructed incompletely.

An **accessible name** identifies a control to assistive technologies. It can derive from text, a label, or defined ARIA relationships. ARIA can express states and relations absent from native elements, but it does not add keyboard behaviour automatically. Prefer native semantic controls, then use ARIA to fill genuine gaps.

Forms serialise named successful controls under an encoding. A checkbox can be absent when unchecked; repeated names can yield several values; file controls use multipart encoding; submit buttons can contribute different names. Server code must parse a multimap rather than assume one scalar per name.

Client-side validation improves feedback but is not an authority boundary. Requests can bypass the browser, constraints can be altered, and concurrent state can change. The server repeats all material validation and authorisation. Return errors associated with fields and a summary usable without colour alone.

HTML responses can support **progressive enhancement**: links and forms perform core navigation and mutation, while JavaScript improves interactivity. This reduces dependency on a successful client bundle and often creates cleaner HTTP semantics. It is an architectural option, not a requirement that every interface avoid rich client state.

### 18.10.4 CSS, JavaScript, and the rendering pipeline

CSS selects elements and applies a cascade of declarations. The final value depends on origin, importance, cascade layer, specificity, scoping, source order, inheritance, and computed-value rules. “The last rule wins” is an incomplete summary.

Layout algorithms—block, inline, flex, grid, table, positioned layout—solve different constraint systems. Responsive design lets layout respond to available space and user preferences rather than a list of device names. Logical properties support writing directions; relative units and content-driven sizing support zoom and text enlargement.

A browser combines the DOM and style information, performs layout, paints pixels, and composites layers. DOM or style changes can require new style calculation, layout, paint, or compositing work. Repeatedly reading layout after writes can force synchronous recalculation. Measure with browser profiling rather than guessing from framework component count.

JavaScript runs tasks on an event loop. Promise callbacks run as microtasks at defined checkpoints; rendering and user input compete with long tasks. An <code>async</code> function yields only at awaits whose operations genuinely settle later. CPU-heavy parsing or rendering on the main thread blocks input and accessibility.

Modules provide lexical scope and dependency graphs. Bundlers can transform modules, split chunks, minify code, and rewrite asset references; source maps connect generated failures to source but can disclose source if published indiscriminately. A content hash supports immutable caching.

Hydration attaches interactive behaviour to server-rendered markup. If the client renders a structurally different tree, frameworks can discard or repair DOM, lose input state, and report mismatch. Time, randomness, locale, authentication, and browser-only values must be controlled across server and client rendering.

Browser performance includes:

- navigation and server response;
- render-blocking styles and scripts;
- image/font transfer and decoding;
- main-thread long tasks;
- layout stability;
- interaction latency;
- memory and detached DOM;
- third-party scripts.

Optimisation follows measured user-facing metrics and representative devices. A tiny compressed bundle can execute expensively; a large image can be harmless below the fold with correct lazy loading; premature memoisation can increase complexity without reducing work.

## 18.11 Caching and conditional requests

A **cache** stores a representation or result for reuse. HTTP caching can reduce latency and load, but stale or private content creates correctness and security risks. Response fields define freshness and reuse policy. An **entity tag**, or ETag, is a validator associated with a selected representation. A client can send a conditional request and the server can respond that the existing cached representation remains valid.

Caches exist in browsers, service workers, proxies, content-delivery networks, gateways, application processes, and databases. Clearing one cache does not clear all. Cache keys must include every request property that changes the selected representation; otherwise one user or encoding can receive another’s result.

**Cache invalidation** means ensuring reused state ceases to be used when its validity ends. Versioned immutable resource names avoid invalidation for static assets: a changed content hash yields a new URL, while old content can remain cached safely.

### 18.11.1 Freshness and reuse policy

A stored response can be **fresh**, reusable without contacting the origin, or **stale**, requiring validation or permitted stale reuse. <code>Cache-Control</code> directives communicate policy. Examples include:

- <code>max-age</code>: freshness lifetime for relevant caches;
- <code>s-maxage</code>: shared-cache freshness overriding ordinary maximum age;
- <code>private</code>: prevent storage by shared caches;
- <code>no-store</code>: request that caches not store the message;
- <code>no-cache</code>: allow storage but require validation before reuse;
- <code>must-revalidate</code>: constrain stale reuse after freshness;
- <code>immutable</code>: representation is not expected to change during freshness.

<code>no-cache</code> does not mean “do not cache.” <code>no-store</code> is stronger but cannot erase copies already logged or retained outside compliant caches. Sensitive responses need authentication, appropriate cache fields, minimal content, and intermediary configuration.

A cache computes age from response timing and fields; clocks, transit, and revalidation matter. Application-level caches often invent simpler TTL rules and thereby omit HTTP variation or authorisation. Cache design must define key, value, freshness, invalidation, ownership, and failure behaviour.

> **Common misconception 18.24 — “<code>Cache-Control: no-cache</code> disables caching.”**  
> It ordinarily permits storage but requires successful validation before reuse. <code>no-store</code> asks caches not to store, though broader data handling still matters.

### 18.11.2 Validators and conditional requests

A strong ETag identifies byte-equivalent selected representations under strong comparison. A weak ETag, marked <code>W/</code>, can identify semantically equivalent representations unsuitable for byte-range combination. ETag generation must include every representation variation, including encoding when applicable.

A client sends <code>If-None-Match</code> on retrieval; a match allows 304 with fields updating cached metadata and no representation body. <code>If-Match</code> on mutation requires a current match and supports lost-update prevention. Date validators are coarser and vulnerable to timestamp precision; when both apply, defined precedence matters.

~~~python
from hashlib import sha256


def strong_etag(body: bytes) -> str:
    digest = sha256(body).hexdigest()
    return f'"{digest}"'


body = b'{"device_id":"A17","status":"ok"}'
validator = strong_etag(body)
assert validator.startswith('"') and validator.endswith('"')
assert strong_etag(body) == validator
~~~

A content hash is a convenient strong validator only if the bytes hashed are exactly the selected representation and collision resistance satisfies the application. Computing it repeatedly for a large dynamic body can cost more than the saved transfer; version columns or stored digests may be preferable.

Cache invalidation strategies include short freshness, explicit purge, versioned keys, write-through updates, tag invalidation, and event-driven eviction. Every strategy has a race. Design which stale values are tolerable and for how long; “eventual consistency” needs a bound and consequence analysis.

Cache stampedes occur when many requests miss or revalidate one popular key simultaneously. Request coalescing, probabilistic early refresh, bounded locks, and serving permitted stale content can protect the origin. Locks themselves need expiry and failure handling.

> **Common misconception 18.25 — “Adding Redis makes an endpoint faster.”**  
> A cache adds network, serialisation, consistency, invalidation, and failure costs. It helps only when reuse probability and saved work exceed those costs under a correct key and policy.

## 18.12 Cookies and application sessions

A **cookie** is a small piece of state a server asks a user agent to store and return under domain, path, lifetime, and security rules. Cookies are automatically attached to matching requests, which is convenient for sessions and central to cross-site request forgery risk.

A **session** associates a sequence of requests with server-recognised state. A common design stores an opaque random session identifier in a cookie and session data on the server. A signed client-side session stores data in the cookie with integrity protection but not necessarily confidentiality. Users can read data that are merely signed.

Cookie attributes include:

- <code>Secure</code>: send only over secure transport under browser rules;
- <code>HttpOnly</code>: deny ordinary script access, reducing some token theft;
- <code>SameSite</code>: constrain cross-site attachment;
- <code>Path</code> and <code>Domain</code>: define scope;
- expiry or maximum age.

Session identifiers must be unpredictable, rotated after privilege changes, invalidated on logout according to policy, and protected from logging. Cookie flags mitigate classes of attack but do not replace output encoding, CSRF controls, or TLS.

### 18.12.1 Cookie selection and scope

A user agent can store several same-named cookies with different paths or domains. Servers should not assume a simple dictionary with one authoritative value. Narrow scope reduces accidental exposure, but <code>Path</code> is a sending rule rather than a robust confidentiality boundary between applications on one host.

A host-only cookie omits <code>Domain</code> and returns only to the setting host. A domain cookie can reach matching subdomains, increasing exposure if any subdomain is less trusted. Cookie-name prefixes such as <code>__Host-</code> let supporting browsers enforce secure, host-only, root-path properties.

<code>SameSite=Strict</code> most strongly restricts cross-site attachment but can disrupt legitimate entry flows. <code>Lax</code> permits selected top-level navigations; <code>None</code> permits cross-site use and requires <code>Secure</code> in modern browsers. “Same-site” is not identical to “same-origin,” so SameSite is defence in depth rather than a complete request-authorisation mechanism.

Cookies have practical size and count limits. Large signed session payloads consume bandwidth on every matching request and can be evicted unpredictably. Do not store secrets merely because the value is opaque-looking or base64 encoded.

> **Common misconception 18.26 — “<code>HttpOnly</code> prevents XSS.”**  
> It blocks ordinary script access to that cookie. Injected script can still act as the user, read page data, issue requests, and alter the interface.

### 18.12.2 Session lifecycle and fixation

A session identifier needs high entropy from a cryptographically secure generator. Store only a verifier or carefully protect the store where risk demands. Bind session state to a principal, creation and activity times, authentication strength, and revocation status.

**Session fixation** occurs when an attacker arranges for a victim to authenticate while retaining an identifier known to the attacker. Rotate the identifier after login, privilege elevation, account recovery, and other trust changes. Preserve only explicitly safe pre-authentication state during rotation.

Timeout policy includes absolute lifetime, idle lifetime, and sometimes renewal. Short lifetimes reduce exposure but can harm usability and create unsafe workarounds. “Remember me” should create a separately revocable long-lived credential that establishes a new session, not make the ordinary session immortal.

Logout should invalidate server-side state and expire the browser cookie. In distributed stores, revocation propagation has latency. Stateless signed tokens cannot be forcibly revoked before expiry without a denylist, key rotation, version check, or introspection, each reintroducing state or broad invalidation.

> **Common misconception 18.27 — “A signed session cookie is encrypted.”**  
> A signature ordinarily protects integrity and authenticity, not confidentiality. The client can read its payload unless it is separately encrypted.

### 18.12.3 Server-side and token-based state

Server-side sessions make revocation and mutable session state straightforward but require a shared durable or replicated store across application instances. Failure policy matters: if the session store is unavailable, failing closed protects authorisation while reducing availability.

Self-contained access tokens carry claims such as issuer, audience, subject, scope, and expiry. A resource server must validate signature, allowed algorithm, issuer, intended audience, time bounds, and application-specific claims. Merely decoding a token is not validation. A token for one service must not be accepted by another because it has a valid signature.

Bearer tokens grant authority to whoever possesses them. Keep them out of URLs, logs, browser local storage where threat models prohibit script access, and referrer-bearing pages. Proof-of-possession mechanisms can bind a token to a key but add protocol and key-management complexity.

~~~python
from secrets import token_urlsafe


def new_session_identifier() -> str:
    return token_urlsafe(32)


first = new_session_identifier()
second = new_session_identifier()
assert first != second
assert len(first) >= 40
~~~

Length is not itself the security proof; <code>secrets</code> uses an operating-system cryptographic source, and 32 random bytes provide ample entropy before URL-safe encoding. The identifier still needs secure transport, storage, rotation, and invalidation.

> **Common misconception 18.28 — “Stateless tokens eliminate session management.”**  
> They move state into signed claims while retaining issuance, expiry, key rotation, audience, revocation, theft, scope, and logout problems.

### 18.12.4 Browser origins, storage, and cross-context communication

The **same-origin policy** limits how a document or script from one origin can inspect another origin’s resources. It is not one rule but a family governing DOM access, network response reading, storage, canvas data, and other capabilities. Cross-origin writes and embeds are sometimes allowed even when reads are blocked.

CORS lets a server opt into selected cross-origin script access. For a non-simple request, the browser sends a preflight <code>OPTIONS</code> request describing intended method and fields. A successful preflight authorises the browser to proceed under the response policy; it does not authenticate the requesting user or constrain direct non-browser clients.

Origins sent in <code>Origin</code> must be compared as parsed exact allowed origins. Reflecting an arbitrary value together with credential permission grants any requesting site access under the victim’s browser credentials. Cache responses varying by origin with an appropriate <code>Vary</code> rule.

Browser storage includes cookies, local storage, session storage, IndexedDB, cache storage, and service-worker state. Their capacity, lifetime, synchronous/asynchronous API, origin partitioning, eviction, and script accessibility differ. Local storage is synchronously accessible to same-origin script and therefore unsuitable for secrets under an XSS threat model.

A service worker can intercept requests and serve cached responses, enabling offline behaviour and creating another cache/deployment layer. An old service worker can continue controlling pages after a server deployment. Version caches, define update and activation policy, and provide a recovery path from a broken worker.

Cross-window <code>postMessage</code> permits explicit communication. The sender should specify an exact target origin, not <code>*</code>, when data are sensitive. The receiver checks <code>event.origin</code>, expected source window, message schema, and authorisation before acting. Message data are untrusted even when the origin is allowed because another application component on that origin may be compromised.

Third-party iframes can be constrained with <code>sandbox</code>, Permissions Policy, CSP, and narrow messaging. Granting both script and same-origin capabilities to untrusted same-origin content can undermine sandboxing. Isolation is a capability design, not a visual border.

## 18.13 From a request to a Python callable

A web server accepts network connections, parses HTTP, enforces protocol limits, and invokes application code through an interface. The application should not reimplement HTTP framing for ordinary work. In Python, two principal server–application interfaces are WSGI and ASGI.

**Web Server Gateway Interface**, or WSGI, defines a synchronous callable contract for Python web applications. A simplified application receives an environment mapping and a callback used to start the response:

~~~python
from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable
from typing import Any


def application(
    environ: dict[str, Any],
    start_response: Callable[..., Any],
) -> Iterable[bytes]:
    body = b"Hello, web\n"
    start_response(
        "200 OK",
        [
            ("Content-Type", "text/plain; charset=utf-8"),
            ("Content-Length", str(len(body))),
        ],
    )
    return [body]
~~~

The body is bytes. The content length uses byte length. This minimal example omits error handling, streaming close hooks, header validation, and server deployment. WSGI represents one request/response exchange through a synchronous call and does not natively model WebSocket or long-lived bidirectional asynchronous events.

**Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface**, or ASGI, defines an asynchronous event interface. An application receives a scope describing the connection plus <code>receive</code> and <code>send</code> awaitable callables:

~~~python
from typing import Any


async def application(
    scope: dict[str, Any],
    receive: Any,
    send: Any,
) -> None:
    if scope["type"] != "http":
        raise ValueError("this application accepts HTTP only")

    await send(
        {
            "type": "http.response.start",
            "status": 200,
            "headers": [
                (b"content-type", b"text/plain; charset=utf-8"),
            ],
        }
    )
    await send(
        {
            "type": "http.response.body",
            "body": b"Hello, ASGI\n",
            "more_body": False,
        }
    )
~~~

ASGI represents HTTP, WebSocket, and lifespan events through typed messages. An <code>async def</code> application is not automatically faster. It improves concurrency for operations that genuinely await non-blocking interfaces. CPU-bound work still occupies an event-loop thread unless moved or redesigned.

### 18.13.1 WSGI’s exact synchronous boundary

WSGI specifies how a server presents one HTTP request to a Python callable and how that callable begins and returns a response. The <code>environ</code> mapping contains CGI-derived strings, server metadata, and extension values. The request body is a file-like byte stream under <code>wsgi.input</code>; reading without respecting content length or server limits can block or consume excessive data.

The application calls <code>start_response(status, headers)</code> before yielding non-empty body bytes. Headers are native strings constrained by the specification’s encoding model; bodies are bytes. If the returned iterable has <code>close</code>, the server must call it, enabling generator cleanup. An application must not depend on the server consuming the entire iterable after a client disconnect.

**WSGI middleware** is both an application to the outer server and a server-like caller of the inner application. It can add correlation identifiers, enforce authentication, alter paths, compress output, or catch exceptions. Order matters: exception middleware outside authentication observes different state from middleware inside it.

~~~python
from __future__ import annotations

from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable
from typing import Any
from uuid import uuid4

StartResponse = Callable[..., Any]
WSGIApp = Callable[
    [dict[str, Any], StartResponse],
    Iterable[bytes],
]


class CorrelationMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, application: WSGIApp) -> None:
        self.application = application

    def __call__(
        self,
        environ: dict[str, Any],
        start_response: StartResponse,
    ) -> Iterable[bytes]:
        request_id = environ.get(
            "HTTP_X_REQUEST_ID",
            str(uuid4()),
        )
        environ["application.request_id"] = request_id

        def wrapped_start(
            status: str,
            headers: list[tuple[str, str]],
            exc_info: object = None,
        ) -> Any:
            headers.append(("X-Request-ID", request_id))
            return start_response(status, headers, exc_info)

        return self.application(environ, wrapped_start)
~~~

The example trusts an inbound identifier for correlation only; a production system validates length and characters and distinguishes externally supplied from internally generated identity. Middleware must not append a second conflicting response field if the inner application already set one under the chosen policy.

> **Common misconception 18.29 — “WSGI is a web server.”**  
> It is an interface specification between servers and applications. A server implementation manages sockets, workers, timeouts, and protocol parsing; a framework or application implements the callable side.

### 18.13.2 ASGI scopes, events, and connection lifetime

ASGI separates a connection **scope** from a sequence of events. An HTTP scope ordinarily covers one request; a WebSocket scope covers the connection. <code>receive</code> yields request-body chunks, disconnects, WebSocket messages, or lifespan events according to scope type. <code>send</code> emits response and protocol events.

Request bodies can arrive in several <code>http.request</code> events with <code>more_body=True</code>. Reading only the first truncates content. Buffering every chunk without a maximum invites memory exhaustion. A streaming consumer processes bounded chunks and responds to disconnect or cancellation.

ASGI lifespan events let a server ask the application to initialise and shut down resources. Connection pools should be created within process/event-loop lifecycle, not arbitrarily at module import, and closed during shutdown. Multiple worker processes each run their own lifespan and own pools.

ASGI middleware wraps the three-callable interface. It must keep request-local state inside the call or scope, not on a shared middleware instance where concurrent connections race. Context variables can propagate request metadata across awaits but require care when spawning tasks.

> **Common misconception 18.30 — “Replacing <code>def</code> with <code>async def</code> converts a WSGI application into an ASGI application.”**  
> The interfaces have different call signatures, event models, lifetimes, and concurrency contracts. An adapter can bridge subsets but cannot invent native streaming or WebSocket semantics.

### 18.13.3 Backpressure, cancellation, and sync/async boundaries

**Backpressure** prevents a fast producer from overwhelming a slower consumer. Awaiting <code>send</code> can allow the server to regulate output; placing generated chunks into an unbounded in-process queue defeats that benefit. Streaming database rows while a client reads slowly can hold a transaction and connection for an unacceptable time.

Client disconnect is a cancellation signal, not proof that server work should always stop. A read-only report can be cancelled; a payment already committed must complete its durable response record even if the socket vanished. Cancellation policy follows side-effect boundaries.

Calling blocking database or HTTP clients directly in an event-loop thread stalls every coroutine on that loop. A thread offload protects the loop but remains bounded by threads and does not make the dependency asynchronous. Conversely, calling an async library from synchronous WSGI requires an event-loop bridge whose lifecycle and cancellation semantics are non-trivial.

CPU-bound Python work should be bounded and usually moved to a process, native implementation that releases the GIL, or background system. Spawning an unbounded task per request only relocates overload.

> **Common misconception 18.31 — “ASGI applications can handle unlimited concurrent requests because waiting is non-blocking.”**  
> Each connection consumes memory, descriptors, task state, dependency capacity, and scheduling work. Concurrency must remain bounded end to end.

### 18.13.4 Server-sent events and WebSockets

Ordinary HTTP is client-initiated request/response. Some applications need continuing server updates or bidirectional messages.

**Server-Sent Events** (SSE) keep an HTTP response open with media type <code>text/event-stream</code>. The server emits UTF-8 text events separated by blank lines. Browsers can reconnect and send a last-event identifier, permitting resumable streams if the application retains a bounded event history. SSE is server-to-client; client-to-server actions use ordinary requests.

A **WebSocket** begins with an HTTP upgrade or extended connection procedure and then exchanges framed messages bidirectionally. Message boundaries are preserved at the WebSocket layer, unlike raw TCP application writes. Frames can fragment a message; maintained libraries reassemble or stream according to their API.

Opening a WebSocket does not supply authentication. Browser cookies can accompany the handshake, creating cross-site WebSocket hijacking risk if the server neglects origin and CSRF-like validation. Tokens passed in query strings leak through logs; subprotocol or first-message authentication has its own exposure and timeout rules.

After connection, authorisation applies to every subscribed resource and command, and may need re-evaluation when roles change. Define:

- maximum connections per principal and globally;
- maximum message size and rate;
- accepted message schema and version;
- heartbeat and idle timeout;
- outbound queue bound for slow consumers;
- ordering and duplicate semantics;
- reconnect and resume behaviour;
- server restart and deployment draining;
- observability without logging sensitive payloads.

A slow client can cause an unbounded outbound buffer unless the server blocks producers, drops defined ephemeral events, coalesces state updates, or disconnects it. Each policy changes semantics.

~~~python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field


@dataclass
class BoundedMailbox:
    capacity: int
    _items: list[bytes] = field(default_factory=list)

    def offer(self, message: bytes) -> bool:
        if len(self._items) >= self.capacity:
            return False
        self._items.append(message)
        return True

    def take(self) -> bytes:
        if not self._items:
            raise LookupError("mailbox is empty")
        return self._items.pop(0)


mailbox = BoundedMailbox(capacity=2)
assert mailbox.offer(b"one")
assert mailbox.offer(b"two")
assert not mailbox.offer(b"three")
~~~

The list has \(O(n)\) removal and is only pedagogical; <code>collections.deque</code> or an asynchronous bounded queue is appropriate. The important contract is that overload becomes an explicit result rather than invisible memory growth.

WebSockets are not a message broker. A disconnected client misses messages unless the application stores and resumes them. Sticky routing can keep a connection at one process, but broadcasts across processes need a shared event system and delivery policy.

## 18.14 Routing and a minimal Flask application

**Routing** maps a request’s method and target pattern to application behaviour. Flask is a deliberately small WSGI-oriented framework that supplies routing, request/response objects, templating integration, configuration, and extension points while leaving many architectural choices to the application.

~~~python
from __future__ import annotations

from flask import Flask, jsonify, request

app = Flask(__name__)

devices: dict[str, dict[str, str]] = {
    "A17": {"device_id": "A17", "status": "ok"},
}


@app.get("/devices/<device_id>")
def get_device(device_id: str):
    device = devices.get(device_id)
    if device is None:
        return jsonify(
            {
                "error": {
                    "code": "device_not_found",
                    "message": "No device has that identifier.",
                }
            }
        ), 404
    return jsonify(device)


@app.post("/devices")
def create_device():
    document = request.get_json(silent=False)
    if not isinstance(document, dict):
        return jsonify(
            {"error": {"code": "object_required"}}
        ), 400

    device_id = document.get("device_id")
    if not isinstance(device_id, str) or not device_id:
        return jsonify(
            {"error": {"code": "invalid_device_id"}}
        ), 422
    if device_id in devices:
        return jsonify(
            {"error": {"code": "device_exists"}}
        ), 409

    device = {"device_id": device_id, "status": "new"}
    devices[device_id] = device
    return jsonify(device), 201, {
        "Location": f"/devices/{device_id}"
    }
~~~

The decorator associates method and path pattern with each function. The path component is decoded and passed as <code>device_id</code>. The GET handler distinguishes absence from an empty value. The POST handler separates malformed/non-object content, a semantically invalid identifier, and a state conflict. A created response identifies its new resource.

The module-level dictionary is not a database. Multiple worker processes hold separate copies; restart erases it; threads can race; and unbounded input consumes memory. It is pedagogical state used to expose HTTP semantics.

Flask’s development server is for development. A production WSGI server controls workers, sockets, limits, timeouts, and graceful shutdown. Import strings and application factories help separate application construction from process launch:

~~~python
from flask import Flask


def create_app(config: dict[str, object] | None = None) -> Flask:
    app = Flask(__name__)
    if config is not None:
        app.config.from_mapping(config)

    from .devices import blueprint

    app.register_blueprint(blueprint)
    return app
~~~

An **application factory** constructs an application under explicit configuration. It supports isolated tests and multiple instances. Importing the blueprint inside the factory can avoid a cyclic import, but module organisation should make dependencies clear rather than rely on arbitrary import timing.

### 18.14.1 Request and application contexts

Flask exposes objects such as <code>request</code>, <code>session</code>, and <code>g</code> through context-local proxies. They resolve to state for the active request or application context; they are not ordinary global singleton request objects. Access outside the appropriate context raises an error rather than identifying an arbitrary request.

The request lifecycle includes URL matching, before-request hooks, view execution, error handling, response processing, session saving, and teardown. Teardown functions run for cleanup even after exceptions but should not conceal the original error. Hook ordering across application and blueprints is part of behaviour and deserves tests.

A **blueprint** records routes, handlers, templates, and static resources for registration on an application. It supports modular composition but is not an isolated process or security boundary. Dependencies should be injected through application extensions or explicit domain services rather than imported mutable globals.

Configuration can arrive from environment-specific objects or mappings. Secrets must not use committed default values. Fail startup if required keys, database URLs, trusted proxy settings, or cryptographic secrets are missing or malformed.

> **Common misconception 18.32 — “Flask’s <code>request</code> object is a process global and therefore unsafe.”**  
> It is a context-local proxy resolved for the active request. Mutable module globals remain shared and unsafe for request-specific state.

### 18.14.2 Separate transport, domain, and persistence

A route should translate protocol input into a domain command, invoke a service, and translate its result into an HTTP response. Embedding all validation, SQL, authorisation, email, and JSON construction in the view makes transaction and test boundaries invisible.

~~~python
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RegisterDevice:
    device_id: str
    site_id: int


def parse_register_device(document: object) -> RegisterDevice:
    if not isinstance(document, dict):
        raise ValueError("an object is required")
    expected = {"device_id", "site_id"}
    if set(document) != expected:
        raise ValueError("fields do not match schema")

    device_id = document["device_id"]
    site_id = document["site_id"]
    if not isinstance(device_id, str) or not device_id.strip():
        raise ValueError("device_id must be non-empty text")
    if type(site_id) is not int or site_id <= 0:
        raise ValueError("site_id must be a positive integer")
    return RegisterDevice(device_id.strip(), site_id)


command = parse_register_device(
    {"device_id": "A17", "site_id": 3}
)
assert command.site_id == 3
~~~

Using <code>type(site_id) is int</code> deliberately rejects booleans, which are subclasses of <code>int</code> in Python but not valid identifiers here. A schema library can express the same boundary more systematically; the domain still decides the rule.

Exceptions crossing the route boundary should map through explicit handlers. A domain “device already exists” result can become 409; a database outage becomes a logged 503 or 500 under policy; an unexpected programming error remains unexpected and must not be mislabeled as bad input.

Template rendering uses automatic escaping appropriate to HTML text and ordinary attributes, but developers must avoid unsafe contexts and deliberate <code>Markup</code>/<code>safe</code> overrides. Static asset URLs, session configuration, maximum request size, and proxy trust are application-wide concerns, not decorations added after routes work.

> **Common misconception 18.33 — “A microframework produces microservices.”**  
> “Micro” describes the framework’s core and extension philosophy. Deployment boundaries, domain coupling, data ownership, and operational independence determine service architecture.

## 18.15 Django as an integrated framework

Django supplies an integrated set of facilities: URL routing, request and response abstractions, templates, forms, authentication, administration, database migrations, and an object-relational mapper. Its purpose is not that every project needs more machinery. It encodes coherent defaults for applications that need these concerns together.

A **project** is the configured site-level application. A Django **app** is a reusable or bounded feature component within a project. The word “app” here is framework terminology and does not necessarily indicate a separately deployed service.

Conceptual model:

~~~python
from django.db import models


class Device(models.Model):
    device_id = models.CharField(
        max_length=64,
        unique=True,
    )
    status = models.CharField(max_length=32)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        return self.device_id
~~~

The class declares fields that Django uses to build Python descriptors, validation facilities, queries, and migration state. <code>unique=True</code> requests a database uniqueness constraint through migrations. Application checks alone cannot enforce uniqueness against concurrent transactions; the database constraint is authoritative.

A **migration** is a versioned transformation of database schema or related state. It is executable history, not a snapshot to regenerate casually. Deployments must sequence schema and application versions so both old and new processes remain compatible during a rolling transition.

### 18.15.1 Requests through Django’s architecture

Django resolves a URL pattern to a view after request middleware runs. A view can be a function or class-based callable and returns an <code>HttpResponse</code> or raises an exception handled by the framework. Response middleware then runs in the reverse direction under the configured chain.

Middleware order affects security and semantics: sessions must exist before authentication middleware uses them; security headers must apply to error responses; transaction middleware changes the duration of database transactions. Installing a component without understanding its order can silently weaken a guarantee.

Forms and model forms combine input parsing, validation, error representation, and controlled model construction. They do not replace object-level authorisation. Excluding an <code>owner</code> field from a form prevents direct binding, but the view must still assign and check ownership correctly.

Django’s administration interface is powerful operational software, not a public application UI. Restrict access, use strong authentication, limit model actions, log material changes, and avoid registering sensitive models casually. Staff status is broad authority under configuration, not a decorative flag.

> **Common misconception 18.34 — “Django is secure by default, so application security is automatic.”**  
> Secure defaults mitigate common classes when used correctly. Domain authorisation, deployment, secrets, dependency updates, unsafe template overrides, raw SQL, and custom code remain application responsibilities.

### 18.15.2 Models, managers, and async boundaries

A model class declares persistence mapping and some invariants. Custom managers and query sets can centralise common selection and tenant scoping, but hidden filters can surprise maintenance code. Database constraints remain necessary because model validation is not automatically invoked for every bulk update or external writer.

~~~python
from django.db import models


class ActiveDeviceQuerySet(models.QuerySet):
    def active(self):
        return self.exclude(status="retired")

    def for_site(self, site_id: int):
        return self.filter(site_id=site_id)


class ManagedDevice(models.Model):
    device_id = models.CharField(max_length=64, unique=True)
    site_id = models.PositiveBigIntegerField()
    status = models.CharField(max_length=32)

    objects = ActiveDeviceQuerySet.as_manager()

    class Meta:
        constraints = [
            models.CheckConstraint(
                condition=models.Q(
                    status__in=["new", "ok", "retired"]
                ),
                name="managed_device_valid_status",
            )
        ]
~~~

The query-set methods are composable and lazy. The check constraint protects the status domain for every database writer using a supporting backend. The example uses an integer rather than a foreign key only to isolate query-set structure; a real relation ordinarily deserves a foreign key.

Django supports asynchronous views and parts of its stack, but synchronous middleware or database operations can force thread adaptation. Long-lived streaming and WebSockets usually use ASGI-oriented infrastructure and, for WebSockets, an additional protocol framework. Measure the actual call chain rather than infer concurrency from one <code>async</code> keyword.

Framework upgrades can change defaults, deprecate APIs, and close security vulnerabilities. Pin compatible versions, read release and deployment checklists, run system checks and tests, and deploy migrations deliberately. Long-term-support releases reduce upgrade frequency but do not eliminate maintenance.

> **Common misconception 18.35 — “A larger integrated framework removes architectural decisions.”**  
> It supplies coherent defaults and facilities. The application still decides domain boundaries, data ownership, authorisation, consistency, deployment, and failure policy.

## 18.16 Relational databases

A **database management system**, or DBMS, stores and retrieves structured state under concurrency, durability, and query semantics. In a relational database, a **table** has named columns and rows. A **primary key** identifies a row; a **foreign key** enforces references between tables under configured actions.

SQL, the Structured Query Language, declares desired relational results. A simplified schema:

~~~sql
CREATE TABLE site (
    site_id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE device (
    device_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    site_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES site(site_id),
    status TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE NOT NULL
);
~~~

The database, not Python type hints, enforces non-null and key constraints for every writer using the database. A check constraint could restrict status to a domain, although a reference table or application evolution may better suit some cases.

SQL query:

~~~sql
SELECT
    s.name,
    COUNT(*) AS device_count
FROM device AS d
JOIN site AS s ON s.site_id = d.site_id
GROUP BY s.site_id, s.name
ORDER BY device_count DESC;
~~~

The DBMS planner chooses an execution strategy using indexes and statistics. An **index** is an auxiliary structure accelerating selected lookups and orderings at storage and write cost. Creating an index on every column can slow writes and consume space without improving actual queries.

### 18.16.1 Relations, keys, and normalisation

The relational model represents data as relations of tuples over named attributes. SQL tables approximate this model with types, nullability, duplicates unless constrained, ordering only when requested, and vendor-specific behaviour. Row order without <code>ORDER BY</code> is undefined even if a test repeatedly returns insertion order.

A **candidate key** is a minimal set of attributes uniquely identifying a tuple. A primary key is the candidate selected as the table’s principal identifier. A **surrogate key** is introduced for identification rather than derived from domain meaning; it does not remove the need for unique constraints on natural invariants such as an external device identifier within a tenant.

Normalisation decomposes data to reduce redundancy and update anomalies. If a site name is copied onto every device row, renaming the site requires many consistent writes. A separate site relation referenced by a foreign key represents the dependency once. Denormalisation can be justified for measured read paths, but it creates a synchronisation rule that must be owned.

NULL represents missing or inapplicable information under SQL’s three-valued logic. Comparisons with NULL yield unknown rather than true or false; use <code>IS NULL</code>. <code>NOT IN</code> with a nullable subquery can therefore behave unexpectedly. Nullability is a domain decision, not merely a convenience during coding.

> **Common misconception 18.36 — “A primary key makes every domain entity unique.”**  
> It makes stored rows unique by that key. Duplicate real-world entities remain possible unless domain identity and additional constraints are defined.

### 18.16.2 Constraints and indexes are executable invariants

Database constraints reject invalid state under concurrent writers:

- <code>NOT NULL</code> requires a value;
- <code>CHECK</code> enforces a row-level predicate supported by the DBMS;
- <code>UNIQUE</code> enforces candidate-key-like uniqueness;
- <code>FOREIGN KEY</code> enforces referential existence and configured update/delete action;
- exclusion or trigger-based constraints can protect more complex relations in supporting systems.

Application validation improves error messages but races: two processes can both observe “name unused” before inserting. The database unique constraint serialises the invariant; the application catches and maps the resulting conflict.

B-tree indexes support equality, range, and ordering patterns over leading columns. A composite index on <code>(site_id, created_at)</code> can serve filtering by site and ordering/ranging by creation time; it is not equivalent to independent indexes for every query. Partial indexes cover rows satisfying a predicate; expression indexes cover computed keys.

Query planners estimate row counts from statistics and choose scans, joins, and sorts. A plan appropriate for ten rows can fail at ten million. Use <code>EXPLAIN</code> and measured execution under representative data, but do not force a plan from one observation without understanding parameter distributions and cache state.

~~~python
import sqlite3

connection = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
connection.execute(
    """
    CREATE TABLE device (
        device_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
        site_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
        status TEXT NOT NULL
            CHECK (status IN ('new', 'ok', 'retired')),
        UNIQUE (site_id, device_id)
    )
    """
)
connection.execute(
    "CREATE INDEX device_site_status "
    "ON device(site_id, status)"
)
connection.execute(
    "INSERT INTO device VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
    ("A17", 4, "ok"),
)
try:
    connection.execute(
        "INSERT INTO device VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
        ("B20", 4, "impossible"),
    )
except sqlite3.IntegrityError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("CHECK constraint should reject status")
~~~

SQLite is useful for this self-contained demonstration; its concurrency, types, DDL, and query planner differ from server DBMSs. Production-dependent behaviour must be tested against the selected production family.

> **Common misconception 18.37 — “Indexes are copies that make all database access faster.”**  
> Each index supports particular predicates and orderings while consuming storage, cache, and write work. Unused or redundant indexes reduce performance.

### 18.16.3 Time, money, identity, and tenant boundaries

Time values need a clock and meaning. An **instant** identifies one point on a time line and can be stored in a UTC-capable timestamp type. A civil time such as “09:30 Europe/London” combines local date/time with a named time zone whose political rules can change. An offset such as <code>+01:00</code> is not a time-zone rule set.

Store instants for occurred events and retain the named zone where future civil schedules must follow local rules. Daylight-saving transitions create nonexistent and repeated local times. Database and Python libraries need an explicit policy for ambiguity rather than silent guessing.

Durations use monotonic clocks for in-process deadlines because wall clocks can jump. Database expiry based on authoritative database time avoids disagreement among application hosts, while clients should not control security expiry.

Money uses an integer minor unit or exact decimal with declared currency and rounding. Binary floating point cannot exactly represent many decimal fractions. Currency determines scale only imperfectly: some currencies have no minor unit, and financial instruments can require more precision. A monetary amount without currency is incomplete.

Identifiers have scope. An account number can be unique within a tenant but not globally; an external provider ID needs provider identity; a user-facing slug can change while an internal key remains. Composite unique constraints should encode the actual scope.

Multi-tenant systems choose among shared tables with tenant keys, separate schemas, separate databases, or hybrid partitioning. Every model affects isolation, operations, migrations, backup/restore, noisy neighbours, and cross-tenant analytics. In a shared-table design:

- every tenant-owned table carries a non-null tenant key;
- unique constraints include tenant scope where appropriate;
- foreign keys prevent cross-tenant references, sometimes through composite keys;
- repository queries require tenant context;
- caches and object storage keys include tenant identity;
- background jobs and logs carry tenant scope without exposing it as unchecked client input.

Database row-level security can enforce tenant predicates below the application, but only if session context is set safely for every transaction and privileged bypass roles are constrained. Connection pooling can leak session variables between requests unless reset.

Deletion is a workflow, not one SQL statement. Foreign keys, audit duties, legal holds, derived indexes, caches, search systems, object storage, backups, and downstream processors can retain data. Define erasure scope and communicate residual backup retention accurately.

## 18.17 Parameterised queries and injection

**Injection** occurs when untrusted data alters the structure of code or a command rather than remaining data. SQL injection commonly arises from constructing SQL with string concatenation.

Unsafe:

~~~python
query = (
    "SELECT * FROM device "
    f"WHERE device_id = '{device_id}'"
)
cursor.execute(query)
~~~

An attacker-supplied quote can terminate the intended literal and introduce SQL syntax. Escaping manually is error-prone and database-specific.

Safe structural separation:

~~~python
cursor.execute(
    "SELECT device_id, status "
    "FROM device WHERE device_id = %s",
    (device_id,),
)
~~~

The placeholder syntax depends on the database driver. The driver transmits or encodes the value as a parameter under protocol rules rather than interpreting it as query structure. Parameters ordinarily cannot substitute identifiers or keywords; dynamic table or column selection requires an allowlist and driver-supported identifier composition.

An ORM reduces direct SQL construction but does not make all expressions safe. Raw fragments, dynamic ordering, template rendering, shell calls, and URL construction each have their own injection boundaries.

### 18.17.1 Values are not identifiers or syntax

Database parameters represent literal values. They cannot ordinarily choose a table name, column, operator, sort direction, or SQL keyword because those positions belong to grammar. Dynamic syntax needs a mapping from an external choice to developer-authored fragments:

~~~python
from typing import Literal

SortChoice = Literal["created", "status"]


def ordering_sql(choice: SortChoice) -> str:
    allowed = {
        "created": "created_at DESC, device_id ASC",
        "status": "status ASC, device_id ASC",
    }
    try:
        return allowed[choice]
    except KeyError as error:
        raise ValueError("unsupported ordering") from error


assert ordering_sql("created").startswith("created_at")
~~~

The returned fragment comes entirely from code. The client selects among capabilities rather than supplying SQL. Driver identifier-composition APIs can quote a validated identifier, but an unrestricted user-selected table is usually also an authorisation and data-exposure defect.

Parameter placeholders differ: DB-API drivers use styles such as <code>?</code>, <code>%s</code>, or named markers. Do not interpolate before passing to the driver. Logging a rendered query should avoid reconstructing secrets and must not become the execution path.

> **Common misconception 18.38 — “Prepared statements sanitise an entire SQL string after interpolation.”**  
> Parameters keep values separate from parsed query structure. Interpolating first has already lost the distinction; dynamic syntax requires controlled composition.

### 18.17.2 Injection is a family of parser-boundary failures

The same structure appears in shell injection, template injection, LDAP filters, regular expressions, email headers, log forging, and code evaluation. Defence follows the target grammar:

1. avoid exposing a programmable grammar where a fixed operation suffices;
2. use structured APIs that separate data from syntax;
3. allowlist the small unavoidable syntax choices;
4. encode output for the exact destination context;
5. run with least authority so a defect has bounded effect.

Input validation alone is insufficient. An apostrophe is a legitimate surname; rejecting it damages data while clever encodings bypass naive filters. Parameterisation permits the full value domain without treating it as structure.

Database accounts should have only required privileges. A read endpoint should not connect as a superuser capable of dropping schemas. Separate migration authority from application runtime authority. Row-level security can add database enforcement for tenant policy, but application context propagation and policy testing remain essential.

Error messages should not reveal query text or schema. Timing and row-count differences can still disclose existence, so authorisation should occur before sensitive query distinctions where feasible.

> **Common misconception 18.39 — “Escaping dangerous characters is a universal injection defence.”**  
> Escaping is grammar- and context-specific and often incomplete. Structural APIs and fixed syntax are preferable; least privilege limits residual damage.

## 18.18 Transactions and concurrency

A **transaction** groups database operations under an all-or-nothing unit and an isolation model. The traditional ACID properties are:

- **atomicity:** a transaction’s changes commit as a unit or are rolled back;
- **consistency:** defined invariants hold across successful transactions, assuming constraints and correct operations;
- **isolation:** concurrent transactions interact as if governed by the selected isolation guarantees;
- **durability:** committed changes survive failures covered by the system’s guarantee.

“Consistency” does not mean the database understands every business rule. It enforces declared constraints and transaction logic.

### Worked example 18.4 — Transfer as one transaction

~~~python
from decimal import Decimal


def transfer(
    connection,
    *,
    source_id: int,
    destination_id: int,
    amount: Decimal,
) -> None:
    if amount <= 0:
        raise ValueError("amount must be positive")
    if source_id == destination_id:
        raise ValueError("accounts must differ")

    with connection:
        with connection.cursor() as cursor:
            cursor.execute(
                "SELECT balance FROM account "
                "WHERE account_id = %s FOR UPDATE",
                (source_id,),
            )
            row = cursor.fetchone()
            if row is None:
                raise LookupError("source account does not exist")
            if row[0] < amount:
                raise ValueError("insufficient funds")

            cursor.execute(
                "UPDATE account SET balance = balance - %s "
                "WHERE account_id = %s",
                (amount, source_id),
            )
            cursor.execute(
                "UPDATE account SET balance = balance + %s "
                "WHERE account_id = %s",
                (amount, destination_id),
            )
            if cursor.rowcount != 1:
                raise LookupError(
                    "destination account does not exist"
                )
~~~

The exact context-manager and placeholder behaviour depends on the driver. The row lock prevents specified concurrent modifications under supported transaction semantics. Both updates commit together or an exception triggers rollback. A database check constraint should additionally forbid negative balances where the domain demands it.

Isolation levels permit or prevent different anomalies. A **lost update** occurs when concurrent operations overwrite one another. A **write skew** can occur when transactions read overlapping state and write disjoint rows while jointly violating an invariant under some isolation levels. “Using a transaction” is incomplete; the invariant, reads, writes, locks, and database isolation must be analysed.

Long transactions retain locks or old versions, increase contention, and complicate retries. Network calls should ordinarily not occur while holding a database transaction open unless the protocol explicitly requires it.

### 18.18.1 Isolation phenomena and serialisability

Isolation levels are named categories with DBMS-specific implementations. Common anomalies include:

- **dirty read**: observing another transaction’s uncommitted write;
- **non-repeatable read**: rereading a row and obtaining a committed change;
- **phantom**: repeating a predicate query and obtaining a changed row set;
- **lost update**: one write overwrites another without incorporating it;
- **write skew**: transactions read shared constraints and write disjoint rows, jointly violating an invariant.

**Serialisable** execution provides outcomes equivalent to some serial order of committed transactions, not necessarily the order they began. Implementations use locks, predicate locks, multiversion checks, or serialisation-failure detection. Applications must be prepared to retry transactions rejected to preserve serialisability.

Snapshot isolation provides a consistent snapshot but can permit write skew. “Repeatable read” means different things across databases. Correct design cites the actual DBMS documentation and tests the invariant with concurrent sessions.

> **Common misconception 18.40 — “ACID transactions execute one at a time.”**  
> Databases interleave concurrent work while providing an isolation contract. The selected level and access pattern determine which observations and anomalies are possible.

### 18.18.2 Locks, deadlocks, and retryable transactions

Pessimistic locking acquires database locks before a conflicting action; optimistic control performs work and rejects a conflicting commit or conditional write. Pessimistic methods can block and deadlock. Optimistic methods can waste work and repeatedly conflict under contention.

A **deadlock** is a cycle of waits: transaction A holds a resource B needs while B holds one A needs. Databases detect a cycle and abort a participant. Acquire resources in a consistent order to reduce deadlocks, keep transactions short, and retry the whole transaction after rollback with a bound and jitter.

~~~python
from __future__ import annotations

from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")


class SerializationFailure(Exception):
    pass


def run_transaction(
    operation: Callable[[], T],
    *,
    maximum_attempts: int = 3,
) -> T:
    for attempt in range(maximum_attempts):
        try:
            return operation()
        except SerializationFailure:
            if attempt + 1 == maximum_attempts:
                raise
    raise AssertionError("loop must return or raise")
~~~

The operation must begin a fresh transaction on every attempt. Side effects outside the database—emails, HTTP calls, file writes—must not be repeated casually. Record an outbox event within the transaction and perform external delivery later.

Savepoints provide partial rollback within a transaction but do not create independent durability. Nested library transaction blocks may join one outer transaction rather than commit separately; know the framework contract.

> **Common misconception 18.41 — “A deadlock means the database is broken.”**  
> Deadlocks are an expected possibility under locking concurrency. The database resolves them by aborting work; applications must minimise cycles and retry safe transaction units.

### 18.18.3 Transactions do not cross systems automatically

A local database transaction cannot atomically commit an email provider, message broker, payment processor, and another database unless a distributed protocol and every participant support it. Two-phase commit can coordinate prepared participants but introduces availability, blocking, and operational costs and is uncommon across public services.

A **saga** represents a multi-step process as local transactions plus compensating actions. Compensation is not time travel: refunding a payment does not make a sent parcel or disclosed email unseen. The process needs explicit states, idempotent commands, retry rules, deadlines, and manual resolution for irrecoverable cases.

The transactional outbox solves one common boundary by committing domain state and an event record together. A relay may publish the event more than once, so consumers deduplicate or make effects idempotent. An inbox table can record consumed event identifiers transactionally with local changes.

> **Common misconception 18.42 — “Wrapping code in one Python <code>with</code> block makes every side effect atomic.”**  
> The database connection controls its own transaction. External services, files, caches, and queues need explicit coordination and recovery semantics.

## 18.19 Object-relational mapping

An **object-relational mapper**, or ORM, maps Python-level classes and expressions to database tables and queries. It solves repetitive mapping, composable query construction, identity handling, and schema integration. It does not make the relational model object-shaped.

~~~python
device = (
    Device.objects
    .select_related("site")
    .get(device_id="A17")
)
print(device.site.name)
~~~

<code>select_related</code> requests a join for a single-valued relation, avoiding a later query when <code>site</code> is accessed. Without deliberate loading, iterating devices and accessing each related site can cause the **N+1 query problem**: one initial query plus one query per row. Query count grows linearly and network/database latency dominates.

ORM query sets are often lazy. Construction does not necessarily execute SQL; iteration, conversion, length, or related operations can trigger evaluation. Debugging performance requires inspecting generated SQL, query plans, row counts, and indexes.

The ORM object identity map, database row identity, and Python object identity are distinct. Two Python objects can represent the same database row at different times and hold stale values.

### 18.19.1 Object graphs and relational sets have different semantics

Objects expose navigation and behaviour; relational queries transform sets or bags of rows. An ORM translates a useful subset, but translation has costs:

- attribute access can trigger I/O;
- a Python loop can become hundreds of SQL statements;
- object creation can dominate bulk processing;
- implicit flushing can issue writes before an apparent commit point;
- equality and identity can differ across sessions;
- database NULL and SQL collation differ from Python values and comparison.

Query expressions should remain in the ORM’s translatable language until execution. Pulling rows into Python to filter wastes indexes and bandwidth; calling a Python-only function inside a query is usually impossible or evaluated in an unexpected place.

An **identity map** returns one in-memory object per database identity within a unit of work in some ORMs. It improves relationship consistency but creates stale caches and memory growth. Django does not provide one general long-lived identity map; other ORMs do. Never assume the pattern from the generic term “ORM.”

> **Common misconception 18.43 — “ORM attributes behave like ordinary in-memory attributes.”**  
> Access can execute queries, lazy relations can fail outside a session, and values can be stale relative to concurrent database state.

### 18.19.2 Query shape is part of correctness

The N+1 problem is one instance of uncontrolled query shape. Joining several one-to-many relations can instead create a Cartesian multiplication, returning enormous duplicate row combinations. Select-in prefetch can use several bounded queries and assemble relations without multiplication. The right strategy depends on cardinality.

Pagination should happen in SQL under a deterministic order. Fetching every row and slicing in Python is not pagination. Counting an enormous filtered set can itself be expensive; APIs should decide whether exact totals justify cost.

Bulk updates bypass per-object hooks, validation, and sometimes timestamp behaviour. They are valuable precisely because they avoid object-by-object machinery. Database constraints and explicit audit logic protect invariants that must survive every write path.

~~~python
# Conceptual Django query: inspect rather than execute here.
query = (
    Device.objects
    .filter(site_id=4, status="ok")
    .select_related("site")
    .order_by("device_id")
)
sql, parameters = query.query.sql_with_params()
~~~

Inspecting generated SQL and parameters helps verify joins and filtering without interpolating values. Actual performance requires the database execution plan and representative data.

Repository or service layers can isolate persistence choices, but mechanically wrapping every ORM method often adds indirection without a semantic boundary. Introduce an abstraction around domain operations and transaction units, not because a pattern catalogue demands one.

> **Common misconception 18.44 — “Fewer SQL queries always means better performance.”**  
> One explosive join can be worse than several selective queries. Measure row cardinality, transferred bytes, plan, latency, memory, and lock duration.

## 18.20 Schema evolution

Changing a live schema is a distributed compatibility problem. Suppose a required column is added. If the database first rejects rows lacking it while old application instances still write the old form, deployment fails.

An **expand–migrate–contract** strategy:

1. add a nullable or defaulted field compatible with old code;
2. deploy code that writes both old and new representations;
3. backfill existing rows in bounded batches;
4. verify completeness;
5. deploy code reading only the new representation;
6. enforce the new constraint;
7. remove the old representation after no supported reader needs it.

Each step is reversible or observable. Large table rewrites can lock or saturate a database; version-specific database facilities determine operational strategy.

### 18.20.1 Schema and application versions coexist

During rolling deployment, old and new processes execute concurrently. A safe migration establishes a compatibility window. Renaming a column directly can break the old version; adding a new column, dual-writing, backfilling, switching reads, and later removing the old one permits coexistence.

Defaults have several meanings: a database default for omitted writes, an ORM default applied in Python, and a backfill for existing rows. They are not interchangeable. A volatile or computed default can rewrite a table in some database versions; consult the selected engine.

Migration files belong in version control and are reviewed like production code. Editing an already-applied migration creates divergent histories. A corrective migration advances from known state. Squashing history is a deliberate maintenance operation that preserves compatibility for supported installations.

> **Common misconception 18.45 — “A migration is just the difference between current model classes and the database.”**  
> It is ordered executable history with dependencies, data assumptions, locking behaviour, and compatibility obligations.

### 18.20.2 Online change, backfill, and rollback

A large backfill should process deterministic bounded batches, commit progress, respect replication and load, and be restartable. Record a high-water mark or select rows still missing the new value. An update without a stable order can revisit or starve rows under concurrent changes.

Creating an index can block writes or consume substantial I/O unless the DBMS provides an online/concurrent form. Adding a constraint can be staged: create it without validating historical rows where supported, repair data, validate, then make application assumptions. Each engine has different syntax and guarantees.

Data migration code must use historical model/schema state rather than importing today’s application class, which may change before a fresh installation replays history. Time zones, locale, external APIs, and nondeterministic defaults make historical replay fragile.

Rollback has limits. Dropping a column destroys data; reversing after new code wrote values unavailable to old code can be lossy. Prefer roll-forward correction and backups tested through restoration. Application rollback must remain compatible with the already-applied schema.

A migration runbook states:

- expected locks and duration;
- compatible application versions;
- preconditions and free-space requirements;
- monitoring and abort thresholds;
- backfill progress and validation queries;
- rollback or roll-forward procedure;
- ownership and communication.

~~~python
def batches(
    identifiers: list[int],
    *,
    size: int,
) -> list[list[int]]:
    if size <= 0:
        raise ValueError("size must be positive")
    return [
        identifiers[start : start + size]
        for start in range(0, len(identifiers), size)
    ]


assert batches([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], size=2) == [
    [1, 2],
    [3, 4],
    [5],
]
~~~

Real backfills should not first load all identifiers as this demonstration does. They page through an indexed stable key and persist progress, with rate control and idempotent updates.

> **Common misconception 18.46 — “Database migrations should always run automatically when an application process starts.”**  
> Concurrent starters, long locks, privilege separation, and failure recovery make migration a controlled deployment operation in many systems.

## 18.21 REST as constraints, not a synonym for JSON

**Representational State Transfer**, or REST, is an architectural style defined through constraints including client–server separation, stateless interaction, cacheability, uniform interface, layered systems, and optional code transfer. In everyday speech, “REST API” often means an HTTP API exposing resources with JSON. The looser usage should not erase HTTP semantics.

Resource-oriented design gives nouns stable URLs and uses methods for operations:

| Operation | Method and target |
|:---|:---|
| list devices | <code>GET /devices</code> |
| retrieve A17 | <code>GET /devices/A17</code> |
| create under collection | <code>POST /devices</code> |
| replace A17 | <code>PUT /devices/A17</code> |
| partially modify A17 | <code>PATCH /devices/A17</code> |
| remove A17 | <code>DELETE /devices/A17</code> |

This is a convention, not automatic correctness. Actions that do not map cleanly to resource replacement can be represented as subordinate resources, commands, or documented POST operations. A clear domain protocol is better than forced noun grammar.

Collection endpoints need filtering, ordering, pagination, and limits. Offset pagination is simple but can duplicate or skip rows as concurrent changes shift positions. Cursor pagination uses a stable ordering key and opaque continuation value. It still requires a deterministic total order and policy for mutations.

### 18.21.1 Uniform interfaces and hypermedia

REST’s **uniform interface** constrains components to shared resource-identification, representation, message, and hypermedia semantics. It enables generic intermediaries and evolvable clients at the cost of application-specific efficiency. Merely using JSON over HTTP does not satisfy every REST constraint.

A resource is conceptual: “the current device A17” can have representations that change while its identifier remains stable. Representations carry state and links. A client applies methods to resource identifiers rather than invoking an in-process object method.

**Hypermedia as the engine of application state** means a response supplies links or controls indicating available transitions. A client need not construct every URI from undocumented templates. In practice many JSON APIs instead publish out-of-band schemas and fixed path conventions. That can be a valid HTTP API, but the distinction should be named accurately.

Links can have relation types such as <code>self</code>, <code>next</code>, <code>collection</code>, or domain-specific registered/documented relations. A URL is opaque to a client unless the protocol defines its structure. Parsing a database identifier from the last path segment couples the client to current routing.

> **Common misconception 18.47 — “REST means mapping CRUD operations to four HTTP methods.”**  
> CRUD mapping is one design technique. REST is an architectural style involving statelessness, cacheability, uniform interface, layers, resources, representations, and hypermedia constraints.

### 18.21.2 Collection protocols and evolution

A collection endpoint should define:

- filter vocabulary and combination rules;
- stable sort fields and tie-breakers;
- default and maximum page size;
- cursor opacity, lifetime, and tenant binding;
- treatment of insertions, deletions, and updates during traversal;
- field selection or expansion;
- total-count semantics and cost;
- error behaviour for invalid or expired cursors.

Keyset pagination asks for rows after the last ordering tuple. For descending creation time with a unique identifier tie-breaker:

~~~sql
SELECT device_id, created_at, status
FROM device
WHERE
    (created_at, device_id) < (%s, %s)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, device_id DESC
LIMIT %s;
~~~

The cursor can encode the last tuple plus version and scope, then be authenticated to prevent tampering. It should not expose a capability the caller is not authorised to use. Changing sort/filter parameters invalidates the cursor.

API evolution prefers additive compatible changes where possible: clients must ignore documented unknown response fields, while servers can reject unknown request fields under a stricter contract. Removing or changing meaning needs deprecation, telemetry, consumer communication, and a version boundary.

Versioning can use media types, fields, paths, or host names. None removes the need to maintain semantics within a version. Dates such as <code>2026-09-22</code> can label a compatibility profile but should not imply that clients automatically understand later fields.

Generated OpenAPI descriptions can document paths, schemas, authentication, and responses, and can drive clients or validation. They do not prove business invariants, authorisation, concurrency safety, or implementation conformance. Contract tests should exercise the description against running behaviour.

> **Common misconception 18.48 — “Once an API is versioned, breaking changes are harmless.”**  
> Clients still need migration time, old versions need security maintenance and retirement, and shared state must support coexistence. Versioning labels incompatibility; it does not remove its cost.

### 18.21.3 Webhooks are outbound APIs under failure

A **webhook** asks one system to deliver event notifications to an HTTP endpoint controlled by another. Delivery crosses administrative domains and must assume timeout, duplication, reordering, endpoint compromise, and long outages.

The event should have an immutable identifier, type, occurrence time, schema version, producing account, and data or a reference to fetch current state. Consumers deduplicate by event identifier. Events describe facts—<code>invoice.paid</code>—rather than demand implementation-specific actions—<code>send_green_email</code>.

The sender signs a canonical byte representation with a per-consumer secret or asymmetric key. Include a timestamp and reject signatures outside a bounded window to reduce replay. Verify the signature over the raw body before parsing or transforming it. Compare through a constant-time library function.

